So the Philistines by their Dagon, framed like a fish, or a mermaid rather, 1 Sam. 5. 4. intended not to worship any fish, or such sea monster, but their tutelar god; whom, out of some superstitious conceit, they were pleased so to portray. This exposition, therefore, seems overmuch forced; and the words are rather to be referred to the first branch of the verse; *they shall cast them to the moles, and to the bats*, that is, into such holes, as the one dig in the ground; and such dark and dusty corners, as the other use to roost in, either about the house, or elsewhere; not the very same, necessarily, but any such. See, *ships of Tarshish*, v. 26.

*{moles*} The word is nowhere else found; but signifies such a beast, as digs, and burrows in the ground. Which some therefore would have to be the *cony*, or the *great mountain rat*, that is rife in the *Alps*. But the Hebrew has another name for the one, Levit. 11. 5. Psal. 104. 18. Prov. 30. 26. And of the other it is uncertain, whether it were at all found, or known, much less frequent in those parts. It is most probable therefore to be, as it is here rendered, *the mole*, though another word also be so translated, Lev. 11. 30. Some would make two several words of it, rendering it, *to dig holes*, or *vaults*; but the former is the more generally received, and the more probable.

*{bats*} Of this all agree, both here, and Levit. 11. 19. Deut. 14. 18. yet the Latin word for *a mole*, is the very same with this. And the one may be derived from the other, in regard of some qualities, wherein those two creatures agree. As in the dimness, and duskiness of their eyesight, not enduring the broad daylight. For neither of them is stark blind; and the same word in Hebrew (yet not this) being used both of a fowl, Levit. 11. 18. and of a creeping creature in the very same chapter, v. 30. Some of the rabbins render it in the former place, *a bat*; in the latter, *a mole*.

**V. 21.** *{To go into the clefts of the rocks*} When he has thrown away his idols, that could not secure him, to assay what shift he can make for himself. See v. 18.

*{clefts*} As Exod. 33. 22.

*{into the tops*} Or, *cliffs*. See ch. 57. 5. To go into the *clefts*; or, up to the *cliffs*. The word in the original, does properly signify a *branch*, chap. 17. 6. & 27. 10. and being applied to rocks, and hills, it signifies such parts thereof, as the main body of the rock, or mount, does branch itself forth into. The *cliffs*, as we term them: between which places of refuge and shelter, are oft-times found; and which being steep, and rising higher than the main bulk, or body of the rock, are not of easy access for an enemy, Judg. 15. 8. Psal. 104. 18. Jer. 48. 20.

*{of the ragged rocks*} The word, *ragged*, is not in the original; nor is it included in the term here used: which signifies any rock in general, Numb. 20. 8. Psal. 40. 2. chap. 32. 2. See chap. 16. 1.

*{for fear of the Lord, and for the glory of his majesty*} See verse 10, 19.

*{when he ariseth to shake terribly the earth*} See before, v. 19.

**V. 22.** *{Cease ye from man*} A dehortation, very fitly inferred upon the former denunciation; and making way for what follows, ch. 3. 1, 2, &c. Seeing that all human helps, and external stays will fail; and no might or height will be able to secure any, when God comes to execute judgment: be admonished, and advised, to cast off your vain confidence in frail and mortal man, Psal. 146. 3. Jer. 17. 5, 6. and remember you have to do with God, before whom no man is able to stand, Psal. 76. 7, 12. Eccles. 6. 10. ch. 45. 9.

*{man*} For, *men*; as v. 20.

*{whose breath is in his nostrils*} Heb. *in his nose*. Whose life is so frail that if his nostrils be but stopped, that he cannot breathe freely, he dies, 2 Kings 8. 15. or whose life, as a puff of wind, passing to and fro through his nostrils, may be very soon and suddenly gone. Or, who may puff and blow, as if he could do great matters, Psal. 10. 5. and be puffed up, and swell, with a high conceit of himself, 1 Cor. 8. 1. 1 Tim. 6. 4. but all is no more, but a little loose wind, that may be soon gone, and he with it, Psal. 78. 39. and 146. 4. Acts 5. 5.

*{for wherein is he to be esteemed?*} What reckoning is to be made of him, Job 7. 17, 18. Psal. 8. 4. & 144. 3, 4. Not, but that man is an excellent creature of himself, bearing God's image, Gen. 1. 27. & 9. 6. and being one of God's masterpieces, Gen. 1. 26. Psal. 139. 14, 16. of more value than the whole world besides Matth. 16. 26. as appears by the price paid for his ransom, 1 Pet. 1. 18, 19. But that, if he come into comparison with God, or if he shall stand in opposition against God, he is a sorry, feeble, worthless thing; a puff of wind, and a pile of dust, Psal. 103. 14. & 78. 39. Eccles. 12. 7. a thing of nothing, or less than nothing; that God is able easily to blow away, and bring to naught, in an instant, Gen. 2. 7. and 3. 19. & 18. 27. Psal. 62. 9. chap. 40. 15, 16, 22, 24. Dan. 4. 35.

### CHAPTER 3

**V. 1.** *{For behold, &c.*} This chapter is part of the prophecy, or sermon, beginning chap. 2. 2. Very suitably subjoined to the dehortation, wherewith the former chapter is concluded. He dehorted, there, from confidence in the creature; man especially, and whatsoever aid or support he is able to afford. And here he renders a reason of that his dehortation; to wit, because all such props and stays God has determined to withdraw.

*{behold*} A note as well of admiration, as of attention; giving warning of some, as well admirable, as remarkable matter to ensue. So Gen. 6. 13. ch. 7. 14. and 29. 14.

*{the Lord, the Lord of hosts*} See ch. 1. 24.

*{doth take away*} Heb. *is taking away*; or, *is withdrawing*: as Prov. 28. 9. he is presently about to do it. He will certainly do it; and he will suddenly do it: It is as sure to be done, and soon done, as if it were in doing, or done already. So Gen. 6. 7, 13. 1 Kings 14. 14. chap. 29. 14. Jer. 4. 6. and 5. 15.

*{from Jerusalem, and from Judah*} See of these, on chap. 1. 1.

*{the stay and the staff*} All means, one and other, whereby, as with a staff, man's life is sustained, v. 1. or a state is supported, v. 2, 3. The words in the original, do both signify one and the same thing; to wit, such a staff, wherewith men, weak through sickness, Exod. 21. 19. Or age, Zach. 8. 4. or for ease in journey, Mat. 6. 8. are wont to stay themselves. They differ only, herein, that the one is a masculine, the other a feminine form; either is used for aught, that a man stays himself with, trusts to, or relies on, Psal. 18. 18. ch. 36. 26. though the latter only be found used for *a staff* properly so termed; both mentioned here, to intimate *stays* of all sorts, more or less.

*{the whole stay of bread*} Heb. *all staff*; or, *stay of bread*. (as *whole* *head*; or *every head*, chap. 1. 5.) Hereby some understand that *power* and *virtue* that bread has to nourish; as if God threatened to deny a blessing to their food. So that albeit they had bread, and did eat; yet what they did eat should not nourish them, should do them no good. A judgment supposed to be threatened, Levit. 26. 26. in those words, *ye shall eat, and not be satisfied*; and to have been put in execution, Hag. 1. 9. where it is said, *ye eat, but are not satisfied*; or *filled*. And true it is, that man's life, health, and strength, depends not on bread, or food; but on God's will and pleasure, Deut. 8. 3. Matth. 4. 4. who, if he deny a blessing unto the creature, or withdraw the power and efficacy from it, which he can do, when he will, and oft does: the creature then, though we have it, and use it can nothing avail us. But even those two Scriptures seem rather to intimate a scarcity of bread; as by the tenor of the context in either may appear; as also by the opposition in the former of them, of *eating their fill*; or, *feeding to satiety*, to the full, Levit. 26. 5. and in the present passage, God seems rather to threaten the taking away, from them, the creatures themselves, that are the ordinary stays of man's life; as the persons also of those, that were the stays of their state, v. 2, 3. By *the stay*, or, *staff of bread*, therefore, I suppose rather to be meant, *bread* itself: *Bread* being put for all manner of food, and sustenance, as the principal, most general, and most strengthening food, Psal. 104. 14, 15. (as 1 Kings 4. 22, 23. Neh. 5. 14, 15, 18. ch. 4. 1.) and *staff of bread*, for *bread*; which is as *a staff*, or, *a stay*, Levit. 26. 26. Judg. 19. 3, 8. Ezek. 4. 14. and 5. 16. as *the daughter of Zion*, for *Zion*; that is, as a daughter, ch. 1. 8. and *the sign of circumcision*, for *circumcision*, which is *a sign*, Rom. 4. 11. God threatening to bring upon them (as he did sometime upon Egypt; where he is said, as here, to have *broken the whole*, or, *all the staff of bread*, Psal. 105. 16.) an extreme scarcity of food. And what was here threatened, we shall find fulfilled, Jer. 37. 21. & 38. 4.

*{and the whole stay of water*} Heb. as before, *all stay*; or, *staff of water*. All manner of drink, as needful as bread, or meat, for the support of man's life: All comprehended under the name of *water*, because water is in those parts, the most general and ordinary drink, Num. 21. 5. Deut. 2. 28. & 9. 9. 1 Kings 18. 4, 5. 2 Kings 6. 22. Jer. 3. 7.

*{stay of water*} As of *bread* before. For, *water* itself. See Amos 4. 8. compared with Hag. 1. 6.

**V. 2.** *{The mighty man, &c.*} Those two mentioned, ver. 1. were the stays of each several man's life. These that follow, being the prime persons: for martial, civil, and ecclesiastical officers are not the chief ornaments only, but the stays and pillars of the joint body politic, both of church and state, Judg. 5. 14, 15. 1 Kings 2. 12. and 13. 14. Psal. 68. 27. & 75. 3. Eccles. 10. 17. ch. 1. 26. 1 Tim. 3. 15. which being removed therefore, the ruin of both must needs ensue; as of a house when the principal pillars are pulled away, that support it, Judg. 16. 29, 30.

*{mighty*} For strength of body, 1 Sam. 14. 52. 1 Sam. 17. 10. or, for power of command, Gen. 10. 8, 9.

*{and the man of war*} Or, *the warrior*. Skillful and expert in military affairs, Judg. 20. 17. 1 Chr. 12. 36.

*{the judge, and the prophet*} The one to act, and by execution of justice, to reform. Jud. 2. 18, 19. The other to instruct; and by instruction, to reclaim. Jer. 23. 22.

*{and the prudent*} The word properly signifies *a diviner*; and is taken, commonly, in an evil sense, for such, as by diabolical ways of divination, undertake to foretell future events, Deut. 18. 10. Josh. 13. 22. Yet here, in the better part, for a man of much sagacity, and depth of judgment, able so to bolt out the truth of things difficult, and abstruse; and to deem of, and guess shrewdly at the consequences, and events of affairs, that he may seem to have a spirit of divination in him. So is the word taken, Prov. 16. 10. and an instance of it we may see in Solomon, 1 Kings 3. 16, 28. See Eccles. 9. 16, 18.

*{and the ancient*} As ch. 9. 15. by reason of years, and age; grave, wise, and experienced; and in that regard, of more authority, Levit. 19. 32. Prov. 16. 31. and 20. 19. Job 15. 9, 10. & 32. 4, 6, 7. Ezek. 7. 20. See 1 Kings 12. 6, 8.

**V. 3.** *{The captain of fifty*} One of the least numbers that commanders took charge of, Exod. 18. 21, 25. 1 Sam. 8. 12. 2 Kings 1. 9, 11, 13. intimating, that hardly any fit to undertake the least and lowest charge, should be left. See verse 7, 8.

*{and the honourable*} Heb. *the man eminent in countenance*; as ch. 9. 15. one that carries authority with him in his countenance, a man of respect, in regard of his birth, (Eccles. 10. 17. chap. 19. 11.) place, or parts, Eccles. 8. 1.

*{and the counsellors*} Such as princes are wont to have near at hand, to advise with in weighty affairs, 2 Sam. 15. 12. and 16. 23. 1 Chr. 26. 14. 2 Chr. 30. 2. Esth. 1. 3. ch. 1. 26. & 48. 13. Such, as being pious and prudent, may be of great concernment for the support of a state; and where such fail, all is like to fail, and miscarry, both at home, and abroad, Prov. 11. 14. and 24. 6. Mic. 4. 9.

*{and the cunning artificer*} Heb. *the wise of the workmen*, in timber, stone, or metal; for in Scripture, as also in other the learned languages, the skillful in such arts are termed *wise*; and skillfulness in them, *wisdom*, Exod. 31. 3, 6. such among them, as are in such affairs more skillful than ordinary; who being of much use in a state, either for civil, or warlike employments; much inconvenience and detriment therefore, may accrue to a state, by want of them, 1 Sam. 13. 19, &c. 2 Kings 12. 11, 12. and 24. 14. Jer. 24. 1. Zach. 1. 20, 21. For I cannot here accord with that learned writer, who would have the words rendered, *one skillful in witchcrafts*; because the Chaldee uses the latter term commonly for *witchcrafts*.

*{artificer*} The word signifies (as also the Latin that answers it) such, as work either in metals; as smiths, braziers, and goldsmiths, Gen. 4. 12. Deut. 27. 5. or, in timber and stone; as carvers, carpenters, masons, and the like, 2 Sam. 5. 11. 1 Chr. 14. 1. and 22. 15.

*{and the eloquent orator*} Or, *skillful of speech*. Heb. *skilled in charms*, ch. 26. 16. and so also would that former learned annotator have it here taken. But it is generally supposed rather, thereby, here to be meant one of that power and efficacy in speech; that he is able by his persuasions, so to prevail with those he speaks to, that his words seem to be as a spell; and the persons he speaks to, to be as charmed by him, Psal. 58. 5. 1 Cor. 2. 4. As is the word of divination used in no ill sense, Prov. 16. 10. Such a one was Abigail, that charmed David, 1 Sam. 25. 24, 34. and such another was the woman of Abel, that charmed Joab first, and then the whole city, and so saved it from being sacked, 2 Sam. 20. 16, 22. Of such Solomon, Eccles. 9. 14, 15. The words, *Orator, Artificer*, and so the rest of them, though in the singular number, are not meant of any one particular person, but are put collectively, for all, or most, of each degree or rank mentioned. So ch. 2. 7, 20. v. 5.

**V. 4.** *{And I will give children to be their princes*} The fearful effect following on the removal of such as are of abilities for government and employment.

*{I will give children to be their princes*} Or, *I will make children their princes*. For, that is the usual sense of the Hebrew phrase here used, Psal. 2. 8. chap. 60. 17. Jer. 9. 10.

*{I will give*} Set up, place in offices of government. For, into such places none come, but either by God's permission, or appointment, Psal. 75. 6, 7. Prov. 8. 15, 16. Dan. 4. 25, 32. and he gives such, as well in wrath, as in mercy, Hos. 13. 11.

*{children*} Either in age, and years, and consequently rude, and raw, wanting experience and discretion for so weighty an employment, Eccles. 10. 16. or of a childish disposition, for wit, skill, carriage, courage, and the like, no better than children; or in some sort worse, because less teachable and tractable than children, Eccles. 4. 12. Such were Ahaz, Manasses, and Josias his successors. See v. 12.

*{and babes shall rule over them*} *Babes*, that is, childish, babyish ones; no wiser or discreeter, than either suckling, or newly weaned babes. For, from the word that so signifies, the most deduce that here used, Psal. 8. 2. ch. 28. 9. Yet some other render it, *men of illusions*, or, *insolencies*; that is, mockers; men of insolent carriage; such as take delight in the scornful usage of others. For so is the word taken, from whence they derive it. But the former seems the genuine sense of the word here, (being nowhere else found) as confirmed by what follows, v. 12.

**V. 5.** *{And the people shall be oppressed*} The necessary consequent, either of none, or of ill government; where either no governors at all are, or in such place of government, as are not able to govern themselves, Judg. 9. 4, 6, 15, 20. & 17. 6. & 18. 1. & 19. 1. & 21. 25.

*{oppressed*} Not by close, and underhand dealing defrauded; but by force, and open violence despoiled, as Judg. 18. 24, 25. So v. 12. Some read it, *and the people shall oppress one another*, or, *among the people, one shall oppress another*. And the sense comes all to one, in either; but the verb here used, is passive, as 1 Sam. 13. 6. & 14. 24. chap. 53. 7.

*{one by another*} Or, *one against another*. Heb. *man by man*; or, *man against man*. This clause some join to the former words, as our English has it. Others begin a new sentence with them, supplying a word, much of the same notion with that which in the next branch is subjoined. *Man shall rise against man*, as Mic. 7. 6. that is, one against another, as 1 Sam. 2. 25. and the points of distinction, in the original, carry it rather this way. See ch. 9. 21.

*{and every one by his neighbour*} Heb. *a man by*, or, *against his neighbor*: or, *friend*. A common phrase in Hebrew, for *one another*; without any special notion, or intimation of mutual relation, or respect, Exod. 21. 14, 18, 35. ch. 13. 8. Jer. 7. 5. Yet, in this place, it seems to have some emphasis in it, as implying, that no respect of vicinity, or amity, would be had among them; but that they would be as forward to wrong a near neighbor, as a mere stranger, a friend, as a foe. See Jer. 9. 4, 5. Mic. 7. 5, 6.

*{the child shall behave himself proudly against the ancient*} There shall be a general confusion of all degrees, without respect of age, or state, ch. 24. 2.

*{behave himself proudly*} Or, *strengthen himself*. For the word signifies as well *power*, as *pride*, Psal. 138. 3. Cant. 6. 5. See *Rahab*, ch. 51. 9. Heb. *behave themselves proudly*; or, *strengthen themselves*. For the noun is singular, the verb plural. Of which form of speech, see before, on ch. 2. 18, 20. The meaning is, every boy, or young stripling, will be taking heart, to carry himself malapertly, or insolently toward the ancient, whom he ought to reverence and respect, Levit. 19. 32. See v. 12.

*{and the vile*} Or, *contemptible*. Heb. *of light esteem*, 1 Sam. 2. 30. & 18. 23. See ch. 16. 14. every base fellow, (as before, every boy) will make bold with, or carry himself saucily, and arrogantly toward those, that be far his betters. So Shimei, 2 Sam. 16. 5, 9.

*{against the honourable*} The word signifies *weighty*, as the other *light*. Men of worth, and weight. For honor and weight go together; and the same word, with little difference, in the three learned languages, imports either, Deut. 23. 58. ch. 23. 9.

**V. 6.** *{When a man, &c.*} Or, as some, *For a man, &c.* as rendering a reason of the former confusion; because every man should shun all public employment, & no man be willing to take any authority upon him, ch. 59. 16. The particle may well signify either; as before, chap. 1. 29, 30. & 2. 19. And according to the former reading, confirmed by what follows, v. 7. It contains a relation of a further evil, mentioned rather as an effect, and consequent of the former; to wit, that the state should be in such a general confusion, that men would be glad to get any to protect them, and to offer place of command and authority to them; but those whom they should make such offers unto, considering how things stood, should utterly refuse that, which ordinarily men are wont most to affect, Num. 16. 3. 2 Sam. 15. 4.

*{when*} Or, *And when*. As some render it, that go this way, (as ch. 8. 19.) for the better connection of it with the precedent discourse. So v. 11.

*{a man*} Or, *any man*; as Levit. 1. 2.

*{shall take hold of his brother*} Any one of his kindred as Gen. 13. 8. Deut. 18. 2. & 25. 5, 9. or, of his nation; as Deut. 15. 7, 12. & 23. 19, 20. For, no stranger was to bear rule with them, Deut. 17. 15.

*{saying*} A needful supply, though not in the Hebrew, as Psal. 105. 15. Jer. 30. 17.

*{thou hast clothing*} You have good apparel, such as few have left them in these times of plunder, and spoil; that, for which the common sort of people, are wont most to regard men, Jam. 2. 2. or, *apparel*, being put more generally for all sort of necessaries; you are furnished with means, and are not unfit therefore to bear office among us.

*{be thou our ruler*} As Judg. 9. 8, 10, 12. & 11. 6.

*{let this ruin be under thine hand*} Help to support, or repair the ruins of the state; or, (the abstract put for the concrete, as chap. 1. 21. & 64. 6.) take the charge and government of this ruinous, or tottering, state, upon you. See Psal. 75. 3. & 82. 5.

*{ruin*} As Zeph. 1. 3. A metaphor taken from a house, or wall, either ready to fall, or ready fallen down, Psal. 62. 3. ch. 30. 13. Amos 9. 11. See v. 8.

*{under thine hand*} Under your *charge*; *hand*, for, *charge*; as Num. 4. 28, 33.

**V. 7.** *{In that day*} Or, *Then*; as ch. 2. 11, 20. answering to the particle *when*, v. 6.

*{shall he swear*} Heb. *lift up*. To wit, his hand. A phrase frequent in Scripture, taken from the rite, in those times used, of lifting up the hand toward heaven, in the solemn taking of an oath, as to him that dwells in heaven, (Psal. 123. 1. chap. 57. 15. & 66. 1.) by whom they swore. See Gen. 14. 22. Deut. 32. 40. Ezek. 20. 6, 15, 63. Rev. 10. 5, 6.

*{saying, I will not be*} Or, *I cannot be*. For the future, in Hebrew, is oft potential. So Job 9. 3. & 14. 4, 14. Jer. 2. 23, 32. and so here for the reason rendered of his refusal.

*{an healer*} Heb. *a binder up*. A metaphor taken from surgery, and the binding up of wounds, and sores for the cure of them. See ch. 1. 6. & 30. 26. I dare not undertake the cure of such desperate evils, as the state is possessed of, and pestered with, chap. 1. 5, 6.

*{in mine house is neither bread nor clothing*} I am not so furnished, as you suppose me to be. Either fear shall make him rather to forswear himself, than to undertake so perplexed and perilous a charge. Or such scarcity shall be of all necessaries, comprehended all under these two heads, (as we use to say, meat, drink, and apparel.) Gen. 28. 20. 1 Tim. 6. 7. that even those shall be found to want them, that were esteemed to have greatest store of them, 2 Kings 6. 27.

*{bread*} See v. 1.

**V. 8.** *{For Jerusalem is ruined, and Judah is fallen*} Or, *when*; as v. 6. So some, continuing the former speech of the party refusing to take charge; and rendering a reason of his refusal to undertake the care and cure of the state: as being so far ruined, that it was not in his power to support & keep it up. But the context runs better, as we have it, or as some other, *surely*. For so the particle here used, is also sometime taken, Job 8. 6. & 20. 20. Psal. 44. 22. or, *Therefore*, as Psal. 116. 10. Jer. 9. 20. For the prophet's intent seems to be, as to relate their ruin, touched upon v. 6. so to show the cause of it, to wit, for their extreme obstinacy, and impudence, in their carriage towards God.

*{Jerusalem and Judah*} The Jewish state, the inhabitants of that city, and people of that land. See ch. 1. 1. For, that he speaks not so much of the city, or land itself; as of the persons, people, and state consisting of them, as ch. 1. 27. the words ensuing show.

*{is ruined*} Or, as some, *hath stumbled*; as Psal. 27. 2. ch. 8. 15. according to that of the apostle, Rom. 9. 32. & 11. 11. but the other agrees better with the former passage, v. 6. and so is the word used, Psal. 107. 12. & 109. 24.

*{is fallen*} Is come to confusion, as ch. 21. 9.

*{because their tongue and their doings, are against the Lord*} They set themselves both in word and deed against *Jehovah*, him from whom they have their being, (Acts 17. 25, 28. See ch. 1. 2.) Psal. 73. 9. Mal. 3. 13. Jude 15.

*{to provoke the eyes of his glory*} As if they spoke, and did things on purpose, to provoke him to his face. So Psal. 78. 17. chap. 1. 4. & 65. 3. Jer. 7. 18, 19. See somewhat the like, Job 17. 2.

*{to provoke*} Or, *by provoking*; or, *in provoking*. So is the particle used, Gen. 3. 22. *by knowing*; or, *in knowing*. For so it would be there rendered, and Deut. 9. 18. *in doing evil*. See ch. 10. 2.

*{the eyes of his glory*} Or, *his eyes, of glory*: as, *his name of glory*, Psal. 72. 19. For, *his most glorious eyes; his most glorious name*. So, *his hill of holiness*, Psal. 15. 1. *his Son of love*, Col. 1. 13. *His word of power*, Heb. 1. 3. For, *his most holy hill, his most beloved Son; his most powerful word*.

**V. 9.** *{The shew of their countenance doth witness against them*} Their lewdness and shamelessness discovers itself in their very face and forehead; neither do they desire, or endeavor, to conceal it, Ezek. 24. 7, 8.

*{shew*} Or, *trial*, as some. For it comes from a word that signifies, *to acknowledge*, Prov. 20. 11. or, *strangeness*; as others: because the same word sometime signifies, *to estrange*, 1 Kings 14. 5, 6. Or, as others *hardness*; from a word that signifies, *to harden*, Job 19. 3. and the word in Arabic, is said so to be used. Nor is it unusual in the Latin tongue, to say, *one of a hard face* for an impudent man. The word (as many other, in this prophecy) is nowhere else found in Scripture; that which makes it the more ambiguous. However, the sense is certainly this, that their very looks alone, were evidence enough, without further proof, to convince them, how they stood inwardly affected; the disposition of their heart therein as evidently offering itself unto view, as if it were even stamped on their faces, or engraven on their foreheads: and that their extreme impudence is implied, the sequel shows. See Jer. 3. 3. *a harlot's forehead*.

*{doth witness*} Does give in evidence against them. Heb. *doth answer*; in reference to such interrogatories, as are wont to be administered to those that come in as witnesses against a party questioned, or accused. So ch. 59. 12. and in the law, *Thou shalt not answer a false testimony against thy neighbor*, Exod. 20. 16. Deut. 5. 20.

*{and*} Or, *yea*. As Neh. 6. 10. Psal. 7. 4. For it is a further aggravation of their shamelessness.

*{they declare their sin*} They tell it out; (as Judg. 14. 16. *thou hast not told it me*,) they not only show it in their face, as, *the heavens are said to show God's righteousness*, Psal. 89. 9. but they publish it with their tongue; not in way of confession, as David, Psal. 32. 5. but in way of profession, as Lamech, Gen. 4. 23, 24.

*{as Sodom*} That is, the men of Sodom, who openly professed what they intended, and commonly practiced, Gen. 19. 5. So Judg. 19. 22. See Jer. 2. 25.

*{they hide it not*} As those seek to do, that are ashamed of their sin, Gen. 3. 7, 8. Job 31. 33. See Ezek. 24. 7. a defect of the pronoun as ch. 9. 9.

*{woe to their soul*} That is, *to them*; or, *to themselves*: as in the next clause, and Lam. 5. 16. *woe to us*. So Psal. 3. 2. *that say to my soul*; that is, *to me*: and ch. 51. 23. *which have said to thy soul*; that is, *to thee*. Yet the phrase makes the speech more passionate; being spoken by the prophet, rather in way of deploration, than of denunciation; as that also in the Lamentations. See ch. 1. 4, 24.

*{for they have rewarded evil to themselves*} They do, by these their untoward and obstinate courses, procure mischief to themselves. They hurt not God, but wrong themselves, Job 35. 4. Prov. 9. 12. & 11. 17. Jer. 7. 19.

*{rewarded*} Or, *done*; or, *procured*. For the word does not always imply, any retribution, or reward; as it does hereafter, v. 11. but oft-times, only a doing of aught, simply, to oneself, or another, be it good, or evil. See Psal. 7. 5. & 13. 6. & 116. 7. Prov. 3. 30. ch. 63. 7. in all which places, is the same word used. And it might well be here rendered in the present tense, (as the like, ch. 1. 1, 3.) *they procure*; or, *do evil to themselves*: or bring evil upon themselves. See Hos. 12. 9.

**V. 10.** *{Say ye to the righteous*} Some take these words, as spoken by way of concession, and preoccupation: you will say, there is a promise made to the righteous that they shall do well; but you are no such, and it belongs not therefore to you; Deut. 28. 18, 19. Others, as in way of reprehension, and castigation of the false prophets, that saddened the hearts of the godly; but preached peace to the wicked, Ezek. 13. 19, 22. Others rather, by way of caution, and consolation, to keep up the hearts, and bear up the spirits of that small company of godly ones, that remained yet among them; and to give them assurance of God's goodness to be showed them, and his care to protect them, amidst those confused and calamitous times, ch. 8. 24. 2 Pet. 2. 9.

*{say ye to the righteous*} Heb. *say the righteous*; or, *tell the righteous*. A defect of the particle, as 1 Sam. 15. 31. *one told David*; and 1 Kings 20. 9. *tell my Lord the king*. Say to them; that is, to them *be it said*. As *say to Archippus*, that is, to *Archippus be it said*. (a place more than one way wronged,) Let the godly man assure himself of this, ch. 49. 9. & 44. 28. Hos. 2. 1, 23. For what God says or bids say, shall assuredly be, Num. 23. 19. chap. 55. 10, 11. See ch. 1. 20.

*{the righteous*} The upright man. Righteous, in regard of inherent righteousness, truly, and sincerely; though not perfectly, and exactly, according to the rigor of the law: for so none is here on earth, Psal. 143. 2. Prov. 20. 9. Eccles. 7. 20.) So Psal. 32. 11. & 58. 10. & 97. 11. Jer. 5. 1. & Luke 1. 6.

*{that it shall be well with him*} Heb. *that good*. As in the next verse, *evil*. A short, but quick, and emphatical form of speech, (the like whereunto, see Job 34. 18.) that good shall betide him; that it shall fare well with him, however it betide others. That howsoever things go, it shall go well with him; for all shall work for his good, Eccles. 8. 12. Jer. 15. 11. Rom. 8. 28.

*{for they shall eat the fruit of their doings*} They shall not fail to fare well, for their well doing, Psal. 18. 24, 25. & 62. 12. Gal. 6. 7, 8. Heb. 6. 10. A metaphor, taken from husbandmen; who are then said to eat, or enjoy the fruit of their labor, when they are fed, and maintained by that, about which they had formerly taken pains, Psal. 128. 2. 2 Tim. 2. 6. So Prov. 1. 31.

*{they shall*} That is, *each one of them shall*. For there is a passage from number to number, as chap. 1. 18, 20. See verse 5.

**V. 11.** *{Woe to the wicked*} Or, *But woe*. A defect of the adversative; as v. 6. *Woe* here, a note of denunciation, as ch. 5. 11. See ch. 1. 4.

*{it shall be ill with him*} Heb. no more but, *evil*. See v. 10. howsoever the godly fare, it shall be sure to go ill with him, Eccles. 8. 12, 13. ch. 65. 13, 15, 20.

*{the reward of his hands shall be given him*} He shall be rewarded according to what he has wrought, Psal. 28. 4. & 62. 12. Prov. 1. 31. Rom. 1. 6. 2 Cor. 5. 12.

*{hands*} For *works*. Because the ordinary instrument of working, Prov. 30. 28. & 31. 16, 31. Eccles. 9. 10.

**V. 12.** *{As for my people*} Heb. *my people*. Put absolutely. See the like, Psal. 11. 4. & 18. 30. Prov. 8. 14. & 16. 33. The prophet, after the former assertion inserted, concerning the different state of good, and bad, according unto either's disposition, and demeanor, returns again to prosecute his former discourse concerning the confusion and disorder of the times.

*{my people*} An emphasis in it, that such confusion and disorder should be among God's own people, who had better means among them whereby to know their duty, had been better taught, and professed better things, Deut. 4. 5, 7, 8. & 5. 27. or, that God's people, those whom he had in a special manner made his, and undertaken to protect, should by persons of no worth, or parts; boys, and women be so baffled, and abused, ch. 52. 5. See ch. 1. 3.

*{children are their oppressors*} Or, *children oppress them*. Heb. *child oppressing them*; or, *oppressors of them*: That is, *every child*, or *every boy, is oppressing them*. Of the phrase, see before, v. 5. Yet some read the words, *My people do their oppressors glean*; that is, their oppressors do so spoil and peel them, that they leave nothing behind. And the word indeed may signify a *gleaner of grapes*, properly; as another is thought to signify (but that doubtful) *of corn*, Psal. 129. 7. and so it should be an allusion to that, in the law, where they were forbidden to pluck their vines so, as not to leave some clusters behind, Levit. 19. 10. Deut. 24. 11. and the meaning were, that they should utterly strip them of all; as Jer. 6. 9. See Jer. 49. 9. But the word rather seems here to be taken in the former sense, as that word near unto it, and of the same lineage with it, does very frequently import, Jer. 6. 11. & 9. 20. & 44. 10. and so the meaning is, that even boys and women abused them, and domineered over them; implying, as the insolent carriage of the one party, so the base spirits of the other: that could endure to be so dealt with by such, Jud. 8. 20, 21. & 9. 34. See v. 4, 5.

*{women rule over them*} Those of the weaker sex, 1 Pet. 4. 7. not so fit for rule, 1 Tim. 2. 12. and yet overruling those, it may be, that should rule; as Jezabel did Ahab, 1 Kings 21. 7, 15, 25. that, which of Jeconiah's mother, some suppose, 2 Kings 24. 12. or, as some, effeminate and womanish men, ch. 19. 16. The word in the Hebrew, wants the first, or head letter, of that which signifies *men*; as denying headship to such. They go too far from the text, that would render the word, either *usurers*, or *oppressors*.

*{O my people*} He turns his speech to the people, as minding them, who they were that were the prime and principal causes of this their ruin.

*{they which lead thee, cause thee to err*} Your leaders, your rulers, princes, priests, & prophets, that should aright lead you, mislead you; partly by their evil examples, and partly by their misgovernment, the one; and their misteaching the other, ch. 1. 10, 23. Lam. 2. 14. & 4. 13.

*{which lead thee*} Or, *that should direct thee*. From a word that signifies, as, *to go*, Proverbs 4. 14. and specially *to go on straight*, or *right*, Prov. 9. 6. So to *right*, or, *righten*, ch. 1. 17. and to *direct*; or, *guide*: *thy directors*, or, *thy guides*, Matth. 15. 14. & 23. 16. or, as others, *those that bless thee*. Your false prophets, that preach peace to you, and that soothe you up in your sins, Jer. 6. 14. Lam. 2. 14. Ezek. 13. 6, 10, 16. and so is the word used, Job 19. 11. Psal. 72. 16. Cant. 6. 9. Mal. 3. 12, 15. But the former seems more agreeable to the scope of the prophet, both here, and ch. 9. 16.

*{cause thee to err*} Heb. only *cause to err*. A defect of the pronoun, or affix, as ch. 1. 15. seduce you, lead you out of the way, ch. 19. 13. Jer. 50. 6. People being more prone to follow bad examples, than good; and to be led aside by irreligious, 1 Kings 11. 5, 13. & 12. 30. & 14. 16. Jer. 44. 17. than to be led aright by their righteous, & religious rulers, 2 Kings 14. 4. and 15. 4, 35. 2 Chr. 27. 2. & 30. 3, 10. & 33. 17.

*{and destroy the way of thy paths*} Heb. *swallow up*. They spoil you, and overthrow you, by causing you to take evil ways, and corrupting your life and courses. So is the word used for *spoiling*, and *destroying*, Psal. 35. 25. & 107. 27. chap. 49. 19. Lam. 2. 2, 5, 16. Or, as others, *they hide*; or, *cover*. As, say they, the word is taken, Num. 4. 20. because things hidden, or covered, as well as things swallowed down or destroyed, are removed out of sight. And they expound it of the priests and Levites, that concealed, and withheld from the people, the doctrine of the law, whereby they should shape their courses aright, Luke 11. 52. But the former sense is more plain, and more frequent. Nor does the word in that place of Numbers, seem to signify simply *to cover*, but *to wrap up*, or *to involve*, and make up in a fardel; where the things so made up, seem, as swallowed up in their outmost wrappings.

*{the way of thy paths*} See chap. 2. 3.

**V. 13.** *{The Lord standeth up*} Heb. *Jehovah*. See ch. 1. 2. The Lord Chief Justice, or Judge General, Psal. 50. 6. & 75. 7. & 82. 1. chap. 33. 22. A description of God's entrance upon, and proceeding in judgment, against those oppressors, and misleaders of his people.

*{standeth*} As Gen. 37. 7. Exod. 15. 8. or rather, *is set*; as Psal. 45. 9. *On thy right hand the queen* (your wife, so the word signifies) *is set*, not standing, but sitting: as the Persian king's wife beside him, Neh. 2. 6. and Bathsheba the queen mother, on Solomon's right hand. 1 Kings 2. 19. and so it would be rendered, Psal. 82. 1. *he is set*, as the judge on the bench, that sits down, to hear causes debated before him, Exod. 18. 13, 14. chap. 6. 1. Dan. 7. 9. Joel 3. 12. Rev. 6. 16. so, *to set themselves*, (to wit, in battle array) and, *to stand*, (or stand still) are mentioned, as two distinct notions, 2 Chr. 20. 17. See the like error in translation, ch. 52. 2.

*{to plead*} Or, *to debate*, Job 9. 3. Prov. 25. 8, 9. either, to plead and debate the matter in their behalf, as their advocate, Jer. 50. 34. or to hear the pleas and debates on either side as a judge, Mic. 7. 9.

*{and standeth to judge the people*} He sat down to hear, and debate; he stands up now, as the manner of judges is, after full debate, to pass sentence. So Acts 7. 56. He appears unto Stephen, as ready to pass sentence for him, against those that had condemned him, and to avenge his blood upon them. Or, *he standeth to judge*; that is, as he is set down about it, so persists in it, he goes on in it, and will not give it over, until he have brought the matter to an issue, and finished his work of judicature, Psal. 94. 14, 15. chap. 42. 3. For, *to stand*, is sometime *to persist* in a business, Eccles. 8. 3. Hos. 10. 9.

*{to judge the people*} To judge for them; in their behalf. To pass sentence against their oppressors, as Psal. 7. 8. & 26. 1. See ch. 1. 17.

*{the people*} *His people*; of whom before, v. 12. Deut. 32. 36. A defect of the affix, v. 12. Heb. *peoples*; as Psal. 7. 8. chap. 2. 3, 4. the whole multitude of them, as well one, as another. He will hear, and right them all, be they never so many, Psal. 145. 14, 21. & 146. 7. God can, and will do it; though Moses could not, Exod. 18. 14.

**V. 14.** *{The Lord will enter into judgment*} Will come to a trial, Job 14. 13. Psal. 143. 2.

*{with the ancients of his people*} Before was showed in whose behalf, v. 13. here, against whom he would proceed.

*{the ancients*} Or, *elders*; that is, as the next word shows, the princes, and rulers. So called, because chosen ordinarily, of such as were well in years. Exod. 24. 9, 11. Num. 11. 16. Deut. 21. 2. and because in maturity of understanding and judgment, they ought to be as such, albeit they be not so far in years as some others, Exod. 18. 21. Deut. 1. 13. In which regard also, the same title is given unto *the ministers of the Gospel*; though sometime, having not attained yet to old age, 1 Tim. 5. 17. & 3. 6. & 4. 12.

*{of his people*} *Elders of the people*, say some, as distinct from *the elders of the priests*. But those of both sorts were herein faulty; and in government they seem to have been conjoined, Deut. 17. 9. 2 Chr. 19. 8.

*{for ye have eaten up the vineyard*} Before, the persons against whom he would proceed. Now the actions and indictments that he enters against them; and the crimes wherewith he charged them; to wit, their oppressions of his people.

*{for*} Or, *because*. Heb. *and*. The copulative for the causal; as Psal. 60. 11. ch. 64. 5. and so it may be taken, 2 Sam. 24. 1. in those words *and he moved David, &c.* *because one* (that is, *Satan*, 1 Chr. 21. 1.) *had moved David*, or, *because David had been moved*. (of which form of speech, see chap. 1. 18, 20.) Others render it, *but*; as if it were the latter part of a speech, partly conceived, and partly expressed: (as some make that of the serpent, Gen. 3. 2.) wherein God having related that their duty was to have done, and what care they ought to have had of his vineyard; does after proceed to show, what a contrary course they had taken therewith; *But ye have eaten it up*. And indeed the copulative is oft used for the adversative, as ch. 2. 6. & 5. 2, 6. Mal. 2. 11. But it is not needful, that it should so be here used; nor are such needless supplies safe.

*{ye have*} Or, *they have*. A change of the person. See the like, chap. 1. 29. Deut. 31. 28, 29. the turning of his speech to them, adds some emphasis to it; as if he had said, *Ye*, even you, are those that I speak of.

*{eaten up*} Destroyed, spoiled; a metaphor taken from beasts, that *depasture*, a ground, Exod. 22. 5. Num. 22. 4. & 24. 22. & 5. 5. & 6. 13. or, that *browse* upon vines, and other plants, and so spoil them, ch. 18. 6. & 27. 10. Some render it, *burnt up*, as the word is taken, Judg. 15. 5. Psal. 80. 16. and 83. 14. ch. 9. 18. laid it as waste, as if it were burnt up with fire, Joel 2. 3.

*{the vineyard*} Either God's vineyard; that is, his church; ch. 5. 1, 7. his people, v. 15. *vineyard*, for, *my vineyard*, as, *people*, for, *his people*, v. 13. or, *vineyard*, for, *vineyards*, Judg. 15. 5. and with the article also, Deut. 22. 9. *the vineyards*, that is, the lands, and possessions of his poor people; of whom he speaks, v. 13, 15. See 1 King. 21. 1, 7, 15. Neh. 5. 3, 5.

*{and*} The defect of the copulative, makes the sentence the quicker.

*{the spoil of the poor*} Not taken by them: but taken from them: as, *my wrong*, not done by me, but done to me, Jer. 51. 35. and *his snare and his gin*; not set by him, but set for him, Job 18. 10.

*{spoil*} That which you have wrested, and torn from them, as in an hostile manner; or as wild beasts prey upon cattle. See ch. 10. 2.

*{is in your houses*} And that is evidence sufficient against you, Mic. 6. 10. Zeph. 1. 9.

**V. 15.** *{What mean ye, &c.*} Heb. *what to you*. And that all contracted into one word. A quick form of speech, not unfit to express anger and passion, *What have ye to do?* Or, *Who gave you authority to use my people in this manner?* A sharp expostulation; as proceeding from, and intimating no small measure of wrath and indignation: not unlike those, Psalm 50. 16. chap. 52. 5. Joel 3. 4.

*{that ye beat my people to pieces*} As Mic. 3. 2, 3. Or, *that ye crush them*; as Job 4. 19. Prov. 22. 22. Lam. 3. 34. Or, *bruise them*; as chap. 53. 5, 10. Or, *make powder of them*; as Psalm 143. 3. (See the like, 2 King. 13. 7. Psalm 18. 42.) That you exercise all manner of cruelty upon them. See ch. 1. 15, 21. The same speech is found, Psalm 94. 5.

*{and grind the faces of the poor*} Cause them by your oppressions, and hard usages of them, so to pine away, that it manifestly appears how it fares with them, by their faces. See ch. 1. 17. Or, as some other, *ye batter, ye beat them black and blue*; you are not content to bereave them of their goods, and means of maintenance; but you exercise your cruelty also upon their persons; the marks whereof they bear about them in their faces. The word here used signifies, as to *grind*, Numb. 11. 8. So to *batter*, Exod. 32. 20.

*{saith the Lord God of hosts*} See ch. 1. 9, 24.

**V. 16.** *{Moreover the Lord saith*} Heb. *And*; as Neh. 12. 8. Here the prophet passes from the actions, that God would proceed for against the men, the rulers, and great ones especially, unto the indictments that he had to commence against the women; and the heavy doom that should be passed, and executed upon them, for the same.

*{because the daughters of Zion are haughty*} The crimes charged upon the women, are principally, their excess of pride, wantonness, and vanity, discovering itself in the manner of their gait, and garb.

*{Daughters of Zion*} Not, as *the Daughter of Zion*; (of which phrase, see chap. 1. 18.) but, as *Daughters of Israel*, 2 Sam. 1. 24. And *Daughters of Jerusalem*, Luk. 23. 28. The women that dwelt in Jerusalem, whereof Zion, being a principal part, is put here for the whole city, as ch. 4. 3. But here the rather, it may be, because many of the women of chief note, and most faulty in the excesses, here taxed, (as those before noted, and taxed for their domineering over God's people, vers. 12.) did, in that part of the city, (the king's court especially, being there situate) reside. So also, ver. 17. ch. 4. 4.

*{are haughty*} Or, *stately*. Heb. *are high, or, lofty*; as ch. 55. 9. or, *lift up themselves*; as Zeph. 3. 9. Carry their heads aloft.

*{and walk*} Heb. *will walk*. And so after, again in the future, but for the present: (as appears by the former) which, in Hebrew, is not unusual; especially where the ordinary doing of, or continuance in the doing of a thing, is intimated. Thus they do, and thus they will do, for it is their ordinary guise. So Numb. 23. 7, 9. & 24. 9, 17. ch. 5. 8.

*{and walk with stretched-forth necks*} Heb. *stretched out in the throat*. For so the word, here used, properly signifies; as ch. 58. 1. But is here put for the *neck*, because part of it; or joined to it; as also, Ezek. 16. 11.

*{stretched forth*} The stretching out of the neck, is sometime of earnest desire and expectation, Rom. 8. 19. Sometime of pride and stateliness, Psalm 75. 5. So here.

*{and wanton eyes*} Heb. *lying, or deceiving; or, dealing deceitfully*, ch. 63. 8. *With their eyes*. (For both the preposition wants; as Psalm 17. 7, 14. and the affix also; as ver. 13.) That which some expound of their painted faces, and counterfeit visages. Of which, Jer. 4. 30. Ezek. 23. 40. (See ch. 1. 15.) Others, of their lewd and enticing looks, Gen. 39. 7. Or as others rather read and render it, *twinkling with their eyes*. That which, as Solomon makes the note of a lewd man, Prov. 6. 13. So the prophet here, the note of a light and loose disposition in the women of his times.

*{walking, and mincing as they go*} Or, *tripping it nicely, as they go along*. Heb. *walk; walking*; or, *go, going, and tripping*; or, *taboring; go, going*; as Psalm 126. 6. That is, *go ordinarily*; or *are wont to go tripping, or, taboring*. The Hebrew word here used, being nowhere else found, is ambiguous. Some suppose it, by interchange of one letter with another, of very near affinity, to come from a word that signifies to *beat, or, play on a tabor*. Which some of them understand of the *creaking of their pantofles*. Others, rather of a set frame of affected pace, not without some noise or sound, as they footed it: and so it may be rendered; *They use to tabor it as they go*. As in another kind, it is said of the court ladies of Nineveh, carried away captive; that they should go along with their queen, in the same condition with them *taboring upon their breasts*, Nah. 2. 7. Others derive it from a word that signifies a *little child*, Jer. 40. 7. & 41. 16. and render it, *Go like little children*; that can scarce go alone, and are fain to be led; imitating such in the niceness of their gait. Or as others, going struttingly, and wantonly, as little boys and girls are wont to do; in a lighter manner than will stand with matron-like gravity. Others, lastly, understanding it of such an affected nice pace, as before, suppose it to come from an Arabic term, used in that language, for a *pacing, or ambling nag*. Which may well be deemed the more probable, from that which next follows.

*{and making a tinkling with their feet*} This word also, as the former two, is nowhere else found. That from whence it has its original, used in the singular number, Prov. 7. 22. signifies a *fetter*, as most render it; though our English, *the stocks* in the plural; we have it, ver. 18. for *garters, or, chains*, worn, usually, about the legs. Some therefore expound it, *going, as if they were fettered*. Others, *tinkling*; that is, making a noise with their *spangles* about their gartering say some; with little bells about their shoes; say others; or with the chains of gold, or silver about their legs; wherewith they used to make a noise of purpose, as they went along in the streets: See vers. 18. Thus, as *twinkling with the eyes*, so *tinkling with the feet*, should be taxed as a note of lightness. But they that render it, *going, as if they were fettered*; understand it of such a nice kind of affected pace, as was in the former term intimated; and here further described, by a resemblance taken, either from captives and prisoners, that having irons upon their legs, cannot go freely and readily; but in a slow, and stalking manner, as their irons will give them leave. Or as others, from those cords, or fetters, that horse-breakers are wont to hamper young colts with, to bring them to a pace. That which sorts well with the notation of the word foregoing, from the Arabic.

*{feet*} For *legs*. as Psal. 105. 18.

**V. 17.** *{Therefore the Lord*} Heb. *And*. So Job 10. 15. & 21. 14. Their crimes were before, their doom now follows. God will punish them in those things, and in those parts, wherein they discover, and wherewith they practice their wantonness, and their pride.

*{will smite with a scab the crown of the head*} So ours, and most interpreters; as deeming the word, (nowhere else used) to come from one, which (with usual change of a letter) signifies a *scab*; used oft in the description of the leprosy, Lev. 13. 2, 6. &c. and without such change also in another form, for the same, ch. 5. 7. So the sense is, God with a *scab*, or, *scall*, will take off their hair, which is a part of women's glory, 1 Cor. 11. 15. and wherein these did pride themselves. This might be effected, either by evil usage, when they came into an enemy's hands; or, by some foul disease otherwise seizing on them; such, as not seldom follows looseness of life, Job 20. 11. Prov. 5. 11. Yet some render it more generally; *The Lord will peel, or, make bald the crown of the head*. Which may also be done, by causing them to be shorn, or shaven by the hand of their enemies, with whom they should be in captivity, which, with slaves and captives, is not unusual, Deut. 21. 12. And is done, on purpose, sometimes, in disgrace; such as it is also usually deemed to be, 1 Cor. 11. 6. Or, by giving them such occasions of grief, as should cause them to cut, yea, or to tear off their hair: that, which in heavy calamities, out of impatience, and impotency of spirit, is oft done, Jer. 7. 29. But the first seems most probable. See vers. 24.

*{the crown of the head*} The natural seat of hair. He will make those their heads, which before they carried so high, not only void of all loveliness, but so loathsome now, that they shall have little desire to have any see them: and others as little lust to look after them, that were formerly taken with them. See Cant. 7. 5.

*{of the daughters of Zion*} As, *the daughters of Moab*, ch. 16. 2. See v. 16.

*{and will discover their secret parts*} Heb. *make naked*; or, *bare*, Levit. 20. 18, 19. By bringing them into that miserable condition, that those, who now exceed in variety of apparel, change of raiment, and unnecessary superfluities, shall want clothes, wherewith to cover their nakedness; shall hardly have to hide those parts, which natural shame, and womanly modesty, do, by all means, desire and endeavor to conceal, and keep out of sight, ch. 20. 4. Mic. 1. 11. Or, the meaning may be that they should, in way of scorn and abuse, suffer such disgraceful usage, by the uncivil, and immodest carriage of the ruder sort of their enemies; into whose hands they should fall, ch. 47. 3. Jer. 13. 22. Ezek. 16. 37. & 23. 10, 26. Hos. 2. 2, 10. Nah. 3. 5.

**V. 18.** *{In that day*} What time this doom shall be put in execution; as ch. 2. 20. See ver. 7.

*{the Lord will take away*} He will strip them of all their ornaments, and habiliments, wherein they now so much abound, Ezek. 16. 39. & 23. 26. Not that such ornaments and attires, were of themselves simply evil and unlawful. (See Gen. 24. 22, 53. 2 Sam. 13. 18. Ezek. 16. 10, 13.) but their excess in them, and their abuse of them, to the fomenting of their pride and lust, is that which is condemned in them; and for which the removal of them is here denounced. So Hos. 2. 8, 9. See ch. 5. 12.

*{the bravery*} Consisting in the great variety of ornaments and attires, hereafter rehearsed, being such as they used to wear in times of feasting and jollity: opposed therefore to mourning weeds, ch. 61. 3. Nor is the word to be restrained to the first of them alone, here mentioned; but has reference also to all the rest that ensue. *The bravery of all these things*; for *all these brave, and goodly things*. As, *bravery of excellency*, for, *brave excellency*, or *excellent bravery*, ch. 13. 19.

*{of their tinkling ornaments about their feet*} Or as some, *their slippers*. The Hebrew word properly signifies, *fetters*, Prov. 7. 22. but *garters* here, as the most; or, *chains*. Such golden chains, as in divers of the Eastern parts women of fashion use, at this day, to wear. This was questionless, aimed at in the last clause of the verse next before going.

*{and the cauls*} Or, as some, *networks*. As others, *embroidered works*, by change of a letter, from that which signifies, *embroidery*, Exod. 28. 4, 39. though some distinguish that, and embroidery. Some would have it to be some ornament about the legs; as the former about the feet: as if the former were some kind of *shoes, or slippers*; these of *hose, or stockings*. But there is little probability of either. The word has no fellow.

*{and the round tires like the moon*} The word is found only here, and Judg. 8. 21, 26. where such ornaments are said to have been on the *camels' necks*; that belonged to the Midianitish princes. It is generally acknowledged, by the interchange of two letters of very near affinity, and in sound almost, if not wholly the same, to be derived from one, which in Syriac (whereof the Syrian deity is so termed) signifies the *moon*; yet not so much the half, as the whole moon. Others render it, *chains, or collars*. Which are indeed round in compass, but do not so fitly resemble the moon. And *chains* are also said to have been on the camels' necks; and that distinguished from these *moon-like ornaments*. Others, and those not a few, take it, for *round looking-glasses*. And such indeed swelling up, and bellying out, do not unfitly resemble the moon, and that at full; for from her *roundness* she has that name. But what should looking-glasses do on camels' necks? Others, lastly, for some kind of ornament about their shoes; such, as the nobility among the ancient Romans, wore: whereby they were distinguished from the meaner sort; or other such jewels, and ornaments, shaped like the moon; as among other nations, (which stories show) have been in use. Nor does it hinder, but that these, here mentioned, should be of the same sort with those; because they resembled not the figure of the round, or whole, but the half-hooked, or horned moon. For albeit the *moon*, from her *roundness*, have that name; and so properly, and primarily design the moon at full: Yet was it, in likelihood, more largely used, to signify that planet, without special respect had to her several shapes. And so the word, here used, may well signify such jewels, or ornaments, as represented her in any shape. Of which sort might well be the silver, or golden bosses, on the camels' furniture, before mentioned.

**V. 19.** *{And the chains*} So some. Others, *collars*; as *collars of Esses* with us. Which may therefore amount much to one. But *chains*, or, *collars*, and these seem to be distinguished, Judg. 8. 26. where both are mentioned. The word, here used, comes from one, that signifies *to drop*. And because *pure myrrh*, is such as drops, or issues from the plant of itself enforced, is by a word of the same original, thence so termed, Exod. 30. 34. Some therefore suppose that by it here are meant, such little boxes, like our *civet boxes*, of gold, wherein they used, either to reserve, or carry about them, myrrh, and other like odors, or sweet ointments; bearing the name of that for which they were first made and used. See ver. 20. Others take it for *pearls*; so termed from the form of them, (as some the like in Greek) resembling the *droppings* of myrrh, or other gummy matter: such as we term, *pendants*; and our great ones were wont to wear at their ears.

*{and the bracelets*} Or, *chains*. Peradventure the lesser sort of them, such as our *bracelets* ordinarily are. The word, as it is here single, is nowhere else found. But in a square, or double form it is oft used, in describing the work about the tabernacle; as Exod. 28. vers. 14. & chap. 39. 15. and there signifies *chains*; it comes of a root that signifies *to wreath*; and has affinity with one, that signifies the *navel*, Ezek. 16. 4. And with another, that signifies, *a coat of mail*; or, *a brigandine*, 1 Sam. 17. 5. And it is most likely to import any such ornaments, as consist of links fastened together; as the mail in the coat thereof consisting or of gold-wire, or thread therewith covered, twisted and wreathed together. Such as those about the tabernacle, and priestly robes seem to have been, of both kinds, whereof *chains and bracelets* are usually made. It may, as some think, comprehend *chains* of all sorts, used about neck, arm, wrist, or leg. Howbeit, the Chaldee paraphrast used the word sometime for *hooks*; whence it may be surmised to intend such golden *hooks, clasps, or taches* as women use oft about their looser garments, to fasten one part to another. Of which mention is made, Exod. 35. 22. though amiss rendered there, *bracelets*, the word being commonly used for *hooks*, ch. 37. 29. Ezek. 19. 4, 19. & 29. 4.

*{and the mufflers*} Or, *masks, or, veils, or, hukes*. Such as women use to veil, or cover their faces with, as Rebekah did, Gen. 24. 65. and of which the apostle speaks, 1 Cor. 11. 10, 15. (For the *head* there signifies not the *skull, or scalp* only, but takes in the face also; as when a man is said to be *beheaded*, 2 Sam. 16. 9.) So some take it, because the word whence it comes, is found used by the Jewish writers, for in that manner to *cover*: who yet from the word here, seem to have taken up that use of it, which in Scripture, is not found. Others therefore expound it *spangle, or spangled attires*, that are wont to quiver, and by quivering to make a more glittering show. Because the original of it, is from a root, as in Scripture signifies *trembling, and shaking, or, quaking*, Psal. 60. 3. chap. 51. 17, 22. Nah. 2. 3. Zach. 12. 2. The word itself, is a sole one.

**V. 20.** *{and the bonnets*} Or, *head-tires, or, hoods*. The word is of the same descent with that translated, *bravery*, vers. 18. And is deemed, sometime, to be taken more largely, for all sorts of goodly garments, ch. 61. 3, 10. But is most commonly used for *head-attire*; and that common to either sex, as appears, Exod. 39. 28. Ezek. 24. 17, 23. & 44. 18. See ver. 22.

*{and the ornaments of the legs*} Thus do divers render it. Some of them so taking it because it comes from a root that signifies, *going, of pacing, or marching*, Judg. 5. 4. Psal. 68. 7. But these notations are not always of certainty. The same word, with an *Aleph* only prefixed, which alters not its original, is rendered, *chains*, Numb. 31. 50. and a *bracelet*, 2 Sam. 1. 10. Whence also it appears, that it was such an ornament as was usually worn, not on the legs, but on the arm. For it is said to have been taken off *Saul's arm*; and yet in that other place in *Numbers*, some translate it also *garters*, as the old Latin also does here: however, it appears that it was an ornament no more, if at all, of the legs than of the arms: and the translation therefore would be altered. See vers. 19. *bracelets*. Of which, these seem to have been some special distinct kind.

*{and the head-bands*} Silken *fillets, or ribbons*; which they used about their heads; therewith either to tie up their hair, or to fasten their other head-gear, or attire to their heads. See Ezek. 24. 17. It was an ornament of special note with them; as appears, Jer. 2. 22. See the note there. Nor is it to be omitted, that the royal *diadem* (as the name itself also imports) was in ancient times, no other than a fair and rich *fillet*. It comes of a word that signifies *to tie, or to bind*. And God seems to allude unto such curious *fillets, or ribbons*; when he wills this people *to bind his precepts for a sign upon their hands*, Deut. 6. 8. As also Solomon, when he charges his son *to tie, or bind* the lessons he taught him, *about his neck, on his heart, and on his fingers*; or *hands*, Prov. 3. 3. & 6. 21. and 7. 3.

*{and the tablets*} Heb. *houses of the soul or breath, soul*, for *breath*: as Gen. 6. 17. & 7. 22. and so some take it not amiss, Jam. 2. 26. By these *houses*, or *receptacles of breath*, some understand *pomanders*; or, *boxes* wherein they carried sweet odors about them; with small holes pierced in them (not unlike the *myrrh-boxes*, by some thought to be mentioned, ver. 19.) by the scent thereof, to refresh their spirits when they pleased. Others, *masks or mufflers*, or the like, that covering the mouth, receive, or keep in the breath. For they seem to stray too far, that render it, *pectorals*; or, *breastplates*; understanding thereby, such jewels as they wore in their bosoms, or between their breasts: Because the *soul*, to wit, the heart, is there situate. Another word is rendered, *tablets*, Exod. 35. 22.

*{and the ear-rings*} Jewels, that hung in, or about their ears. So some of the Jewish doctors, and of ours. But there is another word used in Scripture for *earrings*. Numb. 31. 50. & Ezek. 16. 11. See ver. 21. Others therefore of them, whom some also of ours follow, understand by it, *amulets*, superstitious trinkets, of magical device, supposed to have virtue against charms, and enchantments, or other casual evils: *plates, or medals* of gold, with *spells*, or characters engraven on them to that purpose. This they seem, thence to conceive, because of the near affinity between the word here used, and that that signifies *to charm, and enchant*, Psal. 58. 5. Eccl. 10. 11.

**V. 21.** *{And the rings*} Mentioned among the Midianitish ornaments, Numb. 31. 50. used to be worn on the hand, or fingers, Esth. 3. 10. & 8. 2. Luk. 15. 22. Jam. 2. 2. and in Heb. so called, of a word that signifies *to dip deep*; or, *to fix, and fasten*, Exod. 15. 4. Job 38. 6. Psalm 69. 2, 15. Prov. 8. 25. Either because the finger is dipped deep into the ring, and the ring fastened unto it, Cant. 8. 6. Jer. 22. 24. Hag. 2. 23. Or, because being much used in sealing of deeds, they are as dipped in, and fixed upon that which they seal; or give an impression unto, and add a greater firmness to the deed thereby sealed, Esth. 8. 8, 10.

*{and the nose-jewels*} Such as they used to wear on their foreheads, hanging down toward the nose, Gen. 24. 47. Prov. 11. 22. Ezek. 16. 12. This kind of jewel, it seems, was very rife with them. For we find it oft mentioned, Gen. 24. 22. Exod. 35. 22. Judg. 8. 24. Job 42. 11. Prov. 25. 12. and they were of divers sorts; some, that were hanged in, or about the ears; as appears, Gen. 35. 4. and were so rife with their women, and the younger sort of that sex, that of them alone, was made the golden calf, Exod. 32. 2. From which, to distinguish those here spoken of, they are called *jewels of the nose*; though the word here rendered, *nose*, is oft-times used for the whole *face*, Gen. 3. 19. 2 Sam. 24. 33. and so it may take in also the ears, and be rendered more largely, *the face-jewels*; as comprehending either kind.

**V. 22.** *{And the changeable suits of apparel*} From their jewels, and additional ornaments, he seems to pass here to their clothes and garments themselves, that covered their bodies, or the greater part of them.

*{changeable suits*} The word in Hebrew is but one; and is found but in one place more; to wit, Zach. 3. 4. where it is rendered, *change of raiment*. But a word of near affinity to it, and of the same descent with it, signifies *spoils*, taken from men slain and stripped; whether armor, as 2 Sam. 2. 21. or raiment, as Judg. 14. 19. (where another word also is used, for *change of apparel*) so called from a word, that signifies *to pull away; or, pull off*, Deut. 25. 9, 10. And so it is thought, that *change of apparel* is, here styled; because the one is put off for putting on of the other: as Zach. 3.4. But others rather deem it some special kind of apparel, that covered the body from the waist downward; such as our women's *kirtles*, or *petticoats* are: For it is very near the word, that commonly signifies the *loins*, ch. 5.27. & 11.5. Nor see I any reason, why it may not be so taken, in Zachary also for some such garments, as men used to wear, fastened to them about their loins. Only there seems there, a defect of the epithet; such, as in this prophet, chap. 1.18. & 5.4. & Mal. 1.14. and it may then be rendered, *I will clothe thee with fair robes*: or the like. Some garments and attires were, in name at least, common to both sexes. See *Bonnets*, v. 20.

*{and the mantles*} From *covering* or *enwrapping* the body, so called. For that is the notion of its original, Psal. 73.4. This seems to be some upper garment, as the former an inner: That girt to the body; This hanging loose. The word is but once read.

*{and the wimples*} It is rendered *a veil*, Ruth 5.13. Some would have it *an apron*.

*{and the crisping pins*} Or, *curling-pins*. Such long *pins*, as they were wont to curl, or to fasten their hair with: or, to make use of about their attire and apparel. Otherwise, it comes near to a word that signifies *a pen*, or *pin*, to write with, chap. 8.1. or *a tool*, to engrave with, Exod. 32.4. Some expound it *pin-cases*; or, *needle-cases*. I should rather, *pin-cushions*, or, *pin-pillows*: as resembling the form of such *bags*, as the better sort used to put their money in. For which the word is used, 2 King. 5.23. being not found elsewhere.

**V. 23.** *{And the glasses*} Not drinking; but *looking glasses*; or, *mirrors*. Which yet always were not in those days, if at all, of glass; (for of glass we find no certain mention in the stories, or books of the Old Testament: nor is there any word that I know for it in Hebrew) but of fine and bright brass; or other the like metals. See Exod. 38.8. though two other words, be also used for such: but both from one root, and notion of *sight*: and but once only, as this here also, used either of them; the one in that place of Moses: the other, Job 37.18. The word here given them, has its ground from the use of them, *to reveal*, and show a man's, or woman's own face, to themselves, Jam. 1.23,24. The apostle alludes to them, 1 Cor. 13.12. & 2 Cor. 3.18. Howbeit some of the Jewish doctors would have the word to signify such fine and thin garments of lawn, or silk, as do not so much cover, as discover the body clad with them, and lay it open to view of others; as the heavens, in that regard, are in the opinion of some, in that of Job, compared to glass; because transparent: but that is questionable. Nor is there any notion of glass, in the word there used. And of like uncertainty is that of some others; who suppose some reference to such kind of apparel, as is here intimated in the term used, ch. 8.1. (where alone the singular is found; as the plural here only) which if it should so be, I should then surmise, the word here to signify some kind of *veils*; such as with us also, among the neater, or nicer sort rather, are in use; for there the word certainly signifies *a roll* of paper, or parchment, to write in. But the first exposition is most received; and the same words in the Hebrew sometime signify, one thing in the singular number, and another in the plural; as, that which signifies *a pot* in the singular, signifies *thorns* in the plural, Eccl. 7.6. that which signifies an *asp*, or some kind of serpent, in the singular, chap. 14.29. signifies *excrements* in the plural masculine, Exod. 4.15. *issue*, in the feminine, chap. 22.24. that which signifies *light* in the singular, Esth. 8.16. Psal. 139.12. signifies *herbs* in the plural, 2 King. chap. 4. v. 39. ch. 26.19.

*{and the fine linen*} The name of the stuff, or matter; not of the vesture or thing itself, thereof made. It is translated *sheets* in Sampson's story, Jud. 14.12. and the Greek word answering it, and derived from it, is used by three evangelists, in relation of our Savior's sepulture, for *a winding-sheet*, Matth. 27.59. Mar. 15.46. Luk. 23.53. But might peradventure, in that former place, have been better rendered, *shirts*, than *sheets*: for it is not likely, that those Philistims whom Sampson slew, to make payment of his wager, carried their *sheets*; and much less their *winding sheets*, about them. Besides that it seems used also, for *a shirt*, or such an inner garment of linen, as is wont to be worn next the skin, Mar. 14.51,52. and it may well therefore here be rendered, either *smocks*, or *shifts*; the the more modest term used in these times, comprehending both *shirts*, and *smocks*.

*{and the hoods*} Or, *Turbans*. An attire for the head, different from the *bonnet* before mentioned, v. 20. Levit. 8.9,13. such as the Turks and Persians, or their women use at this day, consisting of many folds, and wreaths; and with some raised up to a great height in the middle: so called of a word that signifies *to roll*; or, *turn round*, chap. 22.18. It is used, both for a royal *diadem*, ch. 62.3. Ezek. 21.26. and for a priestly *miter*, Exod. 28.4. Levit. 8.9. Zach. 3.5. and it is so called, because it was *rolled up* in many folds; and the head *enwrapped* with it, Levit. 16.4.

*{and the veils*} Or, *robes*; or, *frocks*: or, *cassocks*. A loose upper garment, so called of *spreading*: For so signifies the word, from whence it comes, 1 King. 6.32. It is found here, and Cant. 5.7. not elsewhere.

**V. 24.** *{And it shall come to pass, that*} Heb. *it shall be* As chap. 2.2. and a defect of the particle, *that*; as ch. 4.3. Before, was the privative part of the doom; what they should be deprived of: Now follows the positive; what in room thereof should succeed.

*{there shall be instead of sweet smell*} The word comprehends all aromatical, or odoriferous spices, Exod. 30.23. 1 Kings 10.2. Ezek. 27.22.

*{stink*} The word properly signifies *putrefaction*; or, *rottenness*, ch. 5.24. and by consequence *stench*, thence usually proceeding. That which should befall them, either from such filthy sores, and loathsome diseases wherewith God should smite them, Deut. 28.27,60. Job 7.5. & 19.17. Psal. 38.5. v. 17. or from such evil usage, and restraint, in prisons, and dungeons, which they should endure in the time of their captivity, ch. 42.22.

*{and instead of a girdle*} Or, *of girding*. Which the word properly signifies, 2 King. 3.21. as also the like word hereafter used; and may import, either *a girdle*, wherewith they used to gird to them their inner garments, Exod. 29.5. or such garments, as being girt to them, about the *loins*, or paps, 1 King. 18.46. Levit. 13.35. Rev. 1.13.) do fall down to the lower parts of the body; whereof before, v. 22. For it is used of those *aprons*, or *girdings*, which of *twigs twisted*, or *wreathed*, rather than *leaves sewed* together, (for the word there used signifies as well *twigs*, or *branches*; as *leaves*, Gen. 8.11. Neh. 8.15.) our first parents made to cover their shame with, Gen. 3.7.

*{a rent*} *Renting* of garments for extremity of grief, Jer. 41.5. Or, *rags*; having no whole garment to put on. It comes of a word that signifies *to cut down*, ch. 10.34. or *to cut asunder*, ch. 29.1. Some therefore expound it of their garments, by the enemy cut short, in scorn, to the discovery of their shame; as 2 Sam. 10.4. ch. 20.4. Others render it *looseness*, *dissolution*; opposed to *girding*: and the word it comes from, seems so to signify, Job 19.26. Their *rags*, such as they shall have, shall, in a slatternly manner, hang loose about those that were so curious in girding, and fitting their garments to their bodies, before: as it is wont to be with those, who either being in a sad or forlorn condition, are wholly regardless of themselves: Or, whose apparel is so tattered and torn, and by reason thereof so unuseful, that they hold it not worthy of any regard, nor would stand them in any stead, were they never so careful to gird it unto them. See v. 17.

*{and instead of well-set hair*} Heb. *work of even*, or, *smooth setting*; or, *trimming*, to wit of hair; as by the opposite does appear. Hair evenly, and curiously so disposed, as no one hair rises, or stands above the rest, but all lies as smooth as the surface of some gold, or brass-plate, artificially beaten out, and exactly smoothed with the hammer, ch. 41.7. For from a word that signifies such manner of work (Exod. 25.18. Numb. 10.2. ch. 44.12.) is that, here only used; with a small alteration of one vowel only derived. And the word which we render, *setting*, *disposed*, or *trimming*, is applied to the *dressing*, or *trimming* of hair, on head or beard, in the story of Mephibosheth, 2 Sam. 19.24. which place gives light to that other ambiguous one, concerning the captive woman's dealing with her nails, Deut. 21.12.

*{baldness*} Procured either by the scab before mentioned, ver. 18; or the hair plucked, or cut off in scorn, or rage, by the hand of a foe; or torn off in extremity of grief, through impotency of spirit, by themselves. ch. 15.2. & 22.12. Mic. 1.16.

*{and instead of a stomacher*} The Hebrew doctors themselves agree not about this. And indeed in most of these names, as also in the forbidden *fowls*, Levit. 11. & Deut. 14.) their greatest rabbins rove, but, as well as we. Some would have it a silken *swathing-band*; such as they used to wear about their breasts. Which with our version, may not altogether unfitly agree. Others of them a fine upper garment, of fine linen or silk. Some of ours, *a girdle* made of *twist-silk*, or thread: Because it has all the letters of a word that signifies *twist*, Exod. 28.28. (for so it would rather be there rendered, than lace) and a *cord*, or *line*, Ezek. 40.3. and some kind of wearing cloth made of such; but rendered *a bracelet*, Gen. 38.18. Others of them *a farthingale*; a garment consisting of many pieces, that being narrow at the top, where it is girt to the waist, widens still to the bottom, where it carries a large compass; such, as in times past, were among our gentry very rife. These suppose the word compounded of a term that signifies *a piece*, Gen. 18.5. Lev. 2.6. And another that signifies *round*: whence the land of Galilee, 1 King. 9.11. But neither is the former word used of pieces of cloth, but of *bread*, or *cake* only: nor is the deduction very probable: nor would all granted afford ground sufficient for the making up of such a garment, as these authors would piece together out of these notions. Ours may stand, till some more probable can be produced.

*{a girding of sackcloth*} Heb. *sack*; as Gen. 42.25. A word that holds its own in most languages. Such coarse, and sorry stuff, as their sacking was mostly made of; and being the ordinary matter of mourning weeds, was used commonly, as a badge of much heaviness & grief, Gen. 37.34. Job 16.15. Ps. 30.11. & 35.13. ch. 15.3. *Girding of*, or, *with sack*; as ch. 22.12. For putting it on, and wearing it; as *girding on of harness*, 1 King. 20.11.

*{and burning*} *Tanning*; or *sunburning*. Which they had formerly been so curiously careful to shun, that they would not once peep out into the air, much less into the sunshine, without mask, or veil, for fear of abating their beauty, and altering their hue. But should now seize on them with a witness; being exposed to all such kind of occurrences; and having nothing to shelter them from sun, wind, or weather. See Cant. 1.6.

*{and*} A defect of the copulative; as Job 12.4. and 20.17. ch. 5.24. Hab. 3.11. which makes the sentence the quicker.

*{burning*} A defective word, from that which, more entire, so signifies, Exod. 21.25. not found elsewhere, unless ch. 32.13. (See the note there) and here used, partly, to quicken the sentence; and partly to make it comply in sound with its opposite. For in such kind of modulations, this our prophet abounds. Nor is the term, *ci*, from *Cavah*, *to burn*, any more uncouth a deduction, as a learned author, to make way for his own uncouth interpretation, here terms it) than *ri*, from *ravah*, *to water*, Job 37.11.

*{instead of beauty*} Which by all means, they had formerly been so exceeding careful and studious to maintain; whereof they had been so proud, Ezek. 16.14,15. The main sum of all is, that being stripped of all their former goodly raiment, and ornaments, they should, in most pitiful plight, and sorry rags, be carried away barehead, and barefoot, in captivity to Babylon. See Jer. 2.25,37. That construction of a late learned annotator, seems over-harsh; who taking the foregoing word not for a noun but a particle, tears off this clause from the present verse, and glues it to the next, thus rendering the words, *For instead of beauty*, or, *because of beauty, thy men shall fall by the sword.*

**V. 25.** *{Thy men shall fall by the sword*} The men shall suffer; for suffering, and fomenting in the women, the vices and crimes before charged on them; ver. 16. And the whole state, for not restraining and reforming them, ver. 26. Or, the women shall suffer, as in their own persons, by the means above mentioned; so by the loss of their husbands also, and of such as might be a support unto them, and a means of keeping them from reproach. See ch. 4.1.

*{Thy*} Yours, O Sion, your inhabitants; as ch. 1.27. v. 16.

*{men*} Distinguished from women, and children, Deut. ch. 2. v. 34. & ch. 3. v. 6. Of the words, see ch. 2.9.

*{shall fall*} Be slain; as 2 Sam. ch. 21. v. 9. Psal. 78.64.

*{by the sword*} Of the enemy, see ch. 1.20.

*{and thy mighty*} Heb. *thy might*. And so Jer. 49.35. *their might*: as we use to say, *nobility*, *gentry*, *commonalty*, for *nobles*, *gentlemen*, *commons*: so, the *height of people*, for *haughty people*, ch. 24.4. or, *thy men of might*, for *mighty men*; as *wisdom* for a man of *wisdom*: a wise man, Mic. 6.9. and *honor* for men of *honor*, *honorable* men, chap. 5.13. so *strength*, for *strong* ones; or, men of *strength*, Judg. 5.21. See ch. 1.21,26.

*{in war*} Where the mighty fall, as well and as soon, oft, as the weak, 2 Sam. 11.25. Eccl. 9.11. especially then, when God fights against them; and the enemy comes with commission from him; against whom no power can prevail, and before whom no strength can stand, Psal. 33.16. and 76.7. Amos 2.14,16.

**V. 26.** *{And her gates shall lament,}* The city being ruined, shall yield a most lamentable spectacle to all that behold it; or, the whole state and land shall be in such condition; it shall so be with all her cities. See Jer. ch. 34. v. 1.

*{her*} A change of the person, as before verse 14.

*{her gates*} *Her cities*, *gate*, for *city*; as Exod. 20.10. Deut. 16.15. and 31.12. Or, *the gates of Zion*, that is, of Jerusalem, wherein the judges and elders used to sit; for the hearing of causes, and the execution of justice, Ruth 4.1,2. Psal. 127.5. Jer. 37.7.

*{shall lament*} A very pathetical expression, intimating such a woeful condition, as even the very senseless creatures might seem to be sensible of it. So, chap. 24.4. The *gates of Zion* are said to *mourn*: for want of that confluence of people that had wont to be in them; as *the ways of Zion*, are said to *lament* for want of passengers that used formerly to pass to and fro by them, Lam. 1.4.
