That which Job calls, *the general meeting house appointed for all that live*, Job 30.23. and of which Solomon says that *all go to one place*, Eccles. 3.20. which of the grave of man's handiwork cannot be said, Jer. 22.19.

*{hath enlarged*} Or, *doth enlarge*; as ch. 1.2.

*{herself*} Heb. *its soul*: *soul* for *self*, as ch. 3. vers. 9. Jer. chapter 51.6.

*{and opened her mouth without measure*} A very rhetorical and emphatical expression, intimating the numberless multitude of those that by hunger and thirst, and other like judgments were swept away, as if there were scarce room enough anywhere, either underground: or aboveground, to receive them, See Jer. 7.32,33.

*{opened*} Or, *widened*. Men are said to *open* their mouths to speak, Psal. 78.2. Matth. 5.2. to *widen* their mouths, when they gape wider than ordinary, to draw in breath, as Psal. 119.131. or to receive, and take somewhat into the mouth, that they greedily desire. So Job says, that men *waited for him*, (that is, for his *words*, that *dropped upon them*) *as for rain, and opened their mouths wide*, (there is the word here used) *as for the latter rain*: that is, as the earth uses to gape for rain in the time of summer's drought: as also men are said sometime so to do in way of mockage, Job 16.10. where the word is translated *gape*: as another near to it of the like sense and use, is rendered, *make a wide mouth*, chap. 57. vers. 4. The word would therefore be here translated, *hath widened*, or, *doth widen*, as before; *gapes wide*, as one that is to take in some more than ordinary great morsel, or much at once.

*{her mouth*} Or, *with her mouth*, as Job 16.10. (the particle wanting as Psal. 17.14. with ver. 7.) as being no less desirous to take them in, and swallow them down: as it did Dathan and Abiram with all theirs, Numb. 16.32,33. Psal. 106.17. (whereunto David alludes, Psal. 55.15. & 69.15.) than they were greedy to seize on the possessions of others, Mic. 2.2. A *mouth* is ascribed to the *grave*, as to the earth, Gen. 4.11. Num. 17.32. and the *throat* of wicked ones, whose mouths are employed in traducing of innocent persons, is said to be *an open sepulcher*, Psal. 5.9. as being ready *to swallow men down quick, like the grave, or the pit*, Prov. 1.12.

*{without measure*} Heb. *unto no measure*; or, *appointment*; or, *proportion*; or, *ordinance*; as the word ordinarily signifies, Gen. 47.22. Exod. 15.25. Josh. 24.25. beyond all ordinary proportion, or wont. The grave is as unmeasurable, and insatiable, in surprising and devouring of them, as they were, in seizing on the possessions of their poor neighbors, and taking them to themselves, verse 18. chapter 3.14.

*{and their glory, &c.*} Or, *that their glory, &c. may descend, &c.* as noting the end for which the grave gaped so wide; because it had such an huge number of corpses to receive, that she might swallow them down suddenly, without stop, or stay, at once. See that use of the particle, v. 5.

*{their glory*} Heb. *her excellency*; or, *the excellency of her*: as the word is rendered, ch. 35.2. where it is also distinguished from glory. See also ch. 3.10. & 53.2. *excellency*, as most take it (though some, simply, for *excellency* itself, as Ezek. 16.4.) for, men of *excellency*; as *glory* before, for men of *glory*, v. 13. those that were of most state, and esteem, among them.

*of her*, That is, of the city of Jerusalem, as some: or the state of Judah, as others: for the affix is not masculine here, as before, v. 13. but feminine: and has therefore nothing else in the text, whereunto it may be referred. See v. 3,7.

*{and their multitude*} Heb. *her multitude*: as *her excellency*. *Her*, as in the former branch: and *multitude*, as in the verse next before-going: the *many*, or, as we use to speak, the *meiny*, those of the meaner sort, which are the greater number by much, everywhere. And so most here take it. Howbeit a late author, as v. 13. so here, renders it rather *abundance*. Which sorts not amiss here, with what follows. See ch. 16.14.

*{and their pomp*} Or, *noise*, or, *tumult*: as it is rendered, ch. 37.29. their *tumultuous noise*, or, *shouting*: as ch. 16.10. for so the word properly signifies, ch. 13.4. & 66.6. such as is usual in warlike conflicts, ch. 25.25. Hos. 10.14. Amos 2.2. as the like also in disorderly feasting, and revelings, especially where wine has got the upper hand, ch. 24.8. Jer. 48.45. & 51.38,39.

*{and*} Some, *with*: as Exod. 1.5. *and Joseph*, for, *with Joseph*: and Neh. 10.42. *and Jeremiah*, for *with Jeremiah*: as it is there well rendered: their tumultuous shoutings shall cease, or die, and be buried with them, ch. 24.8. & 25.5.

*{their*} Heb. *her*. As before.

*{pomp*} Or, *noise*, or, *tumult*, or, *shout*: as some, for, those that make such *noise*, *tumult*, or *shout*: called *the sons*, or *children of shouting*, Jer. 48.45. as *glory* before, v. 13. and *excellency* in this.

*{and he that rejoiceth*} Or, *and him*. To wit, *and*, with him, as before.

*that rejoiceth*, Or, *revelleth* rather: as the city of Jerusalem is called a *reveling city*, ch. 22.2. the houses thereof, *houses of disport*, or, *merriment*, ch. 32.13. The word properly signifies to *skip*, or *leap* for joy. The word used of John Baptist, answering to it, where it is said, that he *leaped* (or *sprang* rather) for joy, being as yet in his mother's womb, Luk. 1.44. and it is taken in a middle sense, sometime for such expression of joy, either honest, and lawful, on good and just ground: or a degree of joy more than ordinary, albeit no such expression be therein used, as chap. 13.3. Psal. 28.7. & 62.6. & 68.3. Hab. 3.18. Otherwhiles, for loose and disorderly skipping and frisking, out of lightness, wantonness: and other the like motions and gestures, expressions of immoderate and inordinate delight, Jer. 51.39. and so here; *he*, or *him, that rejoiceth and revelleth*, taken collectively, for the whole crew of them. See chap. 1.3. ver. 15.

*{shall descend*} Or, *may descend*, taking the copulative for the finitive; *and*, for, *that*: as was before said, *that there may descend*, to wit, into the grave, *the glory*, or *excellency, &c.* for so the words lie, that they may all, and all sorts of them, go down into the grave. So Job 21.12,13.

*{into it*} To wit, *the grave* before spoken of, according to our version; and so is the particle used, Ezra 9.7. chap. 10.21. but the trajection is too great to admit here that sense. For the word of descending, stands here in the front of the sentence, and not in the close of it, as our version places it. And it ought therefore to be rendered, *he*, or *him that revelleth in her*, or *the reveller in her*; as before, *her excellency, her multitude, her shouting*. Of which, see before.

**V. 15.** *{And the mean man shall be brought down, and the mighty man shall be humbled*} Men of all sorts (as before, ver. 14. save that the greater, and of higher degree and state, are first spoken of there; the meaner condition is first mentioned here) shall alike be laid low, being brought down to the grave, that makes no distinction of states, Job 3.13,19. See chap. 2.9. where the words being the same, this is at large opened.

*{and the eyes of the haughty shall be humbled*} See chap. 2.11.

*{shall be humbled*} Their countenance, or big look, shall then be cast down, Gen. 4.6. Lam. 2.10.

**V. 16.** *{But*} Heb. *And*. Which may well stand here.

*{the Lord of Hosts*} See chap. 1.9.

*{shall be exalted in judgment*} He shall, by his just judgment executed on those wicked wretches, who set so light by him before, manifest and magnify, as well his power, as his purity, Psal. 9.6. See ch. 2.11.

*{and God that is holy*} Heb. *the God: the holy One*. The most holy God; so holy, as *none holy as he*, 1 Sam. 2.2. as none *good* in regard of him, Matt. 19.17. none *wise*, in way of collation with him, 1 Cor. 3.19. 1 Tim. 1.17. So none *holy*, in such manner as he is. They that are holy, and wise, and good, in some kind, by participation from him, are neither holy, nor wise, nor good, when they come into comparison with him, Job 4.17,18. & 9.2. & 15.15. & 25.5,6. See ch. 1.4. & 6.3.

*{shall be sanctified*} His holiness, and hatred of sin shall appear, and he religiously acknowledged, by his punishing of it in obstinate sinners, Levit. 10.2,3. Ezek. 20.41. & 28.22,26. the sparing and forbearing of whom, for a time, causes wicked wretches oft-times, to call in question his holiness, Psal. 50.21. Mal. 2.17.

*in righteousness*, by his righteousness showed in those his judgments. For it is not to be understood, as if he were to be *exalted* by *judgment*, and not by *righteousness*, or *sanctified* by *righteousness*, and not by *judgment*. But it is a rhetorical illustration, amplifying and dilating both the act and the effect: and describing the act by two several arguments: the subject, *judgment*; the adjunct, *justice*: the effect or event by two branches of it, the manifesting and magnifying, partly of God's greatness, and partly of his goodness; the one applied to the subject, the other to the adjunct; though both common to either. So also ver. 15. See of *judgment* and *justice*, chap. 1.27. & ver. 7. Of the manner of speech, ver. 13.

**V. 17.** *{Then shall the lambs feed after their manner*} Heb. *And*, for, *Then*, as Gen. 28.21. or 22 rather, (for the condition of the vow there is in the 21. verse, the matter of it in the 22.) Levit. 4.3. & 6.4.

*{Then*} When by the judgments before threatened, being put in execution, the unjust possessors of those houses and lands before spoken of, being either slain, or expelled; they shall either lie waste, or return again to those unto whom they formerly belonged.

*{the lambs shall feed after their manner*} Some expound it literally, and simply, without any figure, or allegory; of cattle, grazing freely without restraint, in those places, whence before, by enclosures, they had been excluded, after the pasture came into those great men's hands: yea, upon those places, now lying waste, where their either dwellings, or farmhouses, had before stood, as chap. 7.25. & 17.2. But it seems rather, as the most and best, to be understood of the godly poor, who either being left in the land, during the time of the captivity, should enjoy those places, and receive the fruits thereof, which by the destruction, or deportation of their oppressors, were now vacant, Jer. 52.13. Zeph. 3.12. (see chap. 7.21,22. or returning out of captivity, should quietly enjoy their lands and means again, whence by cruel and injurious courses of the mightier sort they had formerly been expelled, Ezek. 34.14,15.

*{the lambs*} God's people are in Scripture termed his *sheep*; in regard of the care that he has of them, as their shepherd, Psal. 77.20. & 80.1. Ezek. 34.15. Joh. 10.10,16,27,28. & 21.16,17. and his *pasture sheep*, in regard of the plentiful provision he makes for them, Psal. 23.1,2. & 100.3. Ezek. 34.31. and *his lambs*, in regard of his tender affection towards them, ch. 40.11. Joh. 21.15.

*{shall feed*} Enjoy those good things, that the land affords. c. 1.19.

*{after their manner*} The word here used, is but twice found in Scripture; here, and Mic. 2.12. For the one of these prophets has much from the other, (see chap. 2.2.) Now in Micah it is apparent, that it signifies a *fold*, whereinto sheep are gathered, for their better security, therein to be folded; alluded unto by our Savior, Joh. 10.16. and so some take it in this place, thus rendering the words *they shall feed besides their wonted fold*, or, *folds*. But the particle is seldom, if ever, found used, for *beside*. Others therefore, and so the most, take it according to another word that comes very near it, used Psal. 110.4. compared with Heb. 6.20. & 7.17. Eccl. 3.18. for *order*, or, *manner*; they shall feed freely and quietly, as they had wont to do, before their disturbance and expulsion, Jer. 23.3,4. & 30.10. & 46.27. Ezek. 34.25,28. See chap. 7.25. Others according to their *conduct*, or *leading*: as their shepherd shall lead them, after the manner of those parts, ch. 40.11. because, the verb it comes from, is in the Chaldee so commonly used.

*{and the waste places of the fat ones, shall the strangers eat*} This some understand of strangers, by God's just judgment, devouring what was found left in the places where they had expelled those great ones before mentioned: and so it should be the same with that, chap. 1.6. *strangers devour your land, &c.* Others, of the expulsion of those great ones out of those places, whence they had expelled the right owners before, and driving them out into the waste wilderness, to seek relief and harbor there: and these render the words, *and the fat ones, as strangers* (to wit, from God) *shall feed on the wastes of the land*: and so it should be as that, Psal. 68.6. *the rebellious shall dwell in a dry land*. But this seems to offer over-much violence to the text. Others therefore understand it of the poor oppressed, as before, returning again to those places, to which they had been for a long time as strangers, after their freedom from captivity, Jer. 12.14,15.

*{the waste places*} Or, *wastes*: as Ezek. chap. 33.24. and 36.33.

*{of the fat ones*} The word whereof this comes, signifies *marrow*, Job 21.24. Hence this word word is used for *fat* beasts, or *fatlings*, Psal. 66.15. and another not unlike it, for the same, ch. 25.6. because the bones of fat ones, men, or beasts, are usually full of marrow. Job 21.24. Some therefore understand here, the pastures, the now wastes, where fat beasts, that they fed on, and feasted with, (ch. 22.13.) did formerly feed. Others, where those fat ones, that is, rich ones, did themselves formerly abide. *Fat*, for, *rich*, or, *great*, for their store of wealth, or high feeding, or both; (as Luk. 16.19. so styled, as Psal. 22.29. & 78.31. ch. 34.6,7.

**V. 18.** *{Woe unto them that draw iniquity, with cords of vanity and sin as it were, with a cartrope*} The third sort of abominable fruits that God's vineyard produced, is the obstinacy and eagerness of wicked ones in the pursuit of sin and wickedness, together with a professed contempt of God and his judgments, v. 19.

*{that draw iniquity*} Some understand this, of drawing others to sin: of men, that are not content to sin and do evil themselves; but entice, persuade, urge, and force others thereunto: the Devil's trade, Gen. 3.2,4. called therefore *the Tempter*, Matth. 4.1,3. Joh. 13.2. 1 Cor. 7.5. 1 Thess. 3.5. Rev. 12.9. & 13.14. & 20.8,10. Of such, see, Gen. 39.7,10,12. 2 Sam. 13.3,11,14. & 16.21. Hab. 2.15. Matth. 29.15. and they suppose, that the metaphor used does very pregnantly express it, wherein the persons themselves are compared to beasts, that draw in a cart, or a wain; the vain, and false persuasions, and arguments, wherewith they draw them on unto evil, to traces, or cart-ropes: and the parties so drawn on by them, to wains, or carts; drawn by beasts, understanding by *iniquity* and *sin*, as the word *iniquity* after an Hebraism not unusual, men of *iniquity*, and men of *sin*, as the word *iniquity* seems taken Psal. 49.5. & 65.3. & 119.133. Of which phrase, see also ver. 13,14. But the place seems rather to most others, to be meant of such, as being desperately bent, and abandoned, to sin, do not lengthen only, and draw out their sinful course and tenor of life, as a man draws out a line, or a cord, either in the unfolding, or in the spinning and framing of it, (for the word sometime signifies *to continue*, or, *protract*, Psal. 36.11.) but by all means, that they can devise, draw sin unto themselves, where there is hardly any matter of profit, pleasure, gain, delight, persuasion by others, enforcement from others, or other like temptations that are wont to lead aside, and carry men on to evil. So that, whereas others are drawn by such motives unto sin, they draw sin unto themselves; whereas, sin is by such inducements pressed and enforced upon others, they press and enforce it upon themselves: they draw sin to them, as a beast draws a cart, or wain, after it, Deut. 21.3. Howbeit, some by *sin*, and *iniquity*, here conceive to be meant, the penalties or punishments due unto either. And so indeed the words are not seldom used, Gen. 4.13. Levit. 20.17. Num. 9.13. according to which interpretation, the meaning should be; such as labor to draw on God's judgments upon themselves by their continuance in impenitency, and adding sin to sin, and thereby provoking God, to come the more speedily in judgment against them, Rom. 2.4,5. and this indeed would well suit with what follows; v. 19. But I suppose rather the genuine meaning to be; such as by all means, and with all their might, apply themselves to the practice of evil, toiling and tiring themselves in it, as a beast tugging at the plow, or drawing in the cart; as Jer. 9.5. See Job 4.8. Prov. 3.29. & 21.4. where the like metaphor is used.

*{that draw iniquity*} Heb. *the drawers of iniquity*, as the early risers, v. 11. See there.

*{with cords of vanity*} By *cords of vanity*, some understand here such vain excuses, and pretenses, as wicked ones use ordinarily to cover, or color, to smooth, or smother their vile practices with, 1 Sa. 15.13,15,20,21. But that is not manner of such desperately professed profane ones, as here spoken of: but with open face, and bare forehead rather, to avow, blaze abroad, and boast of their evil doings, Psal. 52.1. chap. 3.9. By *cords of vanity*, therefore, I rather understand those fetches and devices, toilsome courses and employments, wherein men bent to wickedness, and set wholly thereupon, do labor and toil and take pains incessantly, for the compassing of their intended evil, practices, and the bringing about of their wicked designs, Psal. 36.4. Mic. 1.2.

*{with cart-ropes*} Heb. *the thick rope of a wain*, or *cart*. For the word properly signifies a thick cord, or rope; such as those are usually, wherewith carts or wains are drawn, and whereof traces are made for the beasts, that draw in them: and hereby is intimated the strength of those plots, that they make use of, for the accomplishment of their wicked purposes, that they may not fail, and miscarry before they come to full effect, Psal. 64.5,6.

**V. 19.** *{That say, Let him make speed, &c.*} That scoff at God's menaces, and jest at his judgments; neither crediting the one, nor expecting the other: yea not only, not considering them, or thinking at all on them: as those before wholly drowned in sensuality, and carnal delights, v. 12. but in most impious manner jeering at them, and the prophets that denounced them, as if their words were but wind, and the matter itself a mere mockery; such, as it were a most fond thing for any man to fear, Jer. 5.11,12.

*{Let him make speed, and hasten his work, that we may see it,}* Or rather, *Let him make speed; let him hasten his work*, or, *make haste with his work*. For the copulative is not in the text, & the inserting of it makes the speech less emphatical. The words they are of these desperate atheists; as if they had said, we have heard much, and long, of what God, you say, intends to do, we would fain see it once done. So Jer. 17.15. Ezek. 12.23. Amos 5.18. 2 Pet. 3.3. they speak, as if they thought it long a coming; but will think that it comes too soon, when it does come, Matth. 8.29.

*{his work*} God's work of judgment denounced by his prophets, v. 12.

*{let the counsel*} That is, the matter, as by counsel set down, and resolved upon, Psal. 2.11. ch. 19.17.

*{of the holy One of Israel*} So in mockage they speak of God, as those, Job 21.15. Of the style, see, ch. 1.4.

*{draw near and come, that we may know it*} Heb. *know*. A defect of the particle, denoting the object, or thing to be known: either know it to be true, and you to be true prophets, that now tell us of it. Ezek. 2.5. & 6.10. or know it, by seeing, yea, or feeling, what we now hear, finding that fulfilled, that is now said, Jer. 30.24.

**V. 20.** *{Woe unto them that call evil, good; and good, evil*} Some would have this restrained to matter of judicature; and so it would be in effect, the same with that which follows, v. 23. But it seems more general, and to describe the perverse disposition of those who do not only confound the names and natures of things, and take away all distinction between good, and bad; honest, and dishonest; as some here expound it, (which yet were a most horrible depravation and obliteration of natural reason, and of the remainder of God's image, in man's corrupt heart) as misplace them in a cross and perverse course and manner, (like those that turn night into day; and day into night) transferring the one into the room of the other; and substituting the one in the place of the other; not only confounding vice with virtue, and evil with good, making both alike, either allowable, or disallowable, & such as may alike be either rejected or received: but going further than so, hating that, and rejecting it that ought to be loved, and embraced; and embracing that, and approving it, that ought to be rejected and abhorred, Amos 5.10. Mic. 3.2. that which is the highest degree, if it be done out of judgment, of that *reprobate mind*, or, *unsound judgment*, that the apostle speaks of, which some heathen were given up unto, Rom. 1.28. or if against judgment and knowledge out of a mere willfulness, and perverseness of spirit; is not far from that opposition, which our Savior Christ terms blasphemy against the Spirit of God; and says, shall never be remitted, Matth. 12.32. And this is the fourth evil fruit, or crime, that some part, at least, of this people, are here charged with.

*{call evil, good, and good, evil*} Heb. *say of evil, it is good; and of good, it is evil*: as Mal. 1.8. Prov. 20.14. that so do, either out of unsoundness of judgment, or base calumny, or gross flattery, or mere malice. See Prov. 24.24. *of evil*, or *concerning evil*; and, *of good*, or, *concerning good*: as the particle is used, Psal. 91.11. Esth. 3.2.

*{that put darkness, for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet; and sweet for bitter*} Heb. *put darkness into light*, that is, into the room of *light*; and so of the rest. In these words, is a metaphorical amplification of the thing before spoken, illustrating the practice and carriage of the persons therein taxed, by two similitudes, taken from natural objects; thereby intimating, that this their sentencing of good and evil, proceeded not merely from a natural ignorance; or from some infirmity, or weakness: since that those that are corporally blind, albeit they cannot distinguish between night and day; and they may therefore suppose it to be night, when indeed it is day: yet can they not take darkness itself for daylight, or deem daylight to be darkness; as also those that have their mouths or palates, by some distemper or disease out of taste: although they do apprehend things of themselves sweet, as bitter: yet do they not apprehend things bitter, as sweet. But by these metaphorical illustrations, the prophet implies, that this their cross carriage, in passing such doom on good and evil, and not displacing only, but misplacing of either; proceeded rather from a willful and inordinate love of whatsoever was evil, and repugnant to grace and goodness; and an inveterate hatred of whatsoever was good, or had any relish of grace and goodness in it, Job 20.12,13. & 24.13,17. Psal. 36.2,4. Joh. 3.20.

*{darkness for light*} Grace and goodness is commonly termed light in Scripture, Act. 26.18. Rom. 13.12. Eph. 5.4. 1 Thess. 5.5. because it proceeds from God, the Father of light, Jam. 1.17. from his irradiation shining into men's souls, 2 Cor. 4.6. Heb. 10.32. It makes men lightsome inwardly, that is, pure, and sincere, Phil. 1.10. therein like unto God, 1 Joh. 1.5. and able to discern aright of things that differ, Rom. 2.18,20. Phil. 1.10. it makes them shine forth brightly in their life and conversation, Matth. 5.14,16. Phil. 2.15. Rev. 19.8,14. it is such as can endure the light, Joh. 3.21. it assures of the light of God's favor here, Psal. 36.9. & 89.15,16. by translating men into the Kingdom of light, Col. 1.12. and fits them for that everlasting light, whereof also it is a pledge, 1 Tim. 6.16. Rev. 21.23. As on the other side, sin and evil, or the evil of sin, is commonly compared to darkness; and is so usually styled, Joh. 3.19. Rom. 13.12. Eph. 4.8. 1 Thess. 5.4,5. 1 Joh. 1.6. & 2.11. because it darkens the mind, Eph. 4.13. it affects darkness, Eph. 5.11,12. 1 Thess. 5.7. it is such as cannot endure the light of God's word, Joh. 3.19,20. Eph. 5.13. it is the service of Satan, the Prince of darkness, Eph. 6.12. Col. 1.12. and makes men like unto him, Joh. 6.70. 1 Joh. 3.10. it makes men liable to the gloominess of God's wrath, and clouds his countenance toward them here: and if persisted in, will bring unto utter and eternal darkness hereafter, Matth. 8.12. & 22.13. & 25.30.

*{bitter for sweet, &c.*} God's word, and God's ways, are of themselves sweet and comfortable: and such is his favor following all those that are guided by the one, and walk in the other, Psal. 4.6,7. & 19.10. & 34.8. & 37.7,8. & 119.103. Prov. 3.17. and on the other side sin, and sinful courses, though they may seem pleasant for the present, yet have no true, or sound delight in them: they produce bitter fruits, and will prove bitter in the end, Prov. 5.3,4. & 9.17,18. & 14.13. & 23.32. Jer. 2.19. Act. 8.23. Gal. 5.19,21. Eph. 4.31. and yet is man's corrupt heart over-apt to conceive, that there is no sweetness, or desirableness at all in the former: no sweetness, or desirableness at all, but in the latter, Job 20.12,13. & 21.14,15.

**V. 21.** *{Woe unto them that are wise in their own eyes*} The fifth woe, denounced against those that are puffed up with self-conceit: and a vain opinion of their own wisdom. This most of our interpreters understand, of such an opinion and esteem of themselves, that men commonly are possessed of, in regard of their own knowledge, that they think scorn to be advised and taught by others, and refuse therefore, to hear aught that God's ministers speak to them, as being fitter to teach them, than to be taught by them. And true it is, that such self-conceit, is a great hindrance to proficiency in any knowledge; either human, or divine. Neither can wine, or other liquor, enter into a blown bladder, until the wind be voided, and the bladder quit of it. And the apostle therefore says, that *the man that thinks himself wise, must become a fool, that he may be wise*, 1 Cor. 3.19. and Solomon, that *there is more hope of a fool, than of him that is wise in his own conceit*, Prov. 26.12. But I suppose, that the vice, or crime, that the prophet here aims at, is the vain confidence that many of those times, had in their own wisdom, by means whereof, not a few, great statesmen especially, imagined, that they could devise and contrive such ways and courses, as should be able wholly to avert those evils & judgments, as were either threatened, or expected; and so to secure well enough, both the state, and themselves; that which made them not to regard at all, any the speeches of God's prophets, see chap. 30.1,3. & 31.1,3. and by help whereof, others of them made account, that they should be able to secure themselves at least, and to procure their own indemnity, howsoever matters should go, and whatsoever should befall the state; that which made them also set light by whatsoever was denounced, as being furnished, with armor of proof beforehand, against all that might come; and sure to shift well enough for themselves, however it might fare with others. See chap. 28.15. & 29.14,16. Such kind of self-confidence is that, which Solomon opposes to *trusting with the whole heart in God*, Prov. 3.5.

*{in their own eyes*} That is, in their own opinion, conceit, judgment: or, as the apostle speaks, *with themselves*, Rom. 12.16. So Prov. 3.7. & 12.15. & 16.2. and 21.30. & 26.5,16. & 28.11. & 30.12.

*{and prudent*} Some would distinguish this from the former; referring *wise*, to matters concerning God: *prudent*, to things concerning the world. But the words are in Scripture used promiscuously: and the same thing seems (as with this our prophet is very frequent) in divers words repeated; implying, that none of their prudence, or policy, wisdom, or understanding, term it what, or how they pleased, should be able to prevail against God, or to secure them from his wrath, Prov. 21.30.

*{prudent*} Heb. *understanding*. So Jer. 4.22. where such are opposed to *fools*, or *sottish* ones. The term coming from it, is used, Prov. 3.5. where Solomon admonishes his son, *not to lean upon*, or trust unto, *his own understanding*.

*{in their own sight*} Heb. *before their own face*. The same in effect with that before, *in their own eyes*. Because what stands, or lies before a man's face, is in his sight, or in his eyes. So, *before the eyes of God*, Ps. 18.24. and *before the face of God*, La. 3.35. are one and the same.

**V. 22.** *{Woe unto them that are mighty to drink wine*} The sixth woe is thundered out against those that gloried in their ability to take in much liquor, and go away with it. This some think to be the same, in substance, with what was before dealt with, ver. 11,12. Supposing this chapter to be made up of parcels collected out of several sermons of this prophet; and so repeating the same things, as they were found in those several sermons oft delivered. And so indeed our Savior on several occasions at several times, taught sometime the same thing; as Matth. 5.29,38. compared with Matth. 18.8,9. Matth. 7.16,18. with Matth. 12.23. Matth. 10.33,39. with Matt. 16.24,25. as also, that the apostles out of their former Epistles sometime repeat some things, 1 Cor. 5.9. Phil. 3.1. But little probability is there, that this chapter should be so pieced out, and not be an entire discourse and context, framed out of the sum and substance, at least, of one particular prophecy. Others, though they deny not this to be the same with the former: yet they suppose that the same vice, or crime, might well be more than once reproved, and dealt with in one and the same sermon; as some things are more than once inculcated, sometime in the same Epistle. 1 Cor. 1.10,12. & 3.1,4. & 11.18. Phil. 2.1,2. & 4.2. Phil. 3.1. & 4.4. And that indeed is not unusual in the writings both of the prophets and apostles; howbeit there seems here some difference between the former passage and this. That which some suppose to consist in the persons dealt with; the nobles and courtiers being principally aimed at there; the commanders, soldiers, and men of arms, here: and it is not unlikely, by some terms here used, but that they are specially glanced at among others. But I conceive, that the courses and vices mentioned, and darted at, in either passage, are distinct. There was taxed their sensuality; and their unseasonable immoderacy in mirth, music, drinking, and all manner of delights: here the extreme vanity and vileness of those that gloried in this, as matter of much honor and valor, that they were able to take and pour in more liquor, than many others could do. A practice, that many, who live as loosely and as luxuriously as any, yet cannot, or do not, or desire not to do; much less are ordinarily faulty in. Of which we may well say with the apostle, that the *glory* of such is their *shame*, Phil. 3.19. it being rather the commendation of a tun, than of a man, (for a beast will scarce abide it) to be able to take in and contain much liquor.

*{and men of strength*} It is not unlikely, that in this expression, the prophet indeed to touch their military men. For such in Scripture are commonly so styled, by the term here used, *men of arms*, and *armies*; or *of might and valor*, (for the word imports either) Judg. 3.29. 1 Sam. 9.1. and 31.12. 2 Sam. 24.9. It is therefore, as if he had said of them, They are styled men of *valor*: and they are valorous, but at board, not in field; not to fight, but to drink. For that is it, only wherein they desire to show their valor.

*{to mingle*} So indeed the word here used, primarily, signifies, Psalm 102.11. where the afflicted person complains, that he *mingled his drink with his tears*. Now because it was usual in those parts to *mingle*, and *temper* their wine, when they drank, ordinarily, with water, thereby to allay the heat and strength of it; hence came it to pass, that the word, which properly signifies to *mingle*, or *temper*, is both in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, used for to *prepare, pour out, serve, reach*, or *pour in* wine, or other liquor. So Prov. 9.2. wisdom is said not to have *mingled* (for her wine is not mingled stuff, like that, chap. 1.22. but pure, and sincere, as her *milk*, 1 Pet. 2.2. (but to have *prepared*, that is, drawn out of the vessel, poured out into cups, and made ready to be served out) *her wine*. And hence, those that served and attended at feasts, are said to *mingle*, that is, to serve out wine to the guests, and that then, when they served it to them without any mixture of aught. Yea, hence *mixture* is used for *wine* in general, either mixed, or unmixed. So God is said to have in his hand *a cup full of mixture*, that is, *a cup full of wine*, Psalm 76.8. of which it is said more fully, and expressly, Rev. 14.10. that it is the *unmixed*, or pure *wine of wrath mingled*, that is, poured in to be served out, *in the cup of his anger*. And the drunkard is said, Prov. 23.30. *to seek for mixture*, that is, for *wine*, or full cups of it: not *mingled wine*, as it is amiss rendered; it is not such that they seek after. And here therefore it would be rendered, not *to mingle*, but *to pour in*, or *pour down*. Nor will it help, for the salving the translation, to say, that it may be they used to mingle their wine, or drink, with some drugs, or spices, as we sometime do, to improve thereby the heat and strength of it, and so make it the more heady; for this could not be that, but the taking of it in rather, wherein they should show their strength; That had been matter of art, and skill rather, than of might and valor, as they esteemed it.

*{strong drink*} Some render it *drunkenness*, and expound it of making others drunk by tempering, and tendering of wine and strong drink to them, until they make them drunk: as God is said to have *mingled*, that is, poured out upon, or into the Egyptians, *a perverseness of spirit*, that made them stagger like a man in drink, chap. 19.14. Nor is it improbable, but that such as the prophet here speaks of, were forward and frequent enough in such practices, and accounted it no small glory to be able to lay so many men under the board: as too many among us, do, Hab. 2.15. But the word here used, is nowhere taken for *drunkenness*, (there is another word for that, though of the same stock with this, Ezek. 23.19. & 39.19.) but always for *strong drink*. See v. 11.

**V. 23.** *{Which justify the wicked for reward*} Or, Woe also be to them, *which justify, &c.* This is to be supplied, because this is a new crime, and distinct from the former, as well in regard of the matter of it, as of the persons also ordinarily therein offending. For the former reached the generality: men of all sorts and states: and if it touched any more specially, it was their military men: whereas the present concerns those, only, that are in place of judicature: howsoever some of them also might be in the former kind faulty: but this has more specially relation to them, as in such place and office. And the crime for which a woe is denounced against them, is their iniquity and perverse judgment, together with the root of it, their covetousness. That for filthy lucre, being by wicked men bribed, they would not stick to acquit the guilty, and condemn the guiltless: both which are pronounced to be most abominable in God's sight, Prov. 17.15.

*{which justify*} To *justify*, is not to *pardon*, as some would expound it in the doctrine of the gospel: for the word is never found so used, either in the Hebrew, or Greek writers, sacred, or profane, nor in our common speech; nor as it is a law term, does it ever signify *to make just*: save as we use to say, *you make me a knave*, or *a thief*, when some charge us with that which may seem to infer, or imply, as much of us: and when John says of some, that they *make God a liar*, 1 John 2.10. & 5.10. that is, they carry themselves so toward God, as if they accounted him so to be: or, as we use to say, of one, whose honesty and integrity some strive to maintain, when we deem otherwise of him, *you would make him an honest man*. But to *justify* in a legal way, does always signify to *defend* or to *deem as just* and *guiltless*; free from the offense, where the party called in question is charged; to *defend as just*: and so it is the office of *an advocate*, to *deem as just*, and consequently assoil from guilt and so it is the part of *a judge*: and it is therefore opposed sometime to *crimination*, in regard of the former; sometime to condemnation, in regard of the latter, Deut. 25.1. Matth. 12.37. Rom. 8.33,34. and so it is constantly used in cases of this kind, Exod. 23.7. 1 King. 8.32. 2 Chr. 6.23. Job 13.18. Psal. 82.3. chap. 50.8. Yea, so it is said, that *wisdom is justified of her children*, Matth. 11.19. that is, her children as advocates, plead for her, and maintain the equity of her cause and courses, against those that traduce her and them. As also in private carriages, men are said to *justify* others, when they plead for them, and avow their integrity and honesty, against those that question it, Job 27.5. & 33.32. and to justify, or stand in *justification* of themselves, when they maintain their innocency, and freeness from that which they are suspected of, or charged with, Gen. 44.16. Job 9.20. & 32.2. Luk. 16.15. Here therefore the word *justify*, signifies, as ever in matter of judicature, so far forth as it imports the act of a judge, to doom, acquit, or assoil, as guiltless, or as free from the offense charged on the party questioned. And this constant use of the word, in such cases, well weighed, would much conduce to the clearing of the doctrine of *justification* of a sinner in God's sight. Concerning which, see further, on chap. 53.11.

*{the wicked*} The *guilty*. Whom they ought to pronounce guilty, or condemn, Deut. 25.1. Where the word used, signifies properly to *guiltify*, or to *make wicked*. That is, to pass a doom, or sentence upon one, as such, Prov. 17.15. 1 King. 8.32. 2 Chr. 6.23. Now in some cases, and for some special respect, it may sometimes be lawful for those that are in authority, to spare or pardon an offender. And yet if men do it, there where God requires justice to be strictly executed, they must look, with Ahab, to pay with their own souls, for the sparing of such as he demands unto death, 1 King. 20.42. As in the case of willful murder; God will have no satisfaction to be admitted, Numb. 34.31. and the like. But for persons placed in office of judicature, for hire, or favor, not to spare, or pardon, or connive at only; but to justify, and assoil those as guiltless, whom they should sentence for guilty, is such a crime, as is not abominable only in God's eye, but most odious also with men, Prov. 17.15. and 24.24.

*{for reward*} Or, as some, *for hire of reward*, or *gift*. That is, for gifts given in way of hire: but we need not here so to force the text, when the words of themselves yield a plain and full sense, without transposition, or supply. Since the former word is oft used, simply, to signify, *for*, Gen. 22.18. & 26.5. 2 Sam. 12.6,10. Now for judges to make sale of justice, so as not to do justice, unless hired, is vile; and to take gifts from any that have causes before them, is forbidden Exod. 23.8. Deut. 16.19. But to receive hire on purpose to do injustice, is a far greater offense, Mic. 3.11. Again, to deny justice to the wronged, and to acquit the wrongdoer, is a point of much injustice, ch. 1.23. Jer. 5.18. Ezek. 22.12. But to condemn them as guilty, that are utterly guiltless and to be hired so to do, is yet a further crime of a more transcendent nature, Ezek. 22.12. and such as has a solemn curse set upon it, Deut. 27.25.

*{and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him*} That is, which for hire, or favor, or other sinister respects, (for the one of them is here mentioned, as the most common, the other also not excluded) do condemn, and pass sentence on them, as guilty; as Psal. 94.21. *They make wicked*, or condemn as guilty, *the innocent*, the guiltless; not that any man can take another man's righteousness, or innocency from him, and so make him really unrighteous; but then they are said so to do, when they pronounce them to be such; and so cause them to be deemed, and to suffer as such. That men are said to do, which they endeavor to do; and as far as in them lies, effect. Compare Levit. 24.17,21. with Deut. 19.16,21.

*{take away*} Or, *remove*: as Job of himself: *I will never remove mine integrity from me: I will hold my fast righteousness, and not let it go*, Job 27.5,6. Not meaning, that he would not give over his upright carriage (though that no question, he was also resolved on) but that he would not give over the justifying of himself: he would never condemn himself, as guilty of those things which they unjustly charged him with.

*{the righteousness*} The guiltlessness; as Psal. 7.8.

*{of the righteous*} Or, *righteous ones*. Of persons guiltless; not faulty in that whereof they were accused, whether good, or bad, otherwise. So Deut. 25.1.

*{from him*} That is, *from any of them*, or *each of them*. For the noun is plural, the pronoun singular; and implies such a common course of corrupt carriage in this kind, that they made no conscience of sparing any, whatsoever they were, whom, by any one they might be hired to condemn. See of the manner of speech, ch. 2.20. ver. 26.

**V. 24.** *{Therefore*} Hence follows a general denunciation of an utter destruction, that God would for these crimes, so rife and common among them, bring, and that suddenly, upon the main body of his people. For those things that follow, as inferred upon the former, do not refer unto the branch last before mentioned, alone, but to the whole body of the charge.

*{as the fire devoureth the stubble, and the flame consumeth the chaff; so their root shall be rottenness, and their blossom shall go up as dust*} He returns to, and alludes to the allegory of a vine, or a vineyard, which he began with at first, vers. 1. Because this vine, my people, which I had been at so much charge with, and taken so much pains about, brings forth such vile and abominable fruits, as have been before mentioned; therefore will I without further delay, proceed in judgment against it, and even suddenly consume it, Psal. 81.16.

*{as the fire*} Heb. *the tongue of fire*. The flame of fire; or fire, the flame whereof running out in length, resembles a tongue; and that like a tongue, does lick up, and consume, either liquor, or dry and light combustible matter. So 1 King. 18.38. it is said, *The fire that fell from the Lord, consumed the burnt offering, and the wood, and the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench*. The phrase is used of a thing that is suddenly done; of aught, suddenly destroyed as licked up, and without further ado, swallowed down, in an instant. So Balack of the Israelites, encamping near him in the wilderness: *This company will now lick up all round about us, as oxen lick up the grass of the field*, Numb. 22.4.

*{devoureth the chaff*} Heb. *eateth up*. So *fire that eateth up*, ch. 9.4. & 30.30. A mouth is given to the fire, as well as to the sword, ch. 1.20.

*{the stubble*} Light matter, soon consumed. An usual emblem of destruction, suddenly consummated. As dry stubble, being fired at one end of a land, does in the turning of a hand, run over the whole field, Exod. 15.7. Joel 2.5. Obad. 18. Nah. 1.10. Mal. 4.1.

*{and*} A defect of the particle, making the sentence the quicker, answerable to the matter contained in it. So chap. 3.24.

*{the flame consumeth the chaff*} Heb. *the chaff faileth*, with, or from the flame, so the verb signifies, Judg. 19.9. where the day is said *to fail* towards the evening. The particle noting the efficient, is wanting; as Psal. 17.13,14.

*{so their root shall be rottenness, &c.*} Or, as with a supply some render it. *So shall they be destroyed.* (As according to some translations, Psal. 48.7. so were they destroyed. *the root of them shall be as rottenness*; or cutting it shorter, *so the root of them shall be as rottenness*. The former note of similitude (if not the whole reddition, or second branch of the similitude) is wanting in the Hebrew, as oft elsewhere: the latter is expressed there, and ought as well to be rendered in the translation, as the other to be supplied.

*{their root*} *The root of them*; before spoken of. By *root* some understand strong ones well rooted, Job 21.7. Jer. 12.2. By *blossoms*, weak ones, easily blown away, Psal. 103.15,16. ch. 40.7. Others by *root*, the persons themselves; by *blossoms*, their issue, as if it were said, That they, and their issue, should both be destroyed, Hos. 9.16. Others, their whole might, as well inward as outward. Which precise interpretations, and applications of each term, to several set subjects, if it be deemed here requisite, and by the prophet himself intended; I should rather suppose, that by *root*, or *stem*; as ch. 11.1. were understood, strength and power; by *blossoms*, pomp and glory; as ch. 28.1. & 40.6. But the words seem only to import an utter destruction of that state, as of a plant, which so long as the root is sound, though cut and cropped, yea hewn down to the ground, yet may sprout up and shoot forth, and recover its wonted beauty again, Job 14.7,9. Dan. 4.14,15. But when the root is rotten, all perishes together with it: not the blossoms alone, though here only mentioned, as a goodly part and ornament of it; but fruit, slips, twigs, branches, and whatsoever else springs from it, and appertains to it, Job 18.16. J. 11.19. Amos 2.9. See chap. 9.14.

*{rottenness*} Or, *as rottenness*. That is, it shall molder away, as a thing that is rotten. The word was used before, ch. 3.24. in somewhat another notion, but both alluding to the nature of things putrefied: The word whereof it comes, signifies properly *to rot*, Zach. 14.12. *their flesh shall rot, while they stand upon their feet*, rot aboveground while they live) *and their eyes shall rot in their holes; and their tongues shall rot in their mouths*. The punishment, as of the enemies of God's people there; so of his people, that carried themselves as enemies to God, here.

*{and their blossoms shall go up, as dust*} Their blossoms shall never grow to, or yield any fruit; but shall also, as rotten things are wont to do, moldering to dust, fly up into the air, and being there dispersed, come to naught, Psal. 22.15. chap. 9.18.

*{because they have cast away the law of the Lord of Hosts*} This is by some interpreters, supposed to be added, as the main ground and cause of all the forementioned excesses. And indeed, where men have once shaken off that yoke, and cast off that curb, it is no marvel if they run forth into all excess of sin, Jer. 8.6. But it may as well be understood to be mentioned as an effect of them; to wit, that by these wicked and rebellious courses, they do, as it were, professedly cast off God's law, and refuse to yield any obedience unto him; and give him therefore, thereby, just cause to reject them, and to inflict the heavy judgment here denounced, upon them, as he had before threatened, Levit. 26.43.

*{cast away*} Or, *rejected with contempt*. For so the word usually signifies, Jer. 8.9. Ezek. 20.13,16,24.

*{Lord of hosts*} See ch. 1.9,24.

*{and despised the word of the holy One of Israel*} The same thing in effect for further amplification repeated; that which is very frequent with this prophet.

*{despised*} See ch. 1.4.

*{the word*} Or, *command*: as Psal. 119.67,158. and the like word, Esth. 1.15. & 2.20.

*{the holy One of Israel*} One, as most mighty, and therefore able to punish: so most holy, and one therefore that cannot endure such abominable courses, or suffer them to pass unpunished. See ch. 1.4.

**V. 25.** *{Therefore is the anger of the Lord kindled against his people*} Or, *Therefore hath the anger of the Lord been kindled against his people*. For he speaks here of judgments formerly inflicted, for these, and the like excesses; as some think, in the reigns of Joash, by the Syrians, 2 Chr. 24.23,25. and of Amaziah, by the Israelites, 2 Chr. 25.22,24. But I rather conceive them to be afflictions of latter times under Ahaz, partly, by the Israelites, and partly, by foreign nations, the Edomites, the Philistims, the Syrians, and the Assyrians themselves, whom he called in for assistance against them, 2 Chro. 28.5,8,17,20. See ch. 1.7,9. For I cannot accord with them, that understand these words as spoken of evils to come, and not yet inflicted, but as sure to come, as if already inflicted, and therefore delivered in the time present and past. Which though it be usual in prophecies, as before has been observed, ch. 3.1. Yet the course of the context here will not bear it. He minds them of judgment lately past, and yet fresh in memory; partly, to show what God can further do, contrary to their impious conceits, and scoffing speeches of him, vers. 19. and partly, to intimate their extreme obstinacy in evil being not at all amended by those heavy afflictions, that already had befallen them; as the words following imply.

*{the anger*} Heb. *face*; because anger appears in the face, or the countenance, Psal. 34.16. Or *nose*; because anger expresses itself, in some creatures, more especially, in their nostrils, Psal. 18.8. So ch. 13.9. & 30.30.

*{is kindled*} *Hath been incensed*: or, *hath waxed hot*. Because anger heats, so Numb. 11.33. Hos. 8.5. See on chap. 1.31.

*{against his people*} Whom he had most cause to be angry with, having carried themselves so to him, who had done so much for them, ch. 1.3. Amos 3.2.

*{and he hath stretched out his hand against them*} He has not only been angry with them: but proceeded to manifest his anger, by the dismal effects of it. He speaks of God, after the manner of men, who having conceived displeasure inwardly, discover it first in their looks, gesture, and speech: and when that will not serve to affect, and move those with whom they are offended, to use means of pacification; are wont then to proceed to blows, and stripes, Prov. 29.19. & 26.3.

*{stretched out his hand*} The *hand* is said to be *stretched out*, sometime to help, assist, or relieve, Psal. 136.12. Prov. 31.20. Sometime to hurt and smite, Psal. 55.20. & 138.7. ch. 31.3. Jer. 6.12. Sometime for, and sometime against one. That *hand* therefore, that is, that power and providence, which had formerly been stretched out; that is exercised, and employed in their behalf, against their enemies, for their good; had, of latter times, been turned against them, and employed contrarily for their evil. See Judg. 2.15. As he had threatened it should be, when they should rebel against him, Levit. 26.21,24,28.

*{and hath smitten them*} As men in anger are wont to do, ch. 57.17. Jer. 30.14. See ch. 1.5.

*{and the hills did tremble*} The stroke was so terrible, the judgment so dreadful, that the very senseless creatures, the hills themselves might seem to be sensible of it, Psal. 68.8. ch. 64.1,2. Jer. 4.24. Joel 2.10. Though his people (which manifests their stupidity, and extreme obstinacy) were not, ver. 12. ch. 42.24,25.

*{and their carcasses were torn in the midst of the streets*} Implying, both the multitude of such as were slain, and the hideous, and ghastly sight of the dead corpses, which either for want of people to bury them, or for fear of the enemy, not suffering them to be interred, lay unburied in the streets, Psal. 79.3. Jer. 8.2. Of the havoc of men, made under Achas, in Judea, see 2 Chr. 28.6. where it is said, that by Pekah, *one hundred and twenty thousand were slain in one day*.

*{their carcasses*} Heb. *carcass*, taken collectively; as Psal. 79.2. Jer. 7.33.

*{were torn in the midst of the streets*} Heb. as some, *were cut off*; deriving it from a word that signifies *to cut off*, or *cut down*. Used Psal. 80.16. and ch. 33.12. and so taken, it would be rendered, Being *cut off lay in the streets*. Of which kind of phrase, or form of speech, see ch. 1.4. & 14.12. and 38.14,17. Or as others, *were as dust* or, *dung in the streets*; supposing it to be of the same notion with another very like it, that signifies such *dirt*, or other filth, that from the pavement is wont to be scraped, or swept away. See Lam. 3.45. which I conceive to be the genuine sense of the word, having the the note of similitude prefixed to it, in this place. See Psalm 83.10. Jer. 9.21. & 16.4.

*{in the midst of the streets*} That is, *in the streets*; ver. 8.

*{for all this his anger is not turned away*} Albeit the Lord has so grievously smitten, and plagued his people, that his wrath may seem to have been satisfied; yet he is not as yet pacified, nor turned from his fierce anger, but has further judgments to inflict on them. So he threatened before, that when they offended, if they would not be reclaimed; and amended, by less and lighter judgments, further, and fiercer than the former should follow, Levit. 26.21,24,28. The same is repeated again, and again, ch. 9.12,17,21. & 10.4.

*{for all this*} Heb. *in*, or, *with*, as ch. 7.20. or, *for*, as Gen. 18.28. Which some would refer, not so much to the judgment here denounced, as to the sins before recited, ver. 24.

*{but*} Heb. *and*. The copulative, for the adversative; as ver. 5.

*{his hand is stretched out still*} To smite still, and further: as before, So Josh. 8.18,26.

**V. 26.** *{And he will lift up, &c.*} Heb. *For he will lift up, &c.* as ch. 9.12. The copulative particle, in a declarative notion. For he proceeds now to relate, more particularly, what further judgments should be inflicted upon them, (because they had not profited by the former) by other foreign people, breaking in upon them, and wasting their land, far more than the former had done.

*{lift up an ensign*} The use of an *ensign* in times of war, is either to call people together to come in, that they may be listed, and their names entered for service; or to admonish those that be so listed, to be in a readiness to march: or to fit themselves, where they are, in the field, for fight, and to fall upon the adverse party. Unto the first of these, the prophet seems to have respect in this place; when he says, God will, as some great commander, set up his standard, to call those together, whom he intends to employ in this service against his people; thereby intimating, that he will by a secret work of his, cause them to come together, levy forces, and undertake this service, as if by some potent prince, that had erected his signal for that purpose, under whose power they lived, and at whose command they were, they had been enjoined so to do. See further, chap. 11.12. & 13.2. & 18.3.

*{to the nation*} Or, *for the nations*. Some would have it read, *to*, or, *for a nation*. Supposing, that by a slip of the pen, a letter might be added to this word, from the beginning of the next; because the words following, run in the singular number. But hereof there is no necessity, as shall be afterward showed. Of what *nation*, or *nations*, this is spoken, interpreters differ. Some expound it of the Assyrians under Senacherib, in the time of Hezekiah, that wasted most of Judea, and straitened, but took not Jerusalem. Some, of the Chaldeans under Nebuchadnezzar, in the reign of Zedekiah, who both wasted the land, and sacked the city, and fired the Temple, which yet after some space of time, were in less than an hundred years restored, and raised up again. Others, of the Romans, under Titus Vespasian, who so ruined the Jewish state, that it could never be restored; so razed the Temple, that it could never be re-edified, for sixteen hundred years, and upward, unto this day. These nations, as the principal, together with those of other nations, that were assistant to, as sundry were, and served under each of them. Of these three, few hold with the last; and it is indeed the least probable of the three: most go with the second. I incline rather to the first: because, as notable, so near at hand; and it is not likely, would be overslipped: and when it came, was such, as would meet with those to the purpose: and mar all their mirth, that gave themselves wholly to jollity: and supposing it would never be, wished it, in mockery, once come, ver. 11,12,19. Besides that, the like things are spoken, to what here ensues, concerning the desolation that should, by the Assyrian invasion, be effected, ch. 7.17,25.

*{from far off*} Not *lift up*; or *set up an ensign afar off*: as some: though the word be so used, Exod. 20.21. where it is said. *The people stood afar off*; but *to*, or, *for nations*, that are *afar off*; or, shall come *from far off*: as ch. 43.6. *Bring my sons from far*: and *these shall come from far*, 49.12. This had God threatened before, Deut. 28.49. and would now make good by the Assyrians, that were remote from them, and their confederates, as after by the Chaldeans, of whom the same is said, Hab. 1.8. The less favor to be looked for from people, so unacquainted with; and whose language not understanding, the less able they should be to apply themselves unto, and to sue them for mercy, Deut. 28.49. ch. 28.11. Jer. 5.15. and the less hope of release, or return, for those that should be carried away captive by them, ch. 22.18.

*{and will hiss unto them*} Or, *will whistle to them*. For the word, though it be well rendered, *to hiss*, when it has a notion of contempt; as 1 King. 9.8. Lam. 2.15,16. Yet where it implies a mean of calling to any for access, it would rather, be rendered *to whistle*. So here, and so chap. 7.18. Zach. 10.8. And it seems to allude to the manner of those, that whistle to those that are out of sight in the house; and uncertain where, or how far off, or that being, though in sight, yet further off, than that their voice can well reach unto. Or, rather, and more especially, unto the usual manner of shepherds, that with their whistle, are wont to call their sheep together, when they straggle further than they should, or is safe for them. That which our Savior alludes to, Joh. 10.4,5. God will not once set up his *ensign*, for those near at hand, within the sight of it; but he will *whistle* also to those that are more remote, wheresoever; and his bare *whistle* will be sufficient to bring them together. For the word implies a readiness in those that are whistled unto, to come at the call of him that whistles.

*{unto them*} Heb. *unto him*, or, *unto it*, in the singular number; and so after, *he*, or *it shall come, &c.* as if he had spoken but of one nation before. The pronoun therefore is to be taken, either distributively *it*, or *him*, that is, each of *them*: as ver. 23. Or collectively, as *carcass*, for *carcasses*, ver. 25. but withal implying, that they should meet together, and come along, not as a rude, confused multitude, Act. 19.32. but as united together, or making up one main body, under one commander in chief; as Joel 2.7,8,11.

*{from the end of the earth*} That is, from the utmost places, known to the most of them, in those parts: as *the whole world*; for the whole world commonly known; and that was under the Roman jurisdiction, who had, at that time, command of the greatest part thereof, Luk. 2.1. and *every nation under heaven*: to wit, with whom the Jews had ordinary commerce: or among whom they had proselytes, Act. 2.5. Or from places so remote, that they might be deemed to come from the world's end. So ch. 42.10. & 43.6. Jer. 10.13. & 12.12. Matth. 12.42. Or as some, (which I mislike not) *from the land's end*: as Psal. 51.3. & 72.8. that is, from those remote places, where the land is bounded, either with the sea, or other great water, river of note, large lake, and the like. See chap. 7. ver. 18.

*{and behold*} Look for it; be sure of it, as strange, and unlikely as you think it, yet it shall undoubtedly come to pass, See ch. 1.21.

*{they shall come*} They shall come as readily, as the sheep at the shepherd's whistle: nor shall any remoteness of place, hinder them from hearing of God's whistle; or any length of way, or journey to be performed by them, deter them from undertaking God's service in the present expedition, chap. 7.19.

*{with speed*} Or, with *haste*, Jer. 48.16. The particle is in both places wanting, but to be supplied, and found expressed, Eccl. 4.12. *with speed*, or *haste*: that is, speedily, quickly, hastily; sooner than you think: spoken here, in way of answer to what they had said before: *Let him make speed: Let him hasten his work*, ver. 19. what you seem so much to desire, shall be done.

*{swiftly*} Heb. *lightly*. As ch. 19.1. Jer. 4.24. Because lightness of body, is a special help to swiftness. See Deut. 28.49. Hos. 8.1.

**V. 27.** *{None shall be weary*} There shall none of them be wearied out, with the length of the journey.

*{nor stumble amongst them*} Stumble at aught in the way? (which in rough, or stony ways, oft falls out) as Psal. 91.12. ch. 63.13. Jer. 31.9. Or, one against another: (which in tumult, and haste, oft comes to pass, Jer. 48.6,12.) So Joel 2.7,8. They shall meet with no impediments, that shall hinder, or retard them in their journey: but shall march on, in an orderly manner, without let, or impediment, either from without, or from among themselves.

*{none shall slumber, or sleep*} That is, *none shall slumber, much less sleep*: Because, *to slumber*, is somewhat less than *to sleep*. So Psal. 121.4. & 132.4. Not that they should not rest and sleep, at due times, by the way: but they should not be sleepy, and slothful, Prov. 6.9. & 19.24. ch. 56.16. but lively, and watchful, and attentive to their business, Prov. 6.4. Or, as some, they shall spend as well night, as day, in besieging, and assaulting the city: as Jer. 6.5. But the prophet seems to speak here, rather of their expedition by the way: than of their employment at their work, when come, to their way's end.

*{neither shall the girdle of their loins be loosed*} That is, as some they shall not be weak; the loosing, or want of a girdle, being an argument of weakness; as the *girdle*, and *girding* with it, an emblem of strength. Psal. 18.32,39. ch. 23.10. & 45.5. Or, they shall not be fainthearted: noted by the *loosing* of the loins. Dan. 5.6. But the meaning seems rather, that they should not disarm, lay their weapons aside: but go always with their swords, girt to them, hanging at their belt, or girdle upon their thigh, Psal. 45.3. Cant. 3.8. Or always ready for journey, or action; as men that go girt, not ungirt, as men are wont to be, when they sit still in the house, or lay themselves down to rest, 1 King. 18.46. 2 King. 9.1. Prov. 31.17. Luk. 12.35.

*{nor the latchets of their shoes be broken*} That is, as some, they shall not be busy about any other work. Which I see not how the words will bear. Others therefore expound it of their success and safety in fight, that they should not sustain hurt or loss of aught, not so much as of a shoe-latchet. See Gen. 14.23. But the meaning seems rather to be, (for he speaks of them as yet in journey) that they should have nothing befall them, not so much as the breaking of a shoe-latchet, that might cause them to slacken their pace, or to stay them on the way for the mending of it. The sum of all is, that they should be hearty, lively, ready, and well appointed; and meet with no difficulties, or such common occasions, as might retard them in their way. An elegant and artificial description of a journey, or a march rather, with rare expedition, and without any notable impediments dispatched.

**V. 28.** *{Whose arrows are sharp, &c.*} He proceeds to relate with what arms they come furnished. And he begins with their *bow*, and *arrows*; because that was a principal part of their artillery in those times, Gen. 48.22. Psal. 78.9. Deut. 32.23,42. 2 Sam. 1.22.

*{arrows sharp*} Or, *sharpened*. For so the word properly signifies, Psal. 120.4. & 140.3. Prov. 25.18. *sharpened*, that is, polished, and well kept, to wound the deeper; as ch. 49.2. Jer. 51.11. So Psal. 45.5.

*{and all their bows bent*} Heb. *trodden*. As ch. 21.15. So *to tread the bow*, for, to bend it, Jer. 50.14. because they made use of the foot in the bending of the bow. They have all things continually in a readiness for fight, Psal. 7.12. & 11.2. & 37.14.

*{their horses' hoofs shall be counted as flint*} Or, *rock*; as ch. 2.10. Ezek. 3.9. For firmness, as an *hoof of brass*, or *steel*, Mic. 4.13.

*{and their wheels a whirlwind*} The *wheels* of their chariots, much used then in war, and fight, Exod. 14.7,25. Judg. 4.3. & 5.28. Ps. 20.7. & 76.6. *a whirlwind*, for swiftness. So ch. 66.15.

**V. 29.** *{Their roaring shall be like a lion*} *Like the roaring of a lion*; as Dan. 4.33. *His hairs were grown like the eagles, and his nails like the birds*. That is, like the feathers of eagles, the one; and the nails of birds, the other; for length, both of them. See ch. 13.4.

*{their roaring*} The dreadful shout, that in joining fight, or in storming places of strength they shall make, to the terror, and amazement of all that hear it, Psal. 74.4. See Jer. 25.30. For he passes now to speak of their fierceness, in fight, and assault.

*{like a lion*} Whose voice is, of any living creature, the most dreadful, Amos 3.8. To which therefore, both the wrath of a king, Prov. 19.12. and 20.2. and God's indignation also, is likened, Hos. 11.10. Joel 3.16. Amos 1.2.

*{they shall roar like young lions*} Heb. *he shall roar* (as before) *like young lions*; that is, like a company of *young lions*; or, *like some young lion*; (because *a lion* in the former branch) as *beside streams of water*. That is, *some stream of water*, Psal. 1.3. *like young lions*, which are wont to be more fierce, and to have a stronger voice, as being in the vigor of their age; and their might and fierceness nothing yet abated, or allayed. So ch. 31.4. Jer. 2.15. of the several names of *lions*, in Scripture distinguished, according to their ages, or qualities, See on Job 4.10.

*{yea, they shall roar, and lay hold of the prey*} Or, *they shall both roar, and take hold of the prey*: *and*, for *both*, as Psal. 76.6. Jer. 6.24. & 17.26. or, *they shall roar, I say, in taking the prey*, or; *when they take it*: or, *seize on it*: *and*, for *when*, as Psal. 37.23. *the steps of a man are established by the Lord, when he delighteth in his way*; As the lion is said to roar, when he wants prey: but that in a more lamentable tune, as if he prayed for it, Psal. 104.21. So is he said also to roar over his prey, when he has got it: but that is in another-gates manner, in a more terrible tone, as insulting and shouting over it, ch. 31.4. and so we may reconcile the Psalmist, and the prophet. The one affirming, that he roars when he wants prey, the other, that he roars not, to wit, in such manner till he have it, Amos 3.4. See Ezek. 22.25. and the word here used, imports such an hideous roaring, as wherewith much indignation is expressed, Prov. 20.2. and 28.15.

*{and shall carry it away*} The word here used, signifies in general, *to take, and carry away by force*: aught from those that detain it, and are unwilling to part with it. And it is therefore very frequently used for the *rescuing, recovering, saving*, and *delivering* of one from, or out of the hands of those, that are either ready to seize on him, and to mischief him: or, that having seized on him, detain him in captivity and thraldom. So Psal. 17.13. & 18.2,44. & 22.4,8. Only in this place it is used, for the violent snatching from a man, and going away with what he was quietly, and legally possessed of before. In opposition whereunto, as it is here said by Esay, of the Assyrians, that they should *lay hold of the prey, and carry it away*: so by Micah, who lived in the same time with Esay, of the Jews, by them invaded, that they should *lay hold*, (on what they desired to keep back, and save from the enemy) *but should not* be able to *deliver it*: Using the very same word there, that Esay does here, Mic. 6.14. So that the one should carry away, whatever he laid hands on: the other should not be able to secure, or withhold what he had a desire, and endeavored to keep.

*{and none shall deliver it*} Or, *because none can deliver it*. They shall seize upon, and carry away what they please, because none shall be able to make head against them, or hinder them: much less to rescue aught out of their hands. There is no meeting of a lion, when he is ranging about to seek prey: nor rescuing from him what he has once seized on; unless by some extraordinary power, and help from God: as in Sampson's case, Judg. 14.5,6. and in David's, 1 Sam. 17.34,36. alluded to by Paul, 2 Tim. 4.17. See Psal. 17.11. ch. 31.4. But these came armed with God's commission: and there was no saving therefore of aught from them, ch. 10.5,6.

*{and*} For, *because*: the copulative, for the causal; as chap. 64.5.

*{none shall deliver*} Or, *none shall be able to deliver*. For the indicative, is oft used potentially. So Ps. 50.22. Mic. 6.14.

**V. 30.** *{And in that day they shall roar against them*} Or, as the words lie in Hebrew, *they shall roar, I say, against them*; (for he repeats again, what he had formerly said, with addition of a new similitude, exceeding the former) *then*, or, *at that time*: as ch. 2.20.

*{they shall roar*} They shall make a most hideous noise. It is the latter word used, v. 29.

*{against them*} Heb. *he shall roar against him*. That is, the Assyrian army, against the Jewish people: against whom all the foregoing menaces were denounced.

*{like the roaring of the sea*} With such an hideous noise, as the waves, and waters of the sea, make; where having borne down, or surrounded its banks, with much violence and fury, it breaks in upon the land, and carries all away before it. For to such inundations are hostile invasions oft compared in Scripture, Psalm 93.3,4. chapter 8.7,8. and 17.12,13. and 59.19. Jer. 50.44. and 51.42,55. Lam. 2.13.

*{and if one look, &c.*} This last passage is, by interpreters very variously rendered. Yet so, that herein they all agree, that therein is related the forlorn condition of the Jewish people, by the irruption of so powerful and prevalent an adversary, so perplexed; that turn they, and cast their eye which way soever they could, no hope of help, or relief, should appear. This is described by a metaphor of one so surprised and environed with a thick mist, or fog, on every side, that no glimpse of light, can from any part be descried. See the like concerning the state of this people, upon the Assyrian invasion, closing up the prediction thereof, as here, so there, chap. 8.21,22.

*{and if one look into the land*} Or, *when he shall look unto the land*; or, *down to the earth*, or *the ground*. Whether a man look downward, or upward. *When*, rather than *if*; as not questioning whether they will so do: but making no doubt, but that they will so do; *And*, for, *when*, as before, and Psal. 37.23. there cited. See ch. 8.22.

*{one look*} Or, *he shall look*. To wit, the people, before implied in those words, *against him*. The singular number, but collectively taken, or *him*, for any of *them*; and it may here also be so rendered, *they*; or, as some other, *he*, that is, the enemy *shall look into the land, &c.* As if this his very look (so terrible it should be) would so damp them, that the whole country should seem overspread with such hideous darkness, as Egypt was, Exod. 10.22,23. But the former sense seems more probable, because more agreeable to that, ch. 8.21,22. Again, some read it, *we shall look*; as if the prophet spoke in his own person, including himself amongst the rest of them, as a member of the same body with the rest; as he does, ch. 1.9. & 64.6. But the points, that serve for vowels, and the analogy of the verb, in the original, will not admit it.

*{into the land*} To wit, of Judah; toward any part of it; or, down to the earth: as ch. 8.21. opposed, as there, so, as most suppose, here to the *heaven*, or, *sky*, after-mentioned.

*{behold darkness*} When men shall look any way down, either about them, or abroad, (Psal. 142.4.) they shall see nothing on every side, but darkness, overspreading the whole face of the earth; ch. 60.2.) all involved in the same miseries and calamities, with themselves. *Darkness*, for *affliction*, and *distress*, ch. 50.10. Joel 2.10. Amos 2.10. and 8.9. As on the contrary part: *light*, for *joy*, and *comfort*, Esth. 8.16. Psalm 18.28. and 97.11. and 112.4.

*{and sorrow*} Or, rather, *of sorrow*; or, *of tribulation*, *of affliction*, *of distress*. For the word properly signifies *a strait*, Job 7.11. Ps. 18.6. & 66.4. ch. 63.9. Yet some of the Jewish doctors would have it here signify the *Sun*; and the word translated aright *the light*, in the next branch (unto which they join this) the *Moon*, a name given indifferently, both to *Moon*, and *Sun*, Gen. 1.16. Psalm 136.7,9. And so the sense should be, *both Sun and Moon shall be darkened*; no glimpse of light from either. Which, though it expresses as much as the text intends; & the like manner of speech may be oft found elsewhere, ch. 24.13. Ezek. 32.7. Joel 2.10,31. and 3.15. Matthew 24.29. Rev. 6.12. Yet cannot here be received because we never find the Sun elsewhere so termed, nor does aught in the text, necessarily here require it; and other of their own, therefore, herein control them, and render the words, as we have here done. The pauses in the text here make it very difficult, for the words rendered according to their ordinary acception, run thus; *Behold darkness; straits*, (or, *distress*) *and light*; which a late learned writer therefore renders, *distress and light* are together, or, *distress with light*, distress continues even when it is light. See the next clause.

*{and the light is darkened*} Some read the words with a twofold supply out of the former branch; *And he* shall look (as before) *to the light*, upward to the heavens, from whence light comes) and behold (as above,) *it is darkened*. Others, taking into this branch the last words of the former, and repeating again the next before it; the darkness *of distress*; so soon, *as he*, (that is, the enemy) *shall enlighten all* (making of the noun, a verb) and so the sense should be, that the glory and luster of his army, so soon as it showed itself, should damp and darken all with them. Not unlike that, *he shall destroy him, with the brightness of his appearance*, 2 Thess. 2.8. Others again, *the light itself shall be affliction*; (that is, the hope itself, that they had conceived of some help and relief, shall vex them (when it *shall be darkened*, that is, be defeated, and prove helpless. These several versions and interpretations I relate, because they have authors of great note abetting them; but seem much to force and tear the text: and I adhere therefore here, rather, to our own version, as flowing most naturally from the words of the text, It is, as if he had said, when they shall look up towards heaven, as in misery men are wont to do, chap. 8.21. he shall see no more light, hope of help and relief from above, than from below.

*{in the heavens thereof*} That is, in the land of Judah, before spoken of; in the heavens, that cover that part of the earth, wherein that people dwell. The *heaven*, or *sky*, is in Scripture, as also in other profane writings, said to be *darkened* to men, when they are in such grief, or fear, that they have no joy of the light, because dark and gloomy days work much upon men's spirits, Job 24.13,17. Amos 8.9. as on the contrary, the heavenly bodies are said to give light, and to shine forth with more than ordinary brightness to men, when they have much matter of mirth and rejoicing afforded them, Psal. 112.4. chap. 30.26. because the sight of light is cheerful, Eccl. 11.7.

*{the heavens thereof*} *The heavens*. So called of a word that signifies *to drop*, Deut. 32.2. because the rain and dew drops down from thence, Deut. 33.28. and *his heavens*, there; as, *her heavens*, here. And some therefore render it, *in its distillations*, or *rains*, that is, to wit, the *light* is wont to disperse, and drop, or dart upon the earth. But the word *light*, is masculine, the pronoun here feminine. Others read it, *in the destructions thereof*, or, *its ruins*, to wit, of the land. Because the same verb, sometime signifies also *to destroy*, Hos. 10.8. the verb is but once found in this sense, twice in the former: the noun in this place alone. Which, therefore, the forementioned learned writer derives from the Ethiopic language, wherein it has a notion of *rest*, Matth. 11.28,29. & 26.45. and thus renders the text, *Behold darkness, distress*, or, *anguish with light*; (anguish continuing even when it is light, or light is looked for) *it groweth dark in its rests*; that is, they meet with darkness there, where they might promise themselves rest. But of this let others deem.

### CHAPTER 6

**Vers. 1.** *{In the year that Uzziah died*} Here begins the fourth vision, or sermon, of this our prophet, recorded in this book. Or, according to some, the second book of his prophecies, which they supposed to have been digested, according to the reigns of those four kings under whom he prophesied, ch. 1.1. So that all the three foregoing sermons, or prophecies, should be delivered in the reign of Uzziah, this only, in the beginning of Jotham's reign: the next, ch. 7,8. &c. under Ahaz: some other under Hezekiah. But of this, see more on v. 8.

*{that Uzziah*} Of this king and his acts, written by this our prophet, see ch. 1.1.

*{Uzziah died*} It is the manner of those that write histories, or some remarkable relations, to consign or date them by some special note of those times, whereat they begin their relations, or, in which the things related were done: as the year of such a king's reign, or such an one's birth or death; or some other memorable accident: as Amos, by the earthquake that fell out in this king's days, Amos 1.1. and Isaiah here by his death. Concerning which, yet there is some variety of opinions. For some would have the apparition here spoken of, to have been exhibited, and seen in Uzziah's reign, but in the last year of it, before his decease: as Amos his was, before the earthquake: otherwise, say they, why should he not rather say, *in the first year of Jotham's reign*; than, *in the year that Uzziah died*. But unto others this seems not so probable: who therefore say, that the death of Uzziah is mentioned, to fix the time of it more certainly, and to avoid all ambiguity: because of Jotham's reign, there might be a twofold reckoning: the one, from the time that he governed the kingdom, and exercised royal authority, as next heir to the crown, after that Uzziah was smitten with leprosy: and lived sequestered, as a leper, 2 Chr. 26.21. The other, from the time of Uzziah's decease: when he succeeded him in the throne, for whom before he sat on it, 2 Chr. 26.23. & 27.1.
