Nor want there those among the Jewish doctors, who suppose, that by Uzziah's death is here meant: not his natural decease, but his civil death: such as the leper's estate was esteemed, Num. 12.12. and as David accounted his, when in likelihood, under Saul, he was debarred from access to God's house, and free commerce with God's people, Psal. 31.12. and 84.2,9,10. with 1 Sam. 26.19. and Heman deemed his in some depth of affliction, Psal. 88.3. But this seems not so sound: And when the text taken properly, affords a fit sense; nor does aught appear in the context, or other places collated, that may cross it; it is not safe running out into metaphorical senses.

*{I saw also*} As if this had reference to some foregoing vision. The Hebrew is, *And I saw*; and it is true, the copulative is used sometime, for *also*; as Jer. 1.3. but it is used also, to begin a relation, without any dependence upon former discourse, or matter; as ch. 2.2. and it may well here be rendered, *then I saw*, with reference to the time of the occurrent here expressed. For so is the copulative used, Levit. 4.3. & 6.4.

*{I saw, &c.*} The present chapter consists of two parts; a relation of a most glorious apparition, v. 1,7. and a narration of a most dreadful message, that the prophet was sent to deliver unto his people, v. 8,13.

*{I saw*} I saw in a spiritual ecstasy, and a symbolical apparition, as Eze. 1.1. Joh. 12.41. Act. 10.10,11. & 22.17. 2 Cor. 12.2. Rev. 1.12. See ch. 1.1. & 2.1.

*{the Lord*} The word here used, is not *Jehovah*, (which is yet commonly so rendered) but *Adonai*, which properly so signifies, and is given unto Christ, Psal. 110.1. from which place Christ avers his deity, Matth. 22.42,45. Whence some infer, that it was the second Person, the eternal Son of God, who is here said to sit, as King, on the throne: or the Spirit, or third Person, that spoke unto the prophet; ver. 9. And it is true indeed, that the evangelist John, says of Christ that Isaiah in this vision, *beheld his glory*, Joh. 12.41. as also that the apostle Paul says, that *by the Holy Ghost Esay spake unto their fathers*. The words here enjoined him, by him that sat on the throne, v. 9. Act. 22.25. and so, questionless did he speak also, whatsoever, as from God, he delivered to his people. But to exclude the Person of the Father, from sitting on the throne in such apparitions, is not safe. The rather, for that in such apparitions wherein the Persons are distinguished, the Father is still said to sit on the throne, and the Son to be presented unto him, Dan. 7.9,13. or the Son, and the Spirit, to be *before the throne*; not *on the throne*, Rev. 4.2,3. & 5.6. & 6.16. & 1.4. & 4.5. But in this apparition, no such distinction of Persons appearing; I suppose it safest to say, that one God *Jehovah*, ver. 3,5. the only true God, Deut. 6.4. who is also called *Adonai*, or *Lord*; as the only sovereign Lord of all, Joh. 3.11. Mic. 4.13. Mal. 1.6. in three distinct Persons, as the allegations above mentioned show: and that plural term also used, v. 8. *who shall go for us?* (not unlike those, *our image*, Gen. 1.26. and *one of us*, Gen. 3.22.) seems to imply. If it be demanded, how the prophet could see God, when as it is in Scripture said, that *No man hath seen God at any time*, Jon. 1.18. 1 Joh. 4.12. and *whom no man hath either seen, or can see*, 1 Tim. 6.16. The answer is easy, that no man can see him in his essence, as he is in himself; since that he is a Spirit, Joh. 4.34. and a spirit cannot with corporal eyes be seen, Luk. 24.38,39. nor can he be seen in the infinite excellency of his majesty, Exod. 33.20. 1 Tim. 6.16. but yet in such visible modules of glory, as he is pleased to represent himself unto the view of the creature, so he may, and has oft been seen, Exod. 24.9,10,11. Amos 9.1. and in such manner Esay here saw him, in regard whereof, instead of what the prophet says of himself here, *I saw the Lord*: the evangelist says of him, *he saw his glory*, Joh. 12.41.

*{sitting upon a throne*} As a royal sovereign, 1 King. 2.12. in his Temple, (which by the words following, appears, v. 4,6.) as in his court, or palace, here upon earth. See ch. 14.13. or, as a judge on the bench, ready to execute judgment, as Dan. 7.9,11. Joel 3.12. Rev. 6.16. & 20.11,12. See ch. 3.13,14.

*{high, and lifted up*} That is exceeding high, and stately: as, *men lofty, and lifted up*, ch. 2.12. and *cedars high, and lifted up*, ch. 2.13. or, *high* in regard of the frame, and making of it: *lifted up*, or *set aloft* in regard of situation, and place, (such in some sort, as Solomon's was; stately to sight, and lofty for site, 1 King. 10.18,20. (as high, in likelihood, as the *Porch*, before Solomon's Temple, said to be *120 cubits* high, 2 Chr. 3.4. As we see with us in stately structures, the *portal*, or *gatehouse*, as we commonly term it (far higher, many times, than the main body of the whole fabric besides. See further on ver. 2. *above it*.

*{and his train filled the Temple*} He appeared, as sitting on a stately throne; so clad also in his royal robes, Psal. 93.1.

*{his train*} Or, as some render it, *the train thereof*, to wit, of his throne supposing the utmost part of that chair of state which he sat on, to be thereby meant. But we find not the word, whereby this is here expressed, to be anywhere so used. It is applied ever to apparel; and signifies the *skirts*, that is, such parts of it as hang down to the ground: or being longer, and of more worth than is fit to be trailed along upon the ground, are with persons of state borne up by others: and it is not amiss, therefore, rendered here, *his train*, or, *his skirts*. For the word here is plural: nor is it ever read otherwise, that is, the *train*, or *skirts* of his robes. As *her skirts*, Lam. 1.9. and *thy skirts*, Jer. 13.22,26. that is, the skirts of their garments.

*{filled the Temple,}* Or, *Palace*. For that the word most properly signifies, Psal. 45.8. Prov. 30.28. Dan. 4.4. & 6.18. and so it would be rendered, Psal. 11.4. There is a question moved among interpreters where the *throne* here mentioned, was situated, whether within the Temple, or without it; which I suppose, may not amiss be thus reconciled. The *Temple*, taken in a large sense, comprehends the whole fabric, consisting both of the house, which was all over covered, & the two courts also before it, which were (besides the cloisters about, & within them) uncovered; as the like, before great men's houses, are also with us. So is the word, *Temple*, taken, Jer. 7.10. & 26.10. See chap. 1.12. Secondly, it is taken sometime for the house only, 1 King. 6.9. divided into three parts; the *porch*, or *portal*; the *Palace*, and the *Oracle*, 1 King. 6.3,5. Now it seems to me, that the *throne*, or chair of state, was so situated in the *porch*, or *portal* of the Temple, (the height whereof, you had before; and which comes within the compass of that appellation) that the *train* hanging down from it, though seated far above the door of the Temple, entered into the main body of it, and filled the whole palace. Being so situated then, it stood in some sort without the Temple because, not within the palace, most strictly so termed; and yet within the Temple too, because the *porch*, or *portal*, was a part of it. This, the rather I incline to, because God is generally deemed to appear here, as sitting in, or unto judgment. Now the manner of the kings in those times, was to sit, for judicature, in the *ports*, or *gates*, (which doubtless were not without porches) either of their palaces, or of the city. See 1 King. 7.7. Jer. 26.10. & 37.13. & 38.10. Besides that, the quick coal taken from the altar, implies as much: the altar on which the fire was perpetually burning being situated in the inner court, against the front of the house, 1 King. 8.22. Ezek. 40.47. But see further, on ver. 6.

*{filled the Temple*} As, *when the cloud covered the tent of the congregation, the glory of God filled the Tabernacle*; in Moses his time, at the dedication of the Tabernacle, Exod. 40.34. and, *the cloud filled the house*, at Solomon's dedication of the Temple, in so glorious a manner, that the priest could not enter to do aught there, 1 Kings 8.10,11.

**V. 2.** *{Above it stood the Seraphims*} After the description of God's majestical session upon his throne, is related his attendance, correspondent to his state: as princes and potentates are not wont to sit in state alone; but with their nobles, and chief officers attending upon them: so has God, here, his glorious ministers attending upon him: and so Dan. 7.10.

*{Above it*} Or, as some, *About the upper part of it*: to wit, *the throne*. To clear this, some tell us, that whereas there were three rows of chambers built on either side the body of the Temple, one over another, 1 King. 5.6. the footstool, as Exod. 24.10. or lowest part of the throne, was even with the pavement of the second chamber: and the uppermost part of it, about which the seraphim attended: even with the floor of the third: above which, the rest of that shape of a man, wherein the Lord manifested himself, reached unto the roof of that row. But I guess rather, that the Lord appeared in a far more stately and lofty manner: his head and upper parts above the throne reaching from it well near to the roof of the porch: the throne he sat on, reaching from thence downward, unto the top of the doors of the Temple. By which the train of his majestical robes, filled the whole house. So that the seraphs might well stand attending him, *above the throne*, as the text expressly says, the bodily shape of human nature, wherein he appeared, so far exceeding the throne, whereon he sat. For, as for those, that render the word *above him*, they seem not to consider how incongruous a thing it is, for the servant to stand over his master, on whom he attends, see v. 1. *lifted up*. The celestial spirits stand above, near the upper part of God's throne: the faithful on earth, as attending at his footstool, chap. 66.1. Psal. 99.5.

*{stood*} Sat not, as he did: but stood attending on him: the usual posture of servants attending on their masters: of officers, on their lords, 1 Kings 1.2. & 10.12. & 17.1. 2 Kings 25.19. Prov. 22.29. as ready to go and come at command, about whatsoever they shall enjoin them, Matth. 8.9. applied to the angels, both here, and elsewhere, Dan. 7.10. Luk. 1.19. as ministering spirits, ready to be sent abroad, to execute what God pleases to enjoin, either in mercy, or in wrath, Psal. 103.20,21. ch. 37.36. Heb. 1.14.

*{the Seraphims*} Or, *Seraphs*. A counterfeit author of pretended antiquity, whom our Popish writers follow, makes these *Seraphs*, the first of those nine orders of blessed spirits, as he reckons them: and he affirms them to be seven degrees above the *Archangels*, (being, according to his account, the eighth) and never to stir out of the glorious presence of God, as standing here about his throne. So, that, as he states the rank, those *Seraphs* are the highest; and the *Angels* the lowest. True it is, that some distinction of degrees among those glorious creatures seems to be intimated by a place in Daniel, ch. 11.13. where *Michael* is said to be *one*, (as most) *the first* (as some) *of the chief Princes*. Which can hardly be understood other, than *Angels*. For, whether version we admit, a chiefity of some, in regard of others, seems to be intimated. But to set out certain several and distinct ranks of them, assign them their stations; design them their offices, and cut them out their work, is a presumptuous attempt of ignorance and arrogance, joining together, for the producing of a groundless and frivolous conceit. Nor is that less ridiculous, which some of them tell us, that *Seraphin*, and so *Cherubin*, with *n*, signifies order; but *Seraphim*, and so *Cherubim*, with *m* signifies the spirits of each order. Whereas the one is but the Chaldee, or Syrian rather, plural termination; the other, the Hebrew. But to leave them to their idle and frivolous fancies, the *Seraphim*, or *Seraphs*, rather than *Seraphims*, (as *Cherubs, Cherubim*, or *Cherubin*, rather than *Cherubims*, or *Cherubins*; and *Baals*, or *Baalim*; not *Baalims*, Jer. 2.23. because *im*, is the plural termination in the Hebrew; as is *es*, or *s*, with us in English: and the one therefore is superfluous) are glorious spirits: so termed from a word that signifies *to fire*, or *to burn*: as some think, because they are of a fiery nature, or substance; fire being the most subtle of the elements: as purer than the air, or the purest part of the air: and coming nearest therefore to the nature of spirits. Others, in regard of their *fervency* of love unto God. And others again, in regard of their *agility*: the like unto that, which appears in fire, or of their splendor and brightness, Rev. 10.1. It is said indeed, that God makes *the winds his messengers*, (as he did in fetching back his fugitive servant Jonas, Jon. 1.4.) and *the flame of fire*, or, *flaming fire, his ministers*; which the apostle by way of inversion, applying to the angels, says, *He maketh his Angels Spirits, and his ministers, a flame of fire*, Heb. 1.7. (whence some fondly gather a distinction of angels, that some of them are of an airy substance, therefore called *Spirits*: some of a fiery, therefore termed *Seraphs*:) And we read of angels appearing in the likeness of *horsemen and chariots of fire*; 2 King. 6.17. and of the *cherubs*, or some one of them, *with flaming sword*, or, *swords*; set at the entrance into Paradise, to keep man out, Gen. 3.24. and it may well be, that these did likewise (though having the shape of men, as those other of horsemen, and with those cherubs, the figure of a blade; yet) appear, as all of a flaming fire; and thereof were so termed: but of the reason of the name, here, and nowhere else given to these spiritual attendants, we have nothing more than mere conjecture. Yet because the word is the same with that, whereby those *fiery serpents*, are designed, that were sent to sting with fiery torment and inflammation, those mutinous and rebellious ones in the wilderness, Numb. 21.6. Some thence suppose, they are here so called, because to be executioners of God's fiery wrath on these obstinate and refractory wretches: against whom an heavy doom is here in the words following denounced. And we read of *an Angel*, that *had power over the fire*: and *to scorch men with fire*, Rev. 14.18. & 16.8. But of this also, as of the former. Concerning the number of them that appeared here, is some doubt also made. The most affirm them to have been two only; answerable to those two small cherubs in the Tabernacle, on the lid of the ark, Exod. 37.7,10. and to those two large ones in the Temple, that reached with their wings stretched out from wall to wall, in the Holy of Holies, 1 King. 6.27. against which some object, that the word is not dual, but plural: and howsoever that exception be but weak; for the plural is oft used, as well of two, as of more, Levit. 5.11. & 14.22. yet the assertion is uncertain; since that we find four such in an apparition, Ezek. 1.5. and myriads, yea millions of them, Psal. 68.17. Dan. 7.10. nor is it necessary, that the number of the seraphs, should here answer the number of the cherubs, either in the Tabernacle, or in the Temple, more than the like elsewhere. How many therefore there were of them, cannot certainly be determined; but hereof, see more, v. 3,4. The description of them, in what shape they appeared, here follows.

*{each one had six wings*} Heb. *six wings, six wings*, (the reduplication used by way of distribution: as *morning, morning*, for *every morning*, ch. 28.19. & 50.4.) *were to one, one*, for *each one*; as Ezek. 1.6. & 10.14,21. in which last place also, it is said, *four, four, to one*; for, *four, to each one*: as *six, six*, here. And herein these differed from the form of those two cherubs, in the inner part of the Temple, & those also that appeared in a vision to Ezekiel; that those in the Temple had but *one* pair of wings, 1 King. 6.27. those in Ezekiel *two* pair apiece, Ezek. 1.6. & 10.21. these had *three* pair, six apiece; (as those four living wights had, Rev. 4.8. one pair on their shoulders, wherewith they flew; another, as may be deemed, on either side of their breasts, which being cast upward, might cover their faces: and the third about their hips, which falling across, might cover their lower parts. For such was the use of them, described in the words next ensuing.

*{with twain he covered his face*} With one pair of them, to wit, those on either side the breast, each of them covered (not God's face, as many interpreters would have it; thence extracting mysteries of *not seeing God's face*, Exo. 33.20. as implying an inhibition, of prying curiously into God's secret counsels, and hidden mysteries, Deut. 29.29. Pr. 25.2. Act. 1.7.) but his own face, as not enduring to behold the resplendent brightness of God's glory & majesty; no more than mortal creatures are, with open eye, able to behold the sun shining forth in his full strength. Howbeit, I dare not avow, as some have done, that the angels thus are said to *cover their faces*, in God's presence: because they appear before God in their own righteousness: but that Christian men need not so to do: they may look on him with their faces uncovered: because they appear before him in the righteousness of Christ, 2 Cor. 3.18. & 5.21. For neither are Christian men, while they live here, so pure, in regard of freedom from the taint of sin: as the angels are, who never had, nor have any the least spot or speck of it: nor does that righteousness, which by imputation accrues to them from Christ, further, in this regard, avail, than to cause them to be reputed as perfectly conformable to God's law, which by virtue of their own inherent righteousness, these blessed & glorious spirits, both now are, & ever were. Nor did the apostle, in the place mentioned, intend any such matter, as to make any comparison in this kind, between Christian men and angels; but between the faithful before Christ's coming, and those since his revelation in the flesh; and that, not in regard of righteousness imputed to them; for, and from Christ: (wherein there is no difference at all between those faithful of former times; and those that now live and believe, (but in regard of the clearer manifestation of the mysteries of the gospel unto the one above the other; as elsewhere, he makes use of somewhat the like phrase in comparing the scanter light and sight of God, which the faithful attain here, with the fuller and clearer light, and sight of God and the things of God that they are to enjoy hereafter, 1 Cor. 13.12. as by the whole tenor of his discourse there, may evidently appear. But that men in Christ, and partakers of righteousness, as well imparted from him, as imputed for him, have been smitten with such a reverend dread of God's majesty, as has caused them in like manner to *cover their faces* in God's presence; as the angels here are said to do; and that upon far less glorious apparitions than this was; is apparent by the practice both of Moses, Exek. 3.6. and of Elias, 1 King. 19.13.

*{and with twain he covered his feet*} A second use which the seraphs made of another pair of their wings; to wit, the nethermost of them about the hips, rather, than as some would have it, about the feet: that as with the middlemost of them; (both being under, or within compass of their arms) they cover their faces; so with these lowermost, *their feet*: not *God's feet*, as some fondly, as of his *face*, the like before; (thereby, say they, intimating, that neither God's *face*, or his upper parts, that is, things done before the world began: nor his *feet*, or his lower parts, that is, things after the world's end, are to be curiously inquired into) but their own: where by *feet*, most understand that part of the body that is properly and usually so termed, wherewith we tread upon the ground: which being in that regard more subject to soil: much washing of feet was therefore used in those parts, Gen. 19.2. & 24.32. Judg. 19.21. 1 Sam. 25.4. Luk. 7.44. Joh. 13.10. might seem to be no unfit emblem of some defilement. But I suppose rather, with some other, that by *feet*, (as in the Hebrew tongue frequently) by a modest form of speech, are understood those secret parts, which the apostle terms *uncomely*, 1 Cor. 12.23,24. and which nature has taught many even savage people, to cover, who yet go with all, or most of the body besides, stark naked. So is the word, without question, or contradiction of any used by this our prophet; chap. 7.20. so it is by most interpreters taken, Gen. 49.10. Deut. 28.57. and Ezek. 16.25. And the Jews call *urine*, *the water of the feet*; so reading the text, 2 King. 18.27. & ch. 36.12. where Rabshakeh used (as they suppose, and it may well so be) a broader and more unseemly term. The blessed angels therefore appearing in human shape, did with one pair of their wings, the one of them crossing the other, veil and cover those parts, which, as deeming them to have some uncomeliness in them, both our first parents, and their posterity most of them, are careful to conceal and keep out of sight, Gen. 3.7. and which willfully to discover, is generally deemed a note of impudency; or shame, and misery, to have against the will discovered unto, or by others, Gen. 9.21,27. Hab. 2.15,16. See ch. 3.17. Now this they do not, in regard of any taint of sin, as of spiritual filth in them: (no more, than in regard of any guilt of sin, they are said to have hid their faces) though in that regard, our first parents sometime so did, Gen. 3.7. but as they veiled their faces, as having their eyes dazzled with the exceeding brightness of his glorious appearance; the light whereof, with open face, they could not endure so they cover their feet (take the word which way you will) as abashed, in the apprehension of their own infirmity and imperfection, in comparison of God's incomparable and incomprehensible perfections: to which purpose, some apply those passages in the book of Job, chap. 4.18. & 15.15. which yet seem rather to have reference to the fall of the apostatical spirits. But certain it is, that the nearer the creature makes his approaches to God; and in the more glorious manner God manifests himself unto him; the more apprehensive he is of his own meanness, baseness, vileness, nothingness, in regard of God's infinite greatness, ch. 40.17. See Gen. 18.27. Job 38.1. & 40.4. & 42.5,6. The like imports that, Ezek. 1.11. where the cherubs are said, with one pair of their *wings*, to have *covered their bodies*. Nor can I conceive, why the covering of the body there, or feet here, should denote their unspotted purity, as some great ones would have it.

*{and with twain he did fly*} The uppermost pair at their shoulders were made use of, for flight: not that they were then flying to and fro, or, at present in flight; but that with them they used to fly, and had them stretched out, as ready prest for that employment: like those of the cherubs, 1 King. 6.27. & Ezek. 1.11. Whereas the other two pair were clapped close to their bodies: whereby is intimated, their promptness to, and swiftness in, the execution of God's will and work, whensoever he should appoint them any service whatsoever, Psal. 10.20. Matth. 6.10. Hence it is said, that one of them *flew* unto the prophet, v. 6. and of the angel Gabriel, that he became *flying swiftly*, to Dan. 9.21.

**V. 3.** *{And one cried to another*} Their shape was before, and the use of some parts of them; to wit, their wings, now follows their present exercise; such as is said to be the constant employment of those four *wights*, that attended before the throne, Rev. 4.8.

*{one cried to another*} Heb. *this to this*: as Exod. 14.20. Psal. 75.7. not *one with another*, as singing in a consort jointly together; and yet is the word also sometime found so used. Of which, see Lam. 3.40. but *one to another*; as by course singing out the praises of him, on whom they attended; in such manner, as the men and women did, answering one another, upon the delivery of them at the Red Sea, Exod. 15.1,21. and the Levites, at the laying of the foundation of the second Temple, Ezr. 3.11. And hence some gather, that there were but two of them, See further, v. 4.

*and said, holy, holy, holy*, A threefold repetition, as some would have it, intimating the Trinity of Persons, in the Unity of the Deity as some also, that of *Jehovah, God*, and *Jehovah* again, Deut. 6.4. But there is no great likelihood of that here: and in the latter place much less. Others rather suppose, such repetition to denote the superlative eminency of God's *holiness*; as if they had said, *holy*, yea *thrice holy*; or infinitely holy: so Rev. 4.8. and we shall find the like repetition used, for more vehemency, Jer. 7.4. & 22.29. Ezek. 21.9,14,27. For that of the Jewish rabbins, concerning the three worlds, for the creation whereof, God should be pronounced thrice *holy*; *holy*, in creating the supercelestial world, the angels; *holy*, in creating the celestial world, the heavens: and *holy*, in creating the subcelestial world, the creatures all beneath the heavens: as also, that of some others, that this threefold repetition, should have reference to the threefold distribution of time, into past, present, and future; and so intimate the eternity of God's holiness, Rev. 1.4. seem both, though true, yet not at all to the mind or intention of the text.

*{is the Lord of hosts*} Or, *be the Lord of Hosts*; that is, as he is most holy in himself, and *none holy* like him, 1 Sam. 2.2. so let him be acknowledged of all creatures, to be such the sum and substance of the second petition, Matth. 6.9. *Hallowed be thy Name*; or, as some, *shall be*: as approving God's holiness, and the justness of his judgment hereafter denounced, ver. 9,11. and shortly to be executed on that obstinate people; according to that of the Psalmist, *The Lord is righteous in all his ways, and holy in all his works*, Psal. 145.17. Of the title here given to him, see ch. 1.9.

*{the whole earth is full of his glory*} Heb. *the fullness of his glory*, (as *the fullness of the earth*, Psal. 24.1.) is, shall be, or let be, *the whole earth*; or as some *this whole land*. These expound what is here spoken of the land of Judea, wherein God made his more special abode, and did in more special manner manifest his glory, and make known himself, Levit. 26.12. Psal. 76.1. and in more peculiar manner also yet, in regard of his Temple, which was filled with his glory at the first dedication of it, 1 King. 8.11. Psal. 29.9. and which should be filled with his glory, by the execution of his justice, as Num. 14.21. Others extend it to be the wide world, spoken, as in way of enunciation, that all the world, and whatsoever therein is, does manifest, and set forth God's glory: according to that of the Psalmist *How excellent is thy name in all the earth!* that is, throughout the whole world, Psal. 8.1,9. or by way of exhortation, inciting all men to take notice of it, and to acknowledge it: according to that, Psal. 99.3. *Let them praise thy great and dreadful name; for it is holy*: and, *Let the whole earth be filled with his glory*, Psal. 27.19. or, lastly, by way of prediction, as foretelling, that in succeeding ages, not that land of Jewry only: but the whole world should behold, and partake of that glory of God, which the Jews in more special manner alone then enjoyed: according to those prophecies, *All people shall see his glory*, Psal. 97.6. *And the glory of the Lord shall be revealed; and all flesh shall together see it*, chap. 40.5. The first of these seems most probable. For the phrase, see the very like, chap. 8.8.

**V. 4.** *{And the posts, &c.*} Here follows the dreadful effects, that ensued upon the crying, or loud singing of those blessed and glorious creatures, implying matter of much wrath, already conceived, and ready to be manifested, and put in execution. The Temple doors, and posts shaken; and the body of the Temple, filled with smoke.

*{the posts*} That stood on either side of the door. The word is nowhere else read in Scripture. Yet, because it differs in one point, or vowel only, from that which signifies *cubits*; some of the Jewish doctors so expound it here: hence conceiving the posts, or the transoms removed some cubits, two or three, from the place where they formerly were fixed.

*{of the door*} Heb. *of the transoms*, or, *the thresholds*; as Amos 9.1. to wit, the upper, and the lower, whereunto those posts were fastened, the upper resting on them at the top: the lower, at the bottom, bearing them up; and the doors between the posts so large, and so weighty; as Josephus informs us, that twenty men could hardly open, or shut them; being on either side, both below, and above, with great round sockets of brass, deeply entered into mortises, made proportionably in either, that they might by the help thereof, turn to and fro. In regard whereof, those *transoms*, or, *thresholds*, are here rendered *the door*; because, either put for *the door*; or because *the doors* and they are deemed to have moved here together, the one with the other. The word is sometime rendered *post*, Exod. ch. 21. ver. 6. and *posts*, Amos 9.1. but the *thresholds*, or *transoms*, and *posts*, are distinguished, Ezek. 43.8.

*{moved*} Or, *shook; or, trembled:* as chap. 7.2. & 19.1. & 24.19. & Amos 9.1. where the like is said of them, presaging such a commotion as should be in the state; chap. 24. ver. 19.

*{at the voice of him that cried*} That is, as some, at the voice of one of the angels; not crying, or singing aloud altogether: but in course, one by one, either of them in his turn. Whence also they conclude them to have been two only. But others render it, *at the voice that cried:* that is, of the voice, whether of one alone, or of all of them jointly. Howbeit the words may well be rendered, (and so I suppose they should be) *at a voice that cried:* or, *of one that cried:* as ch. 40.3. to wit, of God himself: *whose voice is said to have shaken the earth,* Heb. 12.26. See Psal. 29.2,9. & 104.7. This implies the terribleness of the voice of an angry God, making the very senseless creatures, and those of them that seem firmest, strongest, and best settled, to shake again; as with a blow given at his command, Amos 9.1. so with a noise only made here. For whether it were by a voice coming immediately from him; or upon the voice of those celestial spirits singing his praises; the power whereby this was effected, was not theirs, but his, as that power whereby Jericho was dismantled, upon the sound of the rams horns, Josh. 6.20.

*{and the house*} That is, the Temple, or, *the palace* distinguished, both from the courts without, and from the Oracle within, 1 King. 6.2,5,17. 2 Chr. 8.9.

*{was filled with smoke*} It is said, sometime, to have been *filled with a cloud,* in token of God's acceptation, Exod. 40.34. 1 King. 8.10. but here, *with smoke,* as a token of his indignation, as a *smoke* is said to have *gone out of his nostrils, when he was angry,* Psal. 18.8. See also Deut. 29.20. And hence further, some gather an argument, to prove, that the throne was situate within the house, at the upper end of it; and that this smoke came from his face there sitting. See further hereof, on v. 6.

**V. 5.** *{Then said I, woe is me, &c.*} The prophet here proceeds, to show how himself was affected with the sight of this glorious appearance, together with that terrible voice, and the dreadful effects of it. He was exceedingly amazed, abashed, and confounded in himself, in consideration of his own wants, weakness, inward remainders of corruption; and by reason thereof, unworthiness to appear in the presence of so glorious a Majesty, and unfitness to praise him, so as those blessed spirits did, Job 42.6. Psal. 50.16. and withal, (it may well be) laying to heart those sad signs of God's heavy displeasure, as Hab. 3.16. See the like dread that the faithful have been smitten with, upon the appearance either of God himself, or of messengers from him, Dan. 8.17,18. & 10.7,15,16. Luke 1.12. Heb. 12.21.

*{Then*} Heb. *And.* So ch. 5.17. or, as some, *wherefore:* as ch. 3.17. the one, as intimating the time: the other, the cause.

*{woe is me*} As, *woe to us,* Lam. 5.10. See ch. 1.4.

*{for I am undone*} Heb. *cut off.* As the word is most commonly used, so ch. 15.1. Hos. 10.7,15. I am a forlorn man, sure to perish. Others render it, *for I thought* within myself, as follows: and so the word signifies, 2 Sam. 23.5. & Psal. 50.21. But it is there in an active: here, in a passive form. Others again, and they not a few, following the old Latin, *Because I have been silent:* as if that were the thing that so much troubled the prophet, that he had been silent, and so faulty, in forbearing to reprove the sins, and excesses, as well of prince, as of people. So a word indeed near unto it signifies: whence our English, *dumb,* ch. 23.2. Amos 5.13. and this also signifies sometime, but in another form, to cease, or forbear, Jer. 14.16. Lam. 3.49. though, in this also, some take it, in the same form, Psal. 49.12,13; as reading there, *the beasts that are dumb.* Others lastly, because the word is passive, *I was silenced,* or, *brought to silence:* as they also render the word, ch. 15.1. that is, I was so astonished, that I could not speak, as Psal. 77.4. I was as one stricken stark dumb, Luk. 1.20. but the first seems to be the genuine sense, of the place, and is the usual signification of the word. So Judg. 13.23. we are undone, *we shall die.* For considering the words of God, to Moses, Exod. 33.20. *no man shall see me and live:* and by the angels cry understanding whom it was that he saw, he began to deem himself, as they themselves, near unto death.

*{because I am a man of unclean lips*} *unclean lips:* as *uncircumcised lips,* Exod. 16.12,30. For, *unclean,* and *uncircumcised,* are both joined together, ch. 52.1. opposed to a *pure,* or, *a purified lip,* Zeph. 3.9. the uncleanness of the *lip:* that is, of *tongue,* or, *language,* as Gen. 11.1,6,7,9. but for all manner of pollution, remainders whereof abide still, so long as they make abode here, in the best, Matth. 7.11. Rom. 7.17,20,24. 2 Cor. 7.1. because faultiness in this kind, is most frequent, and not without much difficulty avoided, Jam. 3.2,7,8. and, as it pollutes the whole man, Jam. 3.6. so it discovers also that pollution that lies hidden in the heart, Matth. 12.34,35,36. & 15.20. Eph. 5.29. The consideration therefore of his inward corruption, tainting the tongue, as well as other parts, and making men unfit to appear before God: who is of so pure eyes, that he cannot endure the sight of sin, Hab. 1.13. and a devouring fire ready to fasten on such fuel, Deut. 4.24. Heb. 12.29. & that of the lips especially, rendering men unmeet, to speak either to God, or from God; and withal, as some suppose, the apprehension of defects and failings, in the delivery, of God's messages, and the discharge of his ministerial duty, may justly seem to have made him cry out in this manner, as a forlorn creature. So Peter, Luk. 5.8. *Lord, depart from me for I am a sinful man.*

*{and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips*} Intimating as some think, a consciousness of some guilt, in forbearing to reprove those, whom he saw and knew to be such; and so closely rendering a reason of his former words, *woe is me, that I have been silent.* But of that before: as others, rather implying, that living among such, he had attracted some contagion and taint, from them; it being a matter of much difficulty, for men to be as fish, that live in the sea, and yet not taste of the salt; to converse with defiled ones, and yet not be defiled, Psal. 1.1. & 26.4,6. & 106.35. & 119.115.

*{dwell*} Heb. *sit:* as ch. 5.8. Ps. 26.3.

*{in the midst*} Or, *among;* as Jer. 40.5,6.

*{for mine eyes have seen the King, the Lord of hosts*} So Manoah; to his wife; *we shall die, because we have seen the Lord,* Judg. 13.23.

*{the King*} *the King of all the earth,* Psal. 47.7,8. yea, *of heaven and earth,* Psal. 103.19. that *great King,* Mal. 1.14. at, or on whose footstool, all the kings of the world sit, holding from him, Prov. 8.15. Dan. 4.21,34,35. and commanding some small piece, or pittance of it, ch. 66.1. But more specially, the King of his people, the subjects of his Kingdom; not of power and might only, but of grace, and mercy, Psal. 44.4. & 47.6. & 74.12. ch. 33.17,22.

*{have seen*} Hence, some say, alleging for it a Rabbinical tradition, that Manasses should cause Esay to be sawn in sunder, (to which they apply that, Heb. 11.37.) as guilty of blasphemy, in saying, that he had *seen the Lord of hosts.* But little heed is to be given to such Jewish relations. See of the kings, under whom he prophesied, ch. 1.1. of his sight of God, ver. 1. Of the style here given to God, ch. 1. ver. 9.

**V. 6.** *{Then flew one of the Seraphims unto me*} The course follows, that God took to quiet and pacify the troubled mind of the prophet; and as to free him from his distracting fears, so to confirm him in his ministry, and to encourage him to a further exercise of it.

*{Then*} Heb. *And.* as v. 5. or, as some, *But.* As ch. 29.13.

*{flew*} See v. 2. Dan. 9.21.

*{Seraphims*} Or, *Seraphs.* See v. 2.

*{unto me*} By God appointed so to do, whose commands they stood ready prest to put in execution, v. 2. and that by commission from him, the seraph did what he did, and in his name, appears by his speech to the prophet.

*{having a live coal in his hand*} Or, *with a live coal in his hand.* Heb. *and.* as ch. 13.5. Ezek. 9.1.

*{a live coal*} The word properly signifies a *quick coal,* or, *a coal of fire:* as it is more fully expressed, Cant. 8.6. that is, *fiery,* or *fired;* (for it is another word, and somewhat more general, that is used, Psalm 18.8,12.) Hence the *sparks,* called *the sons,* or *children of such a coal,* Job 5.7. the rather may the prophet seem to have used this term; because of the vicinity of *Seraph,* and *Resheph.* With which manner of allusions, he seems to have been much delighted. See chapter 5.7. The *quick coal* here, is a note of purification, and expiation of sin, because the nature of fire is to sever and consume dross. See chapter 1.25. Matth. 3.10.

*{in his hand*} For they had *hands under their upper wings,* Ezek. 1.8. & 8.3. & 10.2.

*{which he had taken*} Or, *took.* A defect of the relative; as Gen. 39.4. 1 King. 18.12. *had taken,* or, *took;* as Gen. 12.1.

*{with the tongs*} The word, here used, is by our translator diversely rendered. Sometime, as here, *tongs:* so Exod. 25.38. Numb. 9.4. 1 King. 7.49. 2 Chr. 4.21. Sometime *snuffers;* as Exod. 37.23. Which place yet answers to that, Exod. 25.28. It has a dual form, as our English a plural; because consisting of two branches, or joints: and may well comprehend either, to wit both *tongs,* and *snuffers.* It comes from a word, here used, that signifies *to take:* as if he had said, *He took with the taking instruments,* or *the takers.* There is another name of an instrument, used also about the lamps in the Temple, as well as the former; derived from a word that signifies to *prune, trim, cut,* or, *pare;* translated *snuffers,* 1 King. 7.50. 2 Chr. 4.22. The one might seem to have been of use for the raising of the wick, the other for the topping of it; those of either kinds, used about the lamps, were of gold, Exod. 25.38. 1 King. 7.49,50. Those employed about the altar, as these here of brass, Jer. 52.18. The seraph is here said to take one coal only with the tongs, because for a moderate, and gracious use, about the prophet: but another is said, with his bare hand, to take, and scatter of them by whole handfuls, in way of wrath, and judgment, upon the people, Ezek. 10.2,6,7.

*{from off the altar*} To wit, the brazen altar of burnt-offering, that stood in the inner court before the front of the Temple, or palace, Exod. 40.6. 1 King. 8.64. having fire continually burning upon it, Levit. 6.12,13. So that there are probabilities for conjectures on either side. See on v. 1. & 4.

**V. 7.** *{And he laid it upon my mouth*} Or, *which he laid upon my mouth:* either *and* for *which.* See ch. 4.6. or a defect of the affix, as ch. 5.29. Heb. *made it touch my mouth.* The use he made of the coal, to expiate, and purify the prophet’s lips with it.

*{and said*} Informing the prophet, what, by that act of his he meant, and intended unto him; who might, otherwise, have been thereby more dismayed, than before; mistaking, or misconstruing it, as an argument of wrath: as a thing done, not to purge, but to sear his lips. See Ps. 120.3,4.

*{Lo, this hath touched thy lips, and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged*} This touching of your lips, (not with strange fire, as Levit. 10.1. but) with fire from God's altar, (a type of that altar, that is both sanctified, and sanctifies all that is offered on it, Heb. 13.10. & 9.21,22,23. Matth. 23.19.) may assure you from God, (for in his person he speaks, who alone is able, both to purge away the soil of sin, ch. 1.15. Ezek. 36.25. and to assoil from the guilt of it, Mar. 2.7. 1 Joh. 1.7,9.) that the guilt of your sin, is all utterly removed from you, 2 Sam. 12.13. Psal. 103.12. and you also, in some further measure, sanctified and renewed, than before, Deut. 30.6. Zeph. 3.9. For that which some suppose, that the spirit of prophecy, and infallibility, was now conferred on him, which before he had not; is not certain, nor very likely. See chap. 1.1. and ver. 1.

*{taken away*} Heb. *is departed, is gone.* We are said to *depart from sin,* when we surcease the practice of it, Psal. 34.14. *sin to depart,* or be removed from us, when the guilt of it is remitted, Psal. 32.1. & 103.12. So Nathan to David, *The Lord hath taken away thy sin, thou shalt not die,* 2 Sam. 12.13.

*{purged*} Heb. *expiated.* Which is then most properly said to be done, when propitiation and atonement is obtained, Levit. 1.4. ch. 22.14. Rom. 3.25. Yet the other of purifying, may here be jointly understood.

**V. 8.** *{Also I heard the voice of the Lord saying*} *also;* Heb. *And;* as Jer. 1.3. or, *Then;* as ver. 6. After that he had thus heartened me and prepared me for such employment, as he pleased.

*{I heard the voice*} As did our first parents, but they with dread, which made them flee from it, Gen. 3.8. Esay with refreshing, which made him rather to approach it.

*{of the Lord*} Heb. *Adonai.* Him that sat on the throne, ver. 1. Not speaking to him now by a seraph, as before, but immediately from himself.

*{whom shall I send?*} To wit, on my errand to this people. Not as doubting, or deliberating, as uncertain whom to send; but implying that the errand that he should send on, required some party well accomplished. See Jer. 49.19. & 50.44.

*{and who will go for us?*} Who is willing to undertake the office? or, *who shall go for us?* Whom shall we design, and appoint unto this work? as before. Some make it the speech of God the Father, speaking unto the the Son and Holy Ghost. Certain it is, that it was the voice of the one and only true God, in three Persons distinct, (though inseparable, as well in operations towards the creatures, as in nature and essence) as consulting, among themselves: and speaking therefore, first in the singular number; to note the unity, and singularity of the Godhead, or Divine nature; then in the plural, noting the plurality of the Persons in the Godhead: not that God uses any such like consultations; as for want of perfect understanding of affairs, and events, men are enforced oft to make use of; princes, with their peers, and men one with another; but that hereby, speaking after the manner of men (See chap. 3.3.) the orderly and prudent carriage of God, who is said to do, effect, and bring all things about, *according to the counsel of his own will,* Ephes. 1.11. may thereby be designed. See the like, Gen. 1.26. and 3.22. and 11.7. 1 Kings 22.20. See also chapter 1.1.

*{For us*} A passage, both of instruction to inform him, in whose name, and for whom he should deal, 2 Cor. 4.5. & 11.2. and of confirmation, to encourage him unto, and support him in the execution of his ministry, going for, and from God; who would be sure to be with, and protect him in the faithful performance thereof, Exod. 3.12. and 4.12. Jer. 1.17,19. Matth. 28.18,20. Acts 18.10.

*{Then I said*} Heb. *And,* as before. Then being comforted, and encouraged, by the former assurance of favor confirmed and sealed to me, with so solemn a mystery, I offered myself willingly to be employed in God's work, and to go on his errand.

*{Here am I*} Heb. *behold me.* Or, *Lo I;* as Gen. 22.1. ch. 59.9. Ready prest for whatsoever it shall please you to employ me in. So 1 Sam. 3.4,6,8. Ps. 40.7,8. Mat. 21.29,30.

*{send me*} A great promptness, and forwardness, not to obey only, but to offer himself unto God's service; like the Nethins, or Nethinim, Ezra 2.43,58. And those, of whom the apostle, that they had freely of their own accord, *set themselves apart to the ministry of the Saints,* 1 Cor. 16.15. Contrary to that backwardness, and tergiversation, which upon God's call has sometime appeared in some others, Exod. 3.11. & 4.10. Jer. 1.6. See Psal. 110.3. Yet what some would hence gather, that this should be Esayes first mission, as not entered into prophetical office before, does not, necessarily, hence follow; nor is it very probable; for it is affirmed, chap. 1.1. that he prophesied under Uzziah, whereas this vision seems to have appeared after his decease; See ver. 1. Nor does this appear to be so much a general mission, as a special commission, for a particular message, or errand, that he was at this time to deliver, from God to his people. So Ezek. 8.1,2, &c. & 11.1,4.

**V. 9.** *{And he said, Go*} He is not so forward to be sent, but God is as willing to send him on his errand. So 1 King. 22.22. Though to diverse parties, and of diverse natures, and qualities; yet both to be employed in his work of wrath; by execution, the one; by denunciation, the other.

*{and tell this people*} Heb. *and thou shalt say.* Or, *do thou say to,* &c. as ch. 38.18. Act. 28.26. But here the rather so to be rendered, because he seems rather to speak by way of permission and dereliction, than by way of prediction.

*{this people*} not my people: (as unworthy to bear his name, or to be owned by him) but *this people:* as those that he now made no reckoning of, whatsoever formerly he had done. So ver. 10. ch. 29.13. Jer. 7.16,23. and so, *this fellow,* in scorn, and contempt, as one not worthy to be named, Matth. 26.61. Luk. 23.2. and *the man,* Act. 24.5.

*{Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not*} A most dreadful judgment denounced against this people, to wit, of giving them up wholly to the stubbornness and obstinacy of their own perverse hearts, and rebellious wills. As if he had said, since that you will needs willfully stop your ears against those things that you hear; that you will not conceive them, though they be never so plainly delivered unto you, never so powerfully pressed upon you, again and again, ch. 28.9,11. Zach. 7.11,12. Act. 7.37. and shut your eyes, that you may not see, nor perceive and take notice of such things as are so evidently set before you, that you cannot shun the sight of them, ch. 26.11. & 42.18,20. Since that, I say, you are thus stiffly resolved, and desperately bent, that you refuse to regard, or to be wrought upon by aught that is spoken in your hearing, or done in your sight; go on still in your obstinacy, never once thinking of return, till destruction overtake you. It is like that in the Psalm, *My people would not hear me; Israel would not obey me: Therefore gave I them up unto their own hearts lust; to walk after their own counsels,* Psalm 81.11,12. and, *go, and serve, each of you his own dungy* (or, *dunghill*) *idols,* (for so the word properly signifies, the vilest and basest of them, that are) *both now and hereafter, since you will not hearken unto me:* and be ruled by me, Ezek. 20.39. and *fulfill ye the measure of your fathers iniquity.* Go on to do, as they have done before you: you shall not want of God's messengers (*I will send you Prophets,* and *wise men,*) enough for you to murder, Matth. 23.32,34. and that in the Revelation, *Let him that is unjust, continue unjust still;* or *grow more unjust yet,* than before he was: *and let him that is filthy be filthy still;* or, *Let him be yet more filthy,* (for the words may bear either) Rev. 22.11. This I take to be the genuine meaning of the words. Howbeit, I reject not the sense that many learned and religious writers give, conceiving it to be delivered, as by concession, and prenunciation. As if the Lord had said, prophets indeed you shall not want, nor shall signs and miracles fail with you; you shall have enough to see and hear of either: but you shall receive no more fruit, or benefit by them, than as if you had never, either heard aught of the one, or seen aught of the other, Psal. 78.32. & 106.7. Joh. 12.37. God in just judgment for their former excesses, and obstinacy, denying a blessing unto the means: and either withdrawing, or withholding the efficacy of his Spirit, whereby it might have become beneficial to them, for their spiritual good, Deut. 29.2,3. Ezek. 2.5,7. & 3.7. whether way you take it, it comes much in effect to one.

*{Hear ye indeed*} Or, as some, *hear incessantly:* as others, *plainly.* Heb. *in hearing hear,* as ch. 55.2. the Greek, with whom some of the evangelists concur, read it in the future, *Hearing, you shall hear, &c.* Matth. 13.14. Act. 28.26. which Mark, also, seems to have followed, Mar. 4.12. but the future is not unusually put for the imperative; as in the precepts, Exo. 20.13,17. But according to that version, rendering both branches in the future, the former seems spoken; in way of concession; *ye shall see, ye shall hear:* the latter, in way of commination; *ye shall not understand, ye shall not perceive;* the reduplication adds much emphasis to it.

*{but understand not*} Heb. *and.* And so Mark. 4.12. as ch. 29.13. for, *understand not,* Matt. 13.14. *ye shall not understand.* See therefore also ver. 13. & 19.

*{and see ye indeed*} Heb. *in seeing see.* And so Matt. 13.14. *Seeing ye shall see.*

*{but perceive not*} As before. A heavy judgment that befell this people, as in Esays days, so in Christ's time, Matt. 13.14. and continues on them to this day, 2 Cor. 3.14,15. And it is indeed a just thing with God, when men willfully wink, and shut their eyes against the light, to strike them stark blind, as he did the Assyrians, 2 King. 6.18. the Sodomites, Gen. 19.11. and Elimas the Sorcerer, Acts 13.11. to dash out their eyes, Deut. 28.28. Psal. 69.23. Rom. 1.21,22,26,28. and 11.8,10. Howbeit, by the words of *understanding,* and, *perceiving,* is implied, that it is not a corporal, but a spiritual *deafness,* and *blindness,* that to this people, by the prophet, God here speaks of. See ch. 29.18. & 35.5. & 42.18.

**V. 10.** *{Make the heart of this people fat*} Before God directed his speech to the people: he turns it now to the prophet. Not as enjoining him to do, desire, endeavor, or intend to do that, that is here spoken: (though the words are delivered, as by way of injunction, and precept) but as foretelling him what the fruit, and issue of his preaching would be, and should be: (which yet he must not therefore forbear) not of its own nature: but by means of man's corruption, and obstinate disposition, rising against it, Rom. 7.23. and boiling again with it, as quicklime with water cast on it, Rom. 7.13. Rev. 16.9, 11. And through the just judgment of God, giving them up to themselves, and suffering his word to have such a direful effect on them, as to harden their hearts, and make them grow worse, and worse, until they attain unto that height of impenitency, that becomes irrecoverable. See ch. 28.13. & 29.10. Rom. 2.4, 5. & 11.8, 10. 2 Cor. 2.15, 16. 2 Tim. 3.13. Heb. 6.4, 6, 7.

*{make fat*} This the most, both of ours, and the Jewish doctors, read in the imperative form, expounding it of something to be done by the prophet, but no otherwise than by his preaching: alleging, some of them the like of Jeremie, Jer. 1.10. But that is somewhat of another kind: being not so much the effect of his preaching, as the matter of his prophecy: whereas this here spoken of, respects not so much the subject matter of Isaiah's sermons, as the effect, and work that his words were to have on the hearts of his hearers. A strange thing, that that word of God, whose genuine work is to clear the understanding, and enlighten the mind, Psal. 19.7, 8. & 119.99, 104, 105, 130. Prov. 6.23. should, especially, in the mouth of so powerful a prophet, become a means to make men more stupid and senseless, more brutish than before. Yet some, both of the one and the other, take the word to be of the infinitive mood, and so to make up the sense, supply a preposition, implying the ground of the former doom: for that, *the heart of this people is fatted*: or, for that, *this people have made their heart fat*. And to the same purpose, the Greek, and the Evangelists, Matth. 13.14. Act. 28.27. following the Greek, *For the heart of this people is waxed gross*: Which though retained by the penmen of Scripture, regarding more oftentimes, the sense and intent of the text, than the precise terms, where the one swerves not much from the other, and what is in the words so read, implied, is of undoubted truth: yet the context in the original, is nothing so plain in the latter version, as in the former: nor will the words, without some straining, yield it. Howbeit the Evangelist John, may seem to depart here, from either party: as well the former, as the latter: for he neither reads it, as a charge given to the prophet: nor as a fault committed and contracted by the people: but as an act of God himself, *He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their hearts*, Joh. 12.40. But neither does John cite the entire text, nor tie himself to the precise words of the place, nor observe strictly the order of them, as they lie in the text: but picks only out of them, so much as might serve to his present purpose, which in quotation of places, is sufficient. Nor is there any jar, either between the prophet's relation, and his allegation: or between the writings of the other, his coevangelists, and his. What the prophet is willed to do, God, by his just judgment, also did, c. 29.10. and what was in this kind done, they had before themselves begun, in hardening their hearts, both against the word, and works of God, ch. 5.11, 12, 18, 19, 24. And thereby justly deserved, that God should further so deal with them. So *Pharaoh first hardened himself, his own heart*, Exod. 7.13, 14, 22. & 8.15, 19, 32. & 9.9, 34, 35. and *God after hardened Pharaoh's heart*, Exod. 9.12. & 10.1, 20, 27. & 11.9, 10. and that deservedly; even unto his destruction, Exod. 14.4.

*{the heart fat*} The *heart*, not of the body; but of the soul. The *heart*, in Hebrew, being very frequently put for the *soul*, Psal. 14.1. Jer. 5.23. & 17.9. Matth. 12.35. & 15.18, 19. a heart, *fat*, or *gross*; that is, *dull*, or, *stupid*: alluding to the heart in the body, overgrown, and oppressed with fat. See Luk. 21.34. because such fatness, or grossness about the heart, seems to imply stupidity and dullness, Psal. 119.70. though that place may be deemed rather to look another way, and to intimate either a full body, or fat estate: as Deut. 32.15. Psal. 17.10, 14. & 73.4, 7. Jer. 5.28. & 32.2, 3. or, by a *fat heart*, may be understood a *heavy*, or, *ponderous heart*; as the Hebrew phrase is, for a *hard*, or, a *stiff heart*: alluding to the stiffness of suet, when it is once thoroughly cold; at what time it grows stiffer and harder, than other fat or tallow is wont to do; or, because heavy and ponderous bodies are not easily moved, or stirred: as things stiff, and hard also, are not easily wrought on. Hence a *heavy heart*, Exod. 7.14. and a *hard heart*, Ezek. 3.7. are all one: and God is said in the forementioned place, sometime to make Pharaoh's heart *heavy*, Exod. 7.13. and sometime, to make it *hard*, Exod. 7.3. the term that John uses in citing this place, Joh. 12.40. So that by fatness of heart, here may well be understood such a disposition of mind, or spirit, as makes not dull only, and unteachable; but stiff and untractable; unfit any way to be wrought upon, or to be dealt with.

*{and make their ears heavy*} *Heaviness* is sometime applied to the *heart*; and so it imports *dullness*, and *stiffness*, as was before showed, sometime to the *ear*; and then it imports *deafness*, or, *thickness of hearing*, as we speak, c. 59.1. so, *they made heavy their ear*, Zach. 7.11. By a *heavy ear*, applied to the soul, (whereof it is so oft said, *He that hath ears to hear, let him hear*, Mat. 11.15, 43. Luk. 8.8. & 14.35. Rev. 2.7, 11, 17, 29. & 3.6, 13, 22. & 13.9.) is meant such an ear, as is elsewhere termed an *ear uncircumcised*, Act. 7.51. such a one as cannot endure to hear God's word, or aught that is spiritually good, Jer. 6.10.

*{and shut their eyes*} *Close* them, as some; or *daub* them up with plaster, or other like matter. For so ch. 44.18. *he hath daubed up*, or, *daubed over their eyes, and their hearts*. Others *dim* them, or, *make them dim*. For the word here used is not elsewhere found, thus used; save in another form once, chap. 32.3. where it is expounded by *dimness*. The eyes intended, are the eyes of the mind; of which, Psal. 119.18. Act. 26.18. Eph. 1.18. The Evangelists together with the Greek, render it, *and their eyes have they closed*, Mat. 13.14. Act. 28.27. as pointing to the original of this dreadful evil, their own willful obstinacy.

*{lest should they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their hearts*} Or, a little more plainly; *that they may not see*, &c. *nor hear*, &c. *nor understand*, &c. that they may be like mere images, or statues, that have eyes, but see not, ears, but hear not, &c. Ps. 115.5, 6. & 135.16, 17. sottish, blockish, and senseless creatures, *idol-hearers*; like those *idol shepherds*, Zach. 11.17. profiting not at all, by what they either see, or hear, chap. 42.18, 19. & 44.18. Jer. 5.21. 2 Tim. 3.7.

*{with their eyes, and with their ears, and with their hearts*} Not that without these, or with any other instrument but these, men can *see, hear*, or *understand*: but the expression of them, adds a kind of emphasis, and weight to the sentence, and makes the speech the more affectionate, that men should have such organs, or instruments, and yet have no use of them, no benefit at all by them. See the like manner of speech, Gen. 45.12. Job 42.5. Ezek. 3.10.

*{and convert*} Or, *turn*. That they may not return from their wicked courses, but be hardened in them more and more, according to their own desire: *My people love to have it so*, Jer. 5.31. and it is a just thing with God, to let them have what they love; to afford them what themselves desire, Ps. 81.12.

*{and be healed*} Or, as some, *and health*; or, *healing come to them*, as if it were a noun; but none such is: or *healing come to them*; as that of *coming* being included in the verb: but the verb is active, not passive; as appears, ch. 19.22. & 57.19. Jer. 33.6. Hos. 11.3. It is, word for word, *and he heal him*; that is, taken impersonally, or indefinitely, one *heal him*: or, *he be healed*. For by the passive, yet, are such phrases oft expressed. See chap. 2.19, 28. The Evangelists, as the Greek version before them, render it, *and I should heal them*; to wit, as by pardoning their sins upon their repentance: (as Mark expressly gives it, Mar. 4.12.) so by restoring of safety and prosperity unto them, and repairing the breaches of their state: For by *healing*, is that, also, oft-times expressed, Ps. 60.2. ch. 19.22. & 57.18. Jer. 30.17. See ch. 1.6. & 3.7.

**V. 11.** *{Then said I, Lord how long?*} An abrupt and imperfect speech, as interrupted, and cut short, through excess of passion. Like that of the Psalmist, *But thou, O Lord, how long?* Ps. 6.3. and *How long, O Lord?* Psal. 13.1. How long shall this sad condition last? How long shall I, and other your prophets, preach thus, without fruit, and this people persist in this their wonted obstinacy? Jer. 4.14. and 13.27.

*{And he answered, until the cities be wasted, &c.*} God's answer to the prophet's demand, propounded by way of complaint; as much affected with this desperate condition of his people, with whom God had so long borne, that he could no longer forbear, 2 Chr. 36.16. Jer. 15.6. & 44.22. Ezek. 21.27.

*{until*} Heb. *if*. As ch. 30.17.

*{the cities*} Of Juda, ch. 1.7.

*{be wasted*} By the incursion of foreign forces. The Syrians, ch. 9.12. The Assyrians, ch. 36.1. The Babylonians, Jer. 34.1. & 52.7. Yea, though some restrain what is here spoken to Senacherib's invasion; yet some other extend it, unto the sacking of their chief city, and overthrow of their state by the Romans, under Vespasian first, and afterward by Hadrian.

*{wasted without inhabitant*} That is, *wasted*, and left *without inhabitants*: as; *burnt, without inhabitants*: that is *burnt*, and left *without* them, Jer. 2.15. and *laid waste, without inhabitants*; that is, laid waste, and left *without* them, Jer. 4.7. A defective, or comprehensive speech, wrapping up two notions, in one term; the like whereunto, see ch. 38.17, 21.

*{without inhabitant*} Because emptied of them. See ch. 3.26.

*{inhabitant*} Put collectively for *inhabitants*, as ch. 5.3. or divisively, for any one, as 1 Sam. 27.9.

*{and the houses*} As well within, as without the cities, ch. 5.9. Amos 3.15.

*{without man*} That is, either *men*, as ch. 5.3. or any *man*; as Jer. 4.25.

*{and the land be utterly desolate*} Heb. *country*, or *tilled land*, (as ch. 1.7.) *be wasted with desolation*. See such an *utter desolation* described, Jer. 4.23, 26. & Zeph. 1.2, 3. and of the phrase, see ch. 22.17, 18. Mic. 2.10. Howbeit, we are not so to conceive the words, as if the whole country should be utterly dispeopled; or the people, all, without exception, destroyed. For there is mention of a reserve, ver. 13. but that the devastation should be very general, and a great part, both of cities and houses, wholly emptied of inhabitants, many of them utterly destroyed. See Jer. 39.8, 9. and 52.13, 15.

**V. 12.** *{And the Lord have removed men far away*} Some read the words, as rendering a reason of the forementioned desolation, *For the Lord shall remove men far away*. But that needs not; because the words run well on in a clear tenor, without any such alteration. Further only declaring the principal author of this judgment; whosoever they were that should be the instruments, and executioners in it, See ch.17.17,20. & 10.5.

*{removed men*} By causing them to be carried away captive, chap. 26.15.

*{far away*} Into Assyria, and Chaldea, countries far remote from Judea, ch. 5.26.

*{and there be a great forsaking*} Or, *leaving*, Not of people, left *in the land*, but of people *leaving* it; not a voluntary, but an enforced dereliction of lands and houses; with such other commodities that men therein had enjoyed, but should then be constrained to abandon, being either driven away out of them, or carried away from them, Jer. 9.19. For it seems not so natural, to expound it of God’s forsaking them and their land ; though it be true, that the enemy could not have prevailed so against them, if God had not forsaken them, and given them up into the enemy's hand, Deut. 32.30. Jer. 12.7.

*{in the midst of the land*} That is, *in the land* : as ch.5.8.& 7.22.

**V. 13.** *{But yet in it shall be a tenth*} In this last verse, the foregoing sad prophecy is yet shut up with some matter of comfort, to wit, that notwithstanding this great and general devastation of the land, and dissipation of the state: yet all should not be utterly ruined, & rooted out: a small remnant should be reserved: and that remnant, though it should be cropped again, and again, yet should never be so cut off, or consumed, but that there should continue still, a *seed of saints*, to uphold and perpetuate the race, So he concluded his first, and second sermon, with gracious promises of mercy, and restitution, ch. 1. & 4.

*{But yet*} Heb. *And yet*: ch. 1.28. as spoken in way of mitigation of the foregoing sentence. Yet some read, *And until there be but a tenth left in it*: as in way of continuation of the former doom, and of the stint of time therein designed, But I find not the word that is here, anywhere so used: though the word that signifies until, come near it.

*{in it*} In the land, and among the people thereof, v. 12.

*{shall be a tenth*} A small number, one of ten shall be reserved: as ch. 1.9. & 10.21,22.Either remaining still *in the land*, as many of the poorer sort did, 2 King. 25.21, 22. or preserved in the captivity: and restored again to their land, after it had been long waste, ch.7.3. & 61.4. The word here used, is nowhere else found and being formed, like those proper names, Azaniah, Neh. 10, 9. Azaziah, 1 Chron. 15.21. and Azariah, 2 King. 14.21, It may not improbably be deemed to signify as those, *God's hearing, strength, and help*; so this, *God's tenth*: as a portion dedicated to him, and reserved for him: as the tenths were, Levit.27.30. And that the rather, not unfitly so termed, in regard of the holy seed wrapped up in it. See ch. 19.24. *God's third*. Howbeit we are not to conceive, that such a precise number was to be preserved, either *from captivity*, or under the captivity: to wit, just one of ten : but a certain number is put, as oft for an uncertain : So this number of ten, Gen. 31.41, Numb. 14, 22, Rev. 2, 10, And so some other numbers in this argument: as *two or three on the top; three or four on the side-boughs*, chap. 17.6. And *one of a city, and two of a family*, Jer.3.14. Some of those writers that refer and restrain this to the spoil and waste that Sennacherib made in Judea, under King Ezekiah, understand by this tenth, the city of Jerusalem, which was preserved at that time, when the whole land was overrun, ch. 36.1. & 37.35. and which may well, say they, go for the tenth part of the whole land beside. But the terms used, both, here, and in the rest of this verse: as also in other places where the same subject is handled, do seem rather to point at persons, than places, But divers of the Jewish doctors, and some of ours concurring with them, therein understand, by the tenth, here, a *decade of kings*, that should immediately succeed one another, before this waste of the land, and havoc of the inhabitants should be, For God, say they, to comfort the prophet, and alleviate his grief, concerning this sad message enjoined him to go with; and to meet with such thoughts and doubts, as he might have, as if the same were to fall out, and be executed in his days, informs him, that this doom was not to be put in execution, before the end of ten kings of Judah their successive reigns. And indeed there were just ten of them, that reigned successively in that state ; to wit Jotham, Ahaz, Ezekiah, Manasses, Amon, Josiah, Jehoahaz, Jehojakim, Jeconiah, Zedekiah ; before that heavy downfall of it, by the Chaldeans, fell out, But this seems a mere Rabbinical conceit: nor does it fit so well with the text.

*{and it shall return, and shall be eaten*} Heb. *and it shall return; and be to depasture* ; as the word is taken, Numb. 24.22. and chap. 5.5. That is, *it shall again be cropped, or eaten down*; so is the word of *returning* frequently used, Gen. 26, 18, *He returned and digged*; for, *he digged again*, Psal. 78.41. *they returned, and tempted* : for *they tempted again*: *it shall return, and be built*, for, *it shall again be built*, Dan. 9.21. And this seems to have been fulfilled, in the several renewed deportations, as gleanings of the people, by Nebuzaradan, after that, in the first surprisal of the city, Jer. 52.28,30. Or, as some, in those remains, that after the murder of Gedaliah fled into Egypt, and there perished, Jer. 41.16, 17.& 42.22.Yet some refer the words to the return of the people *from captivity*, rendering them either, *and it shall return, having been consumed*: *or when it shall return and have been consumed*; not a tenth part of those that were carried away captive to Babylon, *returning* in safety home again, And some again read them, *it shall, after its return again, be burnt up or removed*; that is, utterly abolished : understanding it as spoken of the last destruction of the Jews, and their state, by the Romans. And it is true indeed, that the word here used, signifies both these; sometime, *to burn*, sometime also *to remove* as was formerly showed, on ch.4.4. But neither does either of those senses fit well here with the context: nor does this prophecy seem to reach so low, as those times in the primary, and peculiar intendment of it. The first exposition seems the most probable. For as for that which a learned late writer has, who takes the latter word in an active notion, thus rendering the text ; *it shall return*, to wit, *from captivity*, *and shall be to burn*; that is, shall destroy and burn up its enemies; as Zach. 12, 6. Obad, 18, I propound it only, and leave it to the judgment of the learned.

*{as a Teil-tree, &c.*} Or, *howbeit, as, &c.* For the better connection of this branch, with the former; *wherein* God by the prophet declares, for the comfort of his people, that albeit there should be but as a tenth reserved, and that tenth, in a manner, tithed again ; yet should, in that small reserve, so much impeached and impaired, be such a *seed of saints*, as should keep the people in a subsistence, and not suffer them utterly to be razed out, Jer.33.25, 26.And this he illustrates by similitude, as most take it of a tree, that having cast her leaves in winter, ch.1.30. or having been browsed upon by cattle, ch.5.5. or cut and mangled, yea, lopped, and hewn down, yet retains some sap; by virtue whereof, it maintains life, and in due time sprouts forth, and springs up again, Job 14.7, 9. or, as others take it, of certain trees planted on the side of some bank, or causeway, that by the roots thereof piercing into it, help to keep up the earth, that would otherwise be crumbling, and moldering away,

*{a Teil-tree*} Or, *a Line-tree*, A tree of goodly leaves, and spreading branches, fit to make bowers of. And this, and the oak, as some suppose, are here made choice of : because the one, in regard of its fairness, the other, in regard of its firmness, might be unlikely to lose their goodly verdure, in winter ; applicable in that regard, unto the Jewish estate; yet whether the Hebrew word signify that kind of tree, is uncertain. Some render it, *an elm*, some, *a holm* ; some *a fir*, or *turpentine-tree*, so the Greek :) Our translators render it, *an oak*, ch. 1, 30, and so oft elsewhere; as also do most other translators of note. Nor conceive I any reason why it should be rendered otherwise, especially here: the teil, or line, having no affinity at all with *an oak*.

*{and an oak*} This word is likewise so rendered, chap. 2.13. Yet some of the Rabbins tell us, that it signifies *a pine*, Others of them, *a chestnut* ; which by the Arabians is termed the *king of oaks*. As a name, not unlike thereunto, is by the Greeks, and Latins given to the *walnut*. The former word, and this differ, not much in the original: in regard whereof, they are deemed to be trees of a near kind, both oaks, but of divers sorts, as of oaks there be many: for which:both the Greeks, and Latins, have distinct names, though we in English have not. And some of our more exact translators, therefore render them in Latin, both here, and elsewhere: The former, by the word *quercus*; the latter by the word, *robur*, The first word of this passage then, very variously, both translated, and understood, may thus be rendered ; *As an oak*, either of the one, or the other kind; *this oak, and that oak*, for *this, or that*, as *father, and mother*; for *father, or mother*, Exod. 21, 15. and *lion, and bear* ; for *lion, or bear*, 1 Sam. 17.34. Or, *as the oak of either kind*; as designing trees, that grow in a certain well known place: *oak, and oak*; for *oaks of this kind, and oaks of that kind*: as *ox, and ass*, for *oxen, and asses*, ch.1.3.

*{whose substance is in them, when they cast their leaves*} This sense most interpreters, as well Jews as ours, here follow. But this seems not so agreeable to the words in the original; where in the former branch, it runs thus; *which (not whose ) support (rather than substance) is in them*, *which in them*; by a redundancy, very frequent, and familiar in the Hebrew ; for, *in which*, or, *wherein*, So Gen.1.30. *which in it is life*; for, *in which*; or, *wherein is life* : and Job 3.3. *which I was born in it*, for, *on which*, or, *wherein I was born*, And I render the word rather,*support, than substance*, because, in propriety of speech, it signifies a *pillar* ; being used of the *pillar* placed on Rachel's sepulcher, Gen. 35.20, As also of that, which Absolom erected for himself, in the king's dale, 2 Sam. 18.18, put here for *support*, because *pillars*, are means of *support*, Judg. 16.26. And for the latter clause, *when they cast their leaves*; that of *their leaves*, is not in the text. Some other therefore of either;render it, *in the dejection, or depaction* : that is, as they understand it, the thrusting, or driving, and fastening down into the ground of the trees themselves, before spoken of; as if it were said, *as in these trees, when they are thrust, and driven down into the ground*: But howsoever, unto stakes and piles driven for *support* into the ground, the term here used, may not altogether unfitly be applied: yet of trees set in the ground, and planted for that purpose : it seems not so proper: nor do I suppose, that the word can be found so used of either. Others take the word, *Shallekheth*, here used, for the proper name of a place : to wit, of a gate of the temple: so called, as some, because by it, they used to cast out, or carry out the ashes, which the altar of burnt offerings yielded; together with the sweepings, and other soil of the temple; which yet seems to be no very probable conjecture; because it opened upon a principal passage to the king's palace, as appears, 1 Chron. 26.16. compared with 1 Kings 10.5. Or as others, rather so called, from the passage itself, on which it opened, so termed, in regard of the earth that was cast in, to make it up, by raising the ground that lay, formerly, too low. Nor is it needful to put into the text, as some do, *the gate*; it being sufficient to say, the trees *wherein the support, at Shallekheth* consists. For the better clearing whereof, it is to be observed; that toward the west side of the temple, there was a *causeway*, or a *terrace*, 1 Chro. 26.16. that reached from the temple unto the king's palace; and by it the king used to go up unto God's house, 2 Chr. 9.4. Now on either side of this causeway, or terrace, it is supposed, that there was a goodly row of trees, as to beautify the passage, (which made the Queen of Saba, among other things that she saw in Solomon's court, to admire it, 1 King. 10.5.) so to keep up the earth, that it might not molder away, and so the causeway come, in time, to decay. Unto these trees, therefore, are the faithful, among God's people, compared: as those, for whose sake the nation was yet kept in being, and not brought to utter ruin.

*{so the holy seed shall be the substance thereof*} The application of the former similitude. The small number of the truly godly, shall be to their land, or state, as those trees are to the causeway, whose banks they bear up; as supports, and shores to sustain it from being utterly brought to nought. See somewhat the like, Job 22.30. and according to some, Prov. 10.25.

*{so*} The note of similitude is concealed; as Proverbs 26.11.

*{the holy seed*} Not the *holy seed*, in regard of profession only, and external sanctification, being taken into league and covenant with God, as Ezr. 9.2. But the *seed* truly, and sincerely *holy*, in heart and life, answerable to what they professed, ch. 4.3. & 62.12. Heb. *a seed of holiness*; for, a *holy seed*: as a *hill of holiness*; for a *holy hill*, Psal. 15.1. a *seed of God*; for a *godly*, or *precious seed*, Mal. 2.15. those choice ones, which God reserves as seed to propagate his church, Rom. 11.15. Those that restrain this to Senacherib's invasion, do hereby understand those few godly in Jerusalem; for whose sake God then saved the city: but that seems too narrow.

*{shall be the substance*} Or, *support*; as before: or *as a support*; as a *pillar* supporting the note of similitude (as Psalm 11.1.) wanting.

*{thereof*} Either of *the land*, before spoken of, ver. 12. or of *the tenth*, mentioned in the beginning of this verse.

### CHAPTER 7

**Verse 1.** *{And it came to pass, &c.*} Here begins the fifth sermon of Isaiah recorded in this book; which he makes entrance into, by relating the occasion of it; to wit, the fear that Ahaz King of Judah was surprised with, upon tidings brought him, that the kings of Israel and Aram, were entered into a league and confederacy against him; whereupon the prophet is sent, by God, unto him, partly to stay his heart, by assuring him, both of the vain attempt, and speedy decease shortly to ensue, of those two kings that made account to divide his kingdom between them; and partly, to foretell him of what evil should befall his land, from the King of Assyria, whom he trusted too much unto: Withal interlacing, by the way, that remarkable prophecy concerning the Messiah to be born of a virgin; the only sure stay for men to rest and rely on, in all difficulties and distresses.

*{And it came to pass*} Or, *Now it came to pass*. For this discourse has no connection at all, with, or dependence upon the vision, or prophecy, next foregoing: They being of divers dates, and delivered in several kings' reigns; that of Jotham, this of Ahaz; as in the front of either is expressed. Heb. *And it was*: of which, see chap. 2.2.

*{in the days of Ahaz*} See ch. 1.1. *days*; and *Ahaz*. This is the third king, under whom Esay prophesied; who, though a most wicked king, yet had he more than one, and those also very comfortable prophecies under him; for the support of the faithful that lived in those bad times. So that Esay seemed to have been under Ahaz, as Elias under Ahab.

*{the son of Jotham the son of Uzziah king of Judah*} The Jewish doctors move a question here, Why so wicked a king should have his genealogy thus expressed? and they tell us it is in regard of the piety of his two progenitors, therein specified; to intimate, that it was not for his, but for their sakes, that the enemy could not prevail then against him. But this is one of their groundless conjectures. We know well, that it is a thing not unusual in Scripture, to genealogize, as well bad as good, Jer. 22.18. & 26.1. & 27.1. And it may well be, that the prophet mentions these, because he had under these, and these only hitherto prophesied.

*{king of Judah*} See ch. 1.1.
