*{that Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, went up, &c.*} Concerning the time of this expedition, there is some doubt made; which to remove, we are, out of the sacred story, to observe a twofold expedition of these two kings, and their forces, against Judah, under Ahaz. The former, in the very beginning of his reign: having made some attempt before to that purpose, towards the latter end of Jotham's reign, 2 King. 15.37. But that done by them severally: the Syrians by themselves, and the Israelites by themselves; and then they mightily prevailed, 2 Chro. 28.5, 8. The latter, sometime after, when having severally found such success before: they made full account, now joining their forces together, to make a full conquest of them: especially, being so low brought by their several invasion before. But in this they prevailed not, 2 King. 16.5. And this, not the other, is that which is here mentioned: and seems to have been in the third, or at the furthest, about the beginning of the fourth year of King Ahaz: for within the fourth of his reign was Pekah slain: that is, in the twentieth, from the beginning of Jotham's reign, who reigned but sixteen, 2 King. 15.30, 33.

*{Rezin*} See of him, 2 King. 15.37.

*{Syria*} Heb. *Aram*. As also it is found termed by ancient Greek writers. See Strabo, *lib.* 1. & 13. & 16. The country confining on the land of Judah, eastward, ch. 9.11. was so called, from *Aram*: one of Shem's sons, whose posterity sometime possessed it, Gen. 10.22. It was divided into divers regions. Hence *Padan Aram*, Gen. 25.20. and *Aram Naharayim*, or *Mesopotamia*, Gen. 24.10. *Aram Zobah*, Psal. 60. title, 2 Sam. 8.3. & 10.6. And to pass by others, *Aram of Damascus*: that is, whereof Damascus, was the head city, 2 Sam. 8.6. And of this Aram of Damascus, was Rezin king; of the other parts of it, how far, is uncertain. See v. 8. & ch. 9.12. *Syria* it is by some supposed so to have been called from *Shur*, mentioned, Gen. 25.18. Though some other rather think, from the famous haven town, *Tyre*, in Hebrew termed, *Tsor*, in Syriac, *Tsur*: and thence the whole country, *Suria*, and *Syria*: for they mold two countries into one, that suppose it called *Syria*, for *Assyria*: as *Spania*, sometime, for *Hispania*. See ch. 23.1.

*{Pekah, king of Israel*} King of the ten tribes, after their revolt from David's house; under Rehoboam, commonly called Israel, as distinct from Judah. See ch. 1.1. *Judah*. Of *Pekah*, see 2 King. 15.27, &c.

*{went up*} Some conceive this term here used, either because the land of Judah was a mountainous country, and so higher than that from whence they had advanced; or because Jerusalem was situate on a hill: (though it were rather on a knoll in a plain, Jer. 17.3. and environed with hills, Psal. 121.1. & 125.2.) and that therefore it is said, *thither the tribes go up*, Psal. 122.4. Though that is, but as we are said to *go up to London*, from all parts of the land; because that is our chief city. But besides that, the words of *ascending*, and *descending*, are in the Hebrew tongue, frequently used for *going forth*, or, *forward*, simply, without any reference to the situation for height, or lowness of the places, towards which men advance. Of which, see chap. 38.8. & Jer. 34.20. & 37.5. where the Chaldeans are said to *go up*, that is, *to go away*, or *depart* from Jerusalem. It is, besides this peculiar in that language, to say of kings, or commanders, that they *ascend*, or *go up*, when they go forth upon any expedition, when they go out unto war: so *Horam went up to help Lachish*, Josh. 18.33. and *Joshua with all Israel, went up to assault Hebron*, Josh. 10.36. And as here the Syrian is said to *go up*, against Judah; so is Ahab, said to *go up* against the Syrian, *Go up and prosper*, 1 King. 22.6, 12.

*{towards Jerusalem*} Or, *against Jerusalem*. The preposition is wanting; as 1 King. 3.13. Of *Jerusalem*, see ch. 1.1.

*{to war against it*} Or, *unto war with it*. Because of the war he had with it, or against it: for it is the noun, not the verb, that is here used. So Jer. 46.3.

*{but could not prevail against it*} The Lord not permitting it, but inhibiting them from so doing. Heb. *could not war*: the noun was before; the verb is here. And it is used, sometime by a trope; especially with the particle here subjoined, not barely for *to war*; but *in warring to prevail*. So Numb. 22.11. Deut. 20.19. Jer. 21.2. And so 2 King. 16.5. *They besieged Ahaz, but could not war*; that is, prevail by surprising him, or his city.

*{could not*} Heb. *he could not*. Where the Jewish doctors make a needless debate, why the prophet should speak in the singular number, when as there were two of them, *Rezin*, and *Pekah*; and the reason, in general, they give, is, because the one of them commanded in chief: (which some would have to be *Rezin*; others of them to be *Pekah*) and the other was but as adjutant, and subservient to him: but there is no need to fly unto such niceties, and uncertainties; the verb singular is used, as the other of *going up*, before, in a way not unusual, where an action wherein two have a joint hand, is by a verb singular attributed unto either. *He could not*; that is, *neither of them could*. And so 2 King. 16.5. in the plural, *they could not*; as also the Greek, and Latin, have both here.

**V. 2.** *{And it was told the house of David, saying*} Thus was the preparation of these two kings: now follows the effect, that the tidings of it, brought to Ahaz his court, had with him.

*{the house of David*} The Jewish doctors move a question, why he says not to Ahaz, but to the house of David; and they say, that he is not named, because he was a most ungodly man. David's house is named, in regard of the promises made to him, and his house, 2 Sam. 7.25. But it is enough for this manner of speech, that Ahaz, how wicked soever, was of the lineage of David; and his court, therefore, is termed *David's house*: as the throne he sat on, is termed *David's throne*: even then, when the worst kings sat in it: as well as when better, Jer. 13.13. & 22.2. and the rather, he says, *the house of David* here, as also v. 13. because, as he speaks there: so the news was brought here, not to the king alone, but to his princes also, and to other the officers of his house, So Jer. 21.12.

*{Syria is confederate with Ephraim*} The Syrians and the Israelite are entered into a league and confederacy against you.

*{Syria*} The King of Syria, and his kingdom.

*{is confederate with*} Heb. *resteth upon*; relies upon him for assistance. For men are said to *rest*, or *rely* upon those, whom they trust to, as chap. 10.20. Others render it, *is set down with him*. He has joined his camp with his: and so is the word of *resting* used, v. 19. and the particle here used, sometime signifies *with*, as Exod. 35.22. or, *is set down in his country*. For the same particle also, signifies *in*, as ch. 38.20. yet some conceive the word, which we translate, *resteth*, to be of another root, that signifies, *to lead*; and so render it, *hath led*, or *brought his army to Ephraim*. And some would have the letters transposed, to make it signify, *hath pitched his camp*. But that is not so improbable: but this is as presumptuous. Such supplies, where needless: and changes, where groundless, are not to be admitted. The sense is apparent, flowing, not unfitly, from either of the former, that they had entered into a mutual confederacy, and joined their forces together: and that Rezin having got Pekah to join with him, made no doubt now, but to make an absolute conquest of Judah.

*{Ephraim*} *Israel.* Or, the ten tribes: whereof Ephraim being a chief one, Gen. 48.29. does oft-times give the denomination to that whole state. So chap. 28.1. Hos. 12.1. Besides, that the first king that reigned over the ten tribes, after their revolt from David's house, was an Ephraimite, 1 King. 11.26. and the chief seat of that kingdom, to wit, Samaria, was situate in that tribe, 1 King. 16.24. v. 9.

*{and his heart was moved, and the hearts of his people*} Their hearts *shook*, or were *shaken*. For the word signifies such a motion, or concussion, as in lifeless bodies is caused by some overpowering force, or violence used to them. We had it before used of the *posts*, or *transoms*, of the temple, ch. 6. v. 4.

*{as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind*} Heb. *from the face of the wind*. That is, by the blast, or force of it, So Ps. 68.1, 2. & 83.13. their hearts quaked, and quivered, as we say, like an aspen leaf, within them. An elegant expression of the extremity and baseness of their fear, arguing no spirit, or courage at all in them. Though I suppose it overnice, which the Jewish doctors here observe, that therefore Achaz his trembling is compared, rather to the *trees of the wood*, than any other; because fruitless trees make more noise than such as bear fruit; rather, because those that stand in the wood, or on the waste, whether fruitful, or fruitless, are more exposed to the force of wind and storm, than such as are planted in places of some shelter. Now the ground of this their excessive fear, seems to have been, from what they had felt, and suffered before: for having been so beaten, and such havoc lately made of them, by either of these, severally invading them, they supposed it could not be avoided, but that they would make an utter conquest of them, having joined both their forces together, (See somewhat the like, 2 Kings 10.4.) and in regard hereof, they were instantly upon dispatching of messengers for aid, unto the King of Assyria; which God sends here to dissuade them from, 2 King. 16.5, 7.

**V. 3.** *{Then said the Lord unto Isaiah*} In this their consternation, God sends his prophet to Ahaz, as another, sometime, to Ahab, in the like perplexity, 1 King. 20.13. (though both very wicked men) to stay, and strengthen him and his, by giving assurance of deliverance, from what they so much feared: the subversion of their state, and surprisal of their city.

*{unto Isaiah*} For, unto me, who write this. The noun for the pronoun; as ch. 2.1. & 13.1.

*{Go forth now to meet Ahaz*} God sends the prophet to him; though he neither seek to God, nor send to the prophet; which Jehosaphat, and Hezekiah, in the like case did, 2 Chr. 20.3. ch. 37.1. Thus does he prevent, even the wicked oft-times, with mercies, beyond, not their deserts only, but their expectations and desires.

*{go forth*} Not out of your house only, but out of the city. For the place where he was to meet Ahaz, was without the city.

*{to meet Ahaz*} To him, especially, he is sent, because he was most stricken with fear, and the business most concerned him and his safety.

*{thou, and Shear-jashub thy son*} He is willed to take his son with him, not as some would have it, to be as a witness of the delivery of his message, or to add some authority thereto, as ch. 8.2. (for what could so young a child's presence in that kind do?) but, because he was to make use of him in his speech to Ahaz, as a sign to assure him of that deliverance, which from God he brought him tidings of, ver. 16. His name was given him, in a prophetical way, by God's special appointment; as was also the name of our prophet's other son, ch. 8.3. and the names of Hoshea's children, Hos. 1.4, 6, 9. It signifies, *a remnant shall return*: as foretelling a reserve of some portion of people, that should, as some, return to their own homes, after the siege of Jerusalem by Sennacherib, broken up, having fled thither for succor and safety before. Or, as others, that should return to their land again, from the Chaldean captivity: or; as others again, that in all times, even of the heaviest calamities, some should be reserved, to rise and return again to their former condition, as a seed preserved for the perpetuating of God's people, ch. 6.13. Yet some render it, *the remnant shall be converted*; shall return to the Lord, being purged and purified by their foregoing calamities; and reformed, and reclaimed from their former aberrations: and so we find it applied, ch. 10.20, 21. and was to be verified also in those gracious reserves. See ch. 6.13. They pull the text asunder, that would read it, *Jashub thy son, that is left*, (for so the Greek and Latin render it) so called, say some of them, because he was saved, when so many thousands were slain in one day, 2 Chr. 28.6. or, because he stayed with his father the prophet, when Rabshakeh his other son, (a Jewish tale) revolted to the Assyrians in discontent; and they force it no less, who would enforce it to speak, with the Chaldee, not of any natural son of the prophet; but of some of his disciples, whom he had (as Paul says of Onesimus, Philem. 10.) begotten to God by his ministry, and brought to repentance, and which continued still steadfast with him, when many other had fallen from him.

*{at the end of the conduit of the upper pool*} The place where Ahaz, at that time was, as some think, hasting unto the city, upon the news brought him of the intended invasion, while he was somewhere else abroad: as other suppose, being thereupon come out of the city, to view the places near about it, and consider what was fit to be done with them; especially such places, as afforded any great quantity of water, either to make them useful for himself; or to hinder the enemy from help or relief by them, as expecting a siege. And this is the more likely, for that we read the like course taken by Hezekiah on the like occasion, 2 Chr. 32.3, 4. ch. 22.9. Yet some think, that he was only walking there upon pleasure, being a place, though without the city, yet not far from his palace: and there, therefore, Rabshakeh made a stand, when he came to summon Hezekiah in his master's name, to surrender to him the city, chap. 36.2. 2 King. 18.17. But it is not probable, that Ahaz amidst so great fears, should have much lust to make walks out on pleasure. Yet it is somewhat observable, that God should send the prophet to encourage Ahaz, and assure him of deliverance from God, in that very place, in which he was afterward by that blasphemous wretch so railed on and reviled, and destruction, in spite of him and what he could do, threatened to the city.

*{the conduit*} The word in Hebrew, signifies a *going up*, or *ascent*; and it is used sometime for a *trench* made to receive water, 1 King. 18.32, 35. Sometime for a *watercourse*, Ezek. 31.4. And it is here taken, not for a *conduit*, (such as ours are) to receive water derived from the pool; (though some so expound it) but for that *passage*, by which the water was from the springhead conveyed unto the pool. As the word of *ascending*, is used oft for *to pass*, Numb. 19.26, 27. 1 Sam. 6.20.

*{of the pool*} The word is commonly deemed to have a notion of *blessing* in it. Whereupon our Jewish doctors take liberty here to descant upon it; and to tell us, that this *pool* was so termed, because the water that fed it, came from a blessed place. But, beside that the name is common to all *pools*, in general; though the more common opinion be, that pools are in Hebrew so termed, either because that fish multiply in them, by virtue of that primordial *blessing*, Gen. 1.22. or because they are fed and increased with the *blessings* of rain from above, (whence the various readings, by reason of the ambiguity of the word, Psal. 84.6. *the rain fills the pools*, or, *the rain of blessings*; that is, *large, and liberal showers*, Ezek. 34.26. *covereth them*) or because watery places, being ordinarily more fertile, are deemed therefore to be accompanied with a *blessing*, ch. 32.20. Judg. 1.15. (in which place, there is hence also a diverse reading, *give me a pool*: or, *give me a blessing*:) Yet others suppose them to be so called, from the depression, or lowness of the ground, where they are usually situate. The root from whence the word comes, signifying as well to *stoop low*, as *to bless*.

*{the upper pool*} A place enclosed on the south side of the city, to receive and retain of the water that issued from the fountain of Gihon, which the Chaldee, and some other, make to be the same with Siloah; in regard whereof it is, also termed, *the pool of Siloah*, Neh. 3.15. Joh. 9.8. and *the king's pool*, Neh. 2.14. and it is here called *the upper*; because it was situate beside the upper city, on the south, near the king's garden, Neh. 3.15. to distinguish it from the *lower pool*, ch. 22.9. that lay beside the lower city on the west, 2 Chr. 32.30. & 33.14. Neh. 3.16.

*{in the highway*} Heb. *in the causeway*, or *cast-way*. As ch. 11.16. & 19.22. opposed to *a way that is not cast up*, where no causeway is, Jer. 18.15. that which bears somewhat another sense, than the term of *highway*, does with us. See chap. 35.8. and 40.3.

*{of the fuller's field*} That is, that leads to it. It seems there was a causeway that reached from this pool to a field not far distant from it, where the fullers used to dress and dry their cloth, having their dwellings near adjoining to it, and making choice of that place, for that purpose, in regard of the pool affording plenty of water, which they had much use of. And this is more probable, than what some others have; that the *causeway* here mentioned, should be a causeway situate between the two pools, the upper, and the lower, reaching from the one, to the other.

**V. 4.** *{And say unto him*} Heb. *Thou shalt say*: as chap. 6.9.

*{Take heed, and be quiet*} The message that God sends the king by the prophet, the sum whereof is; that he should not be so disturbed and disquieted, as he was.

*{Take heed, and be quiet*} The Jewish doctors are somewhat curious here about the former word: which, in regard that the word that signifies *lees of wine*, (of which, see ch. 25.6.) comes from the verb here used, they will not have it rendered here, as elsewhere generally, *take heed*, but, *rest on thy lees*: according to that of Moab, Jer. 48.11. *he is settled on his lees*: that is, say they, rest content with such power as you have of your own, without seeking of aids from Assyria, or any other abroad. And it is true indeed, that in the latter term, (which some render, *be silent*: Others rather, *be quiet*, as the word is most commonly used) as much is implied, ch. 30.15. where *in quietness, and confidence*, is their safety said to consist: that is, in forbearing to seek to and fro for succors abroad, and relying on God's assistance: but there is no need here to strain the word to such a far-fetched notion, from that which it generally signifies, and does exceeding well fit the place. Nor are there wanting of ours, who, though not so straining the word, yet in the exposition of it, swerve from the intendment of the prophet, some understanding it, as an admonition given the king, to be more wary; and not to venture his person so abroad: which were rather to discourage, than to encourage him, contrary to the end that he was sent for. Others, as an advice, to set sentinels, and keep watch and ward diligently: as implying, that God, though he gave assurance of safety, yet would not have industry neglected. But that had been but to spur on a running horse. There needed no inciting of him, unto that which he was forward enough unto of himself: and in likelihood, looking after at that very time when the prophet came to him. See on v. 3. The former word has reference to the latter. And it is no more than as if he had said, take heed how you be thus unquiet, and restless. Or, see by any means, that you keep quiet: be not disturbed and distracted, but quiet your mind, and look not out for foreign helps: but rest on that aid, that God shall by your own forces assisting them, or otherwise working for you, afford you. Like Moses his speech to the Israelites, pursued by Pharaoh, Exod. 14.13. and Jahaziel's to Jehoshaphat, and his people, 2 Chr. 20.15, 17. *Take heed, and be quiet*, for, *take heed thou be quiet*, as, *take heed see my face no more*, for, *take heed thou see my face no more*, Exod. 10.28. *Take heed of him, and obey his voice*, for *take heed that thou do obey his voice*, Exod. 23.21. *Take heed, regard not iniquity*, for *take heed that thou regard not iniquity*, Job 36.21.

*{fear not, neither be faint-hearted*} The same in effect, in other terms repeated, to put the more courage into him, and the better to settle his unsettled thoughts. Heb. *Let not thine heart be tender*; be not *soft-hearted*. Softness being opposed to firmness, because soft things are ready to yield, and give in, upon the least force or touch, and to receive impression from every approaching object. See the like phrase, Deut. 20.3. Jer. 51.46. a *soft heart*, therefore, is put for such a weak, faint, tender, timorous, childish, or effeminate disposition, as has no courage, or manliness at all in it, 2 Chr. 13.8. as faith or confidence makes the heart firm, Heb. 11.27. so distrust and diffidence makes it to faint and flutter, Luk. 12.29.

*{for the two tails of these smoking firebrands*} Thus the prophet speaks in way of contempt of those two kings, and their forces, which were so formidable to this king and his people, and came on with such fury and fierceness, as if with fire and sword they were resolved to destroy all before them; and made full account so without resistance to carry it. He calls them, in derision, not *two firebrands*, which yet were not much to be feared, unless it meet in some very light matter, Zach. 12.6. but *two tails*, that is, two ends of such brands, in which fire is usually kept, and those two ends, not *flaming and burning*, as those of Sampson's between the foxes' tails, Judg. 15.4. (which yet some suppose, here alluded unto) but *smoking*, as ch. 42.3. So that though they may make some smother, yet have little fire, or force to do much hurt, in them, and are ready to go out: Psal. 118.12.

*{firebrands*} Which being taken off the hearth, retain not fire long, but after a while smoke only, and so at length go out. So Amos 4.11. Zach. 3.2. though there made use of another way. Howbeit, the Jewish doctors, whom some of ours also here follow, affirm by the word here used, to be meant, not a *firebrand*, but a *mash-staff*, or, *stock*; such as they use to stir the fire to and fro with in the oven; which when it is burnt so near to the end, that it cannot longer be held in the hand safely, or further use made of it, is thrown away, and lies smoking on the ground, till it go out. No unfit resemblance to illustrate that, that is by the prophet here intended. But the use of the word in those other places, carries it rather the former way.

*{for the fierce anger*} Heb. *in the fierce anger*: and so it is well rendered, Exod. 11.8. 1 Sam. 20.34. But so is the same particle also used, as it is here rendered, Neh. 5.3. Esth. 4.7. Psal. 150.2.

*{fierce anger*} Word for word, *heat of nose*. Because anger discovers itself in the nose, Psalm 18.8. So also ch. 13.9, 13. As if he had said, all their fierceness, and fieriness of their fury, though they fume at the nose never so much, shall prove nothing but smoke.

*{of Rezin with Syria, and of the son of Remaliah*} The *two brands' ends* before mentioned.

*{with Syria*} Heb. *and Syria*. But so elsewhere, chap. 5.14. *The taber with pipe*: and Neh. 12.42. *The singers sang with Jezrahiah their overseer*. So that, the King of Syria, *with* Syria; That is, all his Syrian forces put together, make but one brand's end.

*{the son of Remaliah*} So he calls him in contempt, rather than by his proper name, Pekah: because his father Remaliah was but an obscure private person: and his son Pekah, might the rather therefore go for the tail of a brand. See ch. 9.14.

*{Remaliah*} Heb. *Remalijahu*; as *Jeshajahu*, ch. 1.1. So constantly, ch. 8.6.

**V. 5.** *{Because Syria, Ephraim and the son of Remaliah, have taken evil counsel against thee, saying*} The words in the Hebrew run thus. *Because Syria hath consulted against thee evil: Ephraim and the son of Remaliah saying*. An elegancy of speech, not unusual in Hebrew, in this prophet especially: whereby divers acts, or attributes, are to divers subjects, as in way of distribution, severally applied: whereas they are to be jointly understood of either party: and alike appertain to either. See chap. 5.13. For we are not to conceive it thus spoken: as if the one party had propounded, or contrived, and counseled: and the other concluded, and resolved: but they laid both their heads together, and agreed both jointly upon the issue; as those Psal. 83.3, 5.

*{Syria, Ephraim, and the son of Remaliah*} God will scarce vouchsafe to give them their names.

*{Syria*} Or, the *Syrian*, in contempt; for Rezin the King of Syria. See ver. 1, 4.

*{Ephraim*} Israel, the ten tribes. See ver. 2.

*{the son of Remaliah*} For, Pekah King of Israel. See ver. 4.

*{have taken evil counsel*} Heb. *have consulted evil*: or, *an evil thing* (for the Hebrews use the feminine for the neuter) Or, *have upon consultation resolved evil*: as 2 Chr. 25.16. Jer. 49.20, 30. See verse 6, 7.

**V. 6.** *{Let us go up against Judah, and vex it*} The result of their forementioned consultation to make war jointly upon Judah.

*{go up*} Of this phrase, see on ver. 1.

*{against Judah*} That is, the kingdom of Judah, say some: the head, or head city of it, Jerusalem, say others: it may well comprehend both, and the land itself with them.

*{vex it*} That is, weary them out, and so compel them to yield up to us, both themselves, and their city. Some other render the word, *let us awake them*, or, *rouse them up*: as if they lived securely, and expected no hostile invasion; which is not so probable, having smarted so much, and that so lately also already. See on ver. 1. Or, as some others, let us make some disturbance among them, let us set them among themselves together by the ears; a ready course to make way for a foreign enemy to enter. But the translation we have is right, and confirmed by that which is objected against it. For whereas it is alleged by some, that the verb in the form here expressed is not used, but for *to awake*, that is, to stir up, and to raise out of sleep: the contrary is true, that the word where it has reference unto *sleep*, in that form, out of which, in such use, it is never read, though the form be usually active, yet has always a passive notion, and signifies; not *to awake*, or *make one to awake*, (to which purpose, another word is ordinarily used, Cant. 2.7. & 3.5. & 8.4.) but *to be awaked*, or *to awake of one's self*: as 2 King. 4.31. Psal. 3.5. & 44.23. & 73.20. and constantly elsewhere. And the sense here rendered, is further confirmed by the use of the same word in another form, with reference to those very words, ver. 16.

*{and let us make a breach therein for us*} That is, as some, *let us violently break in upon it*, or, *through it*: as the word is used, 2 Sam. 23.26. & 2 King. 3.26. and as some expound that, Amos 1.13. so it is said of the Arabians, that *they broke into Judah*, 2 Chr. 21.17. & of Jerusalem, *the city was broken up*, Jer. 39.2. Others, *let us make a breach in it*, to wit, among the people, which may *be for us*, that is, for our advantage, whereby the more readily to surprise it. Others, *let us tear it away* from the king thereof, and adjoin, or annex it to our own territories, *to ourselves*. Others, *let us cut*, or, *divide it to ourselves*; that is, having parted it in twain, (as dividing the spoil, before the field fought, or victory gotten, and making no doubt of a general conquest) let us share it between us, and take either his moiety of it. And such complexive phrases in Scripture are oft found. See on ch. 6.11. Howbeit because the same form is used, where no such partition is, to wit, 2 Chr. 32.1. where Senacherib is said to have entered into Judah, and encamped against the fenced cities thereof *to break*, or, *divide*, or, *by breaking*, or, *dividing, to win*, or, *to gain them to*, or, *for himself*: (wherein also, that complexive form of speaking is found) I suppose there is nothing more here intended, than that, by a forcible surprisal of the land and kingdom of Judah, they intended to make it theirs.

*{and set a king in the midst of it, even the son of Tabeel*} Some read this clause by way of disjunction; *or set a king in the midst of it*. Let us either part it between us, or, if we cannot accord upon the partition, let us set up such a one for a king over it, that may be under our protection, & hold it from us both. And it is not improbable; that their intent was to set up such a king, as might be in a kind of vassalage, to them both; such as the Syrian sometime challenged the King of Israel to be to him, 2 King. 20.2, 6. as also true it is, that the copulative is used oft, as a disjunctive, Gen. 2.6. Exod. 21.19. But of that there is no necessity here; because no such partition before necessarily implied.

*{in the midst of it*} In Jerusalem, the head city, or the center of it; or, *in it*, therein, simply, by a frequent Hebraism: as chap. 6.12. ver. 22.

*{set a king—even the son of Tabeel*} Heb. *let us make to reign in it as king*, or, *for king, the son of Tabeel*. So 2 King. 8.20. & 2 Chr. 21.8. *the Edomites made to reign over them a king*. Who this *son of Tabeel* should be, there is much dispute and debate. Some Syrian, say some; for *Tabeel*, say they, is a Syrian name: as *Tabrimon*, 1 King. 15.18. signifying a worshipper of the God Rimmon: 2 King. 5.18. others, some Israelite; and as some of them conjecture, Zichri the Ephraimite, that slew the king's son, and the chief about him: for the good service he then did, 2 Chr. 28.7. The Jewish rabbis, some of them by a trick of theirs, which they call *Albam*, make of *Tabeel Remala*; but whether thereby they understand *Remaliah*, or no, they tell us not. But their device is this; they write the letters of the Hebrew in two lines, the one half thus, under the other.

א ב ג ד ה ו ז ח ט י כ
ל מ נ ס ע פ צ ק ר ש ת

Then they take them, as they stand in order, the upper for the lower and the lower for the upper: and so of טבאל they make רמלא. Another crochet they have, which they call *Athbash*. Of which, see on Jer. 25.26. Others, of them, whom some of ours also accord with, would have it no proper name, but to signify such a one, as should seem *good to us*, or such a one as shall *not be good* for them. But neither will the word, with any writing, well afford such a sense; nor is it probable, but that some certain person is designed, whose parent bore that name; though, who, and what he was, be uncertain, because nowhere else named. Yet of the same name we find one, but of far later times, Ezr. 4.7. whereby it appears to have been a name not unusual.

**V. 7.** *{Thus saith the Lord God*} God's sentence follows concerning this their resolution; which they made no doubt but to bring about.

*{It shall not stand, neither shall it come to pass*} *It*, that is, this, their counsel, or resolution, enclosed in the word, *have consulted* ver. 5.

*{not stand*} Things are said, in Hebrew, *to stand*, when they take effect, Psal. 33.11. *The counsel*, or purpose *of the Lord shall stand*: or are confirmed, and established, Numb. 30.4, 7, 9. Deut. 19.15. and on the other side, *not to stand*, but *to fall to the ground*, when they take not effect, but are frustrate, Numb. 30.12. 1 Sam. 3.19.

*{neither shall it come to pass*} Heb. *nor shall it be*: chap. 8.10. And this has a further emphasis in it: for things may be produced into act, and so have an existence, and yet not be established, not continued; but this result of theirs shall never have any existence: it shall go no further than words; it shall never come into act. *Thus the Lord bringeth the counsel of nations to nought; and makes people's devices of none effect*, Psal. 33.11. thereby showing, that *there is no counsel against God*, Prov. 21.30.

**V. 8.** *{For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin*} Or, as some other, *But the head of Syria shall Damascus be; and the head of Damascus shall Rezin be*: that is, he shall continue that which he now is: *to be*, for, *to continue*: as Dan. 1.21. So the meaning should be; I have set these kingdoms their limits, Act. 17.26. and they shall not pass the bounds that I have assigned them. As Damascus shall continue still the head city of that part of Syria, 2 Sam. 8.5. 2 Chr. 28.5. so shall Rezin continue, while he lives, king of Damascus: and shall not be, as he makes account to be, king of Jerusalem: nor shall Jerusalem have any relation to Syria, but continue the mother city of Judah, still, as it is. Thus they, howbeit another reading may well be admitted, that neither, forces the text, and seems better to suit with that which ensues: nor requires any such supply as this does, to make the sentence entire. *And though*, (for so the particle is frequently used, Josh. 17.18. Psal. 23.4. ch. 12.1.) or, *For though*, (for one particle sometime includes two: see on ch. 18.5.) *Damascus be the head of Syria, and Rezin the head of Damascus. Yet* (so is the copulative oft taken, ch. 8.9, 10. & 17.6. & 49.5.) *within sixty and five years shall Ephraim be broken,—and Samaria with her head, Remaliah's son, shall likewise be broken*: as if he had said, although the house of Israel carry itself so high, relying on their confederacy with Rezin, who being king of Damascus, the head city of Syria, & by reason thereof, has the greatest part of that country at command; yet that shall not hinder, but that within the term of time here designed, the state of Israel shall be dissolved, and Remaliah's son shortly ruined. And this I suppose to be the genuine, sense of the place. See v. 9.

*{and within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people*} Concerning this prediction, and the stint of time mentioned in it, there is no small difficulty. Since that, from the time of this prophecy, about the third or fourth of Ahaz, as was formerly showed; (see on v. 1.) unto the time that the ten tribes by Salmaneser King of Assyria were removed out of their native soil, and transported into other parts of his dominions; nor had now any settled state, which was in the sixth year of Hezekiah, 2 King. 18.9, 10. cannot be above twenty-three, or twenty-four years at most: yea, there want not, that reduce them to a far narrower compass, to the space of eleven years, two of Pekah, ch. 8.4. and nine of Hoshea, 2 King. 17.6. which difference we shall not now stand to reconcile, because it concerns not this place. This knot some finding not how how to untie, fall to cut it asunder. And pretending the original copies to be corrupted, would have *six* read for *sixty*; as if the prophet had said, *within six, and five*, (that is, *eleven*) *years: shall Ephraim be broken from being a people*: and just so many, say they, are reckoned from the time of this prophecy, unto the ruin of Samaria, 2 King. 17.6. But this, because it seems overbold with the text, and introduces a strange and unusual kind of computation, we let pass. The most generally received solution, given both by Jewish doctors and Christian writers, is, that the head of this account is to be fetched, not from the time that Esay spoke these words: but from the time when this dissolution of the Israelitish state, was by the prophet Amos foretold. This they reckon two ways. Some make up their account by the reigns of the kings of Judah, Amos, say they, prophesied in the days of Uzziah; two years before the earthquake, Amos 1.1. which was in his reign, Zach. 14.5. And fell out, (as the Jewish tradition has it,) just at that time, when he pressed into the temple to burn incense, and was smitten with the leprosy, 2 Chr. 26.16, 20. This they presume to have been in the twenty and seventh of his reign, two years before which Amos began to prophesy: to wit, in his twenty and fifth. Nor do they much swerve from this way of computation, who would have the number of years reckoned from that year, or the next after it, wherein Uzziah was so smitten: because, say they, the Syrians then began (taking occasion by the king's disability) to make inroads on his land, 2 King. 15.37. Though that seem rather to have been in Jotham's reign, and, in likelihood, toward the latter end of it. But however that be; these agree with the former, in that, albeit they make Uzziah's irruption into the temple, two years sooner than they: yet both begin their computation from the same year, to wit, the twenty and fifth of Uzziah; and so cast twenty and seven years of his reign (being, in all, two and fifty, 2 King. 15.2.) into this account; unto which, if we add his son Jotham's sixteen, 2 King. 15.23. Ahaz his sixteen, 2 King. 16.2. and six of Ezekiah's, (for in the sixth of his reign was Samaria taken, and that state ruined by Salmaneser, 2 King. 18.10.) we have the just sum of *sixty and five years*. But against this computation, we have divers weighty exceptions. First, there is nothing more than uncertain tradition, to assert the truth of that terrible earthquake's coincidence, with that inconsiderate act of Uzziah. Secondly, it is not only improbable, but undoubtedly untrue, that Uzziah was smitten with leprosy, either in twenty and fifth, or in the twenty and seventh year of his reign. For his son, and successor Jotham, was twenty and five years old at his father's decease, 2 Chr. 27.1. and was consequently born in the twenty and seventh of his reign, which should be the very same year that he became a leper, according to the one; two years after that sad occurrent, according to the other. Neither of which is agreeable to truth: the sacred story informing us, that Jotham was not either unborn, or an infant, when his father was so smitten: but of those years that he was able, both to manage the private affairs of the royal family, and to sway the state. For so it is said, that his father being sequestered upon that occasion, *Jotham his son, was over the house, judging the people of the land*, 2 King. 15.5. Lastly, it is objected, that Amos his prophecy, which is made the head of this account, was as well in Jereboam's, as in Uzziah's reign, whereas the year of Uzziah, which is here fixed on, was some space of time, after Jereboam's decease. For Uzziah began to reign in Jereboam's twenty and seventh year, 2 King. 15.1. and Jeroboam reigning but forty and one, 2 King. 14.23. his last must fall in with the fourteenth of Uzziah's, some ten, or eleven short of Uzziah's twenty-fifth, the first year of their account. Others therefore to shun these difficulties, make their reckoning by the reigns of the kings of Israel, and carry up their account to the seventeenth, or eighteenth of Jeroboam. From whose reign, taking either twenty and four years: and so not regarding the reigns of Zachery, and Shallum, his next successors, that made up but seven months between them, 2 King. 15.8, 13. or twenty and three years, reckoning one year for them: and thereunto adding Menahem's ten years, 2 King. 15.17. Pekahiah's two years, 2 King. 15.23. Pekah's twenty, 2 Kings 15.27. and Hosheah's nine, 2 King. 17.6. they make the sum, without any overplus, complete. But we meet in Scripture again with that which disturbs also this course of account: for we read there, that Zachery, Jeroboam's son, began his reign in the thirty and eighth year of Uzziah, 2 King. 15.8. Now his father's last falling in with the fourteenth of Uzziah: there must of necessity be an interval of, at least two, or three and twenty years, between the decease of the father, and the short reign of the son; supposed to have fallen out by the infancy of the son, at his father's decease: neglected therefore, and not regarded, while others governed, until that coming to some maturity of years, he got the reins into his hand, but held them not long. Now these years, taken in, will make the product arise far above the sum, mentioned here in the text. Nor does it add any strength therefore, to either of these computations, to tell us, as some of prime note do, and that very confidently, though without any color or ground for it, that this number of years was formerly defined by Amos, and passing by tradition, from one to another, was common in men's mouths, and therefore mentioned thus by the prophet: nor what some other observe, that in Scripture computations are sometime made, not from the time of any matter in present discourse, but from some other forepast: and not there, or then, at all mentioned. To which purpose they produce that of Absolom, who having obtained liberty of access to court again, is said, *after forty years*, to have entered into a conspiracy, 2 Sam. 15.7. which years are not to be reckoned, either from his return from exilement, or his repair again to court, but from some other remarkable term of time, no more expressed, than this in the text. For as the former is a mere presumption, so this latter, is but a misapplication of matters incomplient; the tenor of the speech, running far diversely, in the one, and the other. *At the end of forty years*, such a thing was done says the one: and *yet sixty and five years*, and such a thing shall be done, says the other. But all these difficulties may be easily cut off, if we understand the words, as one would have them; not to intend any set stint of the standing, or fall of the state: but of the time only, at which the fall of it was foretold: for on this wise he gives us the sense of them. *Samaria shall fall, as was sixty and five years ago foretold by Amos.* Which being presumed to be the mind of the prophet, the account may soon be made up. For begin we at the sixth year of Uzziah, concurring with the thirty and third of Jeroboam; there will remain forty and six of Uzziah's reign; unto which, adding the sixteen of Jotham's, and the three first of Ahaz's: we have what we desire. But this author must first show us how this notion of his can be made up, by any grammatical construction out of the words of the text; which indeed he does not, nor can it be done. Thus then having considered the computations of those who fetch the head of the account backward, from before the time of Esay's delivery of this prophecy; and either ending it, some space of time after, or setting no period or stint of it at all. We do not meet with, in them any satisfactory solution of the doubt, concerning it, moved. And undoubtedly the words seem evidently to carry it on entire to the future. Now, as in the former, the main question was concerning the head of the reckoning; so the difference here is most about the other term, the end of it. The most suppose it, to end at the taking of Samaria by Salmaneser the King of Assyria, in the ninth year of Hosheah's reign: and the sixth of Ezekiah's, 2 King. 18.9, 10. But that account falling, (as has been showed) at least forty years short; since that, taking the rise of it from Ahaz his first; (which is earlier, in likelihood, by two, or three year, more than should be,) and adding to his sixteen, 2 King. 17.1, 2. Ezekiah's six; the most that can be produced, is but twenty-two years; forty and three short of sixty-five. To salve this, some take hold of the Hebrew, that it is not said, *Yet*, barely; as Jon. 3.4. *Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be destroyed*; but word for word, as Jer. 28.3. *in yet*, that is, *within sixty and five years*, &c. which is truly accomplished, if at any time within that compass, though never so many years before the expiration thereof, it be fulfilled. And this is true indeed. But neither is God wont to set such large stints of time, concerning matters to be concluded within a far scanter compass; and much less to cut our computations so precisely, not in some one; whole and entire; but in broken numbers, as here, *sixty and five*, where an exact account is not punctually intended. Nor had it been agreeable to what God himself, and the prophet here in propounded; to wit, the encouraging of Ahaz against the fear of these his enemies, to enlarge the limit of their appointed fall, in the acquainting of him with it; so far beyond the set point of time, in God's secret purpose assigned thereunto. It had been far greater matter of encouragement to him, to tell him, that within some *twenty-five*, than within *sixty-five* year, Ephraim should cease to be a state. This course therefore of salving the account of those, that reckon from Ahaz his, though first, to Hosheah's last, carrying little color of probability with it: some try to help it another way, of as little likelihood as the former. The sum, say they, here mentioned, is the term that God, by his prophet, prefixed for continuance of that state, but for the excess of their sins, God hastened their overthrow, and cut the sum a great deal shorter; brought it down, from *sixty-five*, to *twenty-five*, or somewhat lower. It is true indeed, that in Scripture we find reversions of God's, both promises and menaces, upon man's worse, or better carriages; and himself acquaints us with his courses, either way, in that kind; Jer. 18.7, 10. But that God has, at any time, cut short any precise term of time, peremptorily set, for the execution of a judgment, I suppose no example can be produced; and there is little reason to admit that here, which we have no precedent of elsewhere. In the last place therefore, some late writers conclude this account, not at Salmaneser's surprisal of Samaria, and deportation of the main body of the ten tribes: but at a far later, utter removal of them by Esarhaddon; who succeeded Senacherib his father, in the kingdom of Assyria, ch. 37.38. This they gather from Ezr. 4.2. where those, whom the Jews upon their return from Babylon, found inhabiting in those parts; affirm that they were brought thither by Esar-haddon; and had continued there ever since. That which they deem to have been done, when that King of Assyria, by his captains invading Judah, took Manasses prisoner, whom he kept some space of time also, in bonds, at Babel, 2 Chro. 33.11. and withal swept away the remainder of those that Salmaneser had left; in the room whereof he placed those mentioned in Ezra. From the third then, or fourth of Ahaz, at what time this was by Esay delivered, (of which see on ver. 1.) unto the twenty and third, or fourth year of Manasses, about which time he is presumed to have been captived, and the residue of the ten tribes taken away; taking in the latter twelve, or thirteen, of Ahaz his reign, and the twenty-nine of Ezekiah's, 2 Chr. 29.1. the whole product will be, just *sixty and five years*. And this seems the most probable computation of this sum, and exposition of the place.

*{shall Ephraim be broken*} As ch. 14.25. Or, *destroyed*, as Jer. 48.4. Or, *broken in pieces*: as Jer. 50.2.

*{that it be not a people*} Heb. *from a people*, or *from being a people*, Jer. 33.10. & 48.42. So ch. 17.2.

**V. 9.** *{And the head of Ephraim is Samaria: and the head of Samaria, is Remaliah's son*} Or as others, *And the head of Ephraim shall be Samaria: and the head of Samaria shall Remaliah's son be*; as before of Damascus, and Rezin, ver. 8. Samaria shall continue still, the head city of Pekah's kingdom; and Pekah for that short time that he has to reign, and live, the king of it, and not of Jerusalem, which he shall have no power to dispose of. Howbeit, some would rather knit these words with the verse next foregoing: and render them together, thus, *For the head of Syria, Damascus, and the head of Damascus, Rezin*; *shall be broken in pieces*: which is supplied from the next branch (*Then after sixty and five years shall Ephraim be broken from being a people*; *together* *with the head of Ephraim, Samaria, and the head of Samaria Remaliah's son*. To which purpose, also some of the Jewish doctors, do in the former verse, the latter clause, insert, *Aram*, with *Ephraim*; reading the words, *Aram, and Ephraim shall be broken in pieces*. Else, say they, nothing should here be spoken, of the evil that should befall Rezin, and Syria, whereas the fall of both kingdoms are usually joined together in this prophecy, chap. 8.4. & 17.3. See ver. 16. But these readings make overbold with the text: and dismember it overmuch. I rather therefore choose to adhere to that reading, which was pointed to, on ver. 8. *And both the head of Ephraim, Samaria, and the head of Samaria, Remaliah's son*, *shall likewise be broken*. This only in the end, being supplied from the former verse. Than which manner of supply, nothing is more common in Scripture, Gen. 1.16. 2 Chr. 10.11. Job 3.20, 23. & 9.14. & 14.5. & 16.21. & 24.19.

*{If ye will not believe surely ye shall not be established*} If you will not give credit to this message which I bring you from God; and rest on his gracious promises, whereby he engages himself to you; if you will rely on him, and not seek out to the Assyrians for aid and support, to frustrate all the designs and attempts of these your adversaries, whom you stand so much in fear of; and to protect you against them; you will never prosper, nor be firmly settled, either in your state, or in your minds. It comes home to that, and drives to the same end, which that of Jehoshaphat, to his people, does, 2 Chron. 20.20. *Trust on the Lord, so shall ye be established: trust to his prophets, so shall ye prosper.* The same thing, in effect, is in both places intended: the only difference is, that it is propounded negatively, as by way of commination, in the one, with an intimation of some doubt made, not undeservedly; of what they would do: it is laid down affirmatively, as by way of confident and comfortable assurance, in the other: and as with some hopeful expectation of that to be done by them, that was required of them. There is in either place an elegancy in the sound of the words, which our English cannot express. Some other readings there are here, to pass by such as have no footing in the words of the text: some render them thus: *if ye believe not me, nor are ye faithful to God*, according to that; Luk. 10.16. Others, *Do ye not believe? it is because ye are not established*, but continue still in your diffident fear and distrust. Others lastly, *Do you not believe, because you are not confirmed?* Because that which I tell you, is not by some sign confirmed to you? And so they suppose, way is made for the subsequent sign. But the reading we have, seems most plain and proper, and to flow most naturally from the text.

*{surely*} So is the particle here found, oft used, Gen. 3.1. Exod. 3.12. chap. 5.7. Some suppose an ellipsis, in such use of it; as if it were entire: *truth it is, that* it shall so be, or not be. Howbeit, we need not conceive such a defect here, or make such a supply, as some would enforce, as if it were of necessity thus to be read, *it is a sign that ye shall not be established*. Since that the particle is oft used, as a note of asseveration, where the word, *sign*, admitted, will make no good sense: as Psal. 44.22. Job 8.6. & 20.20. & 28.1.

**V. 10.** *{Moreover, the Lord spake again unto Ahaz, saying*} The prophet, by God's appointment, proceeds further to confirm Ahaz, whom he perceived still to stagger, and doubt of what he had said to him, by making him offer of a sign.

*{Moreover*} Heb. *And*, as chap. 3.16. and so rather, than *therefore*, as some. Which though elsewhere it does not amiss, as Neh. 2.20. & 5.2. yet fits not here.

*{the Lord*} God himself, say some, immediately. For, when, Ahaz, say they, stood mute, and returned no answer to the prophet, by his silence bewraying his distrust, and incredulity of what the prophet had delivered; the better to encourage and confirm him, God himself undertakes him, as he did sometime, Job 38.1. But the whole tenor of the context ensuing, shows the contrary, to wit, that God spoke unto him still by the prophet.

*{spake again*} Heb. *added to speak*. A usual Hebraism; of which see ch. 1.5. & 8.5. Yet some would place an emphasis in it, as implying, that though Ahaz continued in his wonted impiety and infidelity; yet God persisted in mercy and goodness to him.

**V. 11.** *{Ask thee a sign of the Lord thy God*} For the further confirmation of your faith, and assurance of the truth of the word from him, told you by me.

*{Ask thee*} A usual and elegant redundancy of phrase, or manner of speech, in most languages: it is in Scripture very rife, Gen. 12.1. 1 Chr. 21.10. yet it is here deemed to have some weight *to thee*, or *for thee*, that is, for your behoof, for your good, as Gen. 13.11. 1 Sam. 13.2. 1 King. 3.5. 2 King. 4.3.

*{a sign*} Somewhat to be done, not ordinarily, unusual: such as God is oft wont to annex to his promises, or threats, either to strengthen man's infirmity concerning the one; or to meet with his obstinacy concerning the other. See Judg. 6.30, 40. chap. 37.30. & 38.7, 8. Jer. 19.1, 10. and 27.2. & 51.63.

*{of the Lord*} Heb. *from with Jehovah*, or, *from Jehovah* as Jer. 11.1. From him, whose word it is, and who by such means is alone able to give further assurance of it.

*{thy God*} Whose people you are king of, and whom you profess to serve, and ought so to do. For the Scripture oft speaks of things according to what should be done; though it be not ever done accordingly, (so Prov. 16.13. & 22.11. & 28.23.) or, according to what men do profess though their practice concur not; with their profession, chap. 48.2. & 58.2.

*{ask it either in the depth, or in the height above*} God puts him to his choice, for what sign he will have, a great favor, and honor: had this wicked wretch had grace to make a right use of it. So did he sometime also with Hezekiah, 2 King. 20.8, 9, 10.

*{as in the depth*} Heb. *make deep petition*, or, *go deep in asking*. So the most, agreeing in sense; but differing in grammar. For some of them would have the word of *asking*, here, a noun; and to signify a *petition*, or, *request*. So it should be, *make deep request*, as chap. 30.6. *they have made deep revolt*: but because no noun so signifying, is found of that form: others will have it a verb; and the most of them, an infinitive. So it should be, *make deep to ask*: as Jer. 49.5, 30. *make deep to dwell*. But then there must be a supply understood, at least, of a particle in this latter place, and so in most, if not all, where the like phrase is found. But some, and so the Jewish doctors, an imperative; which though some of those that mention it, reject, and, the places by the rabbis alleged for it, are not so fit, Yet is it most consonant to the usual phrase of the language, where both verbs so composed without that particle, are wont to be of the same mold. So Hos. 9.9. *they have made deep, have corrupted*: for, *they have deeply corrupted*: and so here; *make deep ask*, for, *ask deep*. In like manner are the Hebrew doctors divided; some going the one way, and some the other, about that, Psal. 51.2. *multiply to wash*, or, *multiply wash me*, for *wash me oft*, or, *much*, over and over, again and again; as if he could never be washed enough. The simple sense, of this clause, then, is no more than *ask deep*. Howbeit, many both of the Greek, and Latin interpreters, whom, some later ones also adhere to, render the word more largely, *make deep*, (to wit, the sign, that you would have) *to hell*, or, *to the grave*, to the depth of the earth; make it as deep as the earth, or hell itself is, Jer. 31.37. (of the word, and its signification, having its name of *asking*, or, *craving*, because it is never satisfied, Prov. 30.15, 16. see on ch. 5.14.) and this they labor from the next clause to confirm, where it is said, *make it high*, or, *lift it up aloft*; that is, say they, fetch it from heaven, unto which somewhat should be here correspondent; but of that there is no necessity: and, as the word is diverse from that, that signifies a *suit*, so it is, as much, if not more, discrepant from that which signifies the *grave*, or, *hell*.

*{or in the height above*} Heb. *make high*, or, *heighten*, or *lift up aloft*, that is, as by instances the Jewish doctors illustrate it, ask some sign, below: as, the moving, or cleaving of the earth, Numb. 16.30, 32. 1 Sam. 14.15. or, some sign above, as the eclipsing of the light of the sun, or the like, Joel 2.30, 31. Luk. 21.25. The meaning may be simply this, let the sign that you ask, be high, or low, a matter of greater or meaner concernment, such a one, as yourself please: God gives you your choice.

**V. 12.** *{But Ahaz said*} Heb. *And*. As ch. 5.12, 25.

*{I will not ask*} To wit, any sign, one, or other. And he refuses to ask a sign; not out of any reverent and religious respect to God, as loath to tempt him, or stint him, like those in the wilderness, Psal. 78.41. though he made that his pretense, but out of diffidence and distrust; either because he believed nothing of that the prophet spoke; but that all was vain, and frivolous; or, because he was resolved to go on another way, than the prophet advised, to seek help from the Assyrian, and not to rely upon God, from whom therefore to ask a sign, would be to no purpose, See 2 King. 16.17.

*{neither will I tempt the Lord*} Some would have the words rendered, *I will not exalt the Lord*, as if he should say, that he would not do the Lord so much honor, as to give glory to him, by craving a sign of him. But albeit, a word of sound and letters somewhat near this, signifies, *to lift up an ensign*; yet is this word, and this form, nowhere found so used: but the same word is used in the like sense, though in the better part, and on the like occasion by Gideon, *I will try*, or *prove*, or, *let me try*, or *prove, this once*, Judg. 6.30. nor is it to be imagined, that Ahaz should speak so blasphemously to the prophet: but it was rather spoken by him hypocritically, as respecting that prohibition, Deut. 6.17. (alleged also by our Savior, to the tempter, tempting him to tempt God, Matth. 4.7. Luk. 4.12.) *Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God*: as if a man should, or could tempt God, by doing that which he is enjoined, or invited by God himself to do. And they therefore also seem to strain here too far, who expound Ahaz his words, as if he should say, that he intended not to try what God would do for him in the present war, and in the danger thence imminent, but take such course, as he deemed, would most conduce to his own safety and indemnity. As also those do, who surmise that therefore Ahaz should not say, *the Lord my God*, as the prophet had before said, *The Lord thy God*, v. 11. but *the Lord*, only, as refusing to own him, as his God: for although it be true, that for such trial, the word is sometime used, 1 Sam. 17.40. Dan. 1.12, 14. nor much otherwise in that, Judg. 6.39. and that Ahaz was a wicked man, and one that in heart was wholly departed from his God, having resolved to rely on an arm of flesh, Jer. 17.5. yet, it is not likely, that he was as yet grown up unto such a height of professed impiety, as openly to renounce God, and dependence upon him.

**V. 13.** *{And he said*} Or, *Then*, (as ch. 6.5.) *said he*, to wit, the prophet.

*{Hear ye now, O house of David*} This compellation the prophet uses, as a preface, to stir up, not the king alone, but the rest of them then present, to attend unto that, as a matter of no small concernment, which he was to speak to them. See the like, ch. 28.14, 23. & 48.1.

*{O house of David*} Some ask here, why he says, *O house of David*, rather than, *O Ahaz*, when as he intended him only? To which, some of the Jewish doctors answer, That it was done in way of disgrace and reproach to the king, as one unworthy to be named; as Saul to Ahimelech, *Hear, now, O son of Ahitub!* 2 Sam. 22.12. and Moses to Corah, and his associates, *Hear, now, O sons of Levi*, Numb. 16.8. But the prophet does not direct his speech unto Ahaz alone; but to the rest of his family, together with him, as faulty also in the same kind with him. And the verb therefore is plural, though the noun be singular, because taken collectively, as ch. 2.5. Howbeit, true it is, that in way of reproach, the prophet seems so to term them, as much degenerating from him, of whose family they professed themselves to be, and esteemed it no small grace and glory to them. So ch. 48.1, 2. Matth. 3.9. Joh. 8.33, 37, 39. And so Saul to his followers, *Hear, now, O sons of Jemini, will the son of Jesse give you lands, &c. that ye conspire with him against me.* He calls him in scorn the son of Jesse, as a man of mean birth; them by way of reproach, the sons of Jemini, Benjamites, (ch. 9.1.) as forgetting their own family, and taking part with one, that sought to divest it of its royalty. See v. 4.

*{It is a small thing for you to weary men, but will ye weary my God also?*} The crime he charges them with, is their wearying and grieving, not so much God's ministers and messengers, as God himself, whom they serve, and by whom they are sent, in refusing to rely on him, and accept of his gracious offers, and choosing rather to seek after, and rely on other means, for their safety. See v. 4.8.

*{It is a small thing*} Some would have it read by way of enunciation: *This is a small thing.* But the particle prefixed, is constantly an interrogative, in this manner of speech, as Gen. 30.15. Numb. 16.9, 13. Josh. 22.17. Ezek. 16.20. & 34.18. and it is a form of speech usually savoring of much indignation and exprobration, with inference of some further and greater, than former, or ordinary guilt; as by view of the place pointed to, may appear.

*{to weary men*} To vex, and molest, (as Job 4.2. *shall we not grieve, or be troublesome to thee*) men; either in general, and those whom by your tyrannies and violences, you wrong and oppress: or rather, more specially God's prophets, whom you set light by, and give no credit to: but repute as vain prattlers, and busybodies, that feed you with fancies and fables, 2 King. 9.11. 2 Chr. 25.16. Jer. 5.13. wherein the crime would be the less heinous, did it reach no further than their own persons, as they are men, and did it not rebound to God himself, 1 Sam. 2.25. as it does, Exod. 10.7. Num. 16.11. 1 Sam. 8.7. Jer. 5.12. Luk. 10.16. Joh. 3.20. 1 Thess. 4.8.

*{but will ye*} Or, *but that ye will*. Making it one continued sentence.

*{weary God*} In distrusting him, and refusing to rely on him. Or, as some, in reputing him unable to do what he promises, and undertakes to effect. So they suppose the word sometime to signify, as Gen. 19.11. *they could not*, or, *were not able to find the door*; and ch. 1.14. *I cannot*, or, *am not able to bear*: and so here, *to make God impotent*, or, unable to do aught; as men are wont to be, when they are tired, and spent, which God never is, ch. 40.28, 29. The sense is good, and sound; (for such conceit of God, is one usual ground of distrust, Psal. 78.19, 20, 22. Rom. 4.20, 21.) but the construction is too coact.

*{my God*} Whom in special manner, and office, I belong unto, as 1 King. 17.1. & 18.10, 15. Rom. 1.8, 9. in regard whereof also, the wrong done, in disregarding the message that I now bring you from him, reflects upon him; and does chiefly respect him, being not my message, but his; 2 Cor. 5.20. & 13.3. 1 Thess. 2.13. Yet some observe, that he says not now, as before *thy God*, ver. 11. but *my God*, because he had seemed not to own him, himself, v. 12. But of that see there.

**V. 14.** *{Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign*} Though by your refusal of God's gracious offer, you make yourself utterly unworthy of any such favor to be showed you; yet will God vouchsafe, of his own free accord, to afford you a sign.

*{Therefore*} Or, *Notwithstanding*, rather, Notwithstanding your wearying of God, and being so troublesome to him by your cross, perverse and distrustful carriage; yet will he do this for you. The particle here used, is, as well a discretive, as a causative, and it is so found used, ch. 30.18. Jer. 16.14. & 30.16. Ezek. 39.25. Hos. 2.14. which being not observed in some of those places, has enforced the expositor to introduce harsh and needless trajections, and bred much difficulty in the text.

*{the Lord*} Of this name, (for it is not *Jehovah*; but *Adonai*, which the Jews commonly read in the room of that,) see on ch. 6.1.

*{himself*} Not by himself, as some; (for he does it here by the prophet) but of himself, of his own accord, unasked: as ch. 65.1. For they mind not the use of the language, that translate the pronoun here, *this*, as if the sense were, *The Lord will give you this for a sign*.

*{shall give*} Or, *will give*. The better, and fitter to express God's own spontaneous act, as *The Lord will give strength*, and *The Lord will bless his people with peace*, Psal. 29.11.

*{give*} Not *exhibit*: as some would have it: to wit, hereafter: but *set*: for so in Scripture, *to give a sign*, is *to assign*, or, *set a sign*, Exod. 13.2. Josh. 2.12. So Matth. 12.39. *No other sign shall be given them*, (that is, set, or assigned them) *save the sign of the Prophet Jonas*. See the note on the place, being a place much mistaken by many.

*{you*} Not those to come, their posterity, in whose days the sign here mentioned, was to be exhibited, as some strain it; but those to whom he then spoke. Nor need we restrain it to the better sort of that people (with some other,) whereof some, at least, might be among the rest there, for the promise of the Messiah was made to the whole body of that people, Rom. 9.4. and the prophet here speaks to none other, than those, whom in the former words he tartly taxed.

*{a sign*} A *sign* indeed: a sign of signs: such a sign, as never was before nor since, *A sign*, both *from above*, and *from beneath*, wherein heaven and earth, God and man, were conjoined in one, Joh. 1.14. Phil. 2.6, 7. But here is a question moved; how this miraculous birth, being a matter to fall out many years; yea, ages after, could conduce as a sign unto those that then lived, concerning the deliverance of them, and their head city, from the surprisal of those two kings that were coming with joint forces against them, and it. Unto which we answer.

2. That things not present only, or past, but long after to ensue, are sometime given for signs: and are not seldom of much force, & efficacy to raise men's minds to a hopeful expectation of such events, as are thereby ensured. So Exod. 3.12. This is by God given, or set unto Moses, for a sign to assure him of the delivery of the people of Israel out of Egypt by him: that after their coming out from thence they should serve God upon that mountain, on which God then spoke to him: which yet was not to be, until the deliverance was effected. So chap. 37.30. It was assigned to Ezekiah and his people, for a sign of their deliverance, and indemnity from Sennacherib, that they should for one year eat of that which came up of itself, and another year of that which sprang from it; and the third year have free liberty to sow, and plant, reap, and pluck without disturbance, or interruption, at pleasure. All which was not to be, until after the departure of him, upon the destruction of his forces, when their delivery was now over. So the stones that Jeremiah was willed to take, and hide in Pharaoh's brick-kiln at Tahpanhes among the clay, for Nebuchadnezzar to spread his pavilion over when he should surprise Egypt, Jer. 43.9, 10. was to be a sign to those perfidious Jews, who had fled into Egypt, though the event were not yet in being nor to take effect till some time after: for that dreadful judgment, by the prophet then announced, both against Egypt and them. For it was not so much the disposing of them there, as the Chaldean king, pitching of his pavilion in that place, that was to confirm the truth of that prophecy, whether they lived, in whose sight those were there laid, to see it, or no. To which we may add, that other stone and the book with it, cast into the midst of the river Euphrates at Babylon, thereby to assure God's people, in captivity there; yea and those that were to come thither after them: of their delivery thence, by, and upon the destruction of Babylon, by that typified, but foretold, and so prefigured to give assurance of deliverance thereby unto them; whom it had been but cold comfort to, had they been to perish likewise, together with it, Jer. 51.63, 64. Nor was the stone and book cast into the river so much, as the irrecoverable downfall of Babel, therein designed, that which was to give the Jewish captives assurance of such deliverance, as was promised them in that book. And yet were many years to pass over their heads; yea, and multitudes of them, (whereto no small number also, not yet captived) in continuance of time, worn out, and laid up in their graves, before that ruin of the Chaldean state, the future sign of that their freedom.

2. The ground & end of the sign given, or assigned here, is to be observed. The ground was Ahaz his distrust of God's power, as doubting, whether he were able to do that which the prophet would have him to believe, and rely on him for, to wit, to protect, and safeguard him and his state, against two such potent adversaries, without assistance of some foreign forces. The end is to assure Ahaz, that God can do as much, yea, and much more than this amounts to; he can do things more incredible, more impossible than this. This was no more than God, at divers times, had formerly done, as stories show, Gen. 14.9, 15, 16. Josh. 10.5, 10. 2 King. 10.4. 2 Chron. 14.9, 11, 12. & 20.1, 25. But the sign here propounded, was of such a thing as never the like was, either before or since, the *birth of a virgin*. So that is, as if he had said unto Ahaz. You doubt whether God can deliver you from the forces of these two kings, without help of some other human aids. I shall tell you of a far greater, and more unlikely matter, that he both can do, and will do, he shall cause a virgin to be conceived, and delivered of a child, without the knowledge, or help of man.

3. It is the usual manner of the prophets, in their prophecies and predictions of restitutions, or deliverances of God's people, to make mention of the Messiah, and to point unto him on whom all those promises of special mercies and favors, made to that people were founded; and for whose sake deliverances were oft afforded, even unto those, who were altogether unworthy of them. In regard whereof, it is not without some good probability, deemed by some, that the prophet, therefore, instead of setting Ahaz any other sign, directs him unto the Messiah, whose miraculous birth, was the most sufficient sign that could be; both of God's power for, and love to his people, by consideration of him, if he had any faith at all in him; to entertain some hopeful assurance of God's word to be made good to him, in the particular now propounded. To which may be added, that it is not unlikely, that from that prediction in Moses, Gen. 1.15. *of the seed of the woman*, that should *bruise the head of the serpent*, which the Jewish doctors also expound of the Messiah, some sense in those times might be had of a woman (so the apostle also styles the mother of our Savior, Gal. 4.4.) that should have seed, or issue, without knowledge of man; that which some other prophecies also are, by the ancients, deemed to glance at: as Gen. 49.10. Psal. 132.11. Besides, Dan. 2.34. and so the prophet might speak unto Ahaz herein, of that which might be already received, or not unheard of, at least, among them.

4. Albeit, this concerning the Messiah be mentioned; yet another sign seems to be further withal, thereunto annexed, taken from that child of the prophet's, whom for that end he was commanded, by God, to take along with him, ver. 3. as we shall hereafter show on ver. 15, 16. Both of them jointly concurring to confirm Ahaz his distrustful heart, if it might have been, in that, whereof the prophet from God endeavored to assure him.

*{Behold*} A note of sedulous attention, and serious consideration duly and deservedly prefixed, before the relation and prediction of a matter so strange, so far beyond, and above the course and power of nature, and of so weighty concernment, the incarnation, and birth of the Lord and King Messiah, the Savior of mankind, Matth. 1.22, 23. and that as pointing unto it with the finger, as John sometime at Christ, now incarnate, Joh. 1.29, 36. as a thing, in God's decree and purpose, already present, and even then, to be seen with the eye of faith; as of Abraham, it had been many ages before, Joh. 8.56. Of the use of the particle, see ch. 3.1.

*{a virgin*} So the Evangelist, Matt. 1.23. and so before him, the ancient Greek version received and allowed among the Jews themselves, and read publicly in their synagogues, with such of them as made use of the Greek: nor could it therefore be so rendered by the authors of that version, in favor of Jesus, the son of Mary, not yet born; or of the Christian profession, not yet in being, yet the later Jewish doctors, since the birth of our Savior, out of hatred of him, in whom the same is fulfilled, would have the word, *Almah*, here to signify any young woman, whether virgin, or other, married, or unmarried, known by man, or unknown of man; and to be a name, not of integrity; but of age, or youth only. Against whom, first, we object the notation of the word; in regard whereof it signifies, properly a *hidden*, a *concealed*, a reserved one; one kept out of ordinary sight and view. One *hidden* from man: that is, one *unknown* of man. For *to be hidden*, is *not to be known*, as 1 King. 10.3. Secondly we reason from the constant use of it, in the whole body of Scripture, in which it is, besides this place, six times only used, thrice in the singular number, thrice in the plural. The first place is, Gen. 24.43. in the prayer of Abraham's steward, mentioning such a wife, as for his young master he desired, which could be no other intended by him, than a pure virgin; such a one as Rebecah is avowed to have been there, ver. 16. Though they mistake, who say, it is there used of her; for of her, another term more large, (See Joel 1.8. where it is ill translated, *a virgin*,) is in that latter place used, but with such restriction, as makes it equivalent unto this; which is, by the old Jewish Greek, there also rendered, as here. The second place, is, Exod. 2.8. where it is used of that other Mary, sister to Moses and Aaron then very young, and a virgin, in all likelihood, all her life long. The third place, is Psal. 68.25. where, amidst the holy train, *are the virgins beating the tabers*. The usual employment of such, in their triumphant solemnities, Exod. 15.20, 21. Judg. 11.34. 1 Sam. 18.6. A fourth, and fifth place, are in the Canticles; where the *virgins* are said to love the spouse's beloved, ch. 1.3. Nor were her associates, or attendants, I suppose, presumed to be other: and where the *virgins* numberless attending on him, are mentioned with distinction, from both *queens* and *concubines*, chap. 6.8. such, to wit, as those that attend on the Lamb, Rev. 14.4. The last place is, Prov. 30.19. where among other things that Agur reckons up, as not easy to be descried: one is said to be *the way of a man with a virgin*, or a *maid*; for that is also, usually, a name of integrity with us. And this is the place, that the later Jewish doctors so much insist upon, & triumph in, as if they had found where the word were used, for one that were no *virgin*, no *maid*. For vindication whereof, to let pass the forced expositions of those, who so wring the text, as if they meant to press blood, or crush mature, rather than to fetch milk out of it: Nor to insist upon these two more specious interpretations, that are generally most received of those, who suppose the word to be taken, not according to the truth of the thing, but according to show and semblance only, or repute, and esteem; and so the party there spoken of, to be termed a maid, or virgin: not as being such indeed, but as deemed, and pretended so to be. Which they seek to confirm by what follows, ver. 20. of the whorish wife, who yet pretends to be honest. Or, that other, which yet many seem to be much taken with, of those, that expound it mysteriously, as the same, in effect with this of Esay; or that, at least, of Jeremie; *A woman shall compass a man*, Jer. 31.22. But to omit that, the whole tenor of Agur's discourse runs constantly in another strain. That very addition of the adulterous strumpet is sufficient to overthrow this: For, undoubtedly, the Spirit of God would never yoke the base carriage of so vile, and abominable a creature, with that sacred mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God, never to be without much reverence mentioned, or minded. To leave these therefore to their several authors, fautors, and abetters. The place, to me, seems not plain only, but very pregnant for that sense of the word, which, as genuine, and general, we avow. For the scope of the place is clearly this, to show how closely, and cunningly, persons, either men or women, can carry themselves, in contriving, and compassing their plots and practices, for the satisfying of their desires, when they are lewdly disposed. And the sense, consequently, apparent; that a *virgin* can hardly be so strictly watched, and kept, but that a man, so affected, will by one way or other, procure access to her, and that so covertly, that no notice, for the present, shall be taken by any that *he hath been with her*; as of Amnon, Absalom to Tamar, 2 Sam. 13.20. in whose case also, nothing would have been suspected other than well, had not the parties themselves, by their own after-carriages, bewrayed it. And the like is added, to make the observation complete, of a married woman, dishonestly minded; who yet can carry on her disloyal practices, so smoothly, and secretly, that no note of dishonesty shall appear with her. And thus this text cleared, and the Jewish doctors' only instance being removed, our reason against them, as well from the constant use, as from the native sense of the word, stands firm against them, that the term here signifies a woman untouched, in Solomon's phrase, and the apostle's, Prov. 6.29. 1 Cor. 7.1. Whereunto we might further add that which puzzles them, not a little; what strange matter it should import, for a young woman to bear a child. And here our great masters in Israel are at a stand; one supposing the sign to consist herein, that the child, this young woman went with, should prove a *son*; another, this to be the strangeness of the matter; that this man-child, as soon as ever he was born, should be able to discern between bad meat, and good; another, that he should eat butter and honey, as soon as he was born, instead of sucking in his mother's milk. These, and the like sorry shifts and surmises, are they enforced to fly unto, while they strive, by all means, to suppress that light, that from this Scripture flashes full in their faces. Howbeit somewhat, by the way, has dropped from one of them, that seems to give an inkling of somewhat muttered, in his time, among them, affording testimony to the truth: He says, some understand it of such a *maid*, or *damsel, as had not been seen to bear a child*. Neither does he pass any doom, at all, upon that their opinion: And what manner of maid, or damsel, but a *virgin*, should such be? As little agreement is there among them, in determining who this mother, or this child should be. Some would have the woman, to be King Ahaz his wife, and the child, Ezekiah, his, and her son.
