But herein, others of their own coat, control them; showing, by just computation, that Ezekiah was born divers years before this prophecy was delivered: for he was five and twenty year old, at his father's decease, 2 King. 18.2. who reigned but sixteen in all, 2 King. 16.2. and was born therefore before his father was king. Others of them, would have the mother to be the prophet's wife, and the child their son; for the prophet, say they, had three sons, having, by God's appointment, names imposed on them, importing some prophetical matter, *Immanuel*, promising God's assistance of them, against the Israelites, and the Syrians, ch. 8.10. *Maher-shallal-bas-bash*, implying the Assyrians' speedy plundering of those two people, chap. 8.3, 4. And *Shear-jashub*, foretelling the return of a residue, chap. 7.3. & 10.21. But, howsoever for the other two we make no doubt, because they give us good ground from God's word: yet for this their assertion concerning such a son of the prophet's, as should be here meant, and so styled, we have nothing from them, but their own conjectures. Against which, to omit what we might object, that the land of Judah is called *the land of this Immanuel*; as having a peculiar right to it, and dominion over it, chap. 8.8. which will not agree to any of the prophet's issue, or any other private person: this I say, to let pass; this we persist to oppose, that neither any son of the king, or of the prophet, can be the party here spoken of, unless he can be avowed to have been born of a virgin. Upon which ground also we deservedly reject, what some of our own writers, in part, therein complying with the Jewish doctors, have suggested, to wit, that this might, in some sort, be spoken and meant of some child then born, whether to the king, or the prophet, or any other, which might be a type of Christ. They pitch most upon the prophet's son, mentioned in the next chapter. The prophet, say they, joined himself solemnly to a virgin, who was also a prophetess; by her he had a child, which had a twofold name, this here foretold, and that other there expressed. And this child, so born of one being a virgin, until the time that he was begotten on her, might be a type of him, who in a supereminent and miraculous manner, was to be conceived in, and born of a virgin, still continuing so to be. To this purpose they allege divers predictions, that were verified, some lower, or meaner way in the type; but some other far more excellent way, fulfilled in the truth, further by that type intended. But although it be true, that in sundry complexed prophecies, the thing propounded, or promised, is found exhibited, and made good in the type or shadow, corporally; in the truth or substance, thereby typified, or delineated, spiritually; as in this prophecy, is frequently showed; Or, though corporally in both, yet not in the very selfsame manner; but analogically, by a kind of proportion, that the one bears with the other, of which, see Jer. 31.15. Yet this cannot hold here. First, because it takes away the strangeness intimated in the thing itself, here propounded; and which is, by this suggestion, pretended to be the type. And secondly, because it may justly be deemed to enervate the authority of the Evangelist Matthew, expounding the prophet's words, as spoke by him, of a babe to be born, not of one that had been a virgin, until in marriage he was begotten of her; but of one, who was a virgin, even then when she was already conceived of him in her womb; as the words precisely, both with the Evangelists, and with the prophet here, import; not *a virgin shall conceive*: as if the meaning were one, that is, now a virgin, shall hereafter conceive: but word for word: *a virgin shall go, great, or, be with child*: as speaking of a virgin, that so continuing should be in that condition: of which, more anon. And as that place therefore of the Psalmist, *Thou wilt not leave my soul*, that is, me (as Psalm 3.2. & 7.2. & 119.25. with 44.25.) *to see corruption in the grave*, Psalm 16.10. may not be expounded, one way of David, though in some things, a type of Christ, and speaking in the person of Christ: and another way of Christ himself: but of Christ only; whose flesh, though laid in the grave, yet was not there corrupted; as the apostle argues, Act. 2.25, 34. So what is spoken of the Messiah, to be born of a virgin, is not applicable in any other way, to any other, not born of a virgin, in that manner, as he was: and as it is certain, that none ever, but he, was. And we shall not a little infringe and abate the force and weight of those two principal, and pregnant testimonies, the one concerning our Savior, his mysterious incarnation; the other, concerning his miraculous resurrection: if we shall thus, as some have done with either, pick out the main pith of them, to make them applicable to any other. The mother, therefore, of the child here mentioned, is a *virgin*: and no other than that ever blessed virgin, the mother of the Messiah, continuing a *virgin*, notwithstanding a *mother*, Matth. 1.18, 23. Luk. 1.27, 35.

*{shall conceive*} Heb. *great*; or, *with child*. For the word here used, is not a verb, as some, who render it, *shall conceive*: nor a participle, as other, who require it to be read, *conceiving*; but a verbal, signifying one *with child*; as it is well rendered, Exod. 21.22. 1 Sam. 4.19. or, one *great with child*, ch. 26.17. Jer. 31.8. as of other creatures, we use to say, *great with young*. Nor indeed does the verb, whereof it comes, properly signify *to conceive*: Nor is the word therefore drawn from it, rightly rendered, *conception*, Gen. 3.16. where the words would rather be thus read, *I will greatly multiply thy pain even the pain*: or, *the pain I mean* (for the copulative is there, as oft elsewhere, exegetical) *of thy child-bearing*, or, *thy going with child*. By childbearing understanding, that interval of time, between conception and birth: during which time, teeming women, as we term them, while they breed, and go great, are subject to many infirmities, and bear a continual burden, for a great part of it, about them. And that is it, indeed, that the word here used, intimates; the affinity in the Hebrew tongue being so near, between woman going great with what she bears in her womb; and a hill, or mountain swelling higher than the ordinary surface of the earth; that in some Scriptures it is somewhat ambiguous, whether of the twain is meant, Amos 1.13. the very same word in the plural form; feminine, signifying as well the one, as the other, Exod. 14.2. It is therefore, word for word, as if the prophet, speaking of a thing present, not to the ear, but to the faith, should say, *Behold a virgin with child*, or *great with child*: As the angel to Hagar, Gen. 16.11. *Behold, thou art with child*. Howbeit it is, though for evidence, and certainty of truth, so delivered, to be understood in the future, as the sequel of the context shows, and one of the Jewish doctors, well observes, paralleling it with that of the angel to Manoah's wife; *Behold, thou shalt be with child*: for so he translates, Judg. 13.5. To be noted the rather, to meet with the vain cavil of those of them, who tax the Evangelist, as warping from the prophet's words, in rendering them by the future; *Behold, a virgin shall have in her womb*: as the Greek has it; that is, as we rightly render it, *shall be with child*, Matt. 1.23. And indeed, so would the words be here also rendered, *Behold, a virgin shall be with child*: which yet is not to be understood, as that other place in this prophet, *The child shall die an hundred year old*: That is, he that is now a child, shall be a hundred year old before he die, chap. 65.20. So *a virgin shall be with child*: That is, she, that is now a virgin, shall hereafter be with child; because the nature of the blessing promised carries it so there; whereas the strangeness of the business propounded, carries it, necessarily another way here: Nor may the prophet's words be otherwise taken, than as the Evangelist expounds and applies them: unless we will say, that the prophet foretold one thing to be done, and the Evangelist relates another thing as done. Whereas the one only reports, as exhibited, what the other had before said, should be. For as for that quaint descant of a late writer, upon the word *fulfilled*, used by the Evangelist, Matth. 1.22. that it is a term of art, taken from the practice of picture-drawers, who having first made a type, or rude draft of their work intended, are wont, after, to fill it up with other materials, and with variety of colors; as if thereby were implied, that to what the prophet had delivered typically, the Evangelist had added somewhat; or intimated, at least, that something had been further added, to make up the full truth, of what was but in part foretold. It may well seem subtle; but it is nothing solid: for the meaning is plain, and obvious to any weak apprehension, that then any prediction is said to be fulfilled, when the thing is done that was foretold. I must crave pardon, that I have been somewhat prolix, in endeavoring to clear this place, containing matter of so great consequence, and concernment.

*{and bear*} Or, *bring forth*: as it is more fitly, and fully rendered, Matth. 1.23. Heb. *and bearing*: or, *bringing forth*; as Gen. 16.11. & 17.19. Judg. 13.5. Spoken, as before was observed, as in the present time, but to be understood, as in the places pointed to, and as all here grant, in the future. And the word *virgin*, reaches as well to this, as to the former. *A virgin with child*; and yet still a virgin. And *a virgin bringing forth*, and yet, for all that, still a virgin. For it is not the opening of the womb by birth, but the knowledge of man only, that procures, or produces any imminution of virginity. *She brought forth*, say the Evangelists of the Virgin Mary, Mat. 1.25. Luk. 2.7. Nor are we to give heed unto those frivolous fancies, devised by the patrons of Popery, to make some color upon their prodigious dotage of transubstantiation, of the Virgin Mary's miraculous delivery of our Savior, without opening of the womb: whereas the Scripture expressly tells us, that therefore he was presented in the temple, as by virtue of a special ordinance, *holy to God*; because the male, that by birth had *opened the womb* of her that bare him, Luk. 2.22, 23. Nor do we therefore, as those of that faction charge us, hereby any whit infringe the continued virginity, of the mother of our Savior; they rather themselves infringe it, in denying that to be consistent with pure and entire virginity, which the Holy Ghost, by the Evangelist, affirms to have been with her. The conception of our Savior, we read to have been extraordinary, and miraculous, Luk. 1.35. we read no such thing of his birth: That a virgin should *be with child*; that is it wherein the miracle, principally, yea, peculiarly, does consist: being a matter, not only beyond the ordinary course, but far above all power of nature. But that, being conceived of a child, she should, at the wonted time, when her days were accomplished, be delivered of that she went with, Luk. 2.6. was agreeable to the ordinary course of nature: yet is joined with the former, in relation of the miracle; because, not only a consequent, but an evidence of it, a manifestation of that, to open view, that before lay hid, and might otherwise have been deemed, but some mere delusion.

*{a son*} So the angel to Mary, *Thou shalt bring forth a son*, Luk. 1.31. and to Joseph likewise, *She shall bring forth a son*, Mat. 1.21. and accordingly it is said of her, *She brought forth her firstborn son*, Mat. 1.25. Luk. 2.7. not a daughter, but a *son*. Though the Messiah came of a woman, Gal. 4.4. yet was he to be a male, a man. A man, though of a woman; that both sexes might have interest in him. *For neither is the man without the woman, nor the woman without the man, in Christ*, 1 Cor. 11.11. in whom there is no difference of male, or female, Gal. 3.28. But a man, more especially, in regard of the eminency of the sex, 1 Cor. 11.7, 9. & 14.34. 1 Tim. 2.11, 12. and in regard of the offices he was to sustain, being designed to be a *prince*, ch. 9.6, 7. Luk. 1.31, 32. a *priest*, Psalm 110.4. Hebr. 4.14. & 5.6. and a *prophet*, Deut. 18.18, 19. Acts 3.22, 23. A *son*, that the same person might be the *Son of God*, in regard of his humanity; who, from all eternity had been the *Son of God*, in regard of his Deity, Proverbs 8.24, 25. Psalm 2.7. Luk. 1.35. Hebrews 1.5, 6, 8. and that the *Son of God*, becoming also, *the Son of man*, Matthew 16.13, 16. might make those who were the *sons of men*, to become the *sons of God*, Gal. 4.4, 5.

*{and shall call*} So the most, yet with some difference; for some would have the word here used, a verbal, or a participle; the like whereunto, they suppose to have found, Exod. 5.16. but that place is questionable; and these read the words, as running on in one continued tenor, *Behold a virgin, going with child, and bringing forth a son, and calling his name Immanuel*. But others, rather, conceive it to be a verb and the greater part go this way, reading it in the third person, *and she shall call*. Which reading they strengthen, by producing a place out of Deut. 31.29. where the same word is found in the same form, though in a different signification, (the reason whereof, is well known to those that are skillful in that language) in those words, *And evil shall meet with you*: it being there a feminine of the third person, as they suppose it here to be. Howbeit others read it in the second person, as the margin of our Bibles also represents it; *Thou shalt call*: Not, as if the prophet spoke unto Ahaz: For the word is feminine; but as directing his speech unto the virgin, of whom he spoke; *Thou, O virgin, shalt call*: So the old Greek renders it, and the vulgar Latin; howsoever many of the ancient Greek copies are reported to have it, *They shall call*: which is as much in effect, according to the Hebrew idiom, as if it were said, *he shall be called*. The like whereunto, see chap. 60.14. & 62.12. and so divers also of the ancient writers, in their allegations of this place, read it. But with our marginal reading the Evangelist concurs; albeit, in some other words, he does not precisely follow the old Greek. And albeit the difference be not material; yet unto this latter, this may, for the further strengthening of it, be added. That this our prophet is found to have used the very same word, in the same form, and in the same sense, chap. 60.18. in those words, *And thou shalt call thy walls salvation*, or, *safety*. As also, that some of the Jewish doctors (though for no good end I suppose) attest thereunto: affirming it to be spoken, in way of injunction, or command, in such manner, as legal precepts are wont to be conceived, Exod. 20.5. & 23.15. And so the angel to Hagar, of the child she went with, Gen. 16.11. *Thou shalt call his name Ishmael*; whether way we take it, as spoken in way of prediction, or in way of injunction, as of her; or to her; apparent it is, that the nomination of the child is attributed to her. That which the Hebrew writers observe, to be according to the usual custom of their nation; with whom the mother ordinarily, named the child. And indeed we find it so, very frequently, in the sacred records. For so it seems, that Eve named her firstborn Cain, Gen. 4.1. and his brother, Seth, Gen. 4.25. and Jacob's two wives, are reported to have named both their own children, and their handmaids', which they reputed as their own, Gen. 29.32, 33, 34, 35. & 30.3, 6, 8, 11, 13, 18, 20, 21, 24. So Hannah named her son Samuel, 1 Sam. 1.20. And of divers other, the like is found recorded, Gen. 38.4, 5. 1 Chron. 4.9. & 7.16. But our writers render a further reason hereof: The right of nomination, say they, is in the father: because imposition of names, in behalf of the party naming, argues a special right in the dominion, or authority over the party named; as appears in Adam, imposing names, as on the other living creatures, by God made subject to him, Gen. 1.28. & 2.19, 20. so on the first of that other sex, a woman, made for him, and as a help fit or meet unto him, both as a woman, Gen. 2.18, 23. and as his wife, Gen. 3.16, 20. And in great personages, giving new names unto those, whom they take into their protection, or service, 2 King. 23.34. & 24.17. Dan. 1.7. The prime right of denomination, therefore, resides in the father, as having the more principal interest in, and power over the child; of whose practice in this kind also, may many precedents be produced out of Scripture: Gen. 5.29. & 38.3. & 41.51, 52. 2 Sam. 12.24, 25. 1 Chro. 7.23. and the mother's right of nomination is from the other parent's either concession or consent deemed hence to appear, in that when they differ, the father's voice carries it; as when Jacob and Rachel, upon the birth of the son of whom she died, gave the child several names, that which the father imposed, stood firm, Gen. 35.18. and Zacharies' hand confirmed Elizabeth's vote concerning their son's name, Luk. 1.60, 63. But the virgin, say they, here has the sole, and entire power of naming her child committed to her; because there was no father on earth, either to claim it from her, or to share in it with her. The Messiah, her son, being, as God, without mother; as man, without father, Heb. 7.3. Without father, I say, here on earth. For God was father to Christ, Joh. 8.19, 54. not as God only, but as man also, Luk. 1.35. And yet unto Joseph his father-in-law, as some expound the word used, Luk. 3.23. in regard of his mother's espousal to him; it is said by an angel, at one time; as well as to the virgin, his mother, at another time; *Thou shalt call his name Jesus*, Matth. 1.21. Luk. 1.31. Yea, of Joseph, it is said expressly, that *he called his name Jesus*, Mat. 1.25. and afterward indefinitely, that at the time of his circumcision, *His name was called Jesus, as he was named by the angel, before he was conceived*, Luk. 2.21. This therefore seems to be a nicety more subtle, than sound.

*{call his name Immanuel*} As, *call his name Jesus*, Matth. 1.21. and *called his name Jabez*, 1 Chro. 4.9. That is, *call him Immanuel*: as Gen. 25.18. *She called his name Benoni; But his father called him Benjamin*; Gave him that name: wherein question may be, how this was fulfilled, when as neither the virgin his mother, imposed that name on him: nor was he, that we read of, commonly so called. Whereunto, the answer is ready at hand: that names, in Scripture, are oft given to persons, or said to be given them: not thereby meaning, or intending, that the persons unto whom those names are attributed, either were, or should ordinarily be so styled. But that, that which those names imported, and was thereby signified, should be so verified of them, or in them: that the name itself might, as justly and deservedly be given unto them, and used of them, as if it were their proper and peculiar appellation. So it is said of Solomon, that David his father, called him, Jedidiah: *Because the Lord loved him*: and by Nathan signified so much to him, 2 Sam. 12.25, 26. alluded also to, Neh. 13.26. Yet read we not where David, elsewhere, so styles him: or that he was usually, so called. So Jeremiah tells Pashur, *The Lord hath not called thy name Pashur; but Magormissabib*; meaning, that such straits and terrors, should pursue, and surprise him, that that might justly be deemed his name, Jer. 20.3, 4. So it is said of Ezekiel, that the name of the restored city, formerly called, Jerusalem: shall thenceforth be, *Jehovah-shammah*, Ezek. 48.35. thereby intimating, that God should, in so conspicuous manner, manifest his presence among his people, and his abode with them there: that the city might well be named, *the Lord is there*. Yea, so of Christ himself also; (as the most) the prophet Jeremie tells us, that this is the name whereby he should be called, *Jehovah-tsidkenu*, Jer. 23.6. & 33.16. His meaning being not there, no more than Esay's here, that our blessed Savior should be commonly known, and called by that as his proper name: but, that what that term imported, should of him be most truly affirmed, and acknowledged to be fully made good in him. And the same is to be said of the name here given: as also of that high, and lofty style, consisting of so many eminent titles, and attributes, wherewith he is dignified, ch. 9.6. and yet is the name, here specified, given again afterward to this virgin's birth, ch. 8.8.

*{Immanuel*} The initial letter being lost, or left out, (in regard of the uncertainty of the sound of it in the Hebrew: or the difficulty of expressing it by any special character, in other tongues) as in *Amos, Obadiah, Jacob*, and other the like; so in this. Or, *Emmanuel*: according to the Greek, Matth. 1.23. which our language is more prone to follow: as in *Eve, Abel, Moses, Jesus, Mary*, and others. The word signifies, *God with us*: as it is expressly expounded, both by the prophet, ch. 8.8, 10. and by the Evangelist, Matth. 1.23. A fit name for the Messiah, and fulfilled in him; who being God, from all eternity, became one with us in time, Joh. 1.1, 14. to bring God, and us together, whom sin had before severed, Rom. 5.10. Col. 1.20. 1 Pet. 3.18. and who coming as a mediator between God and us, 1 Tim. 2.5. became both our *surety* to God, ch. 53.7. (See the note there) and God's *surety* to us, Rom. 8.32. 2 Cor. 1.20. Heb. 7.22. and so made a perfect reconcilement, between God and us, 2 Cor. 5.19. Ephes. 2.14, 18. Heb. 10.19. Unto Jesus Christ therefore does this name most aptly, most exactly agree in the substance of it, or what it imports. Howbeit, I dare not say, as some do, that it is a name incompatible to any other. For as the name *Jesus*, signifying a *Savior*, though it be, in a peculiar manner, proper to Christ, Matth. 1.21. yet was in time past, not unusually among God's people, imposed also on others, Zach. 3.1. Heb. 4.8. Act. 7.45. & 13.6. Col. 4.11. and may as well signify one *saved*, as *saving*. So the name *Emmanuel*, though, in a singular manner, it appertain unto Christ; as it is conceived to import, that inconceivable union of the divine nature with our flesh, in one personal subsistence; yet as it may also have reference to God's gracious acceptance of, and presence with his reconciled ones in Christ, to assist them, & protect them, upon all occasions, at all times, Ge. 28.15. Ps. 73.22. Mat. 28.20. Act. 18.10. He. 13.5. So is it applicable to any of the faithful; and so the prophet himself, having before attributed it to the Messiah, does, speaking in their person, afterward apply it also unto them, ch. 8.8, 10. It is, in this regard, with the name *Emmanuel*, signifying, *God with us*, as it is with the name *Ithiel*, signifying *God with me*, Prov. 30.1. which, though some suppose, to intend there the Messiah; yet seems rather to be the name of some ordinary man, either son, or disciple of Agur. Either name is, in some regard, peculiar to Christ: but in other respects, may be communicable to others. Nevertheless considering, that in that special, or singular notion, rather, the names *Jesus*, and *Emmanuel*, (for of *Ithiel*, I say nothing) have been appropriated unto Christ: I suppose it neither fit, nor safe, to impose, either of them on any other; since that, by such common and promiscuous use of them, they may be liable to much profane and irreverent usage.

**V. 15.** *{Butter and honey shall he eat*} This verse some understand of the prophet's son, Shearjashub: whom he was commanded by God, to take along with him when he went to meet Ahaz, ver. 3. and they conceive them to be spoken to this end, to assure Ahaz, that the city of Jerusalem should not endure any such great hardship and straits, by the invasion, and siege of those two kings, as he expected, and so much feared: since that the child, he had there with him, should be brought up, fed, and maintained, in as free and full manner as children, and those of the better sort, are wont to be in, times of greatest peace and plenty. But this exposition, to the most, seems too much strained: because it fetches in the word, *child* here, out of the verse following: without which the relative, in the next clause has nothing to relate to. They understand it therefore of the virgin's birth, before spoken of, and annexed to the former relation, to show, that the child she should bear, and be delivered of, should not be any fantastical appearance, or mere imaginary matter, (as some wicked heretics have, of Christ's humanity, affirmed) but a very man-child, consisting of a true human nature: as being fed, and brought up with such food, as other children, in those parts especially, are ordinarily wont to be. For, as for those conceits of the Jewish rabbis, that the meaning should be, that the child, spoken of before, either Ahaz's, or Esay's, should, as soon as he was born, be able to eat honey & butter, instead of his mother's milk, which other children cannot do, and should take these, being offered him; and refuse any other meat of unpleasing taste; and that herein the strangeness of the sign given, should consist; they are but frivolous fancies of their own brains: there is nothing in the text, that implies any such feeding of the child, whoever it be, in that manner, so soon as it is born; but of the bringing of him up so afterward, when he is capable of such food, until he come to years of discretion: Nor does that therefore seem probable, which one of prime note has; that the Jews use to this day, to give their newborn babes butter and honey, in the first place, before ever they taste of their mother's milk: which as it makes nothing to the prophet's mind, so it consists not with that, which for matter of fact, the rabbis affirm, therein, rather denying than acknowledging any such wont with them.

*{butter and honey*} Meats that young children affect, and (where plenty of either is) are usually much fed with. *Butter*, with us, and some neighbor nations, is the common food of such. *Honey*, not so, because not so rife in these parts: But in those regions very plentiful, as well as *butter*, or *milk*; the material of it, see Gen. 43.11. Deut. 8.8. & 32.13, 14. 1 Sam. 14.25, 26. 2 Sam. 17.29. 2 Chr. 31.5. Psal. 81.17. ver. 22. Jer. 41.8. Ezek. 16.13. Matth. 3.4. Luk. 24.42. whereunto, add the usual commendation of that country in Scripture: *A land flowing with milk and honey*, Exod. 3.8. & 13.5. Levit. 20.24. Numb. 13.28. & 14.8. Deut. 6.3. & 26.9. Josh. 5.6. Jer. 11.5. Ezek. 20.6, 15. Whence also some gather, that hereby is intimated the nation, both of the mother, and the child: that she should be a Jewish woman, and the child of Jewish breed: implied in the manner of his education, peculiar to that nation: as many people say they, are wont to be described, by the manner of their food and diet. That which to instance in, (seemed it much material) were not uneasy.

*{shall he eat*} Not, *shall he make us to eat*: as some; understanding it of Emmanuel: who should keep them in peace, and plenty, Deut. 32.13, 14. Ps. 81.17. but the Hebrew will not bear it.

*{that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good*} Heb. *that he know*, &c. Hence some would collect, that *butter, and honey*, are a food of singular use for children, to make them ripe-witted, and of quick apprehension. Which, to shift off, others would have the words read, not, *that he may know*; but, *until he know*. But of that use of the particle they bring no fit example: that of 2 Sam. 13.2. reaches not it. Nor need we to use any such refuge, the meaning is plain, that he may grow up, and attain to years of discretion, described here by ability to distinguish between *good* and *bad*; as elsewhere by ability of distinguishing between *the right hand*, and *the left*, Jon. 4.10. It is a defective, or complexive speech, *that he may know*; for, that growing up, *he may know*, or, *that he may grow up to know*, &c. which, but by feeding, cannot, in course of nature, be attained. See the like manner of speech, c. 6.11. v. 1.6. c. 38.14, 17, 21. fulfilled in our Savior, who, as man, had his growth in either, Luk. 2.52.

*{to refuse the evil, and choose the good*} This many expound of distinguishing of meats offered him, so as to refuse what is bitter, and unpleasant of taste, and receive what is sweet and pleasant, Job 34.3. and it is true, that the words, *good*, and *bad*, are sometime so used, Gen. 3.6. Prov. 25.13. Cant. 4.10. Eccl. 12.1. But it seems here, rather, to be understood of *good*, & *evil*, morally so termed. For that ability children have, even from the womb, while they suck, at least: as also the young of other creatures, to discern the taste of what is offered them, and to refuse things of unpleasant savor, yet neither do I conceive, that any extraordinary knowledge of, or judgment in, matters of that nature, is, by the prophet, here intended; but such apprehension, and notice of good and evil as children usually have, when the use of reason and understanding begins first to put out, & exercise itself; which is usually about the fourth, or fifth year. So the very same terms almost, are used by Moses; *Your children, which in that day knew not good, or evil*; that is, had no ability to discern the one, or the other, Deut. 1.39.

**V. 16.** *{For before the child shall know to refuse the evil and choose the good*} There is again much diversity of judgment among interpreters, concerning the child here mentioned. The Jewish writers would have it meant of their *Emmanuel*, the son of Ahaz, or Esay, or, I know not who else, that then lived; but unless they be able to give us assurance of such a one, in those days, born of a virgin; he cannot be the Emmanuel, spoken of by the prophet. Some of our writers expound it of the true *Emmanuel*, the Lord Jesus, long before whose conception and birth, and much more, education and growth, that should be effected, that is here foretold. But little comfort could this afford to Ahaz, or stay of mind against his fears; to tell him, that before such a one were grown up to years of some discretion, as was to be born divers hundreds of years after his decease, his two principal adversaries should be cut off. The most therefore, and the best, understand it, not of Emmanuel the virgin's birth, before mentioned; but of some other, or any other young child, that then was; and here they conceive, the sign, to be directly and expressly delivered, that God had of himself, voluntarily offered to give Ahaz; to wit, that in so short a time, as such a child could be able to discern good and evil, those two, that he so much feared, should both of them be destroyed.

*{for*} Or, *And certainly*, or *surely, assuredly*. As this particle is used ch. 5.7. and before here, ver. 9. Or, *yea*; as adding a further matter to what he had propounded: and so it is taken, 2 King. 18.34. ch. 36.19. Psal. 7.4. Prov. 2.3. For having before given Ahaz assurance of God's power, what he was able to do, by an instance of a far more incredible matter, ver. 14. he now passes to the relation of that, which had he faith to believe it, might having given him assurance that according to his gracious promise, he would do it; and might be an effectual sign to him of the same.

*{before the child*} As some, *a child*; as Num. 11.27. where the article also is used. And as a virgin, ver. 14. Any one that is now a child. But as others rather, *this child*: as pointing to, or singling out one, then in presence: as Gen. 21.12. & 44.31, 32. No other, in all likelihood, than *Shearjashub*, the prophet's child; whom to this purpose, God had commanded him to take along with him, ver. 3. for no other use appears of his presence there, with his father, but this alone. See ch. 8.4.

*{shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good*} Of the meaning of this phrase, see on ver. 15. Nor does it follow, that therefore the same child is here spoken of, that was there intended: because the same thing, in the same phrase, is related of either. For it is a usual thing in Scripture, with our prophet especially, by way of allusion, to apply the same words and phrases, unto divers subjects, where occasion is to speak of them together. See on c. 2.8, 9. & 66.3, 4.

*{the land*} The land of Israel. Or, as some, both of Israel, and of Syria, taken collectively. But the former seems the plainer.

*{that thou abhorrest*} In regard of the evil and mischief that it intends against you. Or rather, *by which thou art vexed*. For the same verb that was used in the active form, *Let us vex her*, ver. 6. (which this manifestly relates unto,) is here used in a neuter form, but of a passive signification. So Exod. 1.12. *The Egyptians were vexed, because of the children of Israel*: And, *Moab was vexed, because of the children of Israel*, Numb. 22.3. whom he feared also exceedingly; as Ahaz did the like here, ver. 2. And so it is said of Rezin, 1 King. 11.25. that *he was vexed at Israel*, or *had a spite at Israel* while he reigned in Syria: for so would the words there be rendered. Of another reading, see the next note.

*{shall be left of both her kings*} Not that the land of Israel had two kings, then reigning in her, at once, but Pekah, and Rezin are called her kings: the one, as her native; the other, as in confederacy with her. And she is said to be left of them, not as voluntarily relinquishing her, but as taken away before they could effect, what by their confederacy they intended. Pekah, being taken captive by Tiglath-Pileser, King of Assyria, and not long after, slain by Hoshea, 2 King. 15.29, 30. and Rezin also taken, and slain by the same Assyrian king, 2 King. 16.9. Howbeit some refer this clause of the two kings, not to the word, *left*, but to the word *vexed*: Rendering the whole branch, (as also the words lie in the original) *the land shall be left*, (to wit, of her inhabitants: of which phrase, see ch. 6.12.) *by whose two kings thou art vexed*. That which fitly answers the speech of those two kings, in consultation together, *let us vex her*, v. 6. & that not those two kings only were cut off, so as was before mentioned: but their lands also much dispeopled by the Assyrian invasion, the Israelitish especially appears by the story, 2 King. 15.29. & 16.9. All which was effected within a year, or two, at the most, after this prophecy, as may appear, by comparing the years of Pekah's reign with those of Ahaz, who began to reign in Pekah's seventeenth year, Pekah not surviving full four more, 2 King. 15.27, 30. & 16.1. So that, supposing *Shear-jashub*, to be one, or two years old, at that time, the event here foretold might well be said to fall out, before the child had attained to any notable measure of being able to discern between good and evil. See more hereof, ch. 8.4.

*{of both her kings*} Or, *by whose two kings*, as above. Heb. *from the face of whose two kings*. The like phrase is, Exod. 1.12. Psal. 38.3. ch. 21.15. & 31.8.

**V. 17.** *{The Lord shall bring upon thee, &c.*} Hitherto the prophet had endeavored to comfort Ahaz, and strengthen him against his excessive fears, by foretelling him, and assuring him of the speedy destruction of those kings, whom he so much feared. Now he proceeds to foretell him, what evil, for his hypocrisy, and impieties, relinquishing of God, and making flesh his arm, should befall him, his people, and posterity, from those, to wit, the Assyrians, whom he so much relied on, as his chief, if not only stay, 2 King. 16.7, 8. 2 Chr. 28.16, 21. It is as if he had said, a far worse evil, than that you now fear, shall befall you and yours, from those whom you least suspect.

*{the Lord shall bring*} As 2 Chr. 36.17. *God brought upon them the King of the Chaldees*. The Assyrian shall come with commission from God, God will send him, ch. 10.5, 6. and so indeed he professed, and pretended to be sent, chap. 36.10. though the truth is, he neither knew, nor intended any such service, ch. 10.7, 11.

*{bring*} Heb. *cause to come*. Make such days to come upon you and yours, as the like have not come: that the elegancy of the phrase may be retained, and expressed in the one member, answering to the other.

*{upon thee*} For even in his lifetime, the evil here threatened, began. So the holy story tells us, 2 Chor. 28.20, 21, 22. that *Tiglath-Pilneser*, (called, elsewhere, *Tiglath-Pileser*, 2 King. 16.10.) *King of Assyria, came to him and distressed him; but strengthened him not. Though* (so the word should be rendered; as Josh. 17.18.) *Ahaz had taken a portion out of the house of the Lord, &c. to give to the King of Assyria*. Of which also, 2 King. 16.8.

*{and upon thy people*} Who suffer commonly, yea, of necessity, with their princes, invaded by foreign forces; as they had already, under Ahaz, 2 Chro. 28.6, 8. and did afterward, from the Assyrians much more, ch. 36.1, 12. Jer. 39.9.

*{and upon thy father's house*} Your posterity. For the greatest, and heaviest shock of this storm, lighted upon the king, and his successors, 2 King. 18.13. 2 Chr. 33.11. & 36.6, 10, 17. ch. 39.6, 7. and the repetition of the word, *upon, and upon, and upon*, is very emphatical, and of much force to make the deeper impression, (the like thereunto, see Josh. 7.11.) it began with him in his lifetime; for he was in distress: not from Syria, and Israel only; but from Assyria, 2 Chr. 28.20, 22. It was grievous on the people, principally under Ezekiah, ch. 36.1, 12. and at last, it fell exceeding heavy on the royal issue, under Manasses, Jehoiakim, Jeconiah, and Zedekiah, 2 Chr. 33.11. & 36. Jer. 39.6, 7. & 52.10, 11.

*{days that have not come*} *Days*, that is, *times*, the manner of the Scripture, to reckon by days. See chap. 1.1. such times of affliction, as have not formerly befallen them. *Evil days*, Eccl. 12.1. Eph. 5.16. and *evil times*, Eccl. 9.12. Amos 5.13. not, that the days, or the times themselves, are evil; but are so called, in regard of the evils that befall men in them.

*{from the day that Ephraim departed from Judah*} Since the time, that the ten tribes revolted from the house of David, and divided themselves from the tribe of Judah, the greatest affliction that ever befell that family, and that tribe; either before that time, or to this present day; and was the ground of continual wars, and grievous calamities, from time to time, unto this people.

*{Ephraim*} See on ver. 2.

*{even the King of Assyria*} So some read the words, as by way of apposition, joined with the word, *days*: and expounding what is by them meant: as ver. 20. but this construction seems here somewhat harsh. Others therefore render it, *with the King of Assyria*, as the particle indeed very frequently signifies; but they expound it here *with him*, that is, *by him*, taking the word instrumentally, as in our language we oft use it. Others, lastly, supplying the defect of a particle requisite to make the sense entire, render it, *from the King of Assyria*; as Eve, Gen. 4.1. *I have gotten a man* (that is a man-child; as Joh. 16.21.) *from the Lord*: and Psal. 81.5. *when he* (Joseph; that is, the Israelites, Psalm 80.1.) *went out from of Egypt*. See v. 20.

*{The King of Assyria*} Whom you so much rely upon, and do unadvisedly call in, to assist you, God will make him, whom you make your stay, to be a sore scourge, both to you and yours, ch. 10.5. Thus it fell out with Ahaz, resting on the King of Assyria, as with Asa, resting on the King of Syria, 2 Chr. 16.7, 9. Now, by the King of Assyria, divers interpreters understand, some one king only, some Tiglath-Pileser, that distressed Ahaz, 2 Chr. 28.20. Some, Senacherib, that put Hezekiah to straits, chap. 37.3. Some Nebuchadnezzar, who had Assyria also subject to him, and swept all away before him. See v. 20. I rather concur with those, who take the words used collectively, and take them in all (together with Esar-haddon, that captivated Manasses, 2 Chr. 33.11.) successively; *king*, for a succession of kings: as Dan. 2.37, 38. *thou king, art this golden head*, that is, you, and your successors in the present monarchy, Dan. 8.21. *The rough goat is the king*, (that is, the *kingdom of Greece*,) *and the great horn, between his eyes, the first king*. The kings of Assyria are mentioned, as the principal vexers and wasters, in those latter times of God's people, Neh. 9.22. (as the kings of Syria had formerly been, 1 King. 11.25. & 15.20. & 20.1. 2 King. 5.2. & 6.24. & 8.12. & 12.17. & 13.22. & 15.37. and 16.6. 2 Chr. 24.23, 25. & 28.5.) who having been at first called in to help against others; and thereby taking some taste of a fertile soil, and wealthy state, were not afterward long at rest; but were from time to time, making incursions into it, and pillaging of it, until at length, they made themselves absolute masters of it, ruined the state, and carried wealth, and people away together, Jer. 50.17. *God gave all into their hands*, 2 Chr. 36.17.

**V. 18.** *{And it shall come to pass, in that day, that*} Of this manner of speech, see on chap. 2.2. & 3.24. & 4.1, 2, 3. He proceeds to describe, both the instruments, by whom God would inflict these judgments upon them; and the calamities, that the land and state should sustain in those times. For the word, *day*, is of large 2. extent, as by the places pointed to, may appear: and so v. 20, 21.

*{the Lord will hiss for*} Or, rather, *whistle for*; will call for them: as men whistle, sometime, to persons that are afar off: or, as the shepherd calls in his sheep with his *whistle*. See chap. 5.26.

*{for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt; and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria*} A description of those people, by whom chiefly, the land of Judah should be so grievously afflicted; or of whom those forces should jointly, consist, by which that kingdom and state should be ruined.

*{the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt*} *Fly* taken collectively, for *flies*, as *bee*, afterward, for *bees*; and *ox*, and *ass*: for *oxen*, and *asses*, chap. 1.3. the verb plural in the next verse shows it. Howbeit, there may be some emphasis in it, as if it intimated, that God would do all that is here threatened, with a *fly*, and a *bee*. By this *fly*, some understand the Egyptians themselves; by whom the land of Judah was invaded, under the conduct of Pharao-Necho, after the death of Josiah, who subdued it, and made it tributary, 2 King. 23.33, 35. And they suppose the Egyptians to be termed *flies*; as for the great multitude of them, that should come like swarms of flies, Exod. 8.21, 23, 24: So, in allusion to the condition of their land, which lying low, and abounding in ponds, ditches, and watercourses, cut out from the river, chap. 19.7, 8, 10. was much pestered with flies. Others understand by it, not the Egyptians themselves, but some other nations, as the Moabites, Edomites, Lybians, and Ethiopians, that bordered upon them, chap. 18.1. the rather, because it is not said, *that is in Egypt*; but, *that is in the uttermost parts of the rivers of Egypt*, that is, of Nilus, which branches itself out into divers channels, where it runs into the sea, chap. 11.15. or, which is cut out into many streams, toward the upper part, where it enters upon Egypt; which they suppose to be principally here intended. Nor is it improbable, but that the Assyrian king, having made conquest, both of Egypt itself, and those adjacent parts, did from thence bring many that served under him, when he invaded the land of Judah, 2 King. 24.2, 7. ch. 20.4, 6. Of whethersoever it be meant, the fly here mentioned, may well be deemed, to have some reference to the *flesh-fly*, as applicable to these people, in regard of its usual practice of sucking, as theirs of shedding blood. Other resemblances between them, interpreters give, which I pass by, because they seem besides the prophet's intention, and somewhat too far-fetched.

*{and for the bee that is in Assyria*} The Assyrians are compared to bees, as for the numerousness of them, wherein they agree with flies; so withal for their fierceness, and eagerness, wherein these go beyond them, being armed with stings, which they want; and, as enabled, in that regard, to do the more hurt; so much fiercer also, than flies, Deut. 1.44. Psal. 118.12. and of the fierceness and cruelty of the Chaldeans, who go also under that name, as subject unto one sovereign; of which before, on ver. 17. See 2 Chr. 36.17. Jer. 8.17. ch. 49.30. Jer. 5.15, 16. where it is said of them, that *their quiver is an open sepulcher*: alluding to their shafts, (whereof, see ch. 5.28.) which, together with their darts, and javelins, might well be resembled by the stings of those creatures; by whose name, also, it is supposed that they are here styled, because the land of Assyria, being a woody country, as much abounded with bees, as Egypt with flies. See Jer. chap. 51.14, 27.

**V. 19.** *{And they shall come*} Those flies and bees shall come at God's whistle, without stay, or delay; and enter upon the land of Judah, ch. 5.26.

*{and shall rest*} What they shall do, when they are come: they shall *rest*; that is, *surprise* or *sit down*; or as some, *pitch their camp*: for so they would have it expounded, both before, v. 2. and here. But that seems neither right there, nor so fit or full here. The meaning of the prophet seems to be, proceeding in the same metaphor, that he had before used, that these foreign forces, should, having entered the country, possess themselves of all places therein; as the flies did in Egypt, Exod. 8.21, 24. Psal. 78.45. & 105.31. and make spoil and havoc of all, where they came; as, besides the flies, the locusts also there did, Exod. 10.4, 5, 6, 14, 15. (where the word of *resting*, here found, is likewise used;) Psal. 78.46. & 105.34, 35.

*{all of them*} The number of them being not wasted, or diminished by the length of their march, or by any opposition in their way, ch. 5.27. as ch. 34.16. *not one shall fail*: none shall hang back, stay behind, or be missing of those that God has thus called and designed to this service.

*{in the desolate valleys*} Heb. *valleys of desolations*, or *wastenesses*. The word is nowhere else used, but here, and before, ch. 5.6. This some understand of the towns, or cities, situate in the vale, near the brooks; as the next branch of the strong cities, and forts, seated aloft, on the rocky and craggy hills: as implying, that all places high, and low, should be seized by them. But it may well be understood as the most, of those valleys, that having been before, rich and fertile, had been depopulated, and spoiled, by the foregoing wars: as implying, that there should be no place left so bare, but that it would be taken up by them to quarter in, (so numerous they should be) and further stripped of what was left. An allusion there is, in the words, to the manner of flies, mosquitoes, and gnats, that are usually most busy in low watery places, being there bred by the moisture of the soil. The word first & properly signifies a *brook*, and thence, in the second place a *valley*, or lower slip of ground, wherein such use to run between the hills, Psal. 104.10. chap. 57.5, 6. Hence, *the valley of Kedron*, as some: and *the brook of Kedron*, as others render it; 1 King. 15.13. 2 King. 23.4, 6.

*{and in the holes of the rocks*} Alluding to the manner of bees; that in such places are wont to harbor. Whence that phrase, not so commonly aright understood, of *honey out of the rock*, Psal. 81.16. and of *sucking honey out of the rock, and oil out of the hard stone*, or, *flint of the rock*, Deut. 32.13; meant, of drawing honey from the bees that hive in the one; and oil from the olive trees that grow on the other. The meaning here seems to be, that no place should be found so secure, or secret, that this people would not pierce into. See ch. 2.10, 19, 21. & Jer. 9.21. & 16.16.

*{and upon all thorns*} Or, *bushes*, or *shrubs*. It appears to be the name of some base plant, in that, chap. 55.13. (and, save here and there, the word is not read) it is said, that instead of it, the *fir-tree* shall spring up. Some render it, *cottages*: and such may in the trope be intended. But the proper signification of the word is such, as has been said; and it suits well with the former metaphor; for the flies and gnats use to gather about such, and that in such abundance, sometime, that the bushes and shrubs seem to be covered all over with them: bushes and thickets are places also of shelter, Gen. 3.8. 2 Chr. 33.11. but should not shelter aught, or any from them.

*{and upon all bushes*} So many of our interpreters render it, taking their rise from some of the rabbis, who tell us (as others of them do, upon better ground, of the former, that the word signifies *trees mean*, or *base*, *of no reckoning*, or *worth*. And these derive it from a word, which though, properly, it signify *to praise, commend, extol, glory in, brag of*: Yet by antiphrasis, say they, signifies *base, ignominious, unworthy of any praise*. But I find not, nor do they produce any place, where either the noun, or the verb, is so used. It is true, that in one form, the verb signifies *to be mad*, Eccl. 2.2. and *to make mad*, c. 44.25. & *to make as if one were mad*, 1 Sam. 21.14. yet, not by antiphrasis neither, but by excess rather; because in excess of glorying & vaunting men either become so sometime, or carry themselves as such: nor does it stand with reason to deduce a term rather to that, (were it found sometime so used) that a word by such an impropriety of speech, & contrary, sometime does signify, than from that which it natively & properly imports; unless there were somewhat else, either to enforce, or induce thereunto, whereof neither here appears. The word therefore, whence this descends, signifying sometime *to praise*, or, *glory in*, and sometime also *to shine*, and *be bright*, ch. 13.10. whereof the *morning-star* has its name, chap. 14.12. Hence, others rather render it, *goodly, fair, beautiful, commendable trees*, and the opposition also seems to carry it this way. Some indeed, suppose it to signify *goodly buildings*, or, *stately palaces*, as the former *cottages*. And the Chaldee seems to go this way. So it is said of the flies in Egypt, that they filled Pharaoh's house, and the houses of his servants, as well as of other his subjects, Exod. 8.21, 24. and houses, of both sorts may well be meant by the plants, or trees, here mentioned; but these in the first place. Nor is it unusual for flies to swarm, as well about fair and tall trees, as about low and sorry shrubs. Others yet understand hereby, *men of state*, or *stature*, in comparison of whom, others seem but as shrubs. See ch. 2.13. But the prophet seems here to speak not so much of persons, as of places; his intent being to show how these flies and bees should ransack all places, and make prey and spoil of all that there they meet with, (See Jer. 5.17. & 8.16.) that which, by another very lively resemblance, is in the next verse further set forth. The word here used, is nowhere else read: and by mistake of a letter, is both in the old Latin, and ancient Greek, rendered *holes*, or *clefts*. Which were spoken of here before.

**V. 20.** *{In the same day*} Or, *at that time*: as v. 18.

*{shall the Lord*} He that, before, called in the fly and the bee, with his whistle, v. 18.

*{shave*} Not *cut*, simply, as ch. 15.2. not *clip*; as Jer. 48.37. not *shear*, as Act. 18.18. 1 Cor. 11.6. or *poll*, as Ezek. 44.20. but *shave*, Ezek. 44.20. 1 Cor. 11.6. For it is one thing *to cut*, or *poll*, or *trim*, which was neglected by them commonly in times of grief; as with Mephibosheth, 2 Sam. 19.24. and is usually done with *scissors*, or the like; and another thing *to shave*, or *to cut close to the skin*; as with the cleansed leper, Levit. 14.9. which is not done, but with the *razor*, Psal. 52.2. and was wont to be done in times of extremest grief, and heaviest mourning, Jer. 41.5. And unto this shaving of themselves upon such occasions, of which, see on c. 3.17, 24. Some suppose that the prophet should here have an eye; as if the meaning were, that so great miseries and grievous calamities should befall them, that for extremity of grief, they should *even shave themselves*. But the *shaving* here mentioned, (as that also done, in a type, at God's command, by the prophet, Ezek. 5.1.) seems to look another way, and to be of another nature. For, that done, in such cases, was voluntary, and performed oft, by themselves, Job 1.20. this enforced and executed by the hand of another, as acting the part of a barber. That was the taking of the hair off some one part of the body, the head only, Job 1.20. or the beard, Jer. 41.5. This is a shaving off all the hair of the whole body, (which on such occasions was never heard of) as by the enumeration of the several parts, whereon hair ordinarily grows, appears; and may rather be deemed, to allude to the shaving of the leper, Levit. 13.8, 9. or the Levites, Numb. 8.7. who at the time of their purification, had their flesh shaved all over: and signifies an utter stripping of them of all that was aught worth.

*{with a razor*} A sharp barber's razor, Ezek. 5.1. So is the enemy, God's instrument, here styled; as being in God's hand, as the razor in the barber's hand, which cuts as deep, and as far as he pleases, but cannot cut deeper, or further than he will. So ch. 10.5, 15.

*{that is hired*} The Greek, by mistake of a point or two, render it; *that is made drunk*: which some of ours seem not to disallow; because it is said, *My sword shall be made drunk*, ch. 34.5. But the word, that signifies *drunk*, 1 Sam. 1.14. though coming near this, yet differs from it, not in the sound of the initial letter alone, as *Shibboleth*, and *Sibboleth*, Judg. 12.6. but in the doubling also of the middle consonant, and the change of its annexed vowel. The word signifies a *mercenary*, or, *hired one*. Which some understand by a trope, so termed, as one that God would make use of to the purpose because men are wont to use things hired more freely, not regarding what they put them to. But we need not step out of the way to fetch in such tropes, when we have a plainer sense at hand. The question is, only, how, or by whom, this razor is said to be, or have been *hired*, for the words will bear either. Some say, by God who, with hope of obtaining a large booty, as with a bait, enticed this great king, to invade that wealthy kingdom: and this they build on those words of God, in Ezekiel, concerning Nebuchadnezzar, *I caused his army to serve a great service against Tyre; yet neither he, nor his army, had any wages for it. I will therefore give him the land of Egypt, and that shall be the wages for his army*, Ezek. 29.18, 19. But others rather understand it, of Ahaz his hiring of Tiglath-Pileser the Assyrian king, to come into his succor, against Pekah and Rezin, Israel and Syria, 2 King. 16.7, 8. 2 Chr. 28.16, 21. and this suits well with the main drift of the prophet's discourse here; which is to let Ahaz understand what an unadvised course he had taken, in betaking himself to the King of Assyria, and feeing him to come in to his assistance, he had in so doing but hired a razor to shave him and his state, of whatsoever was of any worth or use in it; as the event should hereafter show. It is an allusion to the use of barbers, whom men usually hire to barb and trim them.

*{namely*} Or, *to wit*, or, *even*, annexed by apposition to the former, but the particle exegetical omitted. See v. 17.

*{by them beyond the river*} Heb. *by the passages*, (as some render it, Jer. 22.20.) or, *by the sides*, (as Jer. 48.28. & 49.32.) *of the rivers*; that is, by those that abide and inhabit about it; and he says; *in the passages*; as some suppose, because the river spoken of, running not straight on, in a direct current; but with many windings and turnings had therefore many places of passage upon it; but of this there is no necessity: for that, the word is frequently used, for, *sides*, or *borders*, Exod. 32.15. 1 King. 4.24. and may well signify those, that bordered in any place upon it.

*{the river*} This river some would have to be Nilus, the river of Egypt, ch. 11.25. & 19.5. because mention was made of it before, v. 18. but the most rather understand it of the river Euphrates, that divides Syria and Assyria: called the river, Psal. 72.8. Jer. 2.18. where both of them are mentioned.

*{by the King of Assyria*} This shaving was begun by Tiglath-Pileser, 2 King. 16.8. 2 Chr. 28.21. continued by Sennacherib, and Esar-haddon, 2 King. 18.13, 16. 2 Chr. 33.11. consummated by Nebuchadnezzar, 2 King. 24.13, 16. & 25.9, 17. ch. 39.6. whom some suppose, principally, here intended; and to be the rather termed here, King of Assyria, than of Chaldea; though lord of both: partly, because the monarchy then bare that name, ch. 36.4. and partly, to intimate God's retaliation of Ahaz his sin, in wasting his land, by him, whom, refusing to trust unto God, he had wickedly relied upon.

*{the head*} Not by cutting off the head itself, or slaying, as the rabbis most of them, upon the place, do most ridiculously expound it: applying it to the destruction of Sennacherib's forces by the angel, ch. 37.36. to which may be added, that ridiculous tale, reported out of some other of them, of the angel's shaving his head and his beard. But as it is said of the Nazarite, *he shall shave his head*; that is, the hair of his head, Num. 6.9. and that, not some few locks of it, as Judg. 16.19. but all the hair of the whole head. The hair whereof is matter, not of ornament only, but of muniment also, especially in those times, wherein they had wont to go barehead; which was the usual manner of the ancient, both Greeks and Romans: (as by stories and monuments of antiquity does appear: and the apostle may seem to have respected, 1 Cor. 11.4, 7.) only, when need was, in rain, or the like, covering their heads with some part of their gown, or upper garment: and may be conjectured to have been also the common guise of the Jewish people; for that covering of the head, is mentioned, upon occasion of mourning, as a matter otherwise unusual, 2 Sam. 15.30. Howbeit, see Ezek. 24.17. which place requires further consideration.

*{and the hair of the feet*} That is, of the secret, or lower parts of the body, Ezek. 16.7, 25. See on ch. 6.2. concerning which, the Hebrew doctors expressly observe, that they were also shaved in the lepers, and in the Levites, at the purifying of either, Levit. 14.8, 9. Num. 8.7. It is, as if he had said, they shall make all bare, from top to toe.

*{And it*} To wit, this razor. That is here attributed to the instrument, that was before ascribed to the chief actor; to God, that made use of it. They strain too far, that render it, *it shall eat with the beard*.

*{shall also consume the beard*} Not take off some part of it, as Hanun did David's messengers, shaving away only the one half, 2 Sam. 10.4. but *consume* it, make an utter riddance of it, take away the whole beard, the hair whereof is deemed, not an ornament only, but an argument of virility: which God therefore would not have defaced, Levit. 19.27. and it was deemed therefore a contumelious usage of David's servants, whom that Ammonite so disfigured, 2 Sam. 10.5. Now here by the *head*, some understand the king and his princes, ch. 9.15. by the *beard*, the priest, Psal. 133.2. by the *feet*, the common sort of people, Judg. 4.10. & 8.5. And howsoever this may seem somewhat curious: yet certain it is, that an utter stripping of the whole body of that state; and of all estates among them, of whatsoever was, or might be, of use, honor, or ornament with them, is by this shaving of head, beard, and feet intended. It is a speech parallel to that proverbial form, *not an hair of your head shall perish*, Luk. 21.18. Act. 27.34. for, as an absolute indemnity is implied in the one, that they should not sustain so much as a hair-worth's loss: so an utter devastation is imported in the other: that not so much as a hair-worth of aught should be left. As the rabbis say of the leper that is to be cleansed, the priest that shaved him, must not leave a hair; if he do leave a hair or two, all is nothing: they should strip all sorts of them, of all that was aught worth. So it is said, Lam. 1.10. *The adversary seized on all her desirable*, or, *delectable things*: and Jer. 8.16. *they have devoured the land, and all that is in it*, and chap. 39.6. *There shall nothing be left*.

**V. 21.** *{And it shall come to pass in that day, that, &c.*} As ver. 18. From hence, the prophet relates the condition of those that should be left in the land, after Sennacherib's invasion, as some; or rather as others, after the Babylonian deportation: and in what state the whole land should be, after this shaving. For they seem to shoot wide, that turn this to a spiritual notion of God's gracious provision and abundant supply of all necessaries, for his, in times of public calamity.

*{a man shall nourish a young cow, and two sheep*} In these words is noted, the great penury of those that should remain in the land, after it had been so plundered by the enemy. Those that had kept great herds before, should have scarce a cow, or a young heifer left; and those that were possessed of a numerous flock, not above one or two sheep.

*{a man*} One, say some, of the better rank; and so, indeed, sometime it is taken, where opposed to, or distinguished from *Adam*. But, here, I suppose, as elsewhere, more generally, and indefinitely, for any man whatsoever. See ch. 2.9.

*{nourish*} Heb. *quicken*; that is, *keep alive*, as Psal. 22.29. which some understand, of *saving*, as Deut. 20.16. when the rest were destroyed and consumed by the enemy, Deut. 28.31. but it seems rather to be taken here, as 2 Sam. 12.3. for to keep or nourish; or, if you will, *to keep for food*: which is hence, termed, Gen. 45.5. Judg. 6.4. not to *plow*, or *till with*. Few, for fear of some new invasion, having any mind of giving themselves, yet to tillage; and wanting cattle also to till withal.

*{a young cow*} Heb. *a calf*, or, *heifer of the ox*; or, *herd*, as Gen. 12.16. & 26.14. Exod. 9.3. Deut. 12.21. See the same phrase, Deut. 21.3. 1 Sam. 16.2.

*{and two sheep*} Or, *two of the lesser cattle*, sheep or goats. For in way of distinction from the former, it comprehends both; as in the places before pointed to, and Levit. ch. 1.2, 10.

**V. 22.** *{And it shall come to pass, for the abundance of milk that they shall give, he shall eat butter*} Or, *that he shall eat butter*. For the particle would be here supplied, as well, as ver. 21. & 23. This some understand of the great plenty that God would bless the land withal, after the raising of the Assyrian siege under Sennacherib, and the departure of his forces, notwithstanding the great havoc that had been made by them, ch. 37.30, 31. But others rather, with more probability, understand it, as an argument of depopulation, and a great paucity of inhabitants left behind in it, when the main body of them was carried away captive by the Chaldeans; the families left, being so small, that the milk of a few cattle, would be sufficient, both to feed them for the present, and to afford also some overplus, to make butter of for future provision: and those few milch cattle, yield the more, because they should have pastures at large to feed the more freely in; being not now restrained by the enclosures of those that joined field to field before, ch. 5.8, 17.

*{for the abundance of milk that they shall give*} Heb. *from the abundance of making milk*, *to make milk*, for, *to yield milk*: as *to make fruit*, for, *to yield fruit*: and, *to make wine*, for, *to yield wine*. See ch. 5.2, 10.

*{he shall eat butter*} Having but few in family, and none to take it of him.

*{for butter, and honey, shall every one eat, that is left in the land*} To wit, of Judah, Heb. *in the midst of the land*: as 5.8. & c. 6.12. This some suppose to imply great plenty of victuals, through God's blessing, as above: and by *butter, and honey*, to be intimated more delicate diet, as before, ver. 15. Others rather, take it for ordinary, frugal, country fare, as milk, cheese, and butter commonly are: and for *honey*, the woods affording store of it, it may seem by the story of John the Baptist, to have been no extraordinary food, Matth. 3.4. Mar. 1.6. on such food therefore, for scarcity, and want of flesh, corn, fruits, and other variety of food, should the poorer sort, left in the land, (2 King. 25.12. Jer. 39.10.) feed; and that also the more freely and fully, having none (of the richer sort especially; being either consumed, or, captivated, ch. 5.13, 14. & 6.11, 12.) either to deprive them of it, or to utter it unto.

**V. 23.** *{And it shall come to pass in that day, that, &c.*} As ver. 21.

*{every place shall be, where there were a thousand vines, at a thousand silverlings, it shall even be for briers and thorns*} This, and what follows, some take, as if it were said, that such places as had been fertile and fruitful before, should then be waste and desolate; and on the other side, such as had been waste and barren before, should then become fertile and fruitful; ver. 25. To which interpretation, they add spiritual senses, of God's raising the weak and lowly; and pulling the haughty great ones down, 1 Sam. 2.4, 5, 8. Ps. 107.40, 41. & 147.7, 8. Luk. 1.52, 53. See ch. 29.17. Others take it in a plainer and more familiar sense, as importing only the great desolation of the land, in regard of the fruits of it. Such as is described, ch. 1.7. Jer. 4.23, 26. & 8.16. as before, the depopulation of it, in regard of its inhabitants, v. 22. to wit, that the richest and fruitfullest places, for want of husbanding and manuring, should be overgrown with useless and harmful trash, v. 24. ch. 5.6.

*{a thousand vines*} Heb. *a thousand vine*: as we use to say, *a thousand horse*. So 2 Sam. 10.6. *a thousand man*, for, *a thousand men*: and *vine*, for, *vines*, as *briar and thorn*, for, *briars and thorns*, hereafter: and ver. 24, 25.

*{a thousand*} That is, many. A certain number, for, an uncertain: as Ps. 50.10. ch. 3.17. Mic. 6.6. Amos 5.3.

*{at a thousand silverlings*} Heb. *a thousand of silver*. That is, so many *shekels*. For that is usually understood, where the coin or weight is not expressed; as 2 Sam. 18.11, 12. Matth. 26.15. The *shekel*, there being in weight and value, about our half-crown: the sum that such vineyards, being of the best sort, were yearly let for, came to about one hundred and twenty and five pounds. See Cant. 8.11. for they seem to shoot wide, who expound it of the small quantity of wine, and money for it, that vines should, in those times, yield; as if it were said, that the vines having not been pruned and dressed, as formerly, for fear of the enemy, should yield so little wine that no man would give above a *shekel* for the wine that any one of them should yield. See ch. 5.10. The verse following carries it the other way. And those Rabbins are yet wider, who refer this to Ezekiah's times, after Sennacherib's overthrow, when men by that good king's persuasion, giving themselves to the study of the law, and drinking but little wine, should neglect the dressing of their vines.

*{shall be briers and thorns*} Heb. *for briars, and for thorns*. A redundancy of speech. The like whereunto, see ver. 19. see also ver. 24. & 25. not that they should be set apart for such trash, as fields are, some for corn, some for pulse, and the like, ch. 28.25. being places appointed for them; but that through neglect they should be so overspread with them, as if they were for no other use, Prov. 24.32. See ch. 5.6.

**V. 24.** *{With arrows, and with bows shall they come thither*} Heb. *with arrows, and with bow*, (that is, *with bow, and arrows*. For it is a redundancy, such as ver. 23.) *shall he come thither*: that is, *shall men come thither*, as ch. 2.19. or, *shall one come thither*: for the verb is singular. So, *she bare*, for, *one bare*: or, *was born*, 2 Sam. 21.8. thither they shall go thither so weaponed, say some, because of the thickness and greatness of those thorny shrubs, to make their passage through, free, without hurt or annoyance, 2 Sam. 23.6, 7. but a bill, or woodhook were for that purpose fitter, than either bow, or shaft. To hunt, say others, such beasts as use to haunt places of that nature, for covert: and the bow indeed is one of the huntsman's chief weapons, Gen. 27.3. But this sorts not so well with the prophet's scope. Others say, they went so weaponed, for fear of the enemy, by reason whereof, they dare not stir abroad to visit their grounds, or look after their cattle; they went abroad, as those wrought, Neh. 4.17, 18. See Lam. 5.9. but neither does this seem here so probable. Others therefore say, to defend themselves against such either wild beasts, serpents, or other harmful creatures, as they might meet with lurking there; and this, the very next clause leads us to.

*{because all the land shall become briers and thorns*} The land shall be generally overgrown with them, ch. 32.13. as it is said of the slothful person, the whole *surface of his field* was overspread with the like, Prov. 24.31. and consequently, would be overrun also with, wild beasts, and other harmful creatures; as is usual with places, by inhabitants abandoned, and overgrown in such manner, Exod. 23.29. ch. 13.21. & 34.14. See the comminations, Gen. 3.18. Levit. 26.22.

*{briers and thorns*} Heb. *briar, and thorn*: as *vine*, v. 23. So ver. 23, 25.

**V. 25.** *{And on all hills, that shall be digged with a mattock, there shall not come thither, the fear of briers and thorns*} Some read the words, far otherwise, on this manner. *As for all the hills, that were digged with the mattock, thou shalt not come thither, for fear of briars and thorns*: in want of the preposition, as Mal. 2.5. and they conceive the prophet's meaning to be, that those hilly places, which had been before curiously kept, and digged for vineyards, orchards, or gardens, 1 King. 21.2. Luk. 13.8. should likewise be so overgrown with brambles, and briars, that no man should dare to enter upon them. But this agrees not with the latter part of the verse: for how should their cattle then be turned in thither? The most therefore follow the more received reading. Some understand it, of a change for the better: that the barren places on the hills, that before would yield nothing, without a great deal of hard labor and toil, should be free from those obstructions, and overspreading of such noxious shrubs, as infested other places; and becoming fertile, afford their cattle good pasture. And the Hebrew doctors run most this way. See before, on ver. 23. But this seems to cross the foregoing discourse, and the main scope of the prophet's speech. Others suppose it to have relation to those that were before said, not to venture out unweaponed, for fear of the enemy: that they should betake themselves to the mountains, that were likewise overgrown with bushes, and briars, as to places of more security: the enemies fear, overswaying the fear of any hurt, that from those thorny shrubs might accrue unto them, and by the hard labor of their hands, there, help themselves. Others again would have the meaning to be, that no place shall be shunned for fear of briars and brambles; albeit they should require never so much pains to rid them. Others, that men having betaken themselves thither, should so diligently grub up those hilly places, that there should be no fear of briar or bramble there; but that their cattle might safely go at large, and feed there, which for fear of the enemy, they dare not trust on the plain, Lam. 5.9. unto whose footing also, some attribute this immunity from briars and thorns, as treading them down, as fast as they came up. Others lastly, which seems to come nearest the prophet's mind, understand the words of such places on the hills, which the rich had fenced in for pleasure, or profit; that such fences being now cast down, and made away, they should lie open to cattle, as well great, as small.

*{And on all hills*} Or, *And as for all those hills*. The nominative put absolutely, as Ps. 11.4. & 10[unclear].30. or, *And all hills*. See further below.

*{that shall be digged*} As Luk. 13.8. or, *hoed*; which best answers the Latin here; both old, and later, and seems most agreeable to the Hebrew, See ch. 5.6. not *ploughed*; as the Greek renders it. For into such places was not the plow brought, nor there used, that the beasts might not trample on the loose earth, or the tender plants with their footing.

*{that shall be*} Or, *that should be*; or, *had wont so to be*, as Mal. 1.6. *a son will honor his father*, that is, should, or is wont so to do. That used not to be ploughed for grain, but to be digged, for planting of vines, or of trees, either for sight, or fruit, or, for the setting, and sowing of herbs and flowers, 1 King. 21.2. (to which purpose also, the hilly parts were much used, Jer. 3.2, 13. & 31.5.) and to be kept in due order afterward, from time to time, by weeding and hoeing.

*{with the mattock*} Or, *spade*, or *hoe*, an instrument used for weeding, and banking, and loosening the earth.

*{there shall not come thither, the fear of briers and thorns*} That which, as was before said, is understood by some, not of briars and thorns growing up in them, as v. 24. but of such thorny bushes, as had formerly served for hedge and fence about them, Ps. 62.3. ch. 5.2. Hos. 2.6. to keep cattle from breaking in to depasture the ground, and crop or browse upon the vines, and other plants therein; which being now broken down, there should be no fear of them, to hinder beasts from free entrance, to feed there at pleasure, ch. 5.5. Hos. 2.12. But the most expound them of the former, as v. 24. yet much differing in exposition of the place, one from another; whereunto, I shall add, and leave it to be considered of by the learned; whether the words so taken, the text may not be thus read, *And on the hills that, had wont to be digged with mattock or spade, that no fear of briar or thorn, might come thither; shall a place also be for sending in of oxen, and the treading of lesser cattle*. All the difficulty here lies in the defect of the particle, *that*, importing the end, or issue: the want whereof both in that language, is not unusual, as Ps. 10.4. ch. 5.11. & 10.12. Hos. 7.6. as also in the Greek of the New Testament, Rom. 8.29. 1 Cor. 1.8. Jam. 5.

*{but they shall be for the sending forth of oxen, &c.*} They shall all lie open for cattle of all sorts to graze upon, and trample down at pleasure.

*{but they shall be*} Heb. *and it shall be*, *and*, for, *but*, as ch. 6.13. & 29.13. or, *shall also be*, as Jer. 1.3. to wit, *a place*, which, though wanting, as 2 Sam. 7.1. 1 King. 18.12. some also put here into the text: or, without any such insertion, *And those hills, &c.* (that were so carefully fenced, and kept before that no cattle, little or great, could have access to them, nor briar or thorn appear in them; but it was presently weeded out) *shall each of them be for, &c.* a frame of speech, like that, ch. 6.10. of which, see there.

*{for the sending forth*} Or, *sending in*, as others render it. For sending out, or putting of beasts, to wit, there to feed freely, as in places lying open, and unkept; for cattle to graze on, (as, *for briars and thorns*, ver. 23.) as not reserved for any other use.

*{of oxen*} Heb. *ox*, as ch. 1.3. ver. 21. and so afterward here the like.

*{and for the treading*} Going to and fro, into any part of them, without let, or restraint.

*{of lesser cattle*} *Of sheep, or goats*. For the word comprehends either, Exod. 3.1. They shall range and graze freely, after their wonted manner, in those places from whence they and their owners had formerly been ejected and excluded, by the violent oppressions, and undue enclosures of the richer and greater sort, ch. 5.17.

### CHAPTER 8

**V. 1.** *{Moreover the Lord said, &c.*} Here begins the sixth sermon, or prophecy, of Esay, in this book recorded; contained in the five chapters next ensuing, which make all but one continued discourse: and that of the same nature, and subject matter, for the most part, with that next before going, ch. 7. for it consists partly, of denunciation of judgments against Aram and Israel, and partly of a prediction of such evils and calamities, as should befall Judah by Assur, together with a mixture of such matter of comfort, as might support the faithful under the same, and give them ground of hopeful expectation of a gracious issue of them: but the former directed unto Ahaz, and his courtiers; this, directed, and in writing therefore publicly exposed, to the people.

*{Moreover*} Heb. *And*. But so also rendered, Jer. 3.1. & 33.1. by some other here, *For*, as ch. 9.11. & 64.4, 5. But because it is no prosecution of any former narration; but a relation of a new after-revelation, or vision: I suppose it should rather be rendered, *Again*: as Ezek. 16.1.

*{the Lord said*} Or, as some, *hath said*; as if it were a speech delivered at one and the same time with the former: but of that there is no likelihood.

*{unto me*} In a vision, or by special revelation. See ch. 1. ver. 1.

*{Take thee*} As Gen. 6.21. & 14.21. So, *go thee*, Gen. 12.1. and, *Ask thee*, ch. 7.11. see there.

*{a roll*} Or, *a volume*; that is, such a parcel of vellum, or paper; as being fitted for writing, and written in, might be rolled up, and unrolled, as occasion was to make use of it. See of such rolls, Jer. 36.2, 23. Rev. 6.14. Howbeit, when I say, *vellum, or paper*, my meaning is not, that the *roll*, which the prophet made use of, was either of vellum, that is, some kind of *parchment*, such as we now use; or of paper, such as we now commonly so term: for the invention of either of these, seems to be far later than Esay's days; before which the most common and general use for such purposes, as we now use those, was the strip of an Egyptian cane, or reed, which the Greeks and Latins call *papyre*, from whence our English word, *paper*; though our paper be of another matter and manner of making, than that was. See on ch. 19.7. by these terms therefore, I here mean, such materials then in use, as were correspondent to those now in use with us. Howbeit, the word here used, is by some questioned; whether it signifies such a *roll*, or no: And some would have it rendered, not *a roll*, but *a patent*, in allusion to that of the open instrument, Jer. 32.11. or, *a page*, because the Talmudists so term the *marge* of any writing, that is pure and unwritten: the reason is, say they, because the word here used, comes not from the word, that signifies *to roll up*, as that does, Jer. 36.2. but from one that signifies, *to reveal, or, lay open*: of which, see more on ch. 3.23. but the Hebrew doctors go the former way, and derive it from the same root with that other, from which, although it does not so regularly descend, yet it so falls out in that language, that oft-times words retain the signification, not of their own proper root, but of some other near unto it, in sound rather, than in sense. Nor does it hinder, but that it may well be styled, *a roll*, albeit, the words have no such proper notation, the use of such *rolls* being so common in those times, Ps. 40.7. Ezek. 2.9, 10. Others choose rather to render it, *a table*, ch. 30.8.
