Hab. 2.2. and their reason is, because he is willed to *write*, or *engrave* on it, *with a style*; which, say they, on parchment, or paper, is not done; but *with a pen*, or *quill*. And they suppose it therefore to have been *a table of marble-stone*, or of *brass*, or *lead*: or the like, Exod. 34.1. Job 19.24. Jer. 17.1. but the word may as well signify, *a writer's pen*, as *a graver's tool*, as hereafter shall be shown: and the word, *write*, not *engrave*, carries it rather to *a book*, or *roll*: than such a *table* as these talk of. Nor do we read, that the prophets did any of them engrave their sermons on such, nor do those places produced, prove it. See on ch. 30.8.

*{a great roll*} Because much matter to be written in it, and that in a fair and large letter. For this prophecy to be therein engrossed, was longer than ordinary: as that also which Jeremy by Baruch's hand, wrote in *a great roll*, being a draught of all his former prophecies, Jer. 36.2.

*{and write*} That being so written, and exposed to public view, it may the better be weighed, and the more seriously considered, as such things are generally deemed to be weighty, which are solemnly engrossed, as also, that being by means thereof, commonly read and known, the truth of the prophecy, upon the event thereof, might the more fully be cleared and confirmed; the prophet having, as it were, pawned his credit thereupon, Deut. 18.21, 22. Jer. 28.19. And lastly, that it might, as upon record, remain unto posterity, Deut. 31.19. Job 19.23. ch. 30.8. Jer. 32.10, 11, 14. Hab. 2.2, 3.

*{in it*} Heb. *upon it*; as we use to say, *write upon parchment, or paper*. Yet the phrase is elsewhere, *to write in a roll, or a book*, Job 19.23. Ps. 40.7. But the former particle is here rather used; because the latter follows prefixed unto the next word, taken instrumentally, as Job 19.24. Jer. 17.1.

*{with a pen*} Either of *quill, cane, or reed*. For such also were the *pens*, anciently in use. The word here is nowhere else found: but another word that answers it, signifies as well a scrivener's, or writer's *pen*, Ps. 46.1. Jer. 8.8. as a graver, or carver's *tool*, Exod. 32.4. Jer. 17.1. So may the word also, here found, be used for either. And here the rather for the former, for the reason above rendered.

*{a man's pen*} By this some of the Jewish doctors understand to be meant only, *a material pen*; so termed, in opposition to that *imaginary pen*, that he saw in the vision, like that *razor* that Ezekiel saw in the same manner, Ezek. 5.1. which was not *a man's razor*, no more than this *a man's pen*. But this is a mere groundless fancy. For it appears not, that either Isaiah, or Ezekiel had any such apparition representing that, as in some visible or imaginary form, that is here or there mentioned, but by a secret suggestion, or instinct, which was sufficient, an injunction to do the same: as when a man would have a scribe, or notary, to draw some instrument for him, he need not show him a pen, or paper, but give him instruction only, what he would have him to write. Others therefore understand it, not so much of the *pen* itself, as of the *letter*, or the *style*, as we also term it. Some of the *letter*, that it should not be written in some strange character, that few could read, as that doom passed upon Baltasar, Dan. 5.8, 15. but in a plain familiar letter, in an ordinary hand; such as any one might easily read; and that also so fair and large that it might be read aloof off, and without any long stay, Hab. 2.2. Some again of the *style*, to wit, that it should be conceived and delivered, not in an obscure, and dark enigmatical, or symbolical manner; as that few capacities should reach it; that part of it especially, concerning the matter of Ahaz his fear, the overthrow of his two potent adversaries, by the King of Assyria, and the scourging of him and his, afterward with the same rod. For they deserve no regard, who would have it meant to be so written, that no brutish party, but *a man* indeed, a man of wisdom and understanding, Ps. 37.17, 22. & 92.6. Prov. 30.2. Mic. 6.9. should be able to conceive it; as *the number of a man*, Rev. 13.18. The word *Enosh*, here used, (of which, see on ch. 2.9.) will not bear it. Nor does that seem so sound, which some have, who would understand it, neither of the letter, nor of the frame of speech, but of the subject matter of God's injunction; that it should be transacted, not according to the *style* of the Court of heaven, where there needs no more, than God's own will, for the passing of aught, Ps. 115.3. & 135.6. Dan. 4.35. Ephes. 1.11. but according to the *style*, or manner of proceeding in human courts, wherein witnesses are wont to be produced; and nothing done is firm, or of force, without them, Deut. 19.15. 2 Cor. 13.1. and so the prophet also carried the business, by God enjoined him, ver. 2. But that phrase of the *style*, of this, or that court, is of too late an edition; nor has it age enough to give authority to such an exposition.

*{concerning Maher-shalal-hash-baz*} Or, *for Maher-shalal-hash-baz*, as Ezek. 37.16. *for Judah, and for Joseph*. Or, as others, without either, only *Maher-shalal-hash-baz*, because the particle here used, is not afterward repeated, ver. 3. This latter way many, yea, the most run; supposing that there was nothing more written in this great roll, but these four words. Which, because it seems very improbable, they add, some of them, that it is called, *a great roll*, not from the bigness, or largeness of the volume, but because it was to contain great mysteries: and others of them, that princes' patents, though never so short, are wont to be engrossed in large paper, or parchment, and great letters. But not to insist on the forced construction of the one, and the unusualness of such brevity in the other: beside the improbability of the thing itself, it would not reach the main intent, and purpose of this divulging it in writing, when as scarce any one, the prophet himself excepted, would be able to understand what were thereby meant. The former, therefore, that render the particle, *concerning*, or, *for*, suppose this whole sermon, or prophecy, was to be engrossed in it; and that, as they conceive, after the usual manner of the prophets, who used to put their sermons in writing; and having so done, to affix them on some gate of the Temple: whence, after they had hung there certain days, the priests took them down, and so laid them up, if they were by them approved, and so they were laid up, and came to be preserved for posterity. Now what they say concerning this particular prophecy, is acknowledged. But what is affirmed concerning an ordinary custom herein, is groundless, and nothing probable. It appears not, that the prophets used commonly, by writing, and affixing them, in any public place, for the view of all, so to divulge them. The very places that they produce for proof of it; this, and ch. 30.8. & Hab. 2.2. rather intimate the contrary. For what need was there to give order for some special prophecies in this kind, if that were the ordinary dealing with all. Neither is it to be believed, that if most of the prophecies, both of Jeremy's, and divers others, had been so affixed, the priests, that then were, would have taken them in, and had such care of them; and not rather have pulled them down, and torn them in pieces; especially having so maliciously and eagerly persecuted the prophets, as false prophets, for delivering them by word of mouth, Jer. 20.1, 2. & 26.8, 11. & 29.26. This prophecy therefore, as some few other, was by a special command of God, thus written, and divulged; which, with other, the like, was not usual.

*{concerning Maher-shalal-hash-baz*} That is, concerning your son *Maher-shalal-hash-baz*; so to be named; for as yet he was not, but is by that name, here so styled, in way of anticipation; of which there are many the like examples in Scripture. See Gen. 12.18. with Gen. 28.19. & 13.10. with 9.22. & 33.17. Exod. 16.3. Josh. 7.24, 26. Judg. 15.19. The participle is used for *of*, or *concerning*, Gen. 20.13. Ps. 91.11. Howbeit a late learned writer would have it rendered here, as it most usually signifies, *to him*, or *for him*; as if the discourse written, were to be inscribed, and dedicated to him.

*{Maher-shalal-hash-baz*} These words are very variously rendered. Some *in making speed to the spoil, he hasteneth the prey*. Some, *to make speed to spoil*; (as Exod. 12.33.) *and haste to prey*. Some, *to the speedy spoiler; make haste to prey*. Some *a speedy robber: an hasty spoiler*; or, *a speedy spoiler; and one that hasteneth to the prey*. Some, *make speed to spoil; hasten to prey*. And they are as diversely understood. For (to let pass all other) some take them as a name intended, not for the prophet's son; but as the name *Emmanuel*, in the foregoing prophecy; for Christ, who at his coming in the flesh, seized on the strong man, that held possession of men's hearts before, and prevailing against him, as one stronger than he, 1 Joh. 4.4. dispossessed him, disarmed him, despoiled him, and divided his spoils, Luk. 11.21. Ephes. 4.8. Col. 2.15. and they would have them to be the words of God the Father, speaking unto the Son, as encouraging him thereunto. Somewhat like unto those, Ps. 2.8, 7. And this way, as by shoals, run the ancient Fathers, and most Popish Writers; and some few others also of no small note. But others, and so the most and the soundest, understand it, as having reference to the King of Assyria; as intimating what he should speedily do unto Israel and Syria: that which both the subject matter of the foregoing chapter, and so the sequel of the context here leads us unto, ver. 3, 4. Howbeit, I cannot subscribe to the curious nicety of those of them, that would divide the words into two branches; the one containing the inscription of an epistle, that the prophet should be enjoined to write unto the King of Assyria; as John to the seven churches of Asia, Rev. 1.11. the other of them, the epistle itself. *To the speedy spoiler*; there is the inscription. *Make haste to prey*; there the epistle itself. Nor to those that would make them to be distinct names, *Maher-shalal*, the one; and *Hash-baz*, the other.

**V. 2.** *{And I took unto me faithful witnesses to record*} Or, *Then*, as Gen. 18.10. & 32.21, 22. Or, *wherefore*, as Neh. 2.2. Jer. 1.17. & 6.11. & 7.16. Heb. *I will cause to attest to me witnesses*: the future for the preterimperfect: as Ps. 18.36, 37.

*{faithful witnesses*} That which some comment here, concerning witnesses, used in marriage contracts, as if the prophet were about taking him a new wife, is nothing to the purpose. And further yet do they stray, that would hence infer, that all here spoken, as those things also related, Hos. 1.2, 3. & 3.1. were done only in vision, as if the persons here mentioned, were intended to be witnesses of the prophet's companying with his wife. *Witnesses* were used by him, because the matter was of much importance, 2 Cor. 13.1. and *faithful*, or, *firm witnesses*; that is, persons of credit, in regard of their place and authority, and such, as no exception could be taken against; as if they should herein collude with the prophet.

*{to record*} Or, *bear witness*. Both of the name that the prophet imposed on his child, (which was usually done, at the time of circumcision, Luk. 1.59. & 2.21.) either being lately born; as some: or, as yet unborn; as others. (for so also before birth, some have been named, 1 King. 13.2. ch. 45.1. Mat. 1.21. Luk. 1.13.) And of the reason why that name was, by God, enjoined to be given him, see ver. 3. Though some so understand it, as if these men were called in to be present, at the prophet's affixing at the draught of his prophecy on the door of the Temple; or in some other public place, to bear witness of the same: which needed not, when, as his name, without question, was in that writing expressed, and annexed thereunto.

*{Uriah the Priest*} Here some move a question, how this *Uriah* should be termed, *a faithful witness*; when as he was a man unfaithful to God in his place, and complied with the king in his idolatrous courses, 2 King. 16.10, 11, 15, 16. But to this is answered. First, that a man may be a good witness, though he be not a good man. He may be firm to man, though he be not faithful to God. Secondly that the word *firm*, or, *faithful*, is not used to imply the approved goodness, or piety of the party mentioned; but their fitness for such a business, in regard of their esteem with man. Thirdly, that Uriah, for aught appears, might not, as yet, carry himself otherwise, than was befitting his place and profession; albeit, that afterward he revolted. Fourthly, some say, which yet I make some doubt of, that the prophet of purpose, knowing what manner of man he was, made choice of him for the one; because he would have witnesses of both sorts; thereby to intimate, that this prophecy was such, as neither good, nor bad should be able to contradict. Fifthly, that whether he were good or bad, or bore a show of that which indeed he was not; he might be very fit for this business, in regard of his interest with Ahaz, whom the same did so nearly concern.

*{and Zachariah the son of Jeberechiah*} Who this Zachariah should be, is uncertain. The Jewish doctors, according to their idle dotages, (whom yet some of ours also, herein, follow) tell us, as of *Uriah*, that prophesied under Jehojakim, Jer. 26.20. So of those two *Zacharies*, the one that prophesied under Joash, 2 Chr. 24.20. the other, that prophesied after the return from the captivity, Ezr. 5.1. Zach. 1.1. And that these are mentioned, as *witnesses*, because their prophecies, for the matter of them agreed much with this of Esay. And if it be objected, that the one of these was dead long before, 2 Chr. 24.21. the other two were, as yet, unborn. They would put this off, by affirming that all this was done but in a vision; and nothing therefore hinders, but that such might be induced as *witnesses*, who, at that time, were not in being. And those of ours, that herein concur with them, allege Moses, and Elias appearing with our Savior, at his transfiguration; as if that also were but some imaginary matter, Matth. 17.4. But leaving these frivolous surmises to their authors; there is no doubt to be made, but that, this *Zachariah*, as well as the former *Uriah*, was one that then lived. And it is deemed by many, (nor is it altogether improbable) that it was that *Zachariah*, whose daughter, *Abi*, or *Abijah*, was wife to Ahaz, who, by her, had Ezekiah, 2 King. 18.2. 2 Chr. 29.1. And this Zachariah, they suppose to be joined with Uriah; that by two of principal note, the one in the Ecclesiastical, the other in the civil state, this weighty matter might be attested. Others deem it to have been that *Zachariah* the prophet, that prophesied under Uzziah, a great part of his time; and is said to have been a man of *understanding in the visions of God*, 2 Chr. 26.5. and so the two witnesses might be a priest, and a prophet. But this I suppose to be the less probable; for that the holy story seems to imply, that this Zachariah deceased before the fall of Uzziah. Nor is there any ground for that which others guess, of one *Zachariah* a Levite, of some note, in Ezekiah's days, 2 Chr. 29.13. save that he lived in those times.

*{Zachariah*} Heb. *Zecharjahu*. For which the Greek, usually, has *Zacharias*, Luk. 1.5. We in English, commonly, *Zachary*. See ch. 1.1.

*{the son of Jeberechiah*} Heb. *Jeberechjahu*; as before, instead whereof, the Greek and old Latin read, *Barachias*: The latter, in likelihood, the rather, because they found *Zachary the son of Barachias*, mentioned, Matth. 23.35. However the names differ little, and with divers others, both father and son, might have the same names, as *Joseph the son of Jacob*, Gen. 30.25. and Matth. 1.16. and *Zorovabel, the son of Salathiel*, Matth. 1.12. & Luk. 3.27. for they seem not to be the same.

**V. 3.** *{And I went unto, &c.*} From hence some of our chief interpreters collect, and are somewhat stiff in it; that all that is here mentioned, was done in a vision. And some doubts and difficulties, indeed, arise from the words thus read; though not such, as may necessarily enforce, any such matter. But they may all be cut off, by reading the words thus, (which the Hebrew will well admit) *For I had gone into, &c.* As rendering a reason, or relating the occasion wherefore, or whereupon God should give him this charge, concerning his child that was to be named, to wit, because his wife was lately delivered of a son. So both the verb, and particle, are in construction alike used, Gen. 12.1. *For the Lord had said unto Abraham*.

*{went unto*} Or, *had gone into*; as some render it. A modest form of speech, expressing the marriage duty, very frequent in Scripture, Gen. 6.4. & 29.29. and the same more fully, as opening the ground of the phrase, Judg. 15.1. *I will go to my wife, into the chamber*; to wit, where man and wife use to be private. But the Hebrew word here used, signifies properly *to approach*; *I approached*, or, *had approached unto, &c.* and so it is used, Gen. 20.4. Lev. 18.6, 14. Ezek. 18.6.

*{the Prophetess*} That is, a virgin, say some, endued with the gift of prophecy, as Mary, Deborah, and Huldah are said to have been Prophetesses, Exod. 15.22. Judg. 4.4. 2 King. 22.14. groundlessly dreaming, that the prophet should wed him a new wife: and that this should be that *virgin*, the mother of *Emmanuel*, before mentioned, ch. 7.14. But the *Prophetess* here, is no other than the *Prophet's wife*: the same, in likelihood, by whom he had *Shear-jashub* before ch. 7.3. So it is observed, that in divers languages, the wives are styled by their husbands' offices, and dignities; as *Duke, Duchess; Count, Countess; Mayor, Mayoress, &c.*

*{and she conceived*} Or, *had conceived*: or, *was with child*. See on ch. 7.14.

*{and bare a son*} Or, *had born a son*. Was new delivered of a male-child, to wit, before ever he received this vision from God, or the charge was given him concerning the naming of the child, and the engrossing of the prophecy, intimated in that name, together with it.

*{a son*} The same, say some, mentioned, ch. 7.14. A fond conceit, better befitting Jews than Christians.

*{Then said the Lord to me*} That is, after the Prophetess was delivered of the child. Heb. *And*: but so it is rendered, also, ver. 2. And so also, Neh. 2.2. Job 13.22. & 40.3. Hos. 1.9. Yet it may be retained here, in its first and proper sense; as in the like, Hos. 1.4, 6.

*{said*} As ver. 1.

*{Call his name*} Call him; as ch. 7.14. Let this be the name whereby he shall be called; as Jer. 23.6. & 33.16.

*{Maher-shalal-hash-baz*} The Hebrews used oft-times to give names, as well to persons, as to places, consisting of divers words. So Gen. 16.13, 14. & 22.14. and 35.28. Judg. 6.32. 1 Chr. 1.20. & 3.19, 22. & 4.30, 31. Jer. 20.3. of the signification of this name, see on v. 1. Of the reason of imposing it, see ver. 4. Howbeit, they swerve far from the truth, and the intent of the prophet, that would have one and the same child have two names; *Emmanuel*, to intimate God's assistance of them, against those their two enemies, Rezin, and Pekah, ch. 7.1, 5. ver. 10. and *Maher-shalal-hash-baz*, to signify the rifling and ruining of them; and that speedily, by the King of Assyria, ver. 4. The name consists of two parts, both in divers words, but of the same sense, implying the same thing; and that by reduplication thereof, to intimate the infallibility of it, and the nearness of its approach: as Gen. 41.32.

**V. 4.** *{For before the child shall have knowledge, to cry, My Father, and My Mother, &c.*} In this verse is the reason given, why God would have the child so called; to wit, thereby to intimate the speedy direption and destruction of those two kings, and their chief cities, by the forces and followers of the King of Assyria.

*{the child*} This child, that is lately now born, and so named: not Christ, as some; nor *a child*, that is any child indefinitely, as others. See ch. 7.16.

*{shall have knowledge*} Heb. *shall know*; or, *shall be able*. So is the word of *knowing*, oft taken: as ch. 56.11. Jer. 6.15.

*{to cry*} Or, *to call*, as v. 3.

*{My father, and my mother*} Or, *My father, or my mother*: either of both, as Exod. 21.15. *He that smites his father, and his mother*, for, *father, or mother*: and children begin, usually, to call *mother* first; because most frequent about them in that age; and the children therefore most familiar with them. The meaning is, before the child shall be able to speak, and to distinguish his parents from strangers. And this seems a shorter time, than that, ch. 7.16. *before the child know to refuse evil, and choose good*. For children are sooner of ability to speak some few familiar words; than of discretion, to understand what belongs to good and evil: and the reason of the divers form of speech used, concerning either, is; because the one, to wit, *Shear-jashub*, might then be some two, or three year old: whereas *Maher-shalal-hash-baz*, was but newly now born; and yet might be as soon able to speak, as the other might be to conceive difference between good and evil. See further on ch. 7.16.

*{The riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria shall be taken away*} The two kingdoms of Israel and Syria, shall be stripped and spoiled of their wealth, and treasure, by the King of Assyria.

*{the riches of Damascus*} The head city of Syria, ch. 7.8. and a place of great wealth: or, as others, *the power of Damascus*. The word signifies either; and *riches* are one principal thing, wherein the *strength* of a state consists.

*{and the spoil of Samaria*} The head city of Israel, ch. 7.9.

*{the spoil*} Not the people. For he speaks rather of a direption, in the child's name intimated, done by Tiglath-Pileser, under Pekah, 2 King. 15.29. than of an utter depopulation, made by Salmaneser, under Hoshea, 2 King. 17.6, 14. though some people also were in that former invasion captived.

*{shall be taken away*} Heb. *he shall take away*, or, *one shall take away*. The verb being taken indefinitely, or impersonally, (the form of speech, see on ch. 2.19.) and therefore well here rendered.

*{before the King of Assyria*} As conquerors are wont to send their rich spoils oft-times, into their own country before them, to give notice of their victories and surprisals, to their people; or to cause them, as the usual manner of the Romans was, to be carried before their stately chariots in triumph: yet some would have it to be a defective speech, and render the words thus; *he* that is, or stands, *before the Kings of Assyria*; that is, his officers, ministers, or attendants, (for so are men said to *be*, or *to stand before the face* of them whom they serve, or attend on, 1 Sam. 16.16. 1 King. 1.2. & 10.8. & 17.1.) *shall carry away*. But the former seems the more familiar.

**V. 5.** *{The Lord spake, also unto me again, saying*} Heb. *And the Lord further added to speak unto me*, as ch. 7.10. Here begins a second part of this chapter. Wherein, as in the latter part of the former, from ver. 17. he foretells what evils should befall the land, both of Israel and Judah; from the King of Assyria, on the one, for their scorn, and contempt of their brethren, and confederating with the Assyrians, to work their overthrow; on the other, for their distrusting of God, and relying upon the Assyrians, by whom they should also suffer; withal, admonishing the godly among them, to be cautious, and to rest upon God alone, and his Word, who had promised to secure them in those calamitous times.

**V. 6.** *{Forasmuch as this people, &c.*} Who the people there spoken of, should be, is very doubtful. Some understand thereby, the people of Judah, or a great part of them, who considering how low their state was brought, and distrusting those weak provisions, as they esteemed them, that their chief city had to maintain a siege against two such potent princes, as were combined together against them, desired to have one of those two to govern them; or that *Son of Tabeel* before mentioned, ch. 7.6. to be set over them; and had underhand, some treacherous compliance with them, to that purpose. So the Hebrew doctors, whom also many of ours follow. But of this we find little ground, either in the sacred story, or elsewhere, in this prophecy. Others therefore, rather suppose the people mentioned, to be the people of Israel; who slighted, and set light by the kingdom of Judah, as having been by the incursions both of the Syrians and themselves, so exceedingly impaired, and by Rezin and Pekah now joined in one, made full account to make full conquest of it, ch. 7.6. For, as for those that interpret it, of the Jewish people in general, that not contenting themselves with God's promised protection, rested upon the Assyrian: they are enforced, for the making good of this their interpretation (wherein, few, or none follow them) to offer overmuch force to the text.

*{this people*} Spoken, as in contempt of them, who so scorned and contemned God's people, as not desiring once to name them. See the like of the other, ch. 6.9.

*{refuse*} Or, rather, *despise, contemn*: For in that, or the like sense, is the word here used, constantly taken. The word of *refusing*, though coming near to it, does in a letter differ from it.

*{the waters of Shiloah*} A fountain called also Gihon, 1 King. 1.33. issuing forth from the foot of mount Sion; and yielding a rivulet, that watered the lower city, Ps. 46.4. Neh. 3.15. Joh. 9.7. See ch. 7.2. Put here, as some, for the house of David, now at a low ebb; or rather, for such defense, as Jerusalem, and the state of Judah then had. Which they slighted and scorned, as if they had nothing but such a sorry rivulet, as that was, to strengthen and secure their head city; not considering the power of God, by such weak means, though no other were able to protect it. See ch. 33.21. albeit, I suppose they wander wide, that would have *Siloah* here put for God's protection itself.

*{that run softly*} Spoken, in way of opposition, to great rivers, that run with a strong torrent, and stiff stream. This rivulet, or the waters issuing from this fountain, are therefore deemed to run slowly, or softly, partly, because the current was not great; and partly; because in its own course it went not straight forward; but with many windings to and fro, in manner of a serpent, that moves slowly, and slyly, creeping, and crooking, ch. 27.1. supposed therefore by some, to be termed, *the dragon's well*, Neh. 2.13.

*{and rejoice in Rezin, and Remaliah's son*} This, some expound of those malcontents, in the Jewish State, that desired, and would gladly be under another government, either Rezin's, or Pekah's, or, of both jointly. Others, of those, to the Jews ill affected in Israel, that vaunted much of, and promised themselves great matters from the conjunction of those two kings, ch. 7.1. and rejoiced greatly in their successes. The Hebrew, word for word, runs thus, *and joy is with Rezin, and the son of Remaliah*, or *Remaljahu*: as also, ch. 7.4. which some fill up, as if it were a defective speech, on this manner, *and joy, is to them, of fighting with Rezin, &c.* as if he had said, they rejoice, or would fain be fighting with Rezin, and Pekah; relying on the aid they looked for, from the King of Assyria: by whose help they doubted not, but to be able to bicker with, and beat them both. But this exposition, as before was said, offers too much violence to the context. The meaning therefore is, rather, that Rezin and Pekah, as they joined together against Judah; so it was matter of much joy to them, to see it so weakened: as thereby conceiving undoubted hope, to prevail, at pleasure, against it. See ch. 7.7, 8. And this exposition is most agreeable to the tenor both of this, and the former chapter.

*{rejoice*} Or, *joy is*. The noun seems rather to be used, than the verb, to make it sound like the former word of contempt. For with such similitude and nearness of sounds, in terms especially of divers, or adverse notions, our prophet seems to have been much delighted; and they have an elegancy in them. See ch. 3.24. & 5.7.

*{Remaliah's son*} So still the prophet in contempt styles him, as one unworthy to be named, or termed king of Israel, being sprung from base parentage, and having by murder got the crown. See ch. 7.4.

**V. 7.** *{Now therefore*} Heb. *And as therefore*; or, *in like manner*. For a retaliation is implied; as they intend, and desire, to be eftsoon doing with Judah: so by a stronger one, than either Judah, or themselves, shall they be dealt with.

*{behold*} Look for it, and that soon, and suddenly; though you neither expect, nor will easily believe it; yet it shall both surely and speedily be accomplished. See ch. 3.1. & 5.26.

*{the Lord bringeth up*} Heb. *is making to ascend*, or, *bringing*; as Jer. 3.7. and, *is taking away*, ch. 3.1. he is even about to do it; it will, out of hand, begin to be done. See v. 4.

*{bringeth up*} Spoken, say some, of the Jewish doctors especially, who would have their land to be the *navel* of the whole earth, (abusing to that purpose, a passage, in Ps. 72.12. Ezek. 38.12. and the highest land in the world) in regard of the situation of the country of Assyria, in relation to the holy land, as lying far lower than it. See ch. 7.1. but it seems rather, to have respect to the rising of some great rivers, surrounding the lower grounds. See on Jer. 49.19.

*{upon them*} Or, *over them*. The people before spoken of, ver. 6. not those of Judah, (for of them afterwards, ver. 8.) but of Israel, on whom this storm first fell; and were in the first place overwhelmed with it, 2 King. 15.29. & 17.3. See ch. 7.20. It is here opposed to *Shiloah*, a small rivulet, running quietly, without much noise, or strong stream, ver. 6. which they therefore set light by, as unable either to do any hurt to their land, or to impeach them in their passage and approaches to Jerusalem: instead whereof, God would send in upon them a great river, such an one as had water store, and ran with a swift and a strong current, which used to break through, or swell over his banks, and so surround the land near unto it.

*{even the King of Assyria*} See ch. 7.17. The King of Assyria shall break in upon them; not like the waters of Shiloah; but like the streams of Euphrates, his own country river. So are mighty commanders with their forces invading of some land, resembled oft to rivers breaking in upon the lower grounds. See ch. 28.2. & 49.19. Jer. 50.44. Dan. 11.22.

*{and all his glory*} Or, *with all his glory*; as ch. 5.14. His armies, or forces, consisting of valiant soldiers; and led by brave captains and commanders, ch. 10.16. in whom, he much gloried, and of whom he so much vaunted, ch. 16.8. & 36.9. & 37.25. and that made a glorious show generally, in the eyes of the people; because by them, he subdued so many countries, ch. 20.9, 10, 13, 14. and 30.18, 20. & 37.11, 12, 13, 18.

*{and he shall*} That is, the King of Assyria shall; or, as others, *it shall*, to wit, the river before mentioned, the Assyrian's followers, and forces: because in that metaphor the prophet proceeds.

*{shall come up*} As before; *the Lord is bringing up*. See there.

*{over all his channels*} Whereby most understand all the valleys, or lower parts of the land, invaded by the Assyrian, and surrounded by him. But whether they take the word to signify *channels*, as some; or *streams*, or *rivers*, or, *streams of rivers*, as others; from Ps. 78.15. & 42.1. & 126.4. It seems no very fit, or handsome expression, to represent the direption, or destruction of a land, or state, by overflowing, or (if I may so say) drowning of *streams*, or *rivers*: (which may rather be deemed an increasing, and enlarging of them) or, of *channels, and watercourses*, which is rather a filling them, and supplying them, if they were empty, of what they wanted before. Some few other therefore understand it of the great river Euphrates its own *channels*; for it divided itself into divers branches, and ran consequently, in many *channels*, or *streams*. But then to say, that a river should *come up over his own channels*, seems as improper a phrase, as a resemblance of the former. The reading therefore would be altered, and the words rendered, either, *with all his streams*, as the particle is used, Exod. 35.22. where the words are, *the men with the women*: and Job 38.32. *Arcturus with his sons*: or, *from off all his channels*: with supply of a particle, sometime deficient, and left to be supplied; as Gen. 4.1. *I have gotten a son from the Lord*: and Ps. 81.5. *when he went forth from the land of Egypt*. The defective form of speech, the prophet seems the rather here to have used: that there might be the more exact correspondence between the two members of this latter clause. The meaning is, that the King of Assur should bring all the forces he could make, along with him; as before it was said, he should come *with all his glory*: or, rather, should take people, (compared to waters, Rev. 17.15.) to serve him in this expedition, out of all parts of his dominion, which branched itself out into many countries; as Euphrates itself also into many channels and streams.

*{and go*} Heb. *walk*: as Ps. 104.26. *there walk the ships*.

*{over all his banks*} His own banks, as Josh. 3.15. & 4.18. & 12.25. to wit, those of the river before mentioned. For they seem much mistaken, who apply this also, as the former, to the land, whether of Israel, or Judah, invaded; and by banks, understand high places, fortresses, and fenced cities, that should no more escape the Assyrian forces, than lower, lesser, and less fortified places, 2 King. 15.29. & 17.16. & 18.10, 13. nor do they seem to understand the prophet aright, who by surrounding of *banks*, suppose breach of oaths and covenants, to be meant; though that be true in the story, 2 King. 18.14, 17. ch. 33.7. but it seems not so fit here.

**V. 8.** *{And he shall pass through Judah*} Or, *it* (to wit, this flood; v. 8.) *shall pass through also* (as ver. 5.) *unto*, or, *into Judah*: as Num. 16.21. The King of Assyria having subdued Israel, the ten Tribes, shall make his way by them so subdued, and pierce through, as a stiff torrent, with full stream, into the land of Judah. See 2 King. 18.10, 11, 13. and of the Chaldees, Hab. 1.11.

*{he shall overflow, and go over*} Heb. *it overfloweth, and passeth over*, or, *through*. It swells, and goes on, carrying all away before it, and rising higher and higher. See the same form of speech, ch. 28.15, 18. Dan. 11.10, 40. Some would have the former word of *passing*, and this here, though divers terms, to intend the same thing. Others distinguish them over-nicely. The difference, I suppose, in the use of them, is no other than this, that the one denotes the enemy's passage to, and entrance into Judea; the other his progress, in the conquest of it.

*{he shall reach even to the neck*} Or, *it shall*; to wit, the inundation. So ch. 38.28. *an overflowing stream, reaching to the midst of the neck*: And the like, Hab. 3.13. It is a metaphor, say some, taken from those that go into the water by degrees, first up to the knees, then to the waist, and so on, till they have gone up to the neck. But it is rather taken from those, whom waters breaking in upon, in a deluge, rise and swell so high with them, that they can hardly keep head above water. The meaning is, that all Judah should be in danger of being utterly lost: as the whole body is in danger to be drowned, when the water comes up so near the head. Thus it was under Ezekiah; when Sennacherib having surrounded the whole land almost, even to the wall of Jerusalem, their head city, (see Jer. 34.7.) and surprised the most of their cities, did much distress it; and had, questionless, carried it; had not God vouchsafed them an unexpected, and extraordinary deliverance, ch. 36.1, 2, 12. & 37.3, 35, 36.

*{and the stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of thy land*} Or, as some, *and it shall be, that the extensions of his wings shall fill the breadth of thy land*. So they render it, because the verb is singular, the noun plural. But the Hebrew will well bear another construction; to wit, *The fullness of the breadth of thy land, shall be the extension of his wings*; as ch. 6.3. *the fullness of the whole land*, or, *earth, is*, or shall be, *his glory*; or, inserting one particle, which the former place also will well admit; *The fullness of the breadth* (that is, the full breadth) *of thy land, shall be for the stretchings out of his wings*: The meaning is, that the Assyrian troops should overspread the whole land from the one side to the other; like a mighty river, or vast sea, that not breaking in, at some gap, or narrow breach, in the sea-walls, or dams, but with full breadth, all along at once, surrounding its whole banks, does with a joint stream rush on, as it passes forward, overwhelming the whole breadth of the country before it. See ch. 9.15. & 11.14. and of the Chaldee forces the like, Hab. 1.6.

*{the stretchings-out of his wings*} Some suppose that the prophet here passes to a new similitude; whereby he describes further, the Assyrian invasion, as resembling the King of Assyria by some mighty *eagle*, that spreads his wings over the prey, that he either intends to seize on, or has already surprised. And it is true, that great kings going forth with great armies, are oft compared to such, Jer. 48.40. & 49.22. Ezek. 17.3, 7. and it is likewise acknowledged, that military troops, or companies, as well of foot, as of horse, are here termed *wings*, in allusion to the *wings* of fowls, the larger sort of them especially, which in some sort, they resemble; though the word be otherwise taken in that other place, ch. 18.1. which some of them here produce for it. But it follows not thence, that the prophet's intent here is, to compare the Assyrian king, to some mighty fowl of prey, because he calls his troops, *wings*; no more than Daniel had to decipher Antiochus, as some vast giant, when he calls the forces, that stood on his side, and fought for him, *arms*, Dan. 11.31. They only express the companies of either, by a common figurative term, whereby such are wont to be designated.

*{O Immanuel*} The prophet here turns his speech to Christ, whose land the country of Judah is said to be, because he had a more special interest in it, as being not to be born only in it, but to sit on *David's throne*, sometime King of it, Jer. 30.9. Ezek. 34.23. & 37.29. Luk. 1.32. & 2.11. as also wherein he had the royal seat of his kingdom, his church at present, Ps. 2.6. which by his power therefore was to be protected, relieved under, and delivered out of this great danger and grievous distress, v. 10, 14. Of the name itself, and the person so named, together with the notation of it, and reason thereof rendered, See ch. 7.14.

**V. 9.** *{Associate yourselves, O ye people*} Having made mention of *Emmanuel*, now as confident of his assistance, he heartens, and encourages the faithful to depend upon him, with hopeful expectation of security and protection from him, amidst those common calamities; and a comfortable issue of them in his due time. To which purpose, also, he makes entrance into this part of his sermon, by turning his speech to their adversaries, that conspired, and plotted together against them, willing them, as in way of derision, to proceed as unanimously, as politically, and as powerfully, in their combinations, consultations, and preparations, as they could; but withal, assuring them, that all their associations, should be dissolved, their counsels frustrated, and their attempts returned back upon themselves, to their own ruin and confusion. See the like, Ps. 37.12, 15. Mic. 4.11, 13. ch. 45.11, 12. & 54.15, 17.

*{Associate yourselves*} So the Chaldee, and some of the Jewish teachers, and so the old Latin. For the Greek read *γνῶτε*; by mistake of a letter, wherein oft they have slipped. Yet most of the Hebrew doctors render it, either *break*, or, *Break yourselves, be broken*. Whom some of ours also follow, because it is of the same form with that, Ps. 2.9. ch. 24.19. But it is well known, that verbs of near affinity for letter and sound, though divers in notion, do in the holy language oft interchange forms. And so it is here; for the word that signifies *to associate*, Prov. 24.22. & 19.3. having some affinity in sound, with that which signifies, *to break asunder*; as may appear, where they are both found together; Prov. 13.20, which sometime borrows forms from this, which are not regularly its own. Thus, which they that stumble hereat, might have found; not here alone, but elsewhere, Prov. 18.24. Those, the prophet intends, as well that had now combined themselves, under those two kings of Israel and Syria, ch. 7.1, 2: as also that joined themselves unto Sennacherib, in the invasion of Judah, ch. 36.1; & 10.8.

*{O ye people*} Heb. *Peoples*, in the plural; as chap. 10.13, 14. & 11.10. For there were two peoples, that conspired together: Syrians, and Israelites, against Judah under Ahaz, ch. 7.2. and the army consisted of divers nations, that Sennacherib led against them under Ezekiah, ch. 7.18.

*{and*} Or, *but*: as ch. 7.12.

*{and ye shall be broken in pieces*} As Jer. 50.2. Heb. *and be broken in pieces*. So, *and live and dwell*. For, *and you*, or, *ye shall live, and dwell*, Gen. 42.18. Psal. 37.27. Jer. 25.5; for the imperative is oft put for the future; as on the other side, the future for the imperative, ch. 6.9. Deut. 5.17, 20. All shall turn to your ruin. See this fulfilled, ch. 37.36, 37.

*{and give ear all ye of far countries*} Heb. *all the remote persons*, or, *parts, of the earth*. Listen, says he, and take notice of what I say, ch. 33.13: as giving warning to those foreign people afar off, to take heed what they did, in adjoining themselves to those that invaded God's people, lest they perish all together with them: though some understand it, as the former: spoken in way of derision; like that, to the youngsters, Eccl. 11.9. as if the prophet should say, hearken to the King of Assyria, inviting you to join with him; and prepare yourselves so to do, if you desire your own destruction.

*{gird yourselves*} Arm yourselves; fit, and address yourselves, for warlike expedition; as Ezek. 38.7. alluding to the use of the military belt, of which, see as ch. 3.27. so 2 Sam. 22.40; 1 King. 20.11, Psal. 18.32. ch. 45.5.

*{and ye shall be broken in pieces*} Heb. *and be broken in pieces*; as before. And there is an emphasis in that form of speech, implying, that the one would instantly and inevitably follow upon the other. Yea, that by doing the one, they should be sure to bring upon themselves the other.

*{gird yourselves, and ye shall be broken in pieces*} It is thrice repeated, to work it the deeper into the minds and hearts of those that should hear, or read it, and to give the stronger assurance of it. See ver. 4. ch. 7.17. So Psal. 96.13 and 98.7.

**V. 10.** *{Take counsel together*} Heb. *consult a consultation*; to wit, about invading Judah, and surprising Jerusalem, as they did, ch. 7.5, 6. So Psal. 38.3.

*{and it shall come to nought*} *God bringeth to nought the counsel of the nations*, Psal. 33.10. *and the devices of the crafty*, Job 5.12.

*{speak a word*} Conclude somewhat, determine a thing, resolve upon aught, what you please: *a word*; for, *a thing*: as Job 22.28. *thou shalt decree a word*, or, *a thing, and it shall stand*; but contrariwise here.

*{and*} Or, *but*; as ver. 9.

*{it shall not stand*} See ch. 7.7. You shall not be able, by all the power you can make, or policy you can use, to prevail against those whom God protects, Psal. 62.3, 4. & 64.5, 8.

*{for God is with us*} And if God be with us, and for us, what need we care, who be against us? yea, who can so oppose us, as to prevail against us? Rom. 8.31. they must prevail first against him, before they can prevail against us, 2 King. 6.17. & 2 Chron. 32.7, 8. Zech. 2.5. 1 John 4.4. he alludes to the name of Emmanuel, ch. 7.14. and declares in part, what it imports; and promises, in regard of God's people, God's constant presence with them, to assist and protect them against all oppositions and assaults. Psal. 125.1, 2. Yet I cannot assent to those, that render it, *because Emmanuel's land it is*; though that be said, ver. 8. But it is not necessarily therefore repeated here.

**V. 11.** *{For the Lord spake thus to me*} The prophet proceeds to confirm the godly party, against such groundless fears, as the distrustful sort of them were surprised with; and exhorted them, from taking such courses, as they did; and that by relating to them, what charge God, in a more serious and solemn manner, than ordinary, had to this purpose, delivered to him.

*{For*} A confirmation of what he had before delivered, concerning the issue of those counsels and courses, that the adversaries of God's people should take against them, ver. 9, 10.

*{with a strong hand*} The near shape of two letters in the Hebrew, has as elsewhere oft, so here, bred a diverse reading, but such, as alters not the sense. Some reading the text, *as with*, some without that note of similitude. Where, by *hand*, the Jewish doctors, whom most of ours follow, understand the Spirit of Prophecy, according to that, *the hand of God was upon me*, Ezek. 1.3. & 3.14, 22. as if he had said, the hand of God made a strong impression upon me, what time he gave this in charge. Added, here, both to give fuller assurance of what he was to deliver from God to them: and to make his words carry the more weight with them. The words are in Hebrew, *with strength of hand*, as Dan. 11.2, or, as some render it, *by apprehension of hand*. That is, taking and holding me by the hand, to confirm and strengthen me, as 1 Sam. 23.16. ch. 45.1 & 51.18. Psal. 73.23. Or, taking me by the hand, to cause me to mark what he should say to me; or, taking me by the hand, and drawing me near to him, as men use to do those, whom they have some secret to impart unto, or are to have some special conference with, Act. 23.19: or laying hand on me, as a schoolmaster on his scholar, that would fain be gone from him; and by force, as it were, (as Ezek. 34.4. detaining me with him; and restraining me from such courses, as the people of these times commonly took: according to which last, there should be a trajection in the words, thus to be read; *and*, or, *when, with a strong hand, he curbed me*; or, *kept me in*. And of such trajections we have indeed some examples in the Scripture, 2 King. 2.14. Job 23.12. Prov. 23.24. & 24.27. but it fits not so well here; and the pauses oppose it.

*{and instructed me*} Or, *when he instructed me*, *and*, for *when*; as ch. 43.12. Jer. 34.1.

*{instructed me*} The word signifies properly, *to chastise*, as Psal. 118.18. and because the end of correction is instruction, Psal. 35.11 & 94.12. Prov. 29.15. in the next place, *to instruct*, Prov. 31.1. ch. 28.26, here; as some would have it, *to [couch]*, or keep within compass, I should rather render it, *by instructing warned me*. A form of speech somewhat like those, noted on, ch. 1.4. *alienated backward*. The meaning is, by informing me of the issue of such courses, he warned me, both to refrain them myself; and to teach other so to do.

*{that I should not walk in the way of this people, saying*} Heb. *from walking*: as 1 Sam. 30.21. 2 Chr. 25.13. Lam. 4.18. That I should not take such courses, as they did, concerning the safeguarding, and securing of themselves against those two kings that came to invade them. See Jer. 10.2.

*{this people*} The people of Jerusalem, so affected, as was Ahaz their Sovereign, ch. 7.2, 12, 13.

**V. 12.** *{Say ye not, A confederacy, to all them to whom this people shall say, A confederacy*} He declares here more expressly, what the people's way was, that he would have them to avoid. Do not you, nor the other faithful that follow you, enter into any such confederacy with the Assyrian, or any other foreign force, as the main body of this people, therein following their heads, do; for the securing of yourselves. Such confederacies never proved successful to God's people; 2 Chr. 16.2, 3, 9. & 28.16, 20. ch. 20.6. & 30.4, 5. Jer. 2.33, 37. Yet some of note expound this of the confederacy of Israel, and Syria, against them; the fear whereof so much possessed their minds, that there was nothing else in their mouths, but *a conspiracy, a conspiracy*. Two great and powerful kings and states have conspired together against us, and they will utterly ruin us: and this they suppose confirmed, by the words next ensuing. But neither do the words of the text itself so well bear this exposition; nor those following necessarily infer it.

*{Say ye not a confederacy*} Heb. *Ye shall not say*; as, *This shall ye say* for, *thus say*, ch. 30.4. & 37.10: *say not a confederacy*; that is, *Think not on a confederacy* (as Exod. 2.14. *dost thou say*, that is, *think? to slay me*: and 2 Sam. 21.16, *he said* (that is, *thought*) *to smite David*, or, *Say not a confederacy*, for, *make no confederacy*: as Psal. 35.3. *Say to my soul*, (or *to me*, as Psal. 3.2.) *I am thy salvation*, that is, save me: and, *Say to wisdom, Thou art my sister*; for, make wisdom your sister, Prov. 7.4. and *saying to a stock, Thou art my father*; for, making a stock your father, Jer. 2.27.

*{to all them to whom*} Or, *of*; as Psal. 145.18. Joel 2.32. Rom. 10.13. as if he had said, do not follow this people in their unsteady courses, seeking to link themselves in league, one while with one, and another while with another, Jer. 2.18, 36. make not a confederacy with so many as they do; or rather, *to any of these*: as Job 1.11. *touch any thing*, or, *aught, that he hath*, and Ezek. 18.13. *hath done any of these*. For so those places would both be rendered; make no such league with any of those, Assyrian, Syrian, Egyptian, or other, whom this people combine with.

*{to them*} Or, *concerning them*: and so, *to whom*, *concerning whom*; as Psal. 91.11. Esth. 3.2.

*{to whom*} Intending, say some, the Syrians and Israelites, whom they most exceedingly feared, and many desired to join with, (see on ver. 6.) or, the Assyrians rather principally, (though not waiving any other, that they might look after) whom, for fear of those so combined, they sought to for succor; 2 King. 16.7.

*{neither fear ye their fear*} Fear not those, whom they fear. Stand not in such fear of those two kings, as they do, ch. 7.2. Jer. 10.2.

*{their fear*} Taken here subjectively, for the *fear*, wherewith they fear: but by the apostle Peter alluding unto this place effectively, for that *fear*, wherewith they affright, 1 Pet. 3.14.

*{nor be afraid*} Be not frightened, or terrified. The word signifies such a *fright*, as causes a concussion; makes one so to shake and quake, every joint of him, as if he should fall asunder. The word is used, ch. 2.19, 21. See a pattern of it, Dan. 5.6. and in this people, ch. 7.2. the words are doubled, the more to hearten and encourage; as Deut. 1.29. Josh. 1.9. 1 Pet. 4.14. ch. 7.4. And because this latter seems to import more than the former, some would have it rendered, not, *nor*, as most versions have it; but *much less be so affrighted*, as this people are, ch. 7.2.

**V. 13.** *{Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself*} Heb. *the Lord of Hosts him sanctify*. It is a speech redundant; but yet not without some emphasis: like that of our Savior in the like case, Luk. 12.5. *fear him, that hath power to cast into hell: fear him*. As our Savior there, and Matth. 10.28. so the prophet here having showed, whom they should not fear, does now further advise, and admonish, them whom they should fear.

*{sanctify*} Glorify, give honor to him, by fearing him, and not man, against whom he promises to secure you, by trusting in him, and not seeking to such for safety, as are not able to help or save you, Psal. 60.11. by yielding yourselves wholly into his hands, to be swayed and disposed of, as he shall see good. So Levit. 10.3. Numb. 20.12. and 27.14. Deut. 32.51. Ezek. 20.40, 41. and 36.23, 27.

*{sanctify*} As *magnify*, Psal. 34.3. not to *make holy*, or *great*, but to acknowledge, or make known, that we deem and esteem such. So 1 Pet. 3.15.

*{the Lord of Hosts*} See ch. 1.9. Some here more specially apply it to Emmanuel, or Christ, called *the Prince*, that is, *principal captain*, or *commander in chief of the Lord's host*, Josh. 5.14.

*{and let him be your fear*} He shows more particularly, how they should sanctify God, by fearing God, and not man: Or God, rather than man, ch. 51.12, 13. by fearing none so, as God; nothing in comparison of God: by making him ever the chief, in some kind, the only object of their fear: by fearing nothing, that he forbids them to fear, when the fear of him drowns all other fears. Fear not those two great kings; but fear him that is above them both. See 2 King. 6.16. 2 Chr. 32.7, 8.

*{your fear*} The object of your fear, the party whom you fear; and so in the next branch; thus: *Jacob sware by the fear of his father Isaac*; that is, by that God, whom his father Isaac feared, Gen. 31.53.

*{and let him be your dread*} The word answers that other, verse 12. and signifies, properly, *one that terrifieth*, or affrights: and the sentence is repeated, for the more emphasis and stronger encouragement, as there; so ver. 3, 9, 10.

**V. 14.** *{And he shall be for a sanctuary*} The issue of this their fear of God; and their confidence in him.

*{And*} Or, *Then*; as ver. 3. and so the Greek expresses it, *if ye trust in him*.

*{he shall be*} To wit, *unto you*. A defect of the pronoun; as ch. 1.15, & 3.10.

*{for a sanctuary*} The word here used, say some, signifies, both *sanctification*, and *sanctuary*. And they render it here, therefore, following the Greek, in the former way, as they do another also near of kin to it, Psal. 114.2. *Judah was his sanctification*. So here, *He will be for sanctification*, or, *He will be your sanctification*, as he says elsewhere, that *He will honor them, that honor him*, 1 Sam. 2.30. so he will sanctify them, if they sanctify him. But albeit, that word used in the Psalm, signify as well *sanctification*, or *holiness* rather, as a *sanctuary*, or holy place; and in this latter way also, some render that in the Psalm, *Judah was his sanctuary*: Yet the word here used, never signifies other, than as our English renders it, *He will be for a sanctuary*, that is, a sacred and inviolable place of retreat, and refuge, whereunto they may freely resort, and wherein they may safely, and quietly repose themselves amidst all commotions and combustions whatsoever, and have therefore no cause of fear. So, Ezek. 11.16. *I will be as a little sanctuary to them, in the countries where they come*. See ch. 4.5, 6. Psal. 46.1, 2. Prov. 18.10. See also ch. 62.18. where both words, above mentioned, are found together. Howbeit, true it is, that a *sanctuary* implies, as well *sanctification*, as salvation; as well *sanctity*, as safety. Nor are these ever severed the one from the other. Rom. 6.22. 2 Thess. 2.13. Rev. 20.6. See ch. 4.3, 5, 6. & 6.13.

*{but for a stone of stumbling, and for a rock of offence*} Having showed what God will be to the godly, to wit, a sanctuary, strong house, or temple of stone, surely founded upon a rock: which whoso trusts to, need not fear, ch. 28.16. he now proceeds to show what he will be to the wicked and ungodly, both in Judah and Israel, that refuse to be ruled by him, and to rely on him, he will be as a *stone* in their way, for them to *stumble* at, to their mischief and overthrow, as a *snare* to catch them, to their destruction.

*{but*} Heb. *and*, as ver. 9, 10.

*{for a stone*} That is, *as a stone*, or, *like a stone*, or simply, *a stone*; as Ezek. 44.12. *They were for a stumbling block*: instead whereof, chap. 7.19. *It was a stumbling block*. So afterward, *for a snare*, as Josh. 23.13. *They shall be for a snare*, instead whereof, Hos. 5.1. *Ye have been a snare*.

*{a stone of stumbling*} Heb. *a stone of striking, smiting*. Such as lying in the way, the foot may smite or strike against, and a man receive some hurt and harm, some maim or mischief thereby, Psal. 91.12. Prov. 3.23. forbidden therefore to be laid in the blind man's way, Levit. 19.14. and commanded to be removed out of the way of God's people, ch. 57.14. See Jer. 6.21.

*{a rock of offence*} Not a bare *stumbling stone*, or, *block*, only such an one, as a man, yet discovering, may make some shift, either to shun, or to get over; or, though he chance to stumble at, yet he may but fall forward, it may but cast him upon his face, so as, without much hurt he may yet rise, and recover himself again: but a *rock of offense* such as coming in a man's way, he cannot possibly avoid, no more than he is able to remove a rock out of his way; which if a man, or ship run upon, or rush violently against, it will cast the man down backward, ch. 28.13. and lay him on his back: as our Savior's words did those that came to apprehend him, Joh. 19.6. and the tidings of the Ark taken did old Eli, 1 Sam. 4.18. It will split in sunder, and drown the one, batter in pieces, and destroy the other. Matth. 21.44. This is applied in the Gospel to our Savior, whose mean condition, to outward appearance, made many to refuse and reject him, to their own ruin; as did this people here, the means of safety that God offered them; but they refused to rest in, and rely upon, Matth. 21.42, 44. Luk. 2.34. Rom. 9.33. 1 Pet. 2.8.

*{to both the houses of Israel*} Heb. *to the two houses of Israel*. These terms some of the Jewish doctors refer, as to be understood by way of distribution; partly, unto the former branch of the words, foregoing, concerning a *sanctuary*, and partly, unto the latter branch, concerning *a stumbling stone, and a rock of offense*. They suppose two sorts of men in the kingdom of Judah to be meant by these two houses: the one, of those that trusted in God, and were faithful to the house of David: the other of those that were treacherous, and did underhand complot with Pekah, and the Assyrians now: or with the Assyrians in Ezekiah's time: of which sort, say they, were Shebna, and some others: and that God here promises to be a *sanctuary* to the former, but threatens to be *a stumbling stone, and rock of offense*, to the latter. The want of the pronoun, denoting those whom the prophet spoke unto, not observed in the first member of the verse, led those doctors aside, and made them much to mistake the prophet's mind: wherein few therefore follow them. The most, as well of theirs, as ours, understand by *the two houses of Israel*: those two kingdoms, which the whole body of the people of Israel the twelve tribes, were divided into, under Rehoboam; ten falling off from him, and two only cleaving to him; when as before, under David and Solomon, they made but one state; as *one house*, acknowledging but one head, 2 Sam. 5.3, 5. & 8.15. 1 King. 2.12. & 11.41. & 12.16, 17, 21. The main body of both which, being grown very corrupt, unfaithful, and disobedient, God threatens them both to bring those heavy judgments upon them, though he would withal secure, and save those that were godly, and faithful among them, Psal. 125.4, 5. 2 Pet. 2.5, 7, 9. Of Israel, see chap. 1.1, 3.

*{for a gin, and for a snare, unto the inhabitants of Jerusalem*} One of the Jewish doctors, whom the Greek also, and some of the Latins, in part, concur with, conceives these words, not as intimating what God would be to Jerusalem, but what others should be to them and what God would be to such, as were so to them. For thus does the great Rabbi join this branch to the former. *God will be a stumbling stone, and a rock of offense, unto those two houses of Israel, that come to be a gin, and a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem*; that is, to Pekah, and Shebna, with their consorts, says he; to the Israelites, and the Syrians confederate with them, say others; both which laid trains for the taking of Jerusalem. But these are overbold in filling up the text, with stuff of their own. The meaning is plain, that God would be as a gin, or a snare to them also, implying, that it was not either the royal seat, or God's own sanctuary there, that should secure them, but that they also, for their iniquity, should suffer with the rest. See Lam. 3.47. He alters the similitude, passing from the former, to another, taken from the practice of fowlers and hunters, that set gins, and snares, to catch birds and beasts: (the like whereunto, see Psal. 35.7. & 91.3. & 119.110. & 140.5. & 141.9. & 142.3. chap. 24.17, 18. Hos. 5.1. & 9.8.) as some suppose, in way of mitigation, as intending a milder manner of dealing with them, than with the rest; and intimating, that though they should be caught in a snare, yet the snare should be broken, and they escape out of it, Psalm. 124.7. But the words ensuing, verse 15. show, evidently, the same thing to be intended in either. See verse 19. chap. 5.13. And others therefore, would have it to intimate rather, that neither by might, nor flight, they should be able to go beyond God, or to escape his vengeance; he would meet with them in either kind, Job 5.13. 1 Cor. 3.19.

**V. 15.** *{And many among them shall stumble, and fall, and be broken*} The issue of the judgment before threatened, described in terms suitable to the two former similitudes, wherein it was denounced and laid down, ver. 14.

*{And many shall*} Or, *That many may*, as Job 5.11. Psal. 78.11. Mal. 1.9. noting either, the issue, or the end. See Jer. 6.21.

*{many*} Not all. For God will ever reserve a remnant, ch. 1.9. & 4.2. & 6.13. But the most are still the worst, Jer. 5.1.

*{among them*} Of both houses, before mentioned, verse 14. Hos. 5.5. Others read it, *against them*; or, *at them*, to wit, the *stone*, and *rock*, before mentioned: But that construction is more harsh.

*{shall stumble, and fall, and be broken*} These respect the former similitude of a stone, and a rock.

*{stumble, and fall*} A man may trip at a stone, or stumble either, and yet not fall. But those that light on these stones, shall so stumble, that they shall not escape a fall. So Psalm. 27.2. *They stumbled, and fell*, ch. 31.3. & 46.6. & 50.32. See ch. 3.8.

*{and be broken*} As running upon, or rushing against a rock; ch. 28.13. Matth. 21.44. Luk. 20.18.

*{and be snared, and be taken*} As beasts, or fowl are taken in a net or snare, Eccl. 9.12. Luk. 21.35. This answers the latter branch of the foregoing verse, concerning *a gin*, or *a snare*. So ch. 28.13. & 42.22.

**V. 16.** *{Bind up the testimony*} The words of God, as all agree; as some, more specially, of Christ, to the prophet; informing him further what he should do, both concerning the visions of God, and the sacred mysteries therein revealed unto him, and concerning the doctrine of God's word in general.

*{Bind up the testimony, seal the law among my disciples*} These two branches, some conceive to have respect unto two sorts of persons; as if the prophet were enjoined *to bind up the testimony*, in regard of the one, *to seal the law*, in regard of the other. They suppose, that the prophet stood, hitherto, before Ahaz and his people, (which yet appears not) with that *roll*, mentioned, ver. 1. unfolded, and spread abroad in his hand, out of which he read, and withal expounded to them, what was therein contained, therefore called here the *testimony*, or *contestation*, because solemnly entered, and engrossed before witnesses, v. 2. But considering that neither king, nor people regarded what he said, God now bade him roll it up again, and fasten it, that they might hear no more of the matters contained in it. Alluding to the manner of such volumes, as being so rolled up, nothing written in them, can be seen, or read, Rev. 6.14. Yet withal that he should open them, and confirm the truth of them, in private, to the faithful, his followers, that were capable of such mysteries, and ready to receive them, Prov. 23.9. Matth. 7.6. 1 Cor. 2.6, in the word of *sealing*, having respect to such things, as for secrecy are wont to be sealed up, that they may be kept from common, either use, or view, Cant. 4.12. Rev. 5.1, 3. Others suppose them to concern both the same persons. Some, the prophet himself, principally; that though few regarded his ministry, yet he should continue constant in the execution and exercise of it: Both by careful keeping in mind, and observing of it himself: and giving assurance of it also unto others: and confirming them in the truth of it: an allusion, as some of them suppose, to such ligatures, as men use for the memorial of aught, that they may not forget it, Deut. 6.8. Prov. 3.1, 3. As others to wares, that merchants do first wrap up, and bind about with cord, and then seal also for more security: As others again, to letters that are first bound about with thread, and afterward sealed: to which God should compare his word delivered unto the prophet, as matter of authentic truth, having God's seal stamped on it, Esth. 3.12. & 8.8. Others deem it to have special regard to the prophet's scholars and followers; that by diligent instruction he should prepare, fashion, and frame their hearts, to be fit tables for the receipt of the divine testimony, the truth of God to be written, in them, and both to be sealed up to them, & to be sealed unto by them, Jer. 31.35. 2 Cor. 1.23. & 3.2, 3. Eph. 1.13. & 4.30. Heb. 8.10: in which places, they suppose, the Jewish manner alluded to, of taking depositions; a draft whereof being made, under the hands of those that were deposed, was after signed also by those that took them. Others, lastly, suppose the words only to intimate, that these mysteries, especially concerning the Messiah, should be, as recorded, so shut, and sealed up, to be reserved for posterity, unto whom, in future ages they should more clearly be revealed, ch. 30.8. Dan. 12.4, 9. Rev. 10.4. Or that they should be like letters closed, and sealed: neither read, received, nor conceived by any, but such only, as were inwardly enlightened, ch. 28.11, 12. The meaning seems to be no more, but that God would not have the prophet to deal further, in this kind, with these faithless and profane scoffers; but reserve such sacred mysteries to be imparted to the faithful; who would with due reverence religiously receive them.

*{Bind up*} As Deut. 14.25. 1 Sam. 25.29. Or, *fashion, frame*, as Exod. 32.4. Or, *keep*, as Prov. 3.21. & 6.20, 21. The first here seems fittest.

*{the testimony*} So is the word of God, in general, oft styled in Scripture; twenty times, at least, in one Psalm, Psal. 119. & it is so termed because thereby, God not only makes known his will to us; but by a solemn, and severe sanction also, does attest thereunto, 2 King. 17.15. Neh. 9.34. And so also is the word taken hereafter, verse 20. but in this place it seems rather to note that special word of God, that God by the prophet had, not without such like sanction, not delivered only to them, but even pressed upon them at present. Nor does it hinder, but that it may well be taken so here; albeit that it be used more largely there.

*{seal*} For immunity, as Dan. 6.17. or safe custody, as Matth. 27.66. or secrecy, as Cant. 4.12. or assurance and certainty, as John 3.33. & 6.27. Rom. 4.11. Eph. 4.30. of either of these two latter, the term may well here be taken.

*{the law*} Either the word of God in general; as Psal. 19.7. & 119.97. or the law of rites and precepts, the law of Moses, Mal. 4.4. Matth. 11.13. John 1.17. or that particular message, or doctrine, that Esay had at this time delivered, or was further, to deliver to the faithful: and thus it seems to be here taken, as also chap. 1.10.

*{among my disciples*} As ver. 15. *among them*, or, *with my disciples*, as Ezr. 10.17. or, *for my disciples*, as Neh. 13.14. for their behoof; reserve it, to be imparted to them, for the stay and support of them in these calamitous times.

*{my disciples*} Or, *my taught*, or *learned* ones. Such as have been *taught of God*, as the prophet speaks, chap. 54.13. (where the same word is used) such, as have *learned Christ*, and been *taught of Christ*; as the apostle speaks, Eph. 4.20, 21. *But ye not so, ye have learned Christ, if so be ye have heard him, and have been taught of him*: (for so the words would there be read) The word does not properly signify, *a disciple, a scholar*: (save, as we use to say, *a scholar*, for one *skillful*, or *learned*,) or *a learner*, though a term near unto it, denote such an one, and is therefore well rendered, *a scholar*, 1 Chr. 25.8. but that word is of an active form: this is of a passive: and signifies properly, not *a learner*, but one *learned*, one, that has been taught, that has learned, and by learning, is become skillful, and *learned*, as the word is well rendered, ch. 50.4. See more hereof there.

**V. 17.** *{And I will wait upon the Lord*} The prophet's words, professing his resolution of constant depending, and patient attending upon God; notwithstanding the present tokens of his wrath and displeasure towards his people: and notwithstanding the discouragements that he received from them, by no part of his ministry prevailing with them, for their good. For, to me, they seem to strain the text unreasonably, who make them the words of Christ speaking to the prophet; and by his own example; encouraging him to constancy and perseverance in his ministry; with patience; as he does his disciples, John 15.20. Heb. 12.1, 2.

*{And*} Or, *Yet*, rather; as Jer. 2.32, 35. Some render it, *Then I waited*, as if he had said, being thus confirmed, v. 11. I resolved to wait, and so did. But the use of the particle, altering the present to the future, carries it rather the other way.

*{I will wait upon the Lord*} Word for word, *I will stay for the Lord*; for so the word properly signifies, 2 King. 7.9, & 9.3. Job 32.4. I will stay his time. So Psal. 33.20. & 106.13. ch. 30.18. Hab. 2.3. Zeph. 3.8.

*{that hideth his face*} That shows himself to be displeased with his people, by these heavy judgments, partly inflicted, and partly further menaced; and as some also, by commanding the roll to be wrapped up and concealed, ver. 16. It is a metaphor taken from the practice of men, who being displeased with a party, withdraw themselves from him, and will not be seen of him, nor spoken to by him, 2 Sam. 14.24. See the like, Psal. 10.1. & 27.9. ch. 45.15. & 54.8. & 57.17 & 64.7.

*{from the house of Jacob*} See ch. 2.5, 6. v. 14.

*{and I will look for him*} I will with patience and hopeful expectation, depend on him, both for support amidst these sad occurrences, and a comfortable issue of them in his due time: So Job 13.15. & 14.14. Psal. 40.1. ch. 25.9. Jer. 14.22. Mic. 7.7.

**V. 18.** *{Behold, I and the children: &c.*} These words also, many would have to be, not the prophet's words, speaking at all of himself, but Christ's speaking to the prophet, and relating to him, what his own condition would be & the condition of his followers, when he should appear & live, here below, in the flesh; and the reason they build upon, is, because the apostle produces these words, as spoken, either of, or by Christ, Heb. 2.13. But the consequence is not necessary. For to instance the like: It follows not, that those words, 2 Sam. 7.14. *I will be his father, and he shall be my son*, were not spoken by God, to David, of Solomon, as David himself tells him, 1 Chr. 22.10. because the apostle applies them to Christ, Heb. 1.5. or that those words in the apostle, the very next before these, *I will trust in him*, whether they be taken out of Psal. 18.2. as some of these would have it, who are herein the stiffest; or, whether they be drawn from the Greek of this prophet ver. 17. which I rather incline to, were not spoken either by David, or by Esay, of themselves, because they are by the apostle, in the same place, carried up unto Christ. Many speeches of the prophets, concerning themselves; and many prophecies concerning Cyrus, and others, who were types of Christ, are in the New Testament applied unto Christ: being one way, and in one manner verified of them; and another way, and in another manner also, many times, fulfilled in him. Of himself then, there need no doubt be made, but that the prophet speaks in this place; albeit the thing spoken of him, be also verified and fulfilled in Christ; and that in another sort, than with Esay it was. And others therefore, not a few, take them to be the prophet's own words, and these, first, and primarily affirmed, concerning himself, and his own, either children, or disciples; either complaining of the people's vile estimation of them; or the ineffectualness of that service, whereunto God had assigned both him and them, or both: and yet withal, professing a readiness to undergo either.

*{Behold*} Spoken, as those who make the words following Christ's; as in way of admiration, that he and his should be so reputed, and that by his own people, John 1.11. So in way also of instigation, to stir the prophet up seriously, to consider it, that he might with more content of mind endure, and undergo the like. See the like, Jer. 25.29, & 45.5. Or, as those that conceive them to be the prophet's, as in way of lamentation, and complaint; that it should be so with him, and his, or that, so little good was done by what they sustained, as Jer. 17.15. Ezek. 33.32. so withal, in way of profession, or protestation of a willingness to do and endure whatsoever, in this, or any other kind, God should please to call them to, or to employ them in, or exercise them with, as ch. 6.8. or by way of exhortation to God's faithful people, inciting them to look on him, and his children; and to consider his constancy, and undaunted resolution, and what the mysterious names, imposed on them, did import, and might assure them of.

*{I and the children*} By *children*, some understand *disciples*, whether Christ's; or Esay's, such as were before mentioned, verse 16. that is, either such as were termed the children of the prophets, because the prophets their instructors, were as fathers to them, 1 Sam. 10.12. & 19.20. 2 King. 2.3, 5. Amos 7.14. or, such, as by his ministry he had begotten unto God, 1 Cor. 4.15. 1 Tim. 1.2. Tit. 1.4. Philem. 10. But others rather understand the prophet's natural *children*, born to him in wedlock by his lawful wife, whereof mention also was made before, ch. 7.3. ver. 3. that, which must be in another manner understood, when applied unto Christ, Heb. 2.14. as Solomon being *God's Son*, Heb. 1.5.

*{whom the Lord hath given me*} When applied to Christ, whom the Father has, for life eternal, given to him, John 6.37, 39, 65. When to Esay, whom God had made him an instrument to convert: or whom by his blessing on the marriage bed, God had bestowed on him, *They are the children*, says Jacob, *that God hath given me*, Gen. 33.5. & 48.9. and, *I*, says God, *gave Isaac unto Abraham, and unto Isaac, Jacob and Esau*, Josh. 24.3, 4.

*{are for signs and wonders in Israel*} I, and my followers, are accounted as monsters, and are matter of wonderment, as such manner of creatures are wont to be, among this people. David of himself, *I am as a monster unto many*, Psal. 71.7. and, *Thou Joshua, and thy fellows, that sit before thee, are men of wonder*, or *men wondered at*, Zach. 3.8. or, *I, and my children*, are propounded by God for strange and unusual signs to this people: and indeed, so they were: the prophet himself is expressly said, so to be, ch. 20.2, 3. See the note on the place; and so were his children: as has been showed on ch. 7.16. & ver. 3, 4. and this also, no doubt, together with the names thereupon given them, did expose them to the scoffs, and pointing at, of the profane multitude: *There goes Maher-shalal-hash-baz*; and the like.

*{from the Lord of hosts*} Heb. *from with the Lord*. That is, by his appointment: That which seems to carry this branch the latter way, v. 3. ch. 10.2. for *Lord of hosts*, See on ch. 1.9.

*{who dwelleth in mount Sion*} Where his temple, his principal place of special residence on earth, and amongst his people, is, Psal. 76.2 & 132.13, 14. See ch. 2.2, 3.

**V. 19.** *{And when they shall say unto you*} To let pass the great variety of strange and strained connections, and coherences, that sundry interpreters give of this passage, with the former context. The occasion of this caution here inserted, seems to be this. The example of Saul, and others, shows how prone people are in times of straits and difficulties, to seek unto sorcerers, by such hoping to receive information of what is like to be, and advice what course to take for their own safety, 1 Sam. 28.7, 15. 2 King. 1.2. This way, therefore, it is not unlikely that many were looking after, in these troublesome times, (especially, being otherwise much addicted thereunto, ch. 2.8.) and inciting others also thereunto. Against whose enticements, the prophet therefore endeavors to arm the faithful; partly, by discovering the vanity & impiety of such courses: & partly, by directing them unto whom upon all such occasions, they ought for advice, to resort.

*{when they shall say*} *when any shall say*, or, *when it shall be said*. For the verb is here put indefinitely, or impersonally, without designation of, or reference unto, any special, or particular person, or persons, as Matth. 24.26. though it may be presumed, that none but the unfaithful sort of people would so speak.

*{Seek unto them that have familiar spirits*} Or, *Inquire of them* (as Deut. 18.11. 1 Sam. 28.7. 1 Chr. 10.13, 14.) for advice and help.

*{that have familiar spirits*} The term here used, comes from a word, that signifies, *a bottle*, Job 32.19. and the word is put, sometime, for *the familiar spirit* itself, as the text in our version here speaks, as where the witch of Endor is termed, *the owner* of such an one, (for so the original has it, 1 Sam. 28.7, 8.) that is, one, that had such an one at hand, to make use of. Where *the witch*, and the *spirit*, or *familiar*, are distinguished the one from the other: as also they are, Act. 16.16. but sometime it is put for *the witch*, him, or herself, one that has, or is possessed of such an one: as where it is said, that Saul had *put away*, and *cut off the witches*, 1 Sam. 28.3, 10. and so is the word also used in this place. And these *witches* are deemed so to have been at first termed, because the evil spirits, that possessed them, when they gave answers by them, used to swell and blow up their bodies, their breasts and bellies especially, like a bladder, or a bottle, as of the Pythian prophetesses, or witches rather, is recorded: and to cast them withal into a kind of frenzy: during which also, they delivered the oracles by them, with an hoarse, or hollow voice, as if they spoke out of their *bellies*, (whence another name is in Greek given them) or out of a *bottle*. Howbeit, the spirit, or familiar, which the Witch of Endor made use of, seems to have been raised by her, but not to have spoken in her; or through her. The word is used again, ch. 19.3. & 29.4.

*{and*} Or, *or*, as ch. 10.14.

*{unto wizards*} Or, *cunning men*, as some call them; the word is not amiss so rendered.
