For it comes of a word, that signifies, *to know*, to *have skill*, or *cunning*; as 1 Sam. 16.16, 18. *one that knoweth*, that is, has skill, or cunning *to handle the harp*, and ch. 29.11, 12. *one that knoweth a book*, for, one that has skill in it, and, *one that knoweth not a book*, for, one that has no skill in reading. So these men were termed *wizards*, or, *skillful, cunning* men, because they pretended much skill and cunning, in disclosing of hidden matters, and foretelling future events. For, as for what the Jewish doctors tell us, of a strange bird, as some, or beast, as others whereof these should have their name, they seem to be merely fabulous. The two words here used, are found commonly joined together in Scripture, as well in historical relations, as in legal prohibitions, Levit. 19.31. & 20.27. Deut. 18.11. 1 Sam. 28.3, 9. 2 King. 21.10. & 23.24. 2 Chr. 33.6.

*{that peep*} Or, *chatter*, as it is rendered, ch. 38.14. The word properly signifies, such a puling voice, as fowl, in general, ch. 10.14, small, or great, such as swallows, and cranes, ch. 38.14. are wont to make: and it seems, that these familiars used, in such a broken, and scarce articulate sound; or in such an hollow, low, whispering manner, to give out their answers, that those by whom they spoke, or that made use of them, were to relate them more plainly, and expound them unto those that consulted them. See ch. 29.1.

*{and that mutter*} This word seems to import a more doleful and mournful tone, or a more dreadful and hideous grumbling, than the former: For it is used, sometime for that bemoaning kind of noise, that doves use to make, ch. 38.14. & 59.11. sometime, for that grunting, or grumbling, rather, than roaring noise, that a lion is wont to make over his prey, when he is possessed of it, chap. 31.4. And such noises, it is not unlikely, that these impostors also sometime made; to strike a kind of awe and dread of them, into those that repaired to them. Though others also, and so the old Latin; understand it of such muttering, and murmuring, or mumbling, as their enchanters, or charmers, in their spells and charms used; and are not unusual with them, at this day. Some of the Rabbis affirm them to be so called, because they used to set men a-musing. And the verb indeed signifies commonly, *to muse*, or, *to meditate*: and although the notation seems somewhat farfetched; yet if the original of the word, *Magi*, used both by the Greeks, and Latins, be not Persian; (as is most probable) but Hebrew, and be derived, as many deem, from the word here used; I should suppose, that they are so termed, not as *mutterers*, which some have imagined; (for it is not likely, that they should style themselves, by a title of disgrace) but as *musers*, a more honorable appellation: nor was the name anciently otherwise esteemed, Matth. 2.1. But to leave this, I cannot concur with those, who would have the word of *peeping* here, to be referred to the *witches*, the word of *muttering*, to the *wizards*: as if the one peeped, but muttered not; the other muttered, but peeped not: whereas the words seem jointly and indifferently to have relation to either. See ver. 14, 15. & ch. 5.13, 15.

*{should not a people seek unto their God?*} The prophet here, informs the faithful, what answer they should return to those, that endeavored thus to seduce them: and here would therefore, for more perspicuity, these words be inserted, *Say ye*, or, the like, as Psal. 115.15. & 132.14. where the defect is in the latter branch: as the like in the former, Psal. 27.8. Jer. 10.11.

*{Should not, &c.*} Heb. *shall not*, Or, *will not*. Whence some render the word thus, *will not any people seek unto*, (or *inquire of*, as before *their own God?* as convincing them, by the general practice of all people, like that, Jer. 2.11. *Hath any nation changed their Gods?* and that, Mic. 4.5. *All people will walk, each in the name of his God*. But we need not alter our reading: the future is frequently used, to signify, not what *will*, or *shall*, but what *would*, or *should*, be done. So 2 King. 3.27. *He sacrificed his Son, that shall reign* (for, *that should reign*, or, *should have reigned*) *in his stead*: Mal. 1.6. *A son will* (that is, should) *honor his father*. And the prophet seems to argue, rather, from matter of right, and due, than of fact: from office, and duty: than from practice: And it agrees better so, also, with the next branch. It is a thing agreeable both to reason and religion, that whom people profess to be their God, him they should, for advice and direction, resort to. So Elias, to the Israelites, *If Jehovah be God, follow him*. 1 King. 18.21. and to Ahaziah's messengers; *Is it not because ye have no God in Israel, that ye go to inquire after the god of Ekron?* 1 King. 1.3.

*{for the living to the dead*} Or, as others render it, *from the living to the dead*, either way the speech is defective, to be from the former branch thus supplied. Should men go to inquire, *for*, or *from the living to the dead?* And according to the latter reading the meaning should be: Should men go from the living God, and his prophets, to seek for advice unto the dead, either idols, or idolaters? Hos. 3.12. or, to men deceased, whom these sorcerers, therefore called *necromancers*, have dealing with, Deut. 18.11. 1 Sam. 28.8, 12. But I find not where the particle here used, is found in that sense. I know some allege: Gen. 26.8. *He looked out from a window*. And, *He fell down from a lattice*, 2 King. 1.1. But it would rather be rendered, *at a window*, in the one place: and *through a lattice*, in the other: as Joel 2.9. *they shall enter in at*, or, *through the windows*. The former reading therefore, which our last translation has, seems the surer, because the particle is frequently found used in that sense to signify, *for*, or, *in behalf of*, as 1 Sam. 7.9. & 12.23. 2 Sam. 12.16. 1 King. 13.6. Jer. 11.14. and oft elsewhere. And so it is, as if the prophet had said, Should men go to seek help and advice in the behalf of the living, and for their safety, from the dead, who neither have any notice of them, nor are able to afford them any succor? Job 13.21. ch. 63.16. Howsoever, the opposition is principally between *living*, and *dead*, as Eccl. 9.4, 5. Nor will the text therefore admit the exposition of some, though of prime note: who would have the word rendered, *from the living to the dead*: as depending on the foregoing branch, without any supply, and as a parallel phrase to that, Gen. 6.7. *from man to beast*; implying that God alone is all-sufficient both for quick and dead, as he is said to be, *Lord of quick and dead*, Rom. 14.9. and *Judge of quick and dead*, 2 Tim. 4.1. for neither are the particles in either from the same: nor has either of the particles here read, ever that use, nor was there occasion here, of inquiring aught, concerning the dead; but concerning the living only.

**V. 20.** *{To the law, and to the testimony*} Let them seek; or, *At the law, and at the testimony*, let them inquire. For that is to be supplied out of the verse foregoing; as there, also, in the latter branch, out of the former. He shows now, whom, for aid and advice, they should repair unto; as before, to whom they should not. By *the law, and the testimony*, some would here understand that doctrine only, and those particular predictions and directions, that the prophet had from God at present imparted to them. Of which before, ver. 16. But these seem to straiten the words overmuch. Others therefore understand by these two terms, the Word of God, in general, either contained in the sacred volumes already written, and then extant, or delivered to them by word of mouth, through the ministry of his prophets, as 2 Chr. 20.20. & 34.21, 22. not excluding those precepts, predictions, or promises, that the prophet had delivered unto them at present. So Abraham sends them, in the parable, *To Moses, and the Prophets*, Luk. 16.29. Howbeit, I suppose, they go over-nicely to work, who by *the law*, here conceive to be meant, the writings of Moses; and by *the testimony*, the prophetical revelations; as if the former were not God's testimony, as well as the latter: when as, indeed, the name of *testimony*, was first, and primarily, given unto the Law, written in the two tables; in regard whereof also, was the Ark called, *the Ark of the testimony*; because those tables were laid up in it, Exod. 25.16. & 40.20. 1 King. 8.6, 9. by either term therefore, is understood, God's Word in general: as our prophet's manner is oft, to express, in divers terms, the same thing. See on ch. 5.13, 15. and on ver. 14, 15. And, as I suppose, *the law, and the testimony*, is no other than God's word, which is his testimony, as *cloud, and smoke*, for, smoky cloud: *storm, and rain*, for, rainy storm, ch. 4.5, 6. See ver. 18.

*{if they speak not according to this word, it is, because, there is no light in them*} The Jewish doctors are here most ridiculous; who, because oaths are in this form commonly conceived, *If this, or that, be not*; (of which see ch. 5.9.) deem therefore, or dream rather, that the prophet should here swear *by the law, and the testimony*, that the people would speak no otherwise, than as he had before said they would, v. 19. and so it should be like that of Elias, 1 King. 17.1. But to leave them to their dreams and dotages, wherein yet they have followers: our own interpreters are much divided about the meaning of these words. Some read them, as a continued sentence, by way of interrogation, thus; *Do they not speak against the law, and the testimony, in this manner?* or, *Do they not speak on this wise*, (advising resort to witches and wizards) *that have no light* (that is, no true knowledge of God, 1 Cor. 15.34.) *in them?* That which, yet, excepting that frivolous conceit of an oath, is, in effect, the same with that before of the Rabbi: Whereunto may be added, what another of his fellows has; *Do they not speak in this manner of the law, and the testimony, that there is no morning light in it?* It is a night, without morning, like that of the false prophets, Mic. 3.6. Others, thus divide them, *If not*, (if they refuse to listen to God's law, and to take advice of him, and his word) *let them speak according to that word that hath no light in it*; neither of truth, nor of comfort; as if he had said, let them even go on in their willful and obstinate blindness; or, as others, *they shall speak according to such a word, as hath no light at all in it*: no light of sound truth being in any word, that agrees not with God's Word, of which our Savior, *Thy word is the truth*, John 17.17. Others coming nearer to our version, and so the old Latin, (for the Greek here, by mistake of letters somewhat alike, is exceedingly misled) *If they speak not according to this word, no morning light shall be to them*; That is, if this people be otherwise minded, than from God they have been advised, and will resolve to run after witches and wizards, there shall no daylight of prosperity befall them; but all darkness of affliction and misery, shall betide them. A very fit exposition, and well suiting with what follows, ver. 21, 22, if the words of the text will bear it, which we shall further anon discuss. Others lastly, coming full home, in effect, to our last version, though a little differing in some expressions; Our former English, *If they speak not according to this word, there is no light in them*: or, as others, because there is a particle omitted; It is a sign, or it, is certain, that (so the relative is used, Neh. 2.7, 8.) *there is no light in them*: or as ours here has it; *It is* (the like defect whereunto, some would have, ch. 7.9.) *because* (so the relative is rendered, 1 King. 15.13. Psal. 119.158.) there is *no light in them*. According to these last, the meaning should be: If any (for the verb is here indefinite, as before, ver. 19.) shall speak otherwise, than according to God's Word, and to that, which I have now from him delivered, it is an evident sign, that there is no light of truth in such an one; or the reason, why such so speak, is, because there is no truth in them. Not unlike that of Paul, Gal. 1.3, 4. and that of John, 1 Joh. 1.6, 8, 18. Howbeit, that of the old Latin, may be well fitted to the original; either by the like supplement, that these latter versions make use of; or, by omitting the particle, as the old English does, which is oftentimes redundant; as 2 Sam. 1.4. Psal. 2.6. Zach. 8.9, 17. and thereunto I most incline, in regard of what ensues: thus reading it; *If they shall not speak, according to this word*, it shall be, *that morning light shall not be to them*; or, *morning light then shall not be unto them*. They shall enjoy no morning light; no light of comfort, or relief, shall shine forth unto them: as otherwise there would have done, had they kept close to God, and been content to follow the directions of his Word. See Saul's case confirming this, 1 Sam. 28.18, 20. 1 Chr. 10.13, 14.

*{there is*} Or, *shall be*: as Psal. 37.10. ch. 19.7. For the negative here used, admits as well time future as past, or present.

*{no light*} Heb. *no morning*, or *no dawning*. For the word properly signifies *daybreak*, or, *the dawning* of the day, Job 38.12. put here for the light, that then appears; as ch. 58.8. Hos. 6.3. Joel 2.2. Amos 4.13: as if he had said in Job's language, *the eyelids of the morning*, or, *day dawning, they shall never see*. They shall be pursued with perpetual affliction and calamity, without any glimpse of comfort: *light*, for joy and comfort, Esth. 8.17. Psal. 97.11. & 112.4. *morning light*, more specially, for such as comes, upon some foregoing, more than ordinary affliction, or distress, as the morning succeeds the night, Job 11.17. See ch. 21.12.

*{in them*} Heb. *unto him*, or *unto them*. For the number is oft changed, as ch. 2.20. & 3.8, 10. and the singular number is used collectively, as having reference to the body of a people. So ch. 5.26, 30. & 6.9, 10. where the pronouns are all singular, though rendered not amiss (as some of the verbs also are) plural.

**V. 21.** *{And they shall pass through it*} The evil follows more largely described, that shall betide these deserters of God, and his aid graciously offered them, betaking themselves unto other evil and abominable courses: to wit, that they shall in their distresses flit to and fro, but meeting with no means of succor or relief, either from above, or below, they shall be at their wit's end, like those at sea in a storm unavoidable and insupportable, Psal. 107.26, 27. See Jer. 14.18.

*{And*} Or, *For*, as Psal. 108.12.

*{they shall pass*} Heb. *he shall pass*. Which some of the Jewish doctors understand of the King of Assyria, passing with his army, through the land of Judah. But their exposition we may well let pass; and so may we as well theirs also, of the *morning light*, before spoken of, that it should pass away from them, and not abide with them. It is meant, of the wicked Jewish people, either, as some, compelled to pass out of their land, which they made full account to dwell in forever; as God had promised they should, so long as they continued loyal to him, Jer. 25.5. or, as others rather, constrained to flit to and fro in the land, where they had quietly dwelt before, to seek succor in their distress; by occasion of foreign foes, and their forces breaking in upon them, and hunting them from place to place, Jer. 16.6. it is in the singular number, because spoken of the people, as one body; and withal, to show how it should be, with each one of those wicked ones. See ver. 20.

*{through it*} Or, *to and fro in it*; the land of Judah, as chap. 9.1. & Gen. 48.9. *in this*, to wit, land, or place. For they seem to fetch it too far, that render it, *for this*; as implying the cause, for which they thus suffered; their impiety, mentioned, verse 19.

*{hardly bestead*} As the word is used, Gen. 25.16, 17. where it is said of Rachel, that *she had hard labor*; or, word for word, *was hardly bestead in her childbearing*: and Job 30.35. where Job says, *he wept* for the man, that had *an hard day*, or time, of it, that was *at any time hardly bestead*. They render it amiss, that translate it, *hardened*. Understanding it of men either hardened in sin, or grown senseless of the evils they sustained: The one suits not with its yoke-fellow, *hunger*, a corporal evil; the other crosses the main course of the context, describing men exceeding sensible of their calamitous condition.

*{and hungry*} Destitute, as of all necessaries; so especially of food, Psal. 107.5. See ch. 5.13. & 9.20. This some refer to Hezekiah's time, ch. 36.12. some to Zedekiah's, Jer. 38.9. & 52.6.

*{and it shall come to pass*} Heb. *and it shall be*; as ch. 7.21.

*{that when they shall be hungry, they shall fret themselves*} Heb. *when he shall be hungry, and he shall fret himself*, for, *that he shall fret himself*, as Amos 9.1. Mal. 1.9. They shall grow extremely impatient in their necessity and distress. It has a metaphor in it, taken from a pot, that boils with the heat of the fire under it, and casts up its scum and filth, chapter 64.2. Jer. 1.13. Ezek. 24.3, 5. Rev. 16.9, 10, 11. It runs on still in the singular number, as before.

*{and curse their king*} They run far from the text, that would have it meant (as some Jewish masters) of the Assyrian soldiers, that should curse their king, for want of provisions: the contrary whereunto, see ch. 37.25. It is spoken of the Jews, as before; that should in heat of impatience curse, not the king of Egypt: as some of the Jewish writers, for not helping them, chap. 30.3, 5, 7. nor of Assyria, as others, for breaking covenants with them, chap. 33.4. called *their king*, because they had linked themselves to him: but their own king, for not protecting, or relieving them; or imputing to him, the cause of those their calamities, which they suffered from the Assyrian, either, by calling him in, or rebelling against him, or not compounding with him, 2 King. 16.7, 8. & 18.7, 31. & 24.20. 2 Chr. 28.16, 20. & 36.13. See ch. 7.20.

*{and their God*} Either the true God, who deservedly brought these plagues upon them, and by his prophets foretold, what would befall them; as those desperately wicked wretches under the beast, Rev. 16.10. Or, *his Gods*, (as it is said of the Philistine, that *he cursed David, by his Gods*, 1 Sam. 17.43.) that is, his idols, whom they now find unable to help them, and false in that, which by their wizards they had put them in hope of. See ch. 7.20.

*{and look upward*} The Jewish doctors, whom some of ours also here follow, run most in a track; supposing this to be spoken of men returning to God, and resting on him, when they perceive all other means to fail; as Psal. 107.5, 6, 12, 13, 18, 19, 27, 28. ch. 10.20. & 17.7, 8. But it is rather a description of one, in a forlorn, distracted, and desperate condition; at his wit's end, looking one while upward, and another while downward: now this way, now that way: and it might more fitly be rendered, *when they look upward*, to wit, either toward the king's house; or towards heaven: *and*, for, *when*; as ch. 43.12. Jer. 34.1.

**V. 22.** *{And they shall look to the earth*} Which way soever they cast their eye, or whithersoever they betake themselves, they shall meet with nothing, but matter of anguish, and much discontent.

*{they shall look to the earth, and behold*} Or, *when they look to the earth, behold, &c.* as ch. 5.30. So Zach. 1.18. & 2.1. *I lifted up mine eyes, and looked, and behold*, for, *when I lifted up mine eyes, and looked, behold*, Rev. 5.6. *I beheld, and behold*; that is, *when I beheld, behold*.

*{to the earth*} Downward, 2 Chr. 20.18. as before, upward, to heavenward, ver. 21. ch. 40.26. or, abroad, *into the land*, as ch. 5.30. though some of the Rabbis understand it of the land of Egypt, whence they looked for some relief, 2 King. 17.4. & 18.21. ch. 20.5, 6. & 30.1. & 31.1. Jer. 37.5, 7.

*{behold*} What they least looked for; as ch. 5.4, 7. & 8.7. Jer. 3.16.

*{trouble, and darkness*} *the darkness of trouble*: as ch. 4.5, 6. As *light*, is put for joy and comfort, ver. 20. so darkness, for affliction, distress, and discomfort, Psal. 112.4. ch. 5.30. & 9.1. & 50.10. Jer. 13.16. Mic. 7.8.

*{dimness of anguish*} The same thing in other terms. So some of the Jewish doctors; though others suppose it to be in a new form; *dimmed*, or *darkened with distress*. See ch. 9.1. and so it would be translated; and he is, or, they are (for the want of the copulative, the Rabbis also observe) *dimmed*, or, *darkened with distress*.

*{dimness*} So for variety. Otherwise the word seems to import, *utter*, or *extreme darkness*: for so his fellows of the same family, Job 10.22. Amos 4.13. And so Job 11.17. where the words would be rendered, *though thou shalt have been never so much darkened, thou shalt be as the morning*: directly contrary to what is there read. For as for those, who harping upon another signification of the root, whence the word arises, would have it understood, calamities *flying* swiftly to them, and increasing with them, they swerve much from the tenor of the prophet's speech, and detract much from the elegancy of it.

*{and they shall be driven to distress*} Heb. *and a mist driven*; as some one affliction following on the tail of another, and pursuing them whithersoever they go: but the genders agree not; which yet some would salve; as the like Amos 9.14. by deeming it to have respect to the same word, in a masculine form. But others rather, *and driven into a mist*; or *driven on in a mist*. For *a mist*, or *fog*, the word properly signifies, Exod. 10.22. and consequently, *the dark*, Prov. 4.18. & 7.9. this and the former, are both joined together, Job 10.22. So the sense is, they shall be driven on into further miseries and extremities, as men in a mist, either forced into it, or driven on in it; as Job 18.18. *he shall be driven out of the light into the mist*, or the dark. And Jer. 23.12. *They shall be driven on in the dark*. See also, Psal. 35.5. Many words of the same notion are heaped up; as Job 10.22. to express the great extremity of their distresses.

### CHAPTER 9

**Verse 1.** *{Nevertheless*} The first words of this verse, which way soever they be taken, do evidently show that this chapter has dependence upon that foregoing; and is a continuation of the prophet's discourse, concerning the mind and message of God therein delivered. It contains, for the support of the faithful, a gracious promise, both concerning a comfortable issue to them of the forementioned calamities; and concerning the restoration of the church by Christ: yet concluding with a renewed denunciation of sad, and dismal occurrences against the obstinate wicked, because not amended by what was past, v. 8. &c.

*{Nevertheless, &c.*} This verse, or some part of it, some join to the former chapter, as a confirmation of the sad and forlorn estate of the persons there spoken of; and they render the particle here, *for*; as Psal. 12.1. Others, make it an entrance into a new relation, importing some allay of the calamitous condition there mentioned: and they render it, as ours here: or, *Yet*; as Job 5.7.

*{the dimness shall not be such, as was in her vexation*} Some, conceiving the word translated *dimness*, to have a notion, rather, of *flight* in it, as before, chap. 8.22. read the words, according to the old Latin, in part thus, *No flight*, or escape shall be to him, *that is surprised therewith*, as rendering a reason of the perplexity that the persons should be in, that were spoken of before. But there is no doubt to be made, but that the word used here, has reference to that which was made use of there, whereof enough has been said already. And the prophet may well be deemed to have retained the same word, the rather, because it sounds sweetly with another here also used: the elegancy whereof cannot, in our language be expressed. On which ground also, comes not unjustly to be rejected, the interpretation of some other, who read the words thus; *For no defatigation shall be to him that straitens*, or *afflicteth them*: That is, say they, (and they are some of the Jewish writers) the Assyrian king, who is to afflict the land, shall never be weary, or give over vexing; but shall be invading them, again, and again. See chap. 29.2, 7, 8. Or, as some other, and those of ours; *Yet defatigation shall not be to those that are in straits*: That is, those that shall be straitly besieged, to wit, by Sennacherib, yet shall not be tired out, and so constrained to give up. These suppose the word to be a noun, or verb, (which yet is not likely) coming from a root, that signifies *to be weary*. For though verbs of those forms, do oft interchange, as elsewhere has been observed, ch. 8.1. Yet regard must be had to the tenor of the context, in words that are ambiguous, and not extant elsewhere: and that observed, will not easily admit that sense in this place. The most therefore, both Jewish, and ours, read the words much after the same manner, as our version exhibits them. And in the Hebrew it runs thus: *It shall not be darkened unto her, whom*, or *with whom*, it shall *be straitened*. That is, the land (for that all acknowledge is meant, and agree to be supplied, as before, chap. 8.21.) that shall be in such straits, as has been said, shall not be so darkened as in some former times, hereafter mentioned; that which is by divers diversely; yea, two contrary ways understood. For some take it, as spoken in way of aggravation; as if it were said, No marvel, if people shall be in such perplexity, as has been described; for this affliction, when it comes, shall darken the land otherwise, in a far more grievous manner, than was done in the former invasions, or inroads made into it. Others deem it to be delivered in way of mitigation, and allay of the former dreadful denunciation; that though it should go hard with the land of Israel, or Judah, and the inhabitants thereof, in the judgment here threatened; yet it should not be so grievously afflicted, as in those former invasions it had been. Which to me seems, well weighing both the terms, used here, of those former incursions, the one of them especially; and the tenor of the text; not so probable to be the meaning of the prophet in this place. I rather adhere therefore to the former sense. See chap. 7.17. For as for those that would read the words, *It shall not* utterly, or totally *be darkened*: as they force that into the text, which they find not there: so they are met with in that which immediately follows, *as, when at first, &c.* unless they will grant, that it was utterly darkened in those times forepassed, which the prophet here points to.

*{dimness shall not be*} Or, *it shall not be dimmed*, or *darkened*. For some make it a noun, and some a verb. See on ch. 8.22.

*{in her vexation*} Or rather, *unto her*, or, *it*; that is, or shall be so vexed, or *straitened*. Heb. *unto whom it is straitened to her*, or *to it*. Or, *to whom distress*, or *straits*, is, or shall be. Taking the word, as some do, for a noun; *unto whom; to her*, or *to it*. A redundancy in that language, very familiar; as Gen. 1.30. Psal. 1.4. That the word *land* is understood, all grant; but some understand by it, the land of Judah, strictly so termed; and conceive the affliction, here foretold, to be meant of the invasion made by Sennacherib, under Ezekiah, (which seems most probable) or by Nebuchadnezzar, under Zedekiah, which not a few hold. Others suppose it to be the land of Israel, or the ten tribes, because mention is made of some parts thereof, in the words ensuing. I see not why they may not be both included, since that greater troubles were to befall either of them, than as, yet there had: nor was there fit access for the Assyrian, to the one but through the other.

*{vexation*} The *vexation* (or *straits*, rather, or *distress*) here intimated, has reference to that spoken of, chap. 8.22. and there rendered *anguish*: and is not to be carried on, as our English does it, to the next branch where mention is made of forepassed times and troubles. For the prophet lays not the comparison between the *vexation*, or *distress*; but between the *dimness*, or *darkness*, that had in former times been, and that then should be. And though *dimness*, or *darkness*, and *vexation*, or *distress*, may amount much to one; yet for the right rendering of the text, and keeping close to the context of the prophet's discourse; they are here to be distinguished: and the reading to be, not, *the land shall not be so vexed*, or *distressed*, but shall not be in that manner, *dimmed*, or *darkened*, as formerly it had been. See v. 2.

*{as—when at the first he lightly afflicted*} Heb. *as in*, or *at the first time he made light*; or, *according to that first time*, wherein, or when *he made light*; (for there is a want of the relative; as Gen. 34.4. chap. 42.5.) or *dealt lightly with*, which some expound fondly, of lightening the land of its inhabitants, by carrying them away captive, 2 King. 15.25. as the ship is said to be *lightened*, by casting out the wares, Jon. 1.5. but this, (to say no more of it) is by the opposite branch of *aggravation*, sufficiently refuted. By *making light*, therefore is meant, *lightly visiting*, or *afflicting*, or *dealing more lightly* with them; as the false prophets are said to have cured the hurt of God's people, as if they were but *lightly hurt*, Jer. 6.14.

*{when he lightly afflicted the land*} That is, *when God lightly afflicted*, or visited it. Or taking the word indefinitely, and impersonally, when the land was lightly afflicted, or visited, See on ch. 2.19. When this first lighter visitation, or affliction was, and by whom inflicted, is not so clear. Some expound it of the invasion made by Tiglath-Pileser, under Pekah king of Israel, and Ahaz king of Judah, 2 King. 15.29. Which to help out, some of them tell us, of a twofold inroad made into the land, by this king. But I rather, with one of the Jewish teachers, understand it of a former invasion, which he points to, though mistaken in the time, made by Pul king of Assyria, in the reign of Menachem, or Manes king of Israel, and Uzziah king of Judah, 2 King. 15.19. 1 Chr. 5.26. said here to be but a light affliction, to speak of, because the king of Israel, having, with a great sum of money, compounded with him: he stayed not long in the land, 2 King. 15.20.

*{the land of Zebulun, and the land of Napthali*} In which it is probable, that Pul quartered his forces, when he invaded Israel.

*{and afterward did more grievously afflict her*} Heb. *and*, or, *or* (rather, as Gen. 2.6. ch. 19.15.) *in the after time* (supplied from the former branch) *when* (as before) *he aggravated*, or *made heavy* (as ch. 36.1.) That is, dealt more grievously with her, or it; to wit, the land, as before; which some therefore put into the text. This is generally understood of the deportation of the ten tribes, by Salmaneser, who coming after Tiglath-Pileser, (as Tiglath-Pileser after Pul) in the reign of Hoshea over Israel, and Ezekiah over Judah, twice entered the land of Israel, and at the first time only made Hoshea tributary; but in the latter imprisoned him: and having surprised, and sacked Samaria, swept all away before him, 2 King. 17.3, 6. than which, what could be more grievous? But it is more probable, that the prophet speaks here, not of any invasion so long after, but of some nearer at hand, if not wholly past; yet already begun, and in a manner, in being. See ch. 8.4.) And I conceive it therefore to be meant of Tiglath-Pileser, who, about this very time, invited by Ahaz, made an inroad into the land of Israel; took, besides divers strong towns, in sundry other tribes, all Neptali and Galile, the Reubenites, Gaddites, and the half tribe of Manasseh, that dwelt on the other side of Jordan; and carried the people of them into Assyria, 2 King. 15.29. 1 Chr. 5.26. That which, in no reason, could be esteemed to be but as a light, or slight touch of that state. Albeit, that one of the Jewish doctors tells us, that they counted not their land darkened by Tiglath-Pileser's invasion of those two tribes, (and so expounds the prophet's words, not of the thing itself, but of the people's account) until Sennacherib came, and seized on all the rest of them; of whom, he alone, that I light on, expounds this latter, and heavier visitation, than the former. A learned late writer, of special note, walks here alone; (as oft elsewhere) thus rendering the text, *As at the first he exposed to ignominy*, or *contempt toward the land Zabulon, and toward the land of Naphtali: so at last he will give glory, by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, in the confine of the nations*. This he will do, by the light that should there appear. He takes the word rendered, *alleviated*, or *lightly afflicted*, for, *to contemn, set light by*, expose to contempt; as 2 Sam. 19.43. Ezek. 22.7. which was done, by the Assyrians' invasions, and direptions of those parts before mentioned: and the word in the latter branch, rendered, *aggravated*, or, *aggrieved*; for *to honor*; and *make glorious*; as Jer. 30.19. Let others consider of it; I approve rather the other reading.

*{by the way of the sea*} Some read the word, *at*, or *in the way to the sea*, whereby men travel, and wares are conveyed thither; and by *the sea*, they understand that part of the midland sea, called *the great sea*, Josh. 1.4. that lies against the coast of the promised land. But the most, rather take the *sea*, here mentioned, to be *the sea of Cinnereth*, Josh. 13.27. called also, *the lake of Genesareth*, Luk. 5.1. and *the sea of Galile*, Matth. 4.18. and by a later name, *the sea of Tiberias*, John 21.1. for the Hebrews call great *lakes*, as well as the branches of the main sea, *seas*, Numb. 34.11, 12. Josh. 12.3, 18: denominated from the country adjacent, and towns therein, Josh. 19.35. Mar. 1.28. & 6.53.

*{beyond Jordan*} Or, *besides Jordan*. For the country of Galile, coasted all along upon Jordan, not on the further side, or beyond it, in regard of the land of Judah, and Jerusalem; but on the nearer side to them, of it, and the Hebrew word signifies, at large, either *on the one side*, or, *on the other*, 1 Sam. 14.4. and is to be understood, either *on this*, or *on that side*, *hither*, or *beyond*, according to the respective situation of the places, where, and whereof aught is spoken, see Deut. 1.1, 5. & 3.8, 20. & 4.49. Nor need we therefore, for the salving, either of the prophet's, or the Evangelist's chorography, to fly to that shift, as some do, as to say, that this tract of land, is called *Galile, beyond Jordan*, because it had been so termed by the Israelites, before they passed over that river, and were as yet on the other side of it, as France is by the Spaniard, termed the Transalpine Gall-land, because, by the Romans, it had been formerly so styled. For the very same word is, by Moses, used, before they passed Jordan, as well of the places on that side, where they then were, as of the places situate on the other side of it; as by the Scriptures above cited appears.

*{in Galile of the Gentiles*} The particle *in* is wanting, as Hos. 6.9. Mic. 6.11. not unfitly here supplied, as in the former. The whole region of Galile was divided into two parts, the upper, and the lower, so termed, in regard of their nearness to, or remoteness from the head of the river Jordan, on whose stream, and the lake it made, and fed, they coasted. The upper, was in the tribe of Naphtali; the lower in the tribe of Zabulon. Some understand this of the lower Galile, which they will have to be termed *Galile of the nations*; as a populous place, in regard of the fertility of the soil; for which they allege Moses his words, in the blessing of Naphtali, Deut. 33.13. not observing that the lower Galile was not in Naphtali, but in Zabulon. Others suppose that the upper Galile, is here intended, called, as they deem, *Galile of the Gentiles*, because it was much replenished with heathen people, and divers sorts of them mixed with the Israelites in it; partly, in regard of some cities in it, made over, by Solomon, to Hiram, 1 King. 9.11. And partly also, because it lay, some part of it, near upon the confines of Tyre and Sidon, Matth. 15.21. Mar. 7.31. and had therefore by reason of their vicinity, much commerce with them. And so is Harozeth, called *Harozeth of the nations*, or *Gentiles*, Judg. 4.1. in regard of the remainder of the Canaanites there. And Tidal, *king of nations*, Gen. 14.1. As also another king likewise, so styled, Josh. 12.23. in regard of a mixture of divers nations in their cities, or territories; and so under their command. Nor does the Evangelist's relation of our Savior Christ's preaching, and conversing much about the Sea of Tiberias, where he took up for his followers, some of those that exercised fishing there, Matth. 4.18, 22. or his abode at Nazareth, situate in the lower Galile, Matth. 2.23. & 3.13. any whit cross, or contradict this; as some imagine. For it is said expressly, that upon the report of John's commitment, he departed into Galile, and leaving Nazareth, (where he had formerly made his abode) he repaired to Capernaum a city situate in the confines of Zabulon, and Naphtali, Matth. 4.12, 13. and consequently of the upper, and lower Galile, so situate, as was before said, & lying within the limits of the tribe of Naphtali, is justly therefore esteemed to belong, rather to the upper, than to the lower Galile. Besides, it is said further, that our Savior *went preaching about all Galile*, Matth. 4.18. That is, as well the upper, as the lower; and as well that, as this, because it is added, that thereupon *the fame of him went throughout Syria*, Matth. 4.24. which confines upon the upper Galile. Howbeit, I suppose, they are mistaken, who suppose the whole circuit of the holy land, here described; as having its western bound, the midland sea: its eastern, Jordan, its northern, the upper Galile. But of the sea before. And though that were admitted, yet a fourth, at least, wants. Nor can I accord with those, that rent this latter part of the verse from the rest, and annex it to the next; reading the words without any dependence upon the former: as beginning a new period, on this manner, *The way of the sea*, (that is, those that live by the seaside, the Naphtalites, and Zabulonites especially, Gen. 49.13.) *beside Jordan*, (those that dwell on either side of the river) *Galile of the Gentiles*; (the inhabitants of the upper Galile, near to the heathenish country) *people that had walked in darkness, have seen a great light, &c.* And this tearing of the text asunder, they build upon the Evangelist's citation of this prophetical passage, Matth. 4.15, 16. But the Evangelist gives no warrant for any such, either divulsion of this branch from the former, or agglutination of it to the next. For first, in this allegation, they are sorted and severed, just as they are here. Secondly, we may as well upon the same ground, tear off these words, *the land of Naphtali, and the land of Zabulon*, from the former branch, (which yet none do, nor with any color of reason can do) as these words from this latter: since that the Evangelist joins those also with these. The Evangelist picks out only so much of the prophecy, as might concern his present discourse, to apply it thereunto. And mentions therefore these two tribes, and those parts of them especially, pointed to by the prophet, to intimate, that in those places, on which the darkness of affliction had first seized, in those times; there the spiritual light of joy, and life, had, by our Savior's preaching, first sprung forth, Matth. 4.13, 14.

**V. 2.** *{The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light*} Here, I suppose, begins the comfortable part of this discourse, promising light (notwithstanding the formerly denounced darkness) to the godly and faithful: partly by a good and comfortable issue of their present troubles, and deliverance out of their incumbent distresses; and partly, by that spiritual deliverance from the thraldom of sin and Satan, by the promised Messiah: and the abundance of joy and comfort, that should accrue unto them from thence: whereof that other was a type.

*{The people that walked in darkness*} Heb. *The people that were walking*. The noun is singular; the participle plural: because the noun is collective. See ver. 9. By the people here mentioned, some understand the ten tribes, who were to suffer more grievous things, than formerly they had done; partly by Salmaneser, 2 King. 17.3, 6. and partly by Esarhaddon, Ezr. 4.2. because mention is made of them, ver. 1. See ch. 8.7, 8. Others, and those most of the Jewish doctors, whom many of ours also concur with, understand them of the Jews, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, first straitened by Sennacherib, ch. 7.17, 20. & 8.8. afterward surprised, sacked and depopulated by Nebuchadnezzar, 2 King. 18.17. & 19.1, 3. & 25.1, 21. ch. 36. & 37. Jer. 5.39. & 52. I suppose we may well understand both houses, (see ch. 8.14, 15.) in regard of the story, and acts of those times, and the calamities that befell either; which did typically resemble the sad and forlorn estate of persons, continuing in that utter want of all light of grace, and that slavery of sin and Satan, wherein by nature they are, until they be effectually enlightened, and convicted by Christ, Eph. 2.1. & 5.8. 1 John 2.9, 11.

*{walked in darkness*} *sat in darkness*, Matth. 4.16. and so afterward here, that is, lived, and abode in it; because in places, where they abide, men sometime *walk*, and sometime *sit*, at home: as of mutual conversing one with another, (without any such mysteries, as some here, and there make) Psal. 1.1. & 26.4, 5. Yet it may well have reference to *walking in the dark*, without use or help of light, as both discomfortable and dangerous, John 11.9, 10. & 12.35. 1 John 2.11.

*{darkness*} For distress and discomfort, ch. 8.22. & 59.10.

*{hath seen a great light*} This was in part fulfilled to the Jewish people, in those and the ensuing times; first, at the defeat given to Sennacherib, and the breaking up of his siege, ch. 30.31, 32. & 37.36, 37. and afterward, at the overthrow of Babylon, and the deliverance of them out of the Chaldean captivity, Psal. 126.2. ch. 14.3. & 52.9. Jer. 31.4, 5, 7. & 33.7, 11. & 50.4. & 51.48. But most fully and principally, by the ministry of the gospel, whereby people are delivered from that spiritual blindness, and darkness, wherein formerly they abode, Matth. 4.13, 16. Luk. 1.78, 79. & 2.32. John 12.35. Act. 26.18. Ephes. 5.8. and rescued out of the servitude of sin and Satan, whereof that Babylonian bondage was a type, John 8.32, 34, 36. Rom. 6.6, 7, 14, 22. & 8.21. Col. 1.13. 2 Tim. 2.26. Heb. 2.14, 15.

*{hath seen*} He speaks in prophetical manner, of things to come, as already effected, See ch. 3.1. & 9.8.

*{seen*} That is enjoyed, been possessed of; as Psal. 34.12. John 3.3, 5, 36. See Eccl. 11.7.

*{great light*} Much joy and comfort; for *light*, is put for joy and comfort; as Job 18.5, 6. & 30.26. & 38.15. Esth. 8.16. Psalm. 18.28. & 79.11. & 112.4. & for spiritual grace also, John 12.35, 36. Rom. 13.12. 2 Cor. 4.6. Eph. 5.14. 1 Thess. 5.4, 5. 1 John 1.5, 7. & 2.8, 10. as the ground of all true joy and sound comfort, Matth. 13.44. Luk. 10.20. Act. 8.8, 39. & 16.34. Rom. 5.2, 3. & 14.17. 2 Cor. 6.10. 1 Pet. 1.8.

*{they that dwelt in the land of the shadow of death*} The same is repeated; only with some amplification: as ch. 8.9, 10, 14, 15, 22.

*{dwelt*} Heb. *sit*. And so the Evangelist has it, Matth. 4.16. as also Zachary, Luk. 1.79. but *sitting*, is put commonly, for *dwelling, staying*, or, *abiding*, Psal. 23.6. Jer. 39.14. & 40.5. to abide, and dwell in a place, is more than to pass, or walk through it; as Psal. 24.4. & 66.12. So John 12.46. *abideth not in darkness*, and 1 John 3.14. *abides in death*, and *God's wrath abides on him*, John 3.36.

*{in the land of the shadow of death*} Matth. 4.16. *in the region and shadow of death*. Of which phrase, see on ch. 4.5.

*{shadow of death*} As before, so Job 24.17. Psal. 44.19. & 107.10. for *deadly shade*: as, *body of death*, Rom. 7.24. for, *dead body*. Extremity of distress, and misery, compared to such a dreadful shade, or darkness, as with the horror of it, may strike a man even stark dead, Matth. 28.4. or that shadow and darkness, that is said to be in the grave; with those that are laid up in the bowels of the earth, and are lodged in the chambers of death, Job 10.21, 22. Psal. 88.6, 12. and to men dead and buried, are those usually compared, that are in a calamitous and hopeless condition, Psal. 88.4, 6. ch. 26.19. Ezek. 37.11, 12. Dan. 12.2. See further of this phrase, on Jer. 2.6.

*{upon them hath the light shined*} They are, or, shall be (for it is spoken in way of prediction) in as comfortable a condition, as those, unto whom, after a dark, or tempestuous night or season, of some continuance, at sea especially; or at land, in some hazardous, and harborless place, the clear daylight, or bright sunshine, at length suddenly shows forth itself, Act. 27.20, 39. So Psal. 37.6. & 112.4. See ch. 60.1, 2. Mal. 4.2.

**V. 3.** *{Thou hast multiplied the nation, and not increased the joy*} These words, as some, are by an apostrophe directed unto Sennacherib, who came with a vast army to besiege Jerusalem; but was frustrated of his purpose, and retired back with shame: As if the prophet had said to him; You have multiplied your forces indeed; but shall have little joy of them at last. See ch. 36. & 37. But this seems not so suitable unto that that follows. The most therefore are of opinion, that the words are spoken unto God: but in exposition of them, they are much divided. Some refer the words to what was past: And of these, some understand them of the Gentiles; strangers from the commonwealth of Israel. That howsoever God had multiplied them, as he did Israel, and his seed, Gen. 17.20. yet had not imparted that his grace to them, that is the only ground of all true and sound joy, Eph. 2.12. Others rather apply them to the Jewish people: and of these again, some read them on this wise; *Thou hast indeed multiplied this people*, (the Jewish nation, according to your promise unto Abraham, Gen. 15.5. & 22.17.) or, *thou hast magnified them*, (because the word signifies, as well great, and mighty, as *many*, Psal. 25.11, 20. and the verb *to magnify*, or to make great, as to *multiply*, Gen. 3.16. to wit, by many benefits and blessings bestowed on them; victories achieved, and miracles wrought for them) *but yet thou hast not made their joy so great*; that is, have not given them so great cause of joy, as you will do hereafter, in the deliverance of them from the Babylonian captivity, Psal. 126.1, 2. but especially in the spiritual deliverance by Christ, ch. 35.10. Others, *Never since thou multipliedst this people, didst thou give* them such matter of joy; or, *in multiplying* of them, *thou gavest* them no such occasion of joy, as hereafter you intend to do. Thus those of them that refer them wholly to the time past; excepting only, what they annex to them themselves. Those that understand them of the future, either in whole, or in part; do, some of them, apply them to the Jews, thus. *Thou hadst multiplied this people*, or, *Thou wilt multiply them*, at Christ's coming, yet little, or *no joy* will there be of it; because, either so few will receive him, and believe in him, ch. 53.1. John 1.11. & 12.37, 38. or, because, though at first many flocked to him, and followed him, Matth. 15.30, 32, 33. Luk. 12.1. John 4.1. & 11.48. & 12.19. yet afterward they fell as fast away from him, John 6.26, 66. Matth. 21.9. with 27.23, 24. Others to the Gentiles, *Thou hast multiplied this nation*, by accession of the Gentiles called in to them, by the ministry of the gospel, ch. 54.1, 3. Gal. 4.27. Rev. 7.9. *but thou hast not* thereby *increased*, their *joy*; because this vexed and troubled the Jews, Act. 11.2, 3. & 13.45, 50. & 22.21, 22. 1 Thess. 2.15, 16. and because upon the coming in of the Gentiles, they were rejected, Rom. 11.8, 12, 19, 20. Others again, both to Jews and Gentiles, indifferently, that though God be pleased *to multiply*, or *magnify* the body of the faithful, consisting of both nations incorporate into one, Gal. 3.16. Eph. 2.14, 16. & 3.6. yet, he will *not afford* them any *great* measure of such *joy*, as the world affords, John 14.25. & 16.2, 33. or, as worldly men here enjoy, Psal. 4.6, 7. & 17.14. Thus you see how many several ways this Scripture is writhed, (and yet divers senses given it, omitted) and how many fillings are inserted, to make out these notions. The main difficulty arises from the negative particle; which to salve, therefore, some would have the words read by way of interrogation; by which manner of reading, some Scripture scruples, are sometime by some deemed, to be happily removed; as Job 14.14. Psal. 105.28. Hos. 4.14. Mic. 5.2. Eph. 4.26. and so here they suppose, that the words being thus read, *Hast thou not increased their joy?* all the difficulties will be dissolved. The denying interrogative being equivalent to an affirming enunciative. For the sense, I concur with them; but I raise it from another ground. The Hebrew critics, commonly called Masorets, have observed divers readings in sundry places of Scripture, about no one word so many, as about the word, *Lo*, which in Hebrew, according to a diverse writing in that language, signifies one while, *Not*, another while, *To him*. This diversity concerning it, is found, as Exod. 21.8. Lev. 11.21. & 25.30. 1 Sam. 2.3. 2 King. 8.10. 1 Chr. 11.20. Ezr. 4.2. Job 13.15. Psal. 100.3. ch. 49.5. & 63.9. so in this place: the reading therefore being doubtful, whether *not*, or, *to him*, or, *it*; I follow rather this latter; though by ours so generally renounced: not because those Jewish critics prefer it; but because it suits better both with the scope of the place, and with the sequel of the context: & read the words thus: *Thou wilt multiply this nation, thou wilt increase their joy*. The main exception which one of prime note takes to it, is this, that the pronoun in the Hebrew is wont to follow the verb, whereas here thus read, it leads. But so it does also, Job 13.15. where yet most go with the *keri*, the same with this here. And he that takes this exception, yet approves the sense, only reads the words in an interrogative tone, wherein the negative affirms.

*{Thou hast multiplied*} Or, *Thou wilt multiply*. For the prophet runs all along here, in a prophetical strain: speaking of things future, as present, or past.

*{the nation*} Or, *this nation*. For the particle is deictical: as ch. 26.15. *thou hast added to the nation*; to this people, the Jewish. You will cause them to multiply, and thrive again, when they seem to be almost worn out, after the spoil of them, made by Sennacherib, ch. 37.31. after their return from the Chaldean captivity, Jer. 31.27. Zach. 2.4. in the days of the Messiah, by confluence of people out of all parts, that shall join themselves unto them, Psal. 47.1, 9. ch. 2.3. Mic. 4.2. Zach. 8.20, 23.

*{and not increased the joy*} If so read, it should rather be rendered, *but*, than *and*: for it is a discretive; at least, if not an adversative. But for *not*, I read, *to it*, or, *to them*; the word, *nation*, whereunto it refers, being a collective: as ch. 5.25. & 6.9.

*{increased*} Heb. *magnified*; as Gen. 19.19. *increased the joy*, or, *joy to them*, that is, *their joy*. You will give them abundant matter of joy, in delivering them from the Assyrian siege, when they shall be unable to hold out, ch. 37.3, 36, 37. in bringing them back from the Babylonian captivity, when they shall seem to be past all hope of recovery, Ezek. 37.11, 12. and principally, in sending the Messiah unto them, the foresight of whose day, so long before, so much rejoiced Abraham, John 8.56. and whom all the faithful of former times had so earnestly expected, so instantly longed for, Matth. 13.16, 17. Luk. 2.25, 30, 37, 38. to deliver them from the thraldom of sin and Satan, Luk. 1.69, 70. and 2.10, 11. whereof those former deliverances were but shadowy resemblances; and were also exhibited to them, both by him, chap. 63.9. and for him, *in whom all God's promises, are yea, and amen*, 2 Cor. 1.20. See ver. 6.

*{they joy before thee*} As you will give them occasion of much joy, so will they take notice of it, lay it to heart, and in way of thankful acknowledgment thereof, rejoice in your presence. You see how naturally this flows from the former branch; and what strength it hence gives to the interpretation thereof before delivered. So Psal. 9.2, 3. & 20.5. & 21.1. & 35.9. ch. 12.3.

*{they joy*} Heb. *have rejoiced*, or, *shall rejoice*: as before.

*{before thee*} That is, say some, inwardly, sincerely, in your sight, and so the phrase indeed is sometime used, ch. 38.3. Luk. 1.6. to distinguish, as they would have it, this inward and spiritual joy, from that external, worldly, and carnal joy, that worldly men's hearts are so much taken, and taken up with, Psal. 4.6, 7. denied to them in the former branch, Luk. 6.21, 23, 25. but of that branch, and the reference that this has to it, sufficiently has before been spoken. The meaning of the words here, rather is, *in thy presence*: in your sanctuary, in the assembly of your people, the place of *thy face*, or special presence; as it is termed, Psal. 42.2, in reference to that place, where sometime God appeared to Jacob, and he therefore named it *Peniel*, Gen. 32.30. So the phrase is used, Deut. 16.11, 14. Psalm. 68.3.

*{according to*} By two similitudes is the greatness of this their joy further amplified; the one taken from one of the greatest ordinary occasions of joy, in times of peace; the other in times of war.

*{the joy in harvest*} The joy, not so much of hirelings, that reap for others: but of the owners of the grounds, and the grain thereon growing, whether the richer sort, whose revenues consist much in the fruits of the earth, Gen. 26.12. & 27.28. Psal. 4.6, 7. or, those of the meaner rank, the husbandmen, that having taken much pains about the tilling of their grounds, whereupon the livelihood of them and theirs depends, and with long patience and much solicitude expected the return & receipt of it, Jam. 5.7. are exceedingly rejoiced, when they see their labors seconded, and their expectation answered with a plentiful crop, and a seasonable harvest, Psal. 125.5, 6. and are wont therefore with much solemnity, and jollity, to bring in their grain, as the principal support of their life, Gen. 47.15, 19, 25. See ch. 16.9, 10. Yea, by God's appointment, were solemn feasts of rejoicing, upon the bringing in of the fruits of the earth, first, and last, Levit. 23.10, 16, 17, 39, 41. Deut. 16.9, 11, 13, 14.

*{and as men rejoice when they divide the spoil*} Heb. *as they rejoice* (the word put impersonally, as ch. 2.19.) *in their dividing the spoil*: as no greater joy, in times of peace, than when harvest comes well in: so, nor in war, than when victory, after an hazardous fight, especially, is achieved; and rich spoils and booties withal obtained, to be shared among those that were in the fight; as Num. 31.9, 27. Judg. 5.30. 1 Sam. 30.16, 19, 20, 22, 23. 2 Chr. 20.25, 28. Psal. 68.12. See Psal. 119.162.

**V. 4.** *{For thou hast broken, &c.*} Having declared the greatness of their joy, he proceeds to show the ground of it; their deliverance, and freedom, from the straits and thraldom of their enemies; as well corporal, as spiritual. Some read the words, *when*, (as Job 38.8.) *thou shalt have broken*. But we need not alter the received reading.

*{thou hast broken the yoke of his burden*} This some understand of the breaking up of that siege, wherewith Sennacherib begirt Jerusalem, ch. 36. & 37. and of the further deliverance from future vexations and oppressions, from that state then declining, as ch. 13.6. See Nah. 1.13. Others, of the dissolution of the Babylonian captivity, Ezr. 1.1, 2. it may well include both; but both still, as looking further, to the redemption wrought by Christ; of whom, ver. 6.

*{broken the yoke*} You have set them free. For when the *yoke* is taken off, Hos. 11.4. or broken asunder, Jer. 5.5. the beast is at liberty. So Jer. 28.2, 11. & 30.8. *I will break his yoke from off thy neck*.

*{The yoke of his burden*} That is, *his yoke* which is *a burden*. As *the sign of circumcision*, that is, *circumcision*, which is a *sign*, Rom. 4.11. or rather, *his yoke of burden*, that is, *his burdensome yoke*: as *the hill of his holiness*, for, *his holy hill*, Psal. 15.1. and, *his idols of gold*, for, *his golden idols*, ch. 2.20. the syntax is in either place alike; *a yoke*, is in Scripture, put for any grievous or heavy pressure of what kind soever: because *a yoke*, both restrains a beast of his will; and lies heavy also on his neck, Deut. 28.48. 1 King. 12.4, 9, 11, 14. Lam. 1.14. more especially, for servitude, and thraldom; because the beast by it is constrained to do man service, Jer. 27.2, 3, 6, 7, & 31.18.

*{of his burden*} Not which he laid on others; as *thy father's yoke*, 1 King. 12.4, 9. but which was by others laid on him, and wherewith he was burdened: as *our yoke*, 2 King. 12.4, 10. See chap. 3.14.

*{and the staff of his shoulder*} Or, *shoulders*. So ver. 6. the *staff* wherewith God formerly smote them, and laid them, as it were, over the shoulders, ch. 10.5, 24. & 14.29. a metaphor from the manner of some hard and cruel master, that stands over his servants with a *staff*, or a *cudgel*, ready ever and anon to be laying them on: but this *staff*, it is said, God has *broken*, as ch. 14.5. *The Lord hath broken the staff of the wicked*. Thereby intimating, that now his people should not be any longer, as slaves, under the *staff* of such, as formerly they had been.

*{the rod of his oppressor*} Heb. *the rod*, or *scepter of him that exacted on him*. Or as some render it, *from him*, as Ezek. 43.18. So Job 3.18. chap. 3.12. The word properly, signifies, either *a taskmaster*, that imposes a task of work: and requires, accordingly, a strict account of it, Exod. 5.6, 8. chap. 58.3. (whence also it is sometime put for a *driver*, Job 39.7.) Or an *exactor* of tolls and tributes, 2 King. 23.35. and such burdens did foreign princes, the Assyrians, and Babylonians, especially, impose on, and exact from God's people, 2 King. 16.7, 8. & 18.14, 15. Hence, in some versions, *gold-thirsty Babel*, chap. 14.4. but now it is promised, that the *rod*, or *scepter*, that is, the power, or authority, as Psal. 2.9. & 45.6. & 110.2. of these exactors, shall be broken, that God's people may no more be subject to such their exactions, or oppressions. To which purpose it is said, that *the exact shall cease*, & that *they shall make servants those, who exacted* before *from them*, ch. 13.3, 4. See Zach. 9.8. & 10.4.

*{as in the day of Midian*} What time (as ch. 3.18. & 4.1.) God, by Gideon, overthrew the Midianites, Judg. 7.22. ch. 10.26. who had been grievous oppressors of God's people, Judg. 6.2, 6. Unto which overthrow, the prophet is, by some, thought to liken the destruction of Sennacherib's army, because it was not effected by the force and valor of those that went forth against them, but by a sudden fright in the night, Judg. 7.19, 22. all was of God, nothing of man, in either. Others suppose, that Christ's spiritual conquest is thereunto compared, in regard of the trumpets, and the lamps in earthen pitchers, Judg. 7.16. resembling the trumpet of the gospel in the mouth of God's messengers, chap. 58.1. John 5.24, 25, 28. and the ministers, or messengers themselves, though shining, as lamps, in their ministry, John 3.35. Luk. 12.35. whereby they hold out the light of God's word, Phil. 2.15, 16. Yet carrying this precious and powerful light, in earthen vessels only, that the efficacy of it may, appear to be of God alone, not of them, 2 Cor. 4.7. But these things seem a little too curious.

*{the day of Midian*} *Day*, for, *time*: as chap. 3.18. & 4.1. But in more special manner, *the day* of such an one, is used for that time; wherein some more remarkable thing befalls such a person, or people; either for evil, or for good. So, *the day of Jerusalem*, Psal. 137.7. the time when she was besieged, surprised, and sacked. *The day of Gibea*, Hos. 9.9. when for their abominable wickedness, and obstinacy therein, they were destroyed. *In the day of thy brother*, that is, *of his calamity, distress, captivity, destruction*, as it is there expounded, Obad. 12, 14. And so here, *the day of Midian*, that is of his overthrow.

**V. 5.** *{For every battle of the warrior is with confused noise, and garments rolled in blood; but this shall be with burning, and fuel of fire*} So most read this verse; both of the Hebrews, and ours; as consisting of two members; opposed the one to the other. And some of them understand it of the overthrow, given to Sennacherib's army at the siege of Jerusalem: that whereas, in other battles, victory is not wont to be achieved, and the enemy overthrown, without much tumult and noise, and use of arms, and bloodshed, on both sides. Or besmearing, at least, of men's bodies, and their apparel with blood, Psal. 68.23. ch. 63.2, 3. Here should be no such matter, but they should be suddenly smitten, as with a blast of lightning, in the dead of the night, without any noise, or use of soldiers, or arms. See chap. 10.16. Others understand it of Christ's spiritual soldiery, and his conquests, which are carried on and achieved, not with such weapons and conflicts, as others are, 2 Cor. 10.3, 5. but with the fire of his word and Spirit, whereby he both subdues the hearts of men unto himself, unto their salvation, chap. 1.25. & 4.4. Jer. 20.9. & 23.29. Matth. 3.11. 1 Cor. 3.13, 15. and will one day also destroy his obstinate enemies, to their eternal confusion, Psal. 50.3. & 97.3. ch. 11.4. & 26.11. Jer. 5.14. Matth. 3.12. 2 Thess. 1.8. & 2.8. Rev. 1.16. & 19.15. Another going much the same way, but this, rendering the words, *All the conflict of the confligent was, indeed, with noise, and raiment defiled with blood, and yet now is to combustion, is meat for the fire*. That is, although the enemy of God's people, did with much fury and rage assault them, and bedewed their garments with the blood of those whom they slew of theirs, chap. 63.2,3. Rev. 12.17. & 13.7. yet in fine he shall fail of his conquest; being, himself and together with his raiment so stained with the blood of God's people, become matter for the fire, chap. 26.11. Rev. 17.16, 18. & 20.9, 10. And thus they that divided the words of the text into two distinct axioms. But others read the whole verse, as one continued sentence; at least, as speaking of one, and the selfsame matter. And among these, some of the manner of the overthrow, given the Midianites, and their complices; with that which followed thereupon. And they render the words on this wise; *All the whole conflict of those that conflicted*, or that fought either with other, was *with over-confusion*, or *tumult*; *their garments were enfiled in blood, and it became*, or ended *in burning*, even, *food for the fire*. All which they understand of the tumult, or combustion that was in the Midianites' camp; and the slaughter that they made one of another; so great and such abundance of blood thereby spilled, that both the bodies of men, that lay weltering in their own blood, and their garments therewith polluted and spoiled, were fain to be burnt together, the one with the other. See ch. 44.19. Others understand it of the proceedings of Christ, come in the flesh; as rendering a reason, why his deliverance of his church was said to be like that, in Gideon's time, of the Israelites from the Midianites; to wit, because of the preaching, and light of the gospel, like the lights, and trumpets then used, Judg. 7.20. The enemies thereof should be frightened and flighted, Rev. 6.15, 16. The world filled with war and bloodshed, Matth. 24.6, 7. Rev. 6.4. and all, at last, consumed with fire, 2 Thess. 1.8. 2 Pet. 3.7, 10, 12. But as the latter reading seems more plain and suitable, both to the frame of the text, and to the course of the context, than the former; so the former exposition of the latter reading, seems to me more agreeable to either; as more familiar also than the latter.

*{For*} Or, *when*; as Psal. 73.2.

*{every*} Or, *the whole*: See the like ambiguity, ch. 10.7.

*{battle of the warrior*} They are both words of the same root; as if you should say, *war, of warrior*, or *fight of the fighter*. The word is nowhere else found; in regard whereof, some other farfetched notions, are, by some given to it; but with small probability.

*{with confused noise*} *rushing*, or *rustling*, Ezek. 11.12. & 37.7. or, *commotion*, or, *concussion*, 1 King. 11.12. ch. 29.6. Jer. 10.22. Ezek. 38.19.

*{garments*} Heb. *garment*. The singular taken collectively; as ch. 3.6, 7. and, as before, *warrior*; for *warriors*; and *man*, for *men*, ch. 2.20. Some would have the word signify, properly, *a cloak*, or *mantle*, so termed; because the skirts of it used to be cast over the left shoulder, that the right hand, and arm might be at more liberty. But it is used for apparel, in general.

*{rolled*} As of Amasa, 2 Sam. 20.12.

*{in blood*} Heb. *bloods*, gore blood, blood shed in fight, or by other violent means, ch. 1.15. & 4.4.

*{but*} Heb. *and*.

*{but this shall be*} Or, *and it was*, or, *became*: or, *which became*; to wit, the raiment so polluted. For the copulative, is sometime put for the relative; See ch. 3.6. & 5.4.

*{with burning*} So the particle is rendered, Psal. 147.20. and may well be, Job 17.5. or *for, unto burning*, as, *for*, or, *unto desolation*, Joel 3.19. See Gen. 11.3.

*{fuel*} Heb. *meat*; or, *food*: as ch. 10.16. Put, by apposition to *burning*, or having reference to the verb substantive. The whole verse may thus be rendered; *When the whole battle of those that were in battle, was with clashing* of arms, *and raiment rolled in gore blood; which, by burning became food for the fire*, That is, *was, made fuel*. For, *fuel for the fire*, is a mere tautology.

**V. 6.** *{For unto us a child is born*} That these deliverances of God's people, and the subduing and pulling down of such mighty potentates, whether secular, or spiritual, may not seem impossible and incredible; the prophet now proceeds to declare, who it is, and what manner of person, by whom all that has been said, shall be effected: even the Messiah, the eternal Son of the eternal Father, whom God shall raise up to be the King and Governor, of his church. This passage of Scripture, howsoever the ancienter of the Jewish doctors, whom the Chaldee Paraphrast also follows, (as those also testify, that have been versed in the monuments of that nation,) acknowledge to concern the Messiah; yet their later writers, by all means, labor to darken the light of so clear and pregnant a prophecy, by endeavoring to divert it, and to turn it over to Ezekiah. Whom albeit, we deny not, in some things to have been a type of Christ: (of which, see chap. 32.1.) yet the names given unto the party here described, are, some of them, such as cannot agree, either unto Ezekiah, or unto any other mere man, as we shall afterward see. The words may well be rendered; (as before verse 5. as having reference to the deliverance, mentioned, ver. 4. *As a child is born to us*. Not, that such deliverance was not, in part, before exhibited; but because it was then more fully completed; and he manifested in the flesh, by whom, and for whom, all had been done that was formerly effected.

*{a child*} Not Ezekiah, as our new Rabbis would have it, who was born some good space of time before the date of this prophecy, yea, before his father came to the throne; for he was five and twenty year old at his father's death, who reigned but sixteen, 2 King. 16.2. & 18.2. but *Emmanuel*, the Virgin's Son, not as yet born, but to be born, chap. 7.14. though in God's purpose, as born already; *a child*, at his birth, in regard of his human nature, Matth. 2.11. Luk. 2.11, 21, 34. though the Son of God, from eternity, in regard of his Deity, Psal. 2.7. Prov. 8.24, 25. & 30.4.

*{is born*} For, *is to be born*, in the prophetical style; as ver. 4. ch. 7.14.

*{unto us*} Not *among us*, only; Matth. 2.1. but *unto us*, unto our benefit, and behoof, Luk. 2.11.

*{us*} Jews, the seed of Abraham as well according to the faith, as according to the flesh, Luk. 2.10, 11. Rom. 2.28, 29. Gal. 3.8, 3, 16. 1 John 2.2.

*{unto us a son is given*} A second branch concerning the same child, adding some emphasis to the former.

*{a son*} As noting his sex, Luk. 2.7. and so pointing at his twofold nature; being both *Son of man*, and Son of God, also, in one and the same person, Matth. 16.13, 16.

*{is given*} Not *paid*, or returned to us, in way of payment; (for, who has given aught to him, that he should be repaid? Rom. 11.35.) nor *sold* to us, in consideration of aught to be paid by us, (for what can we return to God, that is not his own already, Gen. 32.10. 1 Chro. 29.11, 12. Rom. 11.36.) but *given*, freely bestowed, without any respect of aught in us, that might invite, or induce him thereunto, Rom. 5.6, 8, 10. Tit. 3.5. without expectation of aught from us, that might be beneficial unto himself, Job 22.2, 3. & 35.5–8. Psal. 16.2. Again, not *given*, only, as Isaac was *given* to Abraham, Josh. 24.3. but in a far more eminent manner, in regard whereof, he is, in way of excellency, and in a peculiar manner, termed *God's gift*, John 4.10. and said to be *given by the Father*, John 3.16. & 6.32, 33. See chap. 49.6, 8.

*{unto us*} Both *unto us*, and *for us*; to effect our salvation, Rom. 8.32. See ch. 3.6, 11.

*{and the government shall be upon his shoulders*} Not the power and authority only, of ruling, and governing God's people, is by God his Father, whose Son he is, devolved wholly unto him, Psal. 2.7, 8. Matth. 11.27. & 28.18. John 5.21, 22, 26, 27. Act. 2.36. & 13.22, 23, 32, 33. But the whole care, and charge of protecting his church, and procuring of all things necessary for the safety of it, either corporal or spiritual, temporal, or eternal, is undertaken of him; and borne, and sustained by him, chap. 11.4. & 40.11. & 42.1, 3. & 49.5, 6. & 65.15. 6.35. & 15.16.

*{Government*} Heb. *Principality*, or, *Princedom*, and so ver. 7. It denotes here that place of authority, whereby Christ is made, as viceroy to God his Father, and his Lieutenant General, Psal. 110.1, 2. 1 Cor. 15.25, 27. Col. 1.18, 19. especially, in regard to, and behalf of his church, for the safety and welfare of it, Matth. 28.18, 20. Eph. 1.20, 22.

*{shall be*} So, not amiss; yet the Hebrew syntax requires rather, *is*, or, *hath been*, and so both the Greek, and Latin render it, but the form is prophetical, as in the residue; wherein, either the one expressed, or the other intended, would, without shift, or change, be constantly observed.

*{upon his shoulder*} There seems some allusion here, to what was before said of *the burden*, and *the staff upon the shoulder*, ver. 4. though the Jewish masters make no very good use of it, who to prove this meant of Hezekiah, say, *the rod*, and *the staff*, (they might have said, *the yoke, & the burden* too) were on Ahaz his *shoulders*, because he was but a tributary to the Assyrian, 2 King. 16.8. 2 Chr. 28.20, 21. whereas Hezekiah his son shook off the Assyrian yoke, and refused to be as his vassal, which his father before him had been, 2 King. 18.7. but it is not enough, for the fastening of this prophecy upon Hezekiah, to pick out some piece of it, that may be applied to him: and another manner of regiment is here intimated, as appears, ver. 7. than Hezekiah's ever was. But that we may the better understand the phrase here used, we are to consider, that the *shoulder* is the ordinary part of the body used for the bearing, of heavy especially, and weighty *burdens*. Gen. 21.14. & 24.15. Exod. 12.34. Josh. 4.5. Judg. 9.48. Ezek. 12.6, 11. Now there is a twofold *burden*, there is a *base burden* of servitude, Gen. 49.14, 15. Exod. 2.11. and this burden Christ takes off from the *shoulders* of his. Psal. 81.7. ch. 14.25. and there is *an honorable burden* of care and charge, which attends on, and belongs unto those that are in place of authority; in regard whereof, the same word in divers languages, that signifies *honor* is of near affinity with that which denotes *burden*, and government is therefore by the wiser and better sort, justly deemed no other, than a more honorable kind of service, 1 King. 12.7. Nor indeed is this a light or small; but a great and weighty burden, if it be well weighed; consisting, in a constant care, solicitude, and sedulity, of procuring, and providing for the safety and welfare of those that live under their charge, ch. 32.1, 2. 2 Cor. 11.28, 29. that which, howsoever princes and great personages, oft-times neglect, and regard not, contenting themselves with the state service, and revenues, which they receive, and perceive from their people, without regard of their good: yet Christ does not so: but as he takes the *burden* of servitude from off their *shoulders*: (though not the *burden* of free service neither from off their *shoulders*:) Zeph. 3.9. no more than the *yoke* of willing obedience from off their *neck*, Matth. 11.29.) so he takes the *burden* of care and charge for the providing for them, sustaining of them, and accommodating them with all necessaries, both concerning this life, and a better, and lays it upon his own *shoulders*, Psal. 37.7. & 55.22. & 84.11. Heb. 13.5, 6. 1 Pet. 5.7. See ver. 7. in regard whereof also he is called, not *God's servant* only, ch. 42.1. & 53.11. but *a servant unto God's people* too, Matth. 20.28. Luk. 22.27. Rom. 15.8. Phil. 2.7. What some report of a *key* carried on the *shoulder*, of some officers in court, as here alluded unto, shall be further considered, on ch. 22.22. For the allusion that some suppose here unto Christ's carrying his cross, John 19.17. (not unlike that, which others have, of Isaac's carrying the wood, for the sacrificing of himself, Gen. 22.6. as a type of the same) to more serious authors, seems too light.

*{shoulder*} For *shoulders*; as ver. 4.

*{and his name shall be called*} That is, *he shall be called*, or, *this shall be his name*, to wit, that which follows; not that he should be so commonly styled; but that he should be known, and acknowledged to be such, as these titles all of them import. So ch. 7.14. Jer. 23.6. Ezek. 48.35. Heb. *he shall call*, as Mal. 1.4. *they shall call them*. The active taken very frequently, in an impersonal manner, most aptly expressed by the passive; *He shall be called*, *they shall be called*. Howbeit, the Jewish doctors, some of them, take occasion hereby, most miserably to rent, and tear asunder the text; that they might, if it were possible, by force or slight, wring it out of our hands: yea, and the hands of their predecessors, by applying it to Hezekiah. But they do but as the Madianites, one cross and cut another: and no other weapon needs to refute what one offers, than what is lent us by another. The verb, some of them will by no means have to be impersonal. For God, say they, is expressly said thus to have called Ezekiah: and this to justify, they read, or rend, rather, the words, on this wise. *He who is wonderful in counsel, and the mighty God, and the Father of Eternity shall call his name* (to wit, Ezekiah's) *the prince of peace*; because it is said, *yet shall peace be in my days*, c. 39.8. But another of them observing, that in such speech, of *calling* one's *name*, thus or thus the nominative, or the name-giver, never follows; but where it is expressed, goes ever before the verb; and the accusative referring to the person named, and containing the name given, does always follow next after; he runs across, and hunts counter to his fellow doctors. And the right is, says he, that all that is subjoined, belongs to the party named, to wit Ezekiah, *he shall so name Ezekiah*. Then to make this good, he pulls asunder the terms, whereof both the whole entire style, and each title contained in it, does consist: and so tires himself in struggling against the bright sunshine, to show how they may all be applied to, and verified of Ezekiah. That, wherein the former do directly contradict him, in affirming them to be as indeed they are, the peculiar attributes (some at least among them) of God: and not applicable therefore to any other, than to him that is God. But hereof more, in discussing of the several titles.

*{Wonderful, Counsellor*} These as two distinct titles, those of the Jewish doctors divide, who apply them to Ezekiah, and they say, that he is termed *wonderful*; in regard of that strange wonder of the sun's going backward, wrought in his days, and at his request, 2 King. 20.2, 6–11. and *Counselor*, in regard of the counsel, which, he took with his princes, concerning the service of God, and the safety of his city, and the good counsel he gave in either, 2 Chr. 29.4–11. & 30.1, 9. & 31.3–8. Many also, yea, the most of ours, herein concur with them, though not in applying of them to Ezekiah, (which others, also, of their own, dislike and reject,) yet in disjoining them, and making them two several titles. And true it is, that they may be severally applied unto Christ, and are verified in him. For how can he but be deemed exceedingly *wonderful*, with whom God and man, the divine and human nature, do in one person so mysteriously, and miraculously concur, that the very angels themselves, who do therefore adore him, among other things, admire this in him, as a mystery, even beyond their reach, 1 Tim. 3.16. Heb. 1.6. Eph. 3.10, 11. 1 Pet. 1.12. or, how can the title of *Counselor* be denied unto him, who is the most inward of privy council with God his Father; and imparts unto his, of them, from him, whatsoever is necessary to be known of them? John 1.14, 18. & 3.13. & 5.20. & 15.15. But those other Jewish writers, that expound them of God, join them together, as making up jointly, one title: and so do divers of ours, also, who apply them unto Christ. And indeed to me it seems, that they ought to go together, as the other three following, go also by pairs. For the meaning of them: The word rendered *wonderful*, is not an epithet, but a subject, or substantive: and it signifies properly, *a miracle*, or *a wonder*, such, as being beyond, or above, the course of nature, and the power of the creature, God alone is able to effect, Psal. 136.4. so that to render it, word for word, it is as if one should say, *a wonder*, or *miracle of a Counselor*, that is, a most wonderful, or miraculous counselor, as we use to say, *a mirror*: and *a miracle*, or, *a wonder of womankind*, for a most remarkable, wondrous, and even miraculous woman, and *a miracle of man*, or, *a monster of man*, for, a monstrous, or miraculous man: and it is the usual manner of the Hebrews, in way of amplification, to put the abstract for the concrete: as *desolation*, for *most desolate*, ch. 1.7. *abomination*, for *most abominable*, Deut. 18.12. *pride*, for, *extreme proud*, Jer. 50.31.
