Our blessed Savior therefore, is not unfitly here so styled; as one so exceedingly strange and wonderful, in all his counsels, and courses, especially for his, both in securing them, and in defeating the designs and attempts of others against them, as no ordinary phrase, or form of speech, is able fitly, much less sufficiently, to express it: but what is spoken of Christ herein the noun abstract, that we may the better understand whom the attribute belongs to, is by this our prophet, afterward delivered of God, the Lord Jehovah, in the verb active *He that maketh counsel wonderful*; or, *doth wonderfully in counsel*, ch. 28.28. which place, as it helps to clear this: so it seems to add strength to this latter reading, that joins the two terms together. And indeed, if we take *Counselor* alone, without *Miracle*, or, *Wonder*, here, as *Mighty* alone, without *God* in the next, the title would not seem to contain any such extraordinary, or remarkable matter, as were suitable to the rest.

*{The mighty God*} Or, *A mighty God*, (for there is no article prefixed to any of the titles,) These two terms those Jewish teachers pull asunder, that apply them to Ezekiah. Howbeit, they would have them to signify one and the same thing, as if we should say, *Mighty strong*, as Ezek. 32.21. the *strong* of, or, among, *the mighty*, and so, say they, was Ezekiah, and his name imports as much, signifying, *the strength of God*, or, *strong, and mighty*, from, or through *God*, as David Psal. 18.1. But against this we object, not only the accent in the Hebrew, that carries on the voice without stop, or stay; and inhibits the disjunction of the one from the other: but besides that which they cannot be ignorant of, that the word, *el*, howsoever: in the plural number, some once or twice, it may signify great ones: as Job 41.25. Exod. 15.9. Psal. 89.6. (which two latter places, being in substance the same, are also questionable, and may intend *Gods* as well as *great ones*,) yet in the singular number it is never used, but for *God*; and it is both repeated, chap. 10.21. and in three other places found with the selfsame adjection: *the great and mighty God*, Deut. 10.17. Neh. 9.32. Jer. 32.18. And the title fits well to Christ, who has all the names of the Deity, given to him, in Scripture: *Adonai*, Psal. 110.1. Matth. 22.44. Heb. 1.13. *Elohim*, Psal. 45.6. Heb. 1.8. *Jehovah*, Jer. 23.6. & 33.16. Mal. 3.1. Matth. 11.10. Psal. 83.18. Luk. 1.76. *God*, John 1.1, 14. *the true God*, or *very God*, 1 John 5.20. *the great God*, Tit. 2.13. the same in effect, with *The mighty God*, here, as joined together, elsewhere: and, *God above all, to be blessed forever*, Rom. 9.5. Nor can I pass by the wrong done, both to Christ, and this Scripture, by a professed Christian, but too much addicted to Jewish fancies: who to help out the Rabbis in turning this over to Ezekiah, tears one term away from the former title, and gluing it to this, would have the words read: *The Counselor of*, or, *consulter with the mighty God*. Thus he dares do that, which none of them dared attempt: The stop that stayed them, was no bar to him. But the reason that he gives, why this style, or title, should be given to Ezekiah; to wit, because he should in all his affairs, consult with God, and ask counsel of him, by his prophets, 2 Chr. 29.15, 25. ch. 37.2. may well stop his own mouth. For the word in the Hebrew here used, (which we agreeably, both to the Greek, and Latin, render *Counselors*, he, because that Latin term is more ambiguous, *renders Consulter*,) does never signify throughout the whole Scripture, one that takes counsel of another: but one that gives counsel to another, and so to style Ezekiah, or any mere man, *God's Counselor*, is blasphemous. See ch. 40.13, 14.

*{The Everlasting Father*} They that would have it meant of Ezekiah, render it, some, *the Father of an age*, or, *a long time*, and would have him so styled, because his life was prolonged, when he was at death's door, ch. 38.5. Others, *the Father of a generation*, because, say they, he had an ample posterity. But as for the former, if this title should have had respect to any such thing, he should rather have been termed in Scripture phrase, *the Son of a long time*, than *the Father* of it. For so speaks the Scripture constantly, such an one was *the Son of so many years*, Gen. 5.3, 6, &c. And as for the latter, neither can it be showed, where the phrase, or term, is so used. Nor if it were found so used, would it be any peculiar character of Ezekiah, more than of any other, that had a continued line of issue, after him: yea, of him the less, because for aught we find upon record, he left behind him only one son. The Hebrew has it (as is not denied by those of their writers, that expound it, either of the Messiah, as the ancienter of them: or, of God, as those latter ones, that say, he names Ezekiah here) much to the same effect, as we render it; *A Father of Eternity*, as the word is always taken where applied to God, and his Word, and his reign, Exod. 15.18. Psal. 111.7, 8. ch. 26.4. & 57.15. Christ then is called *the Father of Eternity*; not as the same in person with the Father: For though they be one in nature and essence, John 10.30. Yet are they distinct in person, Matth. 28.19. 1 John 7.5. not so much, in regard of that kind and tender affection, that he bears unto his, and fatherly care he has of them, John 13.1. & 14.18. & 17.12. & 18.8, 9. but more especially and principally, because he is the *Author of Eternity*, that is, of life everlasting, begun in this world, and to be consummate in the next, unto all those that believe on him, and have interest in him, John 6.39, 40, 47, 51. & 8.51. & 10.28. & 11.25, 26. Heb. 5.9. & 7.25.

*{The Prince of Peace*} Of this title applied to Ezekiah, we spoke before: and though the forepart, and latter part of his reign, were prosperous, and peaceable, 2 King. 18.7, 8. & 29.19. yet the midpart was very calamitous and unquiet, 2 King. 18.13–17. ch. 36.1. But unless the whole style, contained in, and consisting of, all these four titles, will suit with him, as well as this, in part, and in some sense, may, all their strife to carry this prophecy over to him, is but frivolous. But unto our Savior, as all the rest; so this also, well suits. As his Father is termed *the God of Peace*, Rom. 16.20. Phil. 4.9. so is he fitly styled, *A Prince of peace*. For he is *our peace*, Mic. 5.5. Eph. 2.14. and *he makes our peace* with God, ch. 53.5. & 57.19. Eph. 2.17. Col. 1.20. and his gospel is *a Gospel of peace*, and his ministers and messengers, are *Ambassadors of peace*, ch. 52.7. Rom. 10.15. 2 Cor. 5.19, 20. Eph. 6.15. and he gives unto all his *peace* outward, inward, temporal, eternal, Mic. 5.5. Zach. 9.10. John 14.27. & 16.33. Rom. 5.1. & 8.16. & 14.17. 2 Thess. 3.17. See ch. 2.4. & v. 7.

**V. 7.** *{Of the increase of his government, and peace, there shall be no end*} From the last title given to the Messiah, whose birth he foretold, he takes occasion to relate, both the amplitude, and the continuance of his principality, and the prosperity accompanying it. All which, how the latter Jewish expositors, and some other treading in their steps, strain their wits to apply unto Ezekiah, will be needless to waste more words.

*{of the increase*} Or, *unto the amplitude*. See v. 3. of the large extent of Christ's kingdom, into all parts of the world; see these predictions, Psal. 2.8. & 72.8–11. ch. 2.2, 3. Dan. 2.35. & 7.27. Matth. 24.14. Rom. 10.18. In the word of *Increase*, (nowhere else found, as a noun, but fitted here to the term of *Government*) there is a close *m* in the middle, where an open one is wont to be; and on the other side an open one is found, in the end of a word, Neh. 2.13. where a close one ought to have been. Whence, divers, both Jewish, and others, pick out hidden mysteries. Some, that the close and square letter signifies firmness and entireness, in the one place; or as the cleft or open one, *a breach*, or *rupture* in the walls of Jerusalem; in the other place, Neh. 1.3. & 2.13. others, that Christ should be enclosed in the womb of a Virgin, ch. 7.14. See Jer. 31.22. Others, that his dominion should extend itself to the four corners of the world, Matth. 24.31. See ch. 66.19. Others, that by this letter, is designed the year of Christ's incarnation to be 600 year after the delivery of this prophecy; but they miss 100 years at least, in their chronography. Yet, some would hence fish out, the name of his mother. But such frivolous toys of wanton wits, the more serious and sober-minded reject and detest. The negligent scribe, in likelihood, forgot to close up his letter, in the one place; and to leave a cleft in the other: which, your Jewish curious critics, when they found in some copies, that they followed, being superstitious of changing aught, retained still, as many other slips of the scribe's pen, only giving a note of it in the margin; or over the word in the text: it is no more, than as if with us, an *s* or an *𝔰* should be in the middle of a word, and an *S* or an *ſ* in the end.

*{of his government*} Heb. *Principality*, or, *Princedom*, as v. 6. answering to the word *Prince*, also, there used.

*{and peace*} Heb. *and to*, or, *of the peace*. For the particle is again, for the more emphasis, expressed. The word, *peace*, is taken from the close of the former verse: and it includes, as there, so here also, not *peace*, barely; but all *prosperity*, ch. 48.18. the meaning is, that all abundance of peace should accompany Christ's government in all places, whither it should be extended, and were entertained, Psal. 72.7. & 116.165. ch. 54.3.

*{no end*} The phrase here used, in this place, implies, not continuance, or length of time; but largeness rather; or extent: as ch. 2.7. Matth. 2.10. & 3.3.9.

*{upon the throne of David*} A defective speech, which the Latin supplies, putting in, *he shall sit*, Luk. 1.32. *God shall give him the throne of his father David*, He shall, as heir to David, of whom he came, Matth. 1.1. Luk. 2.4. Rom. 1.3. sit upon that throne, whereof David was a type, Act. 2.30. and 13.23, 32, 33. in regard whereof, also, he is called by the name of David, Ezek. 34.23. and 37.24.

*{and upon his kingdom*} Or, *and* he shall be *over his kingdom*, as Gen. 41.60. The church of God consisting of Jew and Gentile, whereof David's kingdom was a type, Psal. 2.6. Ezek. 37.22. Luk. 1.33.

*{to order it*} Or, *dispose it*. To settle it, and the government of it, 1 Cor. 12.28. Eph. 1.22. & 4.11, 12. as David, and other religious kings types of him according to their places, had formerly done, 1 Chr. 23–29. 2 Chr. 29. and 30. & 34. and 35. 2 King. 23.

*{and to establish it*} Or, *support it*, Or, *uphold it*. So the word properly signifies, Psal. 94.18. and 119.116, 117. Prov. 20.28. Other princes are upheld by their people: Christ's people are upheld by him, ch. 28.16. Matth. 16.18.

*{with judgment, and with justice*} These two are those, whereby every state, is both aright ordered and upheld. Of David it is said that he sat *executing judgment and justice*, 2 Sam. 8.15. 1 Chr. 18.14. and *justice, and judgment*, are said to be *the inhabitants of God's throne*, Psal. 92.2. *Judgment*, in taking vengeance on the enemies of his church, Psal. 76.8, 9. and on obstinate sinners, Psal. 68.21. Luk. 19.27. and in chastising of his own people also, when they do amiss, Jer. 10.24. & 30.11. 1 Cor. 11.3–32. *Justice*, in righting the wrongs of his people, and rewarding them for their well-doing, 2 Thess. 1.6. 2 Tim. 4.8. Heb. 6.10. For that which some have here of righteousness imputed, and imparted; I suppose, belongs not unto this place. See ch. 1.27. & 16.5.

*{from henceforth even for ever*} Heb. *from now, and forever*. Unto all eternity; for, *the Lord shall reign, as King forever*, and *of his kingdom shall be no end*, Psal. 9.7, 8. & 145.13. & 146.10. Dan. 2.44. & 4.34. & 7.27. Zach. 9.10. Heb. 12.27.

*{The zeal of the Lord of Hosts will perform this*} The eager respect that he has to his own honor, chap. 42.8. & 48.11. Ezek. 36.22, 23. & 39.25. and the tender care, and affection that he bears unto his people, shall cause him to effect, what has here been foretold, ch. 48.9, 10. & 49.15. Joel 2.18. Zach. 1.14. & 2.6, 8. & 8.2. So also, ch. 37.22. Of *the Lord of Hosts* See ch. 1.9.

**V. 8.** *{The Lord sent a word into Jacob*} After these comfortable promises interlaced, for the stay of the faithful; the prophet here returns, again, to relate the calamities that should, for their excess of sin and obstinacy therein, befall the people of Israel, and the Syrian king their confederate.

*{sent*} Or, *hath sent*, as a man, sends a message by some servant, or officer; as Neh. 6.8. So Zach. 7.12. sent by Esay himself, as some, by Amos, as others, The word signifies also, *to cast*, as a man does seed, Eccl. 11.1. Or *to shoot*, as a man, does a shaft, 2 Sam. 22.15. which some think, here alluded to, in regard of what follows.

*{a word*} Of prophecy, concerning evils to betide them, chap. 7.8, 16, & 8.4. The Greek renders it *a plague*, and with other points or vowels, the word signifies either, with two short *ees*, *a plague*, with two long *aas*, *a word*: which latter reading, there is no cause to waive for them, whose version is so full of gross mistakes.

*{into Jacob*} Or, *unto*, as ch. 8.8. & 10.20. *Jacob*, the ten tribes, distinct from Judah, as Hos. 10.11. See ch. 2.5.

*{and it hath lighted upon Israel*} Heb. *and it shall fall upon Israel*. For the copulative turns the form, into the future; as ch. 31.3. and so v. 9. It shall fall, as grain, not light, that may be blown away with the wind, ere it come to the ground, but weighty, that falls into the furrow, and there takes. Matth. 13.8. Or, as the snow, or hail, or rain, that falls on the heads of those that are abroad in it; or on the ground, not without some effect, one way or other, Josh. 10.11. Psal. 11.6. ch. 24.18. & 55.10, 11. Jer. 30.23, 24. Or, as the shaft, of a skillful archer that misses not, but lights full on the place designed, hits the mark that it aimed at, Judg. 20.16. 2 Sam. 1.22. The arrow of God's word, lights ever there whither it is sent, and never fails, ch. 55.9. What God has denounced, against person, or people, they shall never be able to shift off, or avoid, ch. 14.27.

*{Israel*} The same with Jacob. The prophet's manner is, in divers terms, for variety, to deliver the same things. So Psal. 78.71. See c. 1.3.

**V. 9.** *{And*} And whatsoever they now conceive of it; and make account, either to shift it off, or overcome it, and do well enough with it, they shall all of them, by woeful experience, feeling the smart of it, find my words to be truer, than they now imagine.

*{all the people shall know*} Heb. *and they shall know this people*, or, *this people shall know*, (for the verb is plural; because the noun a collective; as, ch. 49.26.) *all of them*, or, *all of it*.

*{the people*} Or, *this people*. For the article does here single out, and specify a particular people. It points us, as by the finger, to the people, before mentioned, v. 8.

*{shall know*} *know it*. A defect of the affix, or pronoun; as ch. 1.3, 15. & 3.9. Rev. 1.1. They shall know the word to be true, which they will not now believe. They shall know it to be no vain word, whatsoever they now think of it, Deut. 32.46, 47. Ezek. 5.13. & 6.10. Or, they shall *know* it experimentally; that is, *feel* it, that is, the evils continued, and threatened in it. So, *to know evil*, for to have experience of evil: whence *the Tree of Knowledge* had its name, Gen. 2.16, 17. and to *know evil*; for, to *suffer evil*, Eccl. 8.5. and to *know sin*, for to *have sin*, 2 Cor. 5.20. See Jer. 23.19, 20.

*{all*} Heb. *all of it*. The whole people, or, *all of them*, as ch. 8.21, 22. all places with them, verse 12. and all sorts among them, 14, 15. even the proudest, and the stoutest of them, ch. 3.9, 11, 12, 17. & 5.15.

*{even Ephraim*} The royal tribe. That which was of chief preeminence with them; and denominating, therefore, oft the whole. See ch. 7.2.

*{and the inhabitants*} For, *inhabitants*, as ch. 5.3.

*{of Samaria*} The royal seat, and chief city of that kingdom. See ch. 7.9. No place so strong with them, that should be able to hold out, c. 8.4. 2 King. 17.5, 6.

*{that say in the pride and stoutness of heart*} That out of their proud and stout stomachs, make full account, easily to repair whatsoever damage, or detriment they have sustained, or may hereafter sustain, from the incursions made by the Assyrians, into their country, and their tribes; and raise themselves again, to a fairer, and more stately condition than before. See the like of the Edomites, with the like success, Mal. 1.4.

*{in the pride*} Heb. *in pride*. Or, *out of pride*; as Matth. 12.34. *out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks*. So Psal. 10.2. *The wicked out of pride, oppresseth the poor*: or, *with pride, proudly*; *that speak with pride* or, *proudly*, Psal. 31.18. Either, *pride*, without the, or, their *pride*, with a defect supplied as before.

*{and stoutness*} Heb. *and in greatness*, as ch. 10.9.

*{say*} Intend, purpose, make full account: as Gen. 27.41. Psal. 30.6. ch. 47.7. Heb. *saying*, say. See the like defect, Jer. 3.1. Howbeit a learned late annotator refers this, not to the Israelites, as simply relating their speech, but to God, as relating *the word sent* by him, v. 8. which they well knew; and checking them for what they say; and would turn the words read by way of interrogation, *Should it be thus said* of you? Or, is it meet for you, so to say? But this, to me, seems an overstrained syntax.

**V. 10.** *{The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones*} Whatsoever the enemy has ruined, we will repair, and reedify in firmer, and fairer manner, than before. As it is said of one of the Roman emperors, that he found Rome, *a brick* city, but he made it *a marble* one.

*{bricks*} Of which their ordinary buildings were, Gen. 11.3. *bricks* for houses built of brick; as *bricks* for altars built of brick, ch. 65.3.

*{are fallen down*} Not decayed of themselves; but overthrown by the enemy, Amos 3.15.

*{but*} Heb. *and*, as ch. 8.9, 10.

*{build*} Them; (a defect of the pronoun; as verse 9.) or, other in room of them, Mal. 1.4.

*{with hewn stones*} Heb. *cutting*, or *hewing*, for stones of hewing, or cutting, as it is more fully expressed, 1 Chro. 22.2. Ezek. 40.42. that is, *hewn stones*. Such were the great men's houses, in Samaria, built with, Amos 5.11. and such they built with, both for strength, Lam. 3.9. and for beauty, 1 King. 7.9, 11.

*{the sycomores are cut down*} The *sycamore*, a kind of wild fig tree, Luk. 19.4. as the fruit, Amos 7.14. so the timber whereof was of small reckoning, and it is said therefore, of Solomon, that he made *cedars* to be as *sycamores*, for the abundance of them, in his days, 1 King. 10.27. put here, not for the trees themselves; the felling whereof had been no such great loss; but for the houses built with the timber of them; (as *cedars*, for houses built with *cedar*, Jer. 22.13, 15. Zach. 11.1.) which the enemy had, or might destroy. Yet some of the Jewish doctors, understand it of the trees themselves, and the spoil made, in the country, of them, by the enemy; (like that by the storm in Egypt, Psal. 78.47.) as the former branch of the havoc, made, of their houses, in the city. But that which follows, of putting cedars in room of sycamores, crosses this conceit: Cedars growing, commonly, on the hills, 1 King. 5.6. and sycamores, on the plains, 1 King. 10.27. Howbeit, being both this, and the former, proverbial forms, it is no great matter whether way we take; though the former sense be the more probable.

*{but*} Heb. *and* as before: and as Mal. 1.4.

*{we will change them into cedars*} Heb. *we will change cedars* for them. Or, *by change* substitute *cedars* in the room of them. A defective form of speech, like those, chap. 38.17, 20, 22. See there: instead of sycamore timber, that our houses were formerly built with, we will now build them with cedar; the choicest timber for building in those parts, in those times; wherewith Solomon built, both God's temple, and his own palace, 1 King. 6.9. & 7.2, 3, 7, &c.

**V. 11.** *{Therefore*} Heb. *And*; as chap. 3.17. as denoting the cause of the judgment following this their insolence, mentioned, ver. 9, 10. Or, *For*, as ver. 13. ch. 64.5. as declaring the means and manner, how the judgment, before denounced, should be inflicted; from whom, and in what sort it should light on them; as he had said, ver. 8. and so, further confirming what was before delivered, verse 8, 9.

*{the Lord shall set up the adversaries of Rezin, against him*} Or, *the Lord will set up, &c.*

*{set up*} Raise up, strengthen, prosper, and make to prevail, as Psal. 20.21. & 59.1. & 69.29. & 91.14. & 107.41.

*{the adversaries of Rezin*} The Assyrians, who invaded Syria, the kingdom of Rezin, subdued it, and slew him, 2 King. 16.9. the rather mentioned here, because the Israelites, were in confederacy with him, and trusted much to his strength, ch. 7.1, 2, 5, 6.

*{against him*} To wit, Rezin. Who being destroyed before them, they might well expect to fare as he did; or, *against them*, the people before spoken of: for of them, the pronoun runs still in the singular number: as ver. 9. *God will bring it upon them*; and cause to prevail against them, the Assyrians who having seized upon Syria, shall not long after do the like with Israel, 2 King. 15.29. & 17.3–6.

*{and join his enemies together*} Heb. *and will mingle his enemies*. The word is but twice found in Scripture; and used in either place, to a diverse purpose: in the one place, *to mingle* men together in fight, and conflict one with another; as in the Hebrew, proud, and contentious people, are said to *mingle* strife, Prov. 15.18. & 28.25. & 29.22. and we use to say, that soldiers *join* in battle: and plaintiff, and defendant are said to *join issue* in law: and so the word is used, ch. 19.2. and so would some of the Jewish doctors also have it taken in this place. But they strain the text too much; here it signifies rather, to *mingle* men together in league, confederacy, and agreement. God will make their adversaries, though bearing little love or goodwill one to another; yet to conspire and join together in one against them.

*{his enemies*} Or, *their enemies*. Not Rezin's; (for some of them were his people) but Israel's: which confirms the exposition before given, of the words, *against them*. These enemies are the Syrians, and Philistines, ver. 12.

**V. 12.** *{The Syrians before*} The Syrians, on whom they so much relied, being now subdued by the Assyrian, and become his subjects, shall come under his conduct, mingled among his forces, to help to surprise and subdue them. Heb. *Aram*. See ch. 7.1.

*{before*} Heb. *from the east*, or, *eastward*. See chap. 2.6. 2 King. 13.17.

*{and the Philistines behind*} Heb. *from behind*; or, *from the west, westward*. For so the Hebrews term *east*, and *west*: the one, the *fore*; the other, the *back* part of the sky, or the world: the south, the *right* side; the north, the *left*, Deut. 11.24. Job 23.8, 9. Now the Philistines lay on the west to Israel; as the Syrians on the east. See ch. 2.6. & 11.14. both being ancient enemies to God's people, were ready upon any occasion, to infest them, and to be used as instruments against them.

*{and they shall devour Israel with open mouth*} The land of Israel shall on either side be so beset by them, that there shall be no way for them to escape; but they must of necessity fall into the hands, or, into the *mouth* rather of the one, or the other.

*{devour with open mouth*} Heb. *with whole mouth*. A metaphorical speech, taken from ravenous beasts, lions, bears, and the like; that open their mouths as wide as they can, to take in, and swallow down their prey, Psal. 124.3, 6. See ver. 16.

*{for all this his wrath is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still*} So ch. 5.25. See the notes there. The first words are repeated here from the close of the former branch, though our English express it not: as if he had said, though *with all mouth* they devour Israel; yet *with all* this is not God's wrath satisfied; an utter riddance must be made of them: the Assyrian must sweep away whatsoever they leave. See 2 King. 17.

**V. 13.** *{For the people turneth not unto him, that smiteth them*} The reason, why God's wrath is not pacified, notwithstanding the forementioned judgment inflicted, but further, & greater, are threatened; because the former have not that work on them, for which God sent them, to wit, to reclaim, and bring them home to him. That, which is so much complained of, about the same time, both by Hoshea, Hos. 7.10, 14, 16. and by Amos, Amos 4.6–11.

*{For*} Or, *Because*. Heb. *And*: as ver. 11. ch. 64.5.

*{the people*} To wit, of Israel, ver. 9.

*{turneth not*} By repentance, and reformation, Prov. 1.23. ch. 55.7. Act. 13.19. God's wrath is not turned from them; because they turn not unto him, Jer. 5.3.

*{unto him, that smiteth them*} Heb. *him*. As ver. 11. unto God, that smites by these, who were but as the Assyrians, his rod, and his cudgel, ch. 10.5.

*{neither do they seek the Lord of hosts*} They seek not, by prayer and supplication for remission of sin, and removal of evils thereby procured, unto him alone; who is able to relieve them, ch. 55.6. Zeph. 2.2. but seek abroad for succor to such sorry helps, as cannot stand them in any stead, Hos. 5.13. & 7.14. Asa's fault, 2 Chr. 16.12. and Judah's too, ch. 22.11. Of the title given God here, see ch. 1.9.

**V. 14.** *{Therefore the Lord will cut off from Israel, head, and tail; branch, and rush, in one day*} He will make an utter riddance of them; and of all sorts among them. *Head and tail; branch and rush*, seem proverbial forms of speech, not unlike that, *the tree with the fruit*; or, *the stalk with the grain*, Jer. 11.19. See the same again, ch. 19.15.

*{Therefore*} Heb. *And*. But so rendered, ver. 11. ch. 3.17. yet, it may be retained in his native notion, here; as in the like place, ch. 5.26. reading the words in a continued series, from ver. 12. *His hand is stretched out still; because the people turneth not, &c.* ver. 13. (enclosed in a parenthesis) *And the Lord will cut off, &c.*

*{branch*} The word is found only in this prophet, and Job 15.32. and the plural, with change of a vowel, Levit. 23.40. put here in likelihood for issue, or children, that are as branches, springing from their parents, as from a stock; so Psal. 128.3. See ver. 17. or, for those of better fashion, that beautify a state, as branches do a tree, ch. 10.33. & 18.5. Ezek. 17.8, 23. and being of more might, seem to be the strength and support of it: See ch. 3.1, 2. as branches of trees, afford staves to stay men up; Zach. 8.4. and scepters to rule with, Ezek. 19.11, 14.

*{and rush*} So called of the pools, or standing water, wherein it is found, put here for the poorer, meaner, and baser sort of people, because it grows commonly, in the mire, or mud, and is therewith fed, Job 8.11. and is a matter of no strength or worth, Job 41.2. ch. 58.5. And we read indeed, that in the deportation of Judah, the poorer and meaner sort were many, if not most of them, left to till and manure the ground, 2 King. 25.11, 12. but in the depopulation of Samaria, there is no mention of any such reserve, of any one sort more than another: but the main body is said to have been carried away; & other from foreign parts, placed in their room, 2 King. 17.6, 23, 24.

*{in one day*} Heb. *one day*. Not on some one day, or other; but, in *one day*. The particle is wanting, as Psal. 56.3. but to be supplied: as ch. 10.18. that is, at one and the same time; together one with another: *day*, for, *time*; as ch. 7.24.

**V. 15.** *{The ancient, and honourable, he is the head*} The application of the former proverbial speech.

*{ancient, and honourable*} Heb. *eminent of countenance*: as ch. 3.3. men of account, for age or office. See ch. 3.2, 3.

*{he is the head*} Or, without *he*, *is the head*. For the pronoun is in Hebrew oft used for the verb substantive, Psal. 44.4. Eccl. 1.5, 12. & 5.9. ch. 10.5. *is the head*: is meant by the head; resembled thereby. So Gen. 41.26, 27. and so, *This is my body*, Matth. 26.26. Nor do the Hebrews speak otherwise.

*{and the prophet that teacheth lies, he is the tail*} Heb. *that teacheth a lie*, (as ch. 32.7.) *he*, or, *is the tail*: as before, the false prophets are so termed: partly, in regard of their base and abject condition, (for such, it is likely, many of them, as well as their priests, were, 1 King. 12.31. 2 Chr. 13.9. Jer. 23.11, 25.) and partly, in regard of their vile and base flatteries, whereby, as dogs with their tails, they fawned upon the great ones, especially for their own behoof, & soothed them up in their sins, ch. 56.10, 11. Jer. 8.10, 11. & 23.14, 17. Mic. 3.5. so rather, than, as some that suppose, an allusion to a serpent, that gliding toward a man, as in kind manner, gets within him, and then stings him; or to such dogs, as come fawning toward men, as playing with them, until they have fastened upon them, and then worry them. Nor do I think, that the prophet's intention was to compare the body of that state, as some hence infer, to a beast: because he mentions a tail, as well as a head; no more, than, where he uses the same phrase of the Egyptian state, ch. 19.15. it being a common proverbial speech. See ch. 3.8.

**V. 16.** *{For the leaders of this people cause them to err*} Heb. *And the leaders of this people*, or, *those that bless this people*, as alluding to the false prophets, that soothed them up in their sins, ver. 15.) *have been misleaders*; such as have led them out of the way, and made them go astray. See ch. 3.12. Some read it, as a prediction, *shall be seducers*, that is, say they, shall appear to be such. But that seems somewhat too coact.

*{For*} Or, *because*: as ver. 13. as rendering a reason, why God would *cut off, head and tail, &c.* ver. 14. because the people by their bad leaders, had been led into such bypaths of error, and bad life, as must needs end in destruction.

*{and they that are led of them*} Or, *blessed by them*; that is, pronounced to be in a happy and blessed condition, as Mal. 3.15. Jam. 5.11. whom they soothe up in their sins, Ezek. 13.22. but I rather approve the former.

*{are destroyed*} Heb. *are swallowed up*, as Lam. 2.2, 5. a metaphor, from ravenous beasts, or great fishes, that swallow down the bodies of those creatures, which they prey upon, Jer. 51.44. See ver. 12.

**V. 17.** *{Therefore the Lord shall have no joy in their young men*} The Lord will spare no sort of them; he will have no regard of sex, age, or state, ver. 9, 14. Deut. 32.25. 2 Chr. 36.17. Jer. 6.11.

*{have no joy in*} As ch. 57.6. *what comfort can I have in such?* he will take no delight in them, as he is wont to do in his people, Psal. 147.10, 11. ch. 62.7. & 65.19. and having no joy in them, taking no delight in them, will take no care of them, have no regard to them, his affection being disjointed and disjoined from them, Jer. 6.8. or *shall have no joy* in them, by a phrase of diminution; for *he will detest*, and abhor them, as ch. 2.6.

*{so shall have no joy*} For, shall have much grief, Prov. 17.21. and, *if any love not the Lord Jesus*, for, be maliciously affected towards him or, out of mere malice set himself against him, 1 Cor. 16.22. a place, much mistaken, and by too many misapplied, to the wounding of many weak ones, and so, *can I have comfort in them?* No, they are as *smoke in my nose*, very troublesome to me. ch. 65.5.

*{their young men*} Heb. *choice young men*, or, *choice ones*; as chap. 40.30. *young men*, as some, because such lovely, Ruth 3.11. as others, because such cheerful, Eccl. 11.9. Lam. 5.14. Zach. 9.17. and God is wont to delight in the prosperity of his servants; as a father or master, to see those of his family cheerful and merry, when they do well, Psal. 35.27. or, *young men*, & such young men; because such are the strength and stay of a state; and the goodly, and beautiful branches before spoken of: which God there threatened to cut off, and hew down, ver. 14.

*{neither shall have mercy, on their fatherless and widows*} I suppose it would more fitly be rendered, *nor will have mercy, &c.* and so before: as those of the *branches*, the strong ones; so these of the *rushes*, the weak ones, ver. 14. He will have no compassion on any of them whatsoever, ch. 27.11. such as these, being the most usual and eminent objects of pity and compassion, both with God and man, Deut. 16.11, 14. & 24.19, 20. Psal. 68.7. & 82.3. c. 10.2. He that commands, and pleads pity for them; will himself have no pity on them; because they are all alike extremely wicked. So chap. 1.4. and 2.6, 9.

*{because every one is a hypocrite, and an evildoer*} They are all exceeding faulty, and corrupt in their carriage, both towards God and man.

*{every one*} Heb. *all of him*, or, *whole he*; that is, the whole people, the whole body of them: as ver. 9. high and low; great and small; mighty and feeble ones: the excess of sin is general.

*{an hypocrite*} So some of the Rabbis; one inwardly evil, and outwardly good: & the main, if not the whole stream of our translators, and expositors, runs in this track; but it is not likely, that any profession of piety & true devotion, about which hypocrisy is most conversant, ch. 48.1, 2. and 58.2. 2 Tim. 3.5. should be so rife, among those that were generally idolaters, and worshipers of the calves and other idols, 2 King. 17.7–12. the word does properly signify *profaneness*; as the verb from whence it comes, *to pollute*, or *profane*, Num. 35.33. Psal. 106.38. chap. 24.5. Jer. 3.1, 2, 3, 9. & 23.11. Mic. 4.11. Dan. 11.32. nor is it ever used otherwise. So would, therefore the noun epithet also be accordingly rendered, *profane*, Job 8.13. & 13.16. & 15.34. & 17.8. & 20.8. & 27.8. & 34.30. & 36.13. as also ch. 33.14. and in this place: for there is no reason in any of these places, to force the word from his native notion, clear reason requiring it to be so rendered, Psal. 35.16. and the noun substantive thence deduced, *profaneness*, ch. 32.6. as it is also rendered, Jer. 23.15. And this being the genuine notion of the term used, it is here put for all abusive, and dishonorable carriage towards God, his sacred Majesty, and holy rites, or aught consecrate unto him, and his service.

*{an evildoer*} As ch. 1.4. *a race of evildoers*, or, *is doing evil*, as making it their practice to do mischief and evil to others, Prov. 17.4. Some would have it, *a maker to do evil*, one that not only is evil himself, but incites others thereunto, like Joram, 2 Chr. 21.11. but I find not the word so used. It here comprehends all injurious and noxious dealings with, and carriages towards man; as the other, all contumelious and irreligious demeanor towards God. The evil in either kind, is so universal, that the whole body of the people may seem to be, as one profane person, as one evildoer, the manner of speech implies as much.

*{and every mouth speaketh folly*} Or, *villainy*; as it is rendered, ch. 32.6. & Jer. 29.21. *lies*, says the Chaldee. But the word is of larger extent, and includes all vile and shameful wickednesses, Gen. 34.7, 13, 31. Deut. 22.21. it is taken from flowers, fruits, leaves, or branches of plants, or trees; that being fallen, shed, and withered, do not only grow useless, and of no worth: but do putrefy and rot, ch. 5.24. & 14.19. & 64.16. such vile and rotten stuff, is all their talk. Eph. 4.29.

*{for all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still*} As before, v. 12.

**V. 18.** *{For wickedness burneth as the fire*} Or, *Because wickedness burneth as a fire*. So some read it, as rendering a reason, why God's anger is not yet pacified, but continues still incensed against them; to wit, because they continue still in sin, and wickedness grows with them more and more, as a fire, that spreads, and arises higher and higher, as it meets with combustible matter. Others rather, *For wickedness shall burn as a fire*; that is, your wickedness shall kindle such a fire among you, as shall consume and burn up all before it, as confirming what was said before, of the continuance of wrath. So ch. 24.6.

*{wickedness*} By *wickedness*, some seem to understand *wicked* ones, as *the rod of wickedness*, Psal. 125.3. others, *the punishment of wickedness*, as Prov. 13.6. *wickedness overthrows the sinner*: and indeed, *sin* is oft used in Scripture for *punishment*, as Gen. 4.13. Levit. 20.17. but we need not go from the propriety of the word: *wickedness* is said to *burn as fire*; as *the rust of their gold and silver*, is said, to *eat the flesh* of covetous persons, and cruel oppressors, *as fire*, Jam. 5.3. because it kindles God's wrath upon them, that shall torment and consume them as fire, Num. 11.1, 3. Psal. 37.20. & 106.18.

*{as fire*} Grievous judgments, are commonly compared to fire, that wastes, as we say, without mercy, Deut. 32.22. Psal. 97.3. chap. 10.16.

*{it shall devour the briers and thorns*} Or, it may be read and rendered, with reference to the former words, *as fire which devoureth, &c.* for the omission of the relative is very frequent. See ch. 10.1. The dreadful wrath of God, procured by their wickedness, is here resembled by such a fire, as either by lightning from heaven, or by some negligence, or casualty, or of set purpose, being kindled, in a great wood, or forest of large extent; first takes hold of the underwoods, the low bushes, and shrubs: after that, seizes on the great timber trees, where they grow thickest together, and having now surprised them, mounts up aloft, and overspreads all, with a thick cloud of smoke. So Psal. 83.14. ch. 10.17, 18.

*{devour*} Heb. *eat up*, as Psal. 56.3. c. 26.11. hence, *a tongue of fire*, c. 5.24.

*{briers and thorns*} The underwood, the meaner and weaker sort, compared before to *rushes*, ver. 14. which in such invasions and calamities, as are here intimated, do usually suffer first: *briers and thorns*, indeed, are wicked men compared to, 2 Sam. 23.6. ch. 27.4. Ezek. 28.24. and so some understand them here. But they are here taken, in another notion: as opposed to the *thicket* after-mentioned. See ch. 10.17.

*{and it shall kindle in the thickets of the forest*} Or, *and kindleth*, or *burns upon the thickets, &c.* that from the lower shrubs, gets up to the taller trees, especially, where they grow thick together, and their boughs are entangled one with another; and do the more readily therefore, take fire one from another. The great ones, by such *branches* resembled, ver. 14. See chap. 10.34. the judgment thus deciphered, will take hold of the stoutest, and loftiest of them, ver. 9.

*{and they shall mount up, like the lifting up of smoke*} Or, *so that they mount up*, or, *go rolling up, with a pillar of smoke*. For he goes on in the comparison he began with, comparing their country to a forest so fired, that nothing can, aloof off especially, be seen for smoke, or but smoke, mounting up from it, as Josh. 8.20, 21. Judg. 20.40. Gen. 19.28.

*{and they*} Or, *so that they*, to wit, the thickets: *and*, for, *that*, or, *so that* as Psal. 78.7. Jer. 14.19.

*{shall mount up*} Or, *do mount up*; or, *they go rolling up*. The word is nowhere else read; but it has near affinity, with a word, that signifies to *wrestle*, Gen. 32.24, 25. whence, some take it, to signify, *a going up, with rolling together*, as the limbs, arms, and legs, of those that wrestle, are in a confused manner twisted together. Others, because a word, that signifies *small dust*, such as men, in wrestling raise, and wrestlers anciently made use of, comes from the same root, Deut. 28.24. Exod. 9.9. ch. 29.5. Nah. 1.3. render it, *go to dust*, or, *fly up into dust*. See ch. 5.24. but the former suits better with the prophet's comparison.

*{like the lifting up of smoke*} So most read it, and the Hebrew commenter observes a defect, of the similitudinary particle, which is not unusual, Psal. 11.1. ch. 21.8. but it needs not here; it is in the Hebrew, *pride of smoke*, as Psal. 89.9. *the pride of the sea*, where we say, *the raging of the sea*, in which place it denotes, not barely a lifting up of the sea water; but a lifting of it as with state, in great abundance, and with much force and might: so *pride of smoke*, implies not barely, a *lifting up* of smoke, a small pillar of smoke, ascending up from some tunnel of a chimney, but such a large quantity of it, as arising from some town, or forest fired, that mounts up amain, rolling to & fro, as it rises, and overspreading all the air about and above the place, whence it rises; so that it darkens the sky, and prevails against the daylight; such a smoke, as rose from that bottomless pit, Rev. 9.2. or from Sodom and Gomorrah and those towns of the plain destroyed together with them, Gen. 19.28. and it may well therefore be rendered, *with a vast pillar of smoke*. See ver. 19.

**V. 19.** *{Through the wrath of the Lord of hosts is the land darkened*} Or, *shall the land be darkened*. But the style is prophetical, speaking of things future, as already, in being. For he proceeds in pursuit of the calamitous condition, that should betide this people, together with the ground of it.

*{Through the wrath of the Lord*} Incensed by their wickedness, v. 18.

*{The land*} Of Israel, the ten tribes. ver. 2, 8. ch. 8.22.

*{darkened*} The Chaldee renders it, *desolated*, or, as others read it, *burnt up*; as Joel 2.3. but the Hebrew doctors from the Arabic, expound it, *darkened*, as we do: *darkened*: that is, overspread, & overwhelmed with calamities and afflictions, as ch. 8.22. & ver. 1. the effects of the fire, and smoke, mentioned, ver. 18. which he has here an eye unto. For what divers divines of note have here, of the darkness of sin and ignorance, and the like spiritual evils, seems to be wholly beside the drift and sense of the place.

*{and the people shall be as fuel of the fire*} Heb. *as meat*, for it; as ver. 9. the people of the land so darkened, shall be consumed by that fire of divine wrath and vengeance, before mentioned, ver. 18.

*{no man shall spare his brother*} Or, *they shall not spare one another*. For so the Hebrew phrase is very commonly used; without respect to kindred, alliance, or any other the like relations, Gen. 26.31. Exod. 16.15. Numb. 14.4. Ezek. 47.14. they shall, as men that are in the dark, and as it falls out in a tumult, when a house or city is on fire, and all is full of smoke, fall foul one upon another; and as if they wanted enemies from without, fall out among themselves at home; or plunder one another, prey one upon another, devour and consume one another, Gal. 5.25. See Jer. 13.14. Yet there, may well be an emphasis here in the word, *brother*, implying, that the nearest bonds of nature should not restrain men from wronging any, or preying upon any, in those civil combustions among themselves, or, in the times of difficulty and distress otherwise. See ver. 19. The intestine broils here described, some suppose to have been in those concussions of the state, by the change of their kings murdered successively one by another. Shallum by Menahem, Pekahiah by Pekah, and Pekah by Hoshea, 2 King. 14.16, 25, 30. Of the last whereof, it may be not improbable. Of the rest it cannot be, because they were before the time of this prophecy, which was delivered in Pekah's reign, and began to take effect shortly after, not long before his death. See ch. 8.4.

**V. 20.** *{And he shall snatch on the right hand, and be hungry; and he shall eat on the left hand, and they shall not be satisfied*} They shall plunder and spoil one another on every side; and yet never have enough; like men sick of that disease, which they call the *doggish desire*, who though they eat never so much, yet are no less hungry, than as if they had fed, but in a dream, ch. 29.8. & 56.11. Prov. 30.15, 16. Howbeit, there want not, that expound it of extremity of famine, that should be in the land. So that as it is said of those, in time of scarcity, they did *eat*, but were *not satisfied*, having not sufficient to free them from hunger, Hag. 1.5. So these persons, with all that they could rap and rend from others, yet should not get enough to answer nature's necessity. But this seems beside the sense of the place.

*{And*} Or, *but*: as ver. 10.

*{snatch*} Heb. *cut*, or, *cut away*, or *cut off*; as ch. 53.5. *rend*, or take away by force, as Hab. 3.16. or, as some, *gnaw*; because of eating the speech is.

*{on the right hand*} *right, and left*; for this side, and that side; either side, or, any side, indifferently, Gen. 13.9. Psalm. 91.7. Prov. 4.27.

*{hungry*} Unsatisfied, in regard of their greedy desire of more: they shall be in their rapines insatiable, Eccl. 5.10.

*{eat*} Spoil, waste, consume, as we say, *eat upon* one. So Jer. 50.17. *Assur ate upon him*, made a spoil, and prey of him.

*{they shall not be satisfied*} A change of the number, as ver. 13. because the former was spoken collectively.

*{they shall eat every man the flesh of his own arm*} That is, say some, for extreme famine, they shall eat their own flesh, as chap. 49.26. But rather, as before, they shall prey upon those that are nearest unto them, and whom they have most need of, until they have even consumed them. The like in another kind. See Jer. 19.9.

*{every man*} Heb. *man*, only, for, *each one*, or *every one*: as ch. 14.18.

*{eat the flesh*} Devour the substance, consume their means, as Mic. 3.3. *they eat the flesh of my people*.

*{his own arm*} His brethren, or near kindred: as ver. 19. See Jer. 19.9. *brethren*, as *arms*, that belong to, and spread out from the same body, or, *arms*, those, that might be means of strength, and support unto them; a man's strength lying most in his arms: So *an arm of flesh*, 2 Chr. 32.8. and, *that makes flesh his arm*, Jer. 17.5. But the former seems most probable.

**V. 21.** *{Manasseh Ephraim; and Ephraim Manasseh*} The speech being deficient, must be supplied from the former; *Manasseh* shall eat, or devour *Ephraim, and Ephraim* shall eat, or devour *Manasseh*. The posterity of these two, though brethren, the sons of Joseph, Gen. 41.51, 52. yet shall one help to spoil and consume another, being divided into factions among themselves, either standing some for one head, and some for another; (as it falls out usually, when by treachery, or other evil courses, those aspire to a crown, that have no right thereunto, 1 King. 16.21, 22. and such an one was Hoshea, who slew, and succeeded Pekah, 2 King. 15.30.) or, some complying with the enemy, whom others oppose. See ch. 8.6.

*{and they together shall be against Judah*} Or, as some read it; *though they together* be *against Judah*; or, though both of them rise up *together against Judah*: whose brethren also they were, Gen. 49.8. the word, *rise up*, is supplied: as chap. 3.5. though they were divided among themselves, yet ready enough to combine together against Judah; as those, that were otherwise at enmity among themselves, against Christ and his church; Psal. 2.2. & 83.5–8. chap. 7.2, 5. Luk. 23.7, 8, 11, 12. Act. 4.27.

*{for all this, his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still*} As before, ch. 5.25. ver. 12, 17.

### CHAPTER 10

**Verse 1.** *{Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, &c.*} The first four verses of this chapter would have been joined to the former; as some report, that anciently they were. For they contain matter concerning the house of Israel, or the ten tribes: and deliver in a charge, with a denunciation annexed unto it, against them, wherein they are attainted of oppression, and wrong, in matter of judicature, as one of the reigning, and crying sins among them; for which God's hand was, and would still be so heavy upon them. Yet some suppose them to concern the kingdom of Judah, which to me seems not so probable.

*{woe unto them*} Some of the Jewish commenters, and of ours also, read the words, as spoken by way of compellation: *Ho they that, &c.* (*Ho they*, for, *O you*: as *O he*, for, *O thou*, Job 18.4.) and so carry it on to those words, ver. 3. *what will ye do?* the syntax, so conceived, is very like that in Job. See ver. 5. & ch. 18.1.

*{that decree*} Or, *draw up*. For the word signifies properly, *to portray*, Ezek. 4.1. or *paint*, Ezek. 23.4. or, *engrave*, ch. 22.16. or, *write*, ch. 30.8. or, *delineate, circumscribe*, as with a compass, set, or limit out, as by line and level, Prov. 8.27, 29. hence it is translated to matter of judicature, Prov. 8.15. and some translate it here, *prescribe*; because, judiciary sentences, are not only wont to be drawn up and described, or engrossed, but to prescribe also what men are to do, or to endure; and circumscribe them, or keep them within compass. The charge therefore is against such wicked rulers and judges, (for to those in authority is this title given, in regard of their legislative, or sentencing power, Gen. 49.10. Numb. 21.18. Judg. 5.9.) as enact injurious and cruel decrees, or ordinances; or deliver dooms and sentence of that nature, to the grievous affliction and vexation of poor people, Psal. 58.1, 2.

*{unrighteous decrees*} Heb. *decrees of iniquity*, or, *wrong*; as Psal. 36.12. Or, *of vexation*, or, *affliction*; as Job 5.6. & 15.35. chap. 58.9. & 59.4. Such as wrongfully vex, molest, and afflict.

*{and that write grievousness, which they have prescribed*} Or, *and to the writers, that write grievous things*. Or, *unto those, that writing write* such things: or, *and to those, that make to be written grievous* things *which they have prescribed*; that is, of their own prescription. Or lastly, *to those that write* grievous things; which *they*, that is, the judges *have prescribed*, or appointed to be written. For, all these ways is this clause rendered.

*{and that write*} These, most interpreters, both Jewish and Christian, distinguish from the former, according to those divers readings, before specified. And some would have them to be the scribes, or registers, such under-officers, as sat, say they, at the judges' feet, (Gen. 49.10. though that place, neither imports any such thing, nor would make for them, if it did) drew up their sentences, and entered them, Jer. 8.8. Others, take them to be such scribes and lawyers, as expounded the law to the people; or to those in authority, when called upon for their advice; Matthew 2.4. Luk. 11.44–46. But it seems to me, to be no other, than a repetition of the former; in terms every way equivalent, the one to the other: save, that a little more emphasis may be in this latter branch: as if he had said, that do not enact them only, but enter them; cause them to be entered, that they may not be reversed; but duly, and straitly executed, Dan. 6.8, 9.

*{grievousness*} That is, decrees, or acts *of grievance*; as *justice*, for decrees, or acts *of justice*; just ones, Prov. 8.15. and so here *grievance*, for *grievous* ones. This word, and the former, as they are oft joined together, Numb. 23.21. Job 4.8. & 5.6. & 15.35. Psal. 7.14. & 10.7. & 55.10. & 90.9. ch. 59.4. Hab. 1.3, 13. so they are in effect and substance, the same. The Psalmist's words, rightly rendered, afford a pregnant parallel of this place, Psal. 94.20. *Shall the judgment seat of vexations, have fellowship with thee?* or, *he that frames grievance, instead of an ordinance*.

*{which they have prescribed*} The defect of the relative is, in Hebrew, very frequent, verse 3. Gen. 39.4. Exod. 13.8. Psal. 71.18. ch. 42.5. Yet I suppose, there is no necessity of supplying it here. Since that the words may be rendered well enough, as was, among the rest, above hinted, *and that writing, write grievous* decrees. That are not afraid, or ashamed to cause their cruel and injurious decrees to be entered, that they may remain, as a public monument of their injustice and oppression, upon record. There is a double emphasis, both in the doubling of the middle letter, (in which form the verb is nowhere else found) and in the doubling of the word.

**V. 2.** *{To turn away the needy from judgment*} Some read the words, *To pervert the judgment seat*, or *the judgment of the needy*. And somewhat the like phrase of speech is found, Prov. 17.23. where it is said, that *a wicked man draws a bribe out of his bosom, to pervert the way of judgment*. And other places of the same nature might be produced; whereof, see on chap. 29.21. Howbeit, since that concerning the word that they here render judgment seat, or *judgment*, no other place yet appears, where it is so used, nor any such like form produced; I leave it to the consideration and judgment of the learned. Others yield it, *To make to decline the needy from* *judgment*. And indeed, the word signifies, in its first form, to *decline* or *turn aside*, used of Balaam's ass, Num. 22.23. and applied to matter of judicature, Exod. 23.2. In his next form; to *to make to decline*, or *turn aside*: used of Balaam's causing his ass to *decline*, or *turn aside*, back again, in the same place. So that to *turn aside the needy from judgment*, or *from* their *suit*, or *cause*, (for that the word primarily signifies, Jer. 30.15.) is to stop them from proceeding in their cause, or bringing it to any good issue; as we use to say, to put them beside it. *The righteous*, says Solomon, *knows* (the meaning is not, takes notice of, or considers the case or condition; as Psal. 31.7. & 41.1. but hears, *takes cognizance of the cause*, or suit *of the needy*, (the very words, here used,) *but the wicked knows it not*. He refuses to give them hearing, or to take cognizance of their cause, ch. 1.23. Which if it be a wicked part in a judge, how much more, upon hearing, to turn them away without relief, or, by an unjust doom, to force them from their right, as it is in the next branch more fully expressed. Howbeit it is well observed, by some, that the words may well be rendered, not, *To turn aside, &c.* as denoting the end of that they were said to do, v. 1. but *in turning aside*. And so in the next branch *In taking away*; as importing the manner how, and matter wherein, the vexation and grievance, before mentioned, was committed, and did consist. See of the like use of this form, c. 3.8. Deut. 22.21. & 28.63. 1 Sam. 12.17.

*{the needy*} Heb. *the attenuated*, or *thin* ones. See ch. 17.4.

*{and to take away the right from the poor of my people*} The same thing, in effect, repeated in other terms; as the manner of our prophet is, but with some emphasis added to it.

*{take away*} The word signifies, *to snatch, pull*, or *tear away*, by force. As a man's cattle, or chattels are by a hostile hand, Deut. 28.31. Or the flesh, or skin of a beast is torn away, or pulled off, by beast, or butcher, Mic. 3.2.

*{the right*} Heb. *judgment*. That which of right, should, by judgment, have been assigned them. So Psal. 9.4.

*{from the poor*} The word properly signifies *afflicted*, and is distinguished from *poor*, Psal. 35.10. & 94.21.

*{of my people*} Hence, some would infer, that this prophecy should not concern Israel, but Judah, because the prophet terms them, his people. But the prophet seems to speak, rather here in God's person, than in his own, as ch. 3.12, 15. and God had his people, no doubt, as well in Israel, as in Judah, 1 King. 19.18. Nor does God forbear, notwithstanding their revolt from him, which made them, deservedly, not to be deemed his people, Hos. 1.9. Yet, in regard of his right of interest in them, their former profession, and present duty, to style them still *his people*, Hos. 4.6, 12.

*{that widows may be a prey; and that they may rob the fatherless*} He shows here, who the *needy*, and poor, or *thin*, and *afflicted* ones were, that he spoke of before, as oppressed by them, in matters of judicature; the *widows*, and the *fatherless*. Fit objects, rather of mercy, ordinarily, in regard of their misery, and want of help, and whom God, therefore, had given them special charge to see righted and relieved when they should be wronged and oppressed, by others. See ch. 1.17, 23.

*{widows*} That is, the houses, lands, and livelihood of such.

*{their prey*} Esteeming what they strip them of, as lawful purchase, like prey taken from an enemy in war, Ezek. 38.12. chap. 49.24.

*{and that*} A defect of the particle, intimating the end. See ch. 5.11. & 7.25.

*{rob*} Make a spoil and prey of them; a warlike term, as the former; both joined together, chap. 8.1, 3. verse 6. The Assyrian was to do to them, what they did to their own people, chap. 8.4.

**V. 3.** *{And what will ye do? &c.*} Their wickedness went before; their punishment now follows. Those that read the first words of the chapter, as uttered, in way of compellation; render these, *Now what will ye do? &c.* Of which use of the copulative, see on chapter 8.1.

*{what will ye do in the day of visitation?*} How think you to escape the just judgment of God? as Matth. 23.33. Rom. 2.3. Or, what course will you take, when he comes to reckon with you? as Job 31.14, 23.

*{day of visitation*} *Visitation*, and *day of visitation*, is twofold; in mercy, or offers of mercy, Ruth 1.6. Luk. 1.68. & 19.44. And in wrath and judgment, Jer. 10.15. & 11.23. Ezek. 10.1. Hos. 9.7. the latter is here meant: and therefore follows.

*{and in the desolation, which shall come from far*} Which shall be effected, by a people that comes from a country, far remote: That is, by the Assyrian, ch. 7.17. & 8.7. & 9.11. v. 5, 6. whose country lay far from the land of Israel, c. 5.26. & 7.18. a defect of the relative; as v. 1. ch. 9.18.

*{to whom will ye flee for help?*} You shall be more helpless, than those are, that in vain seek for help and relief, unto you. They have God to help them, Psal. 9.9. & 10.14. & 68.5. but none shall be able to help you, against him, Hos. 5.13. & 7.11.

*{and where will ye leave your glory?*} Where will you find any place of security; where you may with safety, dispose of your wealth, and your bravery, wherein you now so much glory, chap. 28.15. Amos 6.13. But neither shall you know then, where to bestow it, nor shall it be able to stand you in any stead, Prov. 11.4. Ezek. 7.19. Jer. 22.23. See chap. 15.7. His exposition is scarce worth the mentioning, who would have the words rendered, *where will you quarter* your *vaunting* soldiers then? and requires the former passages to be understood, not of judiciary abuses; but of wrongs done by enquartering of soldiers, and their commanders; the sense of those calamities that thence accrued to his own countrymen, and many, at present, are sensible of with us; did so much transport him, that he is so bold, as confidently to avouch, that they do all wrest the text besides its genuine sense, who interpret it otherwise. Of whom, notwithstanding, I must needs acknowledge myself one, till I see better ground for his exposition thereof, than I yet do.

**V. 4.** *{Without me, they shall bow down under the prisoners, and they shall fall under the slain*} This passage has undergone many interpretations, which, in part, arise from an ambiguity in the first word of the verse: That some suppose to include in it a pronoun, as our version renders it, and as sometime it does; as Hos. 13.4. And these two ways expound it. Some, *But for me*; that is, if I did not support them, they would come to extreme misery, either be murdered, or captivated. Others, *Without me*, that is, because they have left me, and I have withdrawn myself from them, they will come unto ruin, Hos. 5.6. & 7.13. Or, *without me*; that is, any fault of mine, it is, that these evils befall them; their destruction is of themselves, Hos. 13.9. But the greater part of interpreters, both Jewish and Christian, conceive the negative, or exceptive particle, to be simple and single, without the pronoun affixed to it; and so indeed it is most frequently used: and herein these agree; but in exposition are much divided. To pass by the rest, and to point at some one, or two, that are deemed to carry more probability with them, than the rest. Some would have it to be in nature of an oath; as if God did, in a defective kind of speech, declare, that no other way, or course, should serve the turn with them, but to be either bound, or slain. But I find not any oath in Scripture, conceived in the form, here used. Others render the words, *But that ye bow down below the bound, and fall below the slain*: That is, say they, there will be no way for you to save yourselves, save by the most base submission to the enemy, that can be imagined; described here in an hyperbolical speech, of bowing lower than men in bonds, and falling lower than the dead; not unlike that, ch. 57.9. *Thou didst debase thyself, even unto hell*: (which yet, some other, to allay, render it, *As if they were bound; as if they were dead*.) And they understand it of Ezekiah's submiss seeking to Sennacherib by his messengers, 2 King. 18.14. But we need have no recourse to such rank excesses, where the letter will endure a familiar sense. Nor does the text seem to be so fitly applied. Others therefore, retaining the same reading, understand it, not of any means of escape, or attempts to save themselves; but that there will be nothing for them to do, or to endure; but as high and great as they now are, to stoop under their fellow prisoners, thrust, and crowded together; and to lie under slain, heaped, and piled one upon another. Lastly, the ancient Greek, and old Latin, referring it to the two first branches of the verse, next foregoing, the former whereof, (some here repeat,) render the words, *That ye may not be bowed under bonds, or fall among the slain*: As if it were said, *What will ye do then?* or *to whom will ye flee for help? &c.* That you may not be either taken prisoners, or put to the sword? As much as to say, you shall by no shift of your own, or help from others, be able to escape, either the one or the other. And this to me seems to be the plainest sense of the place, and most agreeable to the tenor of the context. Only, for *under bonds*, would rather be *among the bound*, or *prisoners*; as after *among the slain*. Or, to come more nearly, and exactly home to the proper sense of the particle; *in the place of the bound; in the place of the slain*; as, *Am I in place of God?* Gen. 30.2. & 50.19. See v. 16.

*{they shall bow down*} Heb. *he shall bow down*. Indefinitely, used for one, or any one, or each one of them. *bow down*. as ch. 2.20. & 6.2.

*{prisoners*} Heb. *prisoner*. Collectively, as chap. 24.22. & 42.7.

*{and*} Or, *or*: As Exod. 21.15. Some of them shall be carried away captive, some killed.

*{fall*} To the ground; as the blood, and bodies of men are wont to do, 1 Sam. 26.20. & 31.1. 2 Sam. 1.19, 25. & 3.34, 38. Judg. 3.25.

*{slain*} By the enemy.

*{For all this, his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still*} The close of the denunciation against Israel begun ch. 9.8. and continued hitherto; where it is shut up with a commination of further wrath, again repeated. Of which, see before, on ch. 5.25. & 9.12.

**V. 5.** *{O Assyrian*} Because the Assyrian king, had been formerly declared, to be the instrument that God would use, as well for the scourging of Judah, chap. 7.17, 20. as for the sweeping away of Israel, ch. 9.11, 14. God, therefore, by the prophet, for the support and comfort of his faithful ones, those of Judah especially, inserts here a denunciation of destruction to befall that king, when God had done his work by him, and a gracious promise of deliverance of his people from him, and from those evils, that either by him they had sustained; or were likely further to sustain.

*{O Assyrian*} Or, *Ho Assyrian*: as spoken by way of compellation, ch. 55.1. as calling upon him, to come, and take his commission; and undertake his charge, v. 2. And so most of the Jewish commenters. Others, and so some of them, *Ah*, or, *Alas*, as delivered in way of commiseration. God, thereby, expressing his grief for those calamities, that, by the Assyrian, were to be inflicted on his people; ch. 1.4, 5, 24. Others, by way of denunciation; as v. 1. *Woe to the Assyrian*, See ch. 18.1.

*{Assyrian*} Heb. *Ashur*. The name of Shem's second son, Gen. 10.22. from him was so named, the country he lived in, Gen. 10.11. and his issue, Psal. 83.8. It is here put for the king of that people, and country: and more specially for Sennacherib, together with his forces: as v. 24. Ezek. 31.3.

*{the rod of mine anger*} Or, *my rod of anger*. The rod, or instrument that God is wont to make use of, for the chastising, and punishing of those with whom he is angry, ch. 30.31. so his *rod of wrath*, or, *wrathful rod*, Lam. 3.1.

*{and the staff in their hand, is mine indignation*} That is, as some expound it, all the power they have to smite, and afflict, is mine indignation, wherewith they come armed. *Staff*, for *power*; as Psal. 110.2. ch. 14.5. Others read it, *though*, or *albeit the staff in their hand be mine indignation*. The copulative, for the discretive; as Hos. 5.2. That is, albeit I make use of him; yet woe be to him, verse 12. Others again. *For the staff, which is in their hand, is my wrath*: as rendering a reason of the former branch, the copulative, for the causative: as Psal. 60.11. Our two ancient versions seem to have come nearest the right. They render the whole verse thus, *O Ashur, which art*, or *woe also to Ashur, which is the staff of my wrath; and in whose hand is the rod of my indignation*, or *my punishment*. Which version is also backed with the authority of some of the Jewish writers, and with a small supply, will thus, I suppose, exactly come home to the original. *Woe to the Assyrian, who is the rod of mine anger*, or, *my rod of anger: and the staff in their hand*, (that is, in the hand of him, and his forces) *is the staff of mine indignation*, or *my staff of indignation*. The relative, is wanting, as ver. 1. the pronoun put for the verb substantive; as ch. 9.15. the word *staff* is supplied, in the latter member, as is usual in the like form. Dan. 4.33. *his hairs were grown like eagles* for feathers of eagles; *and his nails, like birds*, that is, as nails, or claws (for the same word, in Hebrew, signifies either) of *birds*. See the like also, ver. 10. I shall add what one of the Jewish writers has, because I find it followed, and approved by some of ours. He thus renders it, *The staff that is sent*, or that is to be sent (supplied from, v. 6.) *into their place*, that is, into the land of the Israelites) *in mine indignation*. It is true that the word signifying *an hand*, is in Hebrew, sometime used for *a place*, Deut. 23.12. Jer. 6.3. but that seems not to have place here. The same thing is related again in the latter branch, that was mentioned in the former; as ver. 1. but with some aggravation. For the *staff* seems a heavier, and sorer instrument of correction than a *rod*, which may be but a twig: And *indignation* a degree above *anger*, ch. 30.30. Mal. 1.4. There is a *staff* to *stay*, see ch. 3.1. and *a staff* to *strike* with, Numb. 22.27. and this latter, is the *staff* here alluded to. See ch. 9.4.

**V. 6.** *{I will send him*} The commission, wherewith God would furnish the Assyrian king to go up, and proceed with, against his own people for their sins and excesses. Not that God did intimate any such matter unto him; (albeit he pretended as much, ch. 36.10.) but that God would by his secret, and unsearchable providence, so dispose things, that he should, though upon other grounds, and for other ends, invade that people, ver. 7. So 2 King. 17.25. & 24.2. 2 Chr. 33.11. & 36.17.

*{against an hypocritical nation*} Or, rather, *a profane nation*, or, *a polluted* people, See ch. 9.17.

*{and against the people of my wrath*} Which, by their wickedness, are become liable to wrath, and with whom, for the same, I am highly displeased, ch. 47.6. & 57.17.

*{will I give him a charge*} By a secret instinct; and an unseen, yea, unperceived, but efficacious disposal, Jer. 34.22. & 49.14. & 50.21. 2 Sam. 16.10.

*{to take the spoil, and to take the prey*} Heb. *to spoil the spoil, and prey on the prey*: as Ezek. 38.12. that is, to spoil, and plunder to the purpose. For such repetitions, either in the same term, or, in words of the same notion, are wont to amplify, and exaggerate: as Psal. 76.5. *they slept their sleep*; that is, were cast into a deep sleep: and 1 King. 1.40. *they rejoiced with great joy*, that is, exceeding great joy: and Jer. 33.11. *the voice of joy, and the voice of gladness*, that is, of much rejoicing. See ver. 16. And we have here an interpretation of the name, given to the prophet's son, *Maher-shalal-hash-baz*, ch. 8.3. and a just retaliation of judgment, on those wicked wretches reproved, and threatened before, ver. 2. a spoiling of them by strangers, who had spoiled their own brethren. The spoils that they had taken, together with the rest of their substance, being surprised; and carried away by the enemy: and that fulfilled, that is afterward threatened, to those also, that now spoil them; *Woe to thee, that spoiledst, when thou wast not spoiled; when thou ceasest to spoil*, (being interrupted by the enemy) *thou shalt* then be *spoiled* yourself, ch. 33.1.

*{and to tread them down like mire in the street*} Heb. *to lay him* (to wit, the people before mentioned) *as the mire*, or, *dirt of the streets*, So Psal. 18.42. ch. 41.21. Mic. 7.10. not to make havoc of their goods only; but to seize on their persons, and to use them in most cruel and despiteful manner; to beat them down, and trample on them, and even batter them to pieces, ch. 28.3, 18. 2 King. 9.33. Dan. 7.7. & 8.7. which barbarous cruelty, though God approved not in them; yet was he pleased to make use of, for the punishing of this profane and wicked people, Lam. 3.34–39.

**V. 7.** *{Howbeit he meaneth not so, neither doth his heart think so*} He intends nothing less, whatsoever he pretend, ch. 36.7, 19. than the doing of my work, and the fulfilling of my will.

*{Howbeit*} Or, *Yet*. Heb. *And*: as v. 4. Hos. 1.10.

*{meaneth not*} Heb. *imagineth not*. For it signifies properly, to conceive an image, similitude, or likeness of a thing in the imaginative faculty: A term, taken from artificers, painters, limners, gravers, or builders, that are wont to draw models of those works, that they intend to show their skill in. See ch. 14.24. and chap. 40.18, 25.

*{neither doth, &c.*} The same thing conceived, and expressed in other terms.

*{but it is in his heart to destroy, and cut off nations, not a few*} His intent and purpose is, only, to satisfy his cruel, enormous, and ambitious desires, by conquest of countries, and making havoc of people. Which yet God is said to cut off by him, c. 9.14.

*{it is in his heart*} That is, it is in his purpose: as 1 Sam. 2.35. 1 Chr. 28.2.

**V. 8.** *{For he saith*} In his heart, or, to his people, say the Rabbis; as Lamech to his wives, Gen. 4.23. but the former rather; he thinks with himself: as, *the fool saith in his heart*, Psal. 14.1. and, *I said in my prosperity*, Psal. 30.6. For, to God the heart speaks; and the thought of it he hears, Matth. 9.3, 4. Heb. 4.12, 13.

*{Are not my princes altogether kings?*} A vaunting speech, attributed to the Assyrian king, expressing his inward insolency, arrogancy, and impiety; much of it in effect related again, as delivered from Sennacherib, by his messengers to Ezekiah, ch. 36.9, 15, 18–20. & 37.10, 13, 24, 25. whereby it appears, that Sennacherib and the invasion made by him, into the land of Judah, even unto Jerusalem, is here principally pointed at, chap. 36.1, 2. His meaning in this branch seems to be, that they held now of him, as their sovereign; and served under him, as their commander, who had before been absolute kings; but having been subdued by him, were now but as his princes. And he might well be termed a king of kings, as Nebuchadnezzar is styled, Ezek. 26.7. Dan. 2.37. or that his princes and favorites, were for place, power, and authority, as good, and as great, as kings, so Rabshakeh vaunts of them, as the meanest of those, that took charge under him, being compeers with Ezekiah, ch. 36.9. who at every word, therefore, in mention of him, names him, *The great King*, ch. 36.4, 13.

**V. 9.** *{Is not Calno as Carchemish?*} Have not I subdued all these kingdoms, and places, as well one, as another.

*{Calno*} Called *Calach*, Gen. 10.10. & Amos 6.2. one of Nimrod's great cities. Some have supposed it to be the same with *Calinisum*, a city mentioned by Ammiane, l. 23. situate upon Euphrates: but that seems to have been by a slip of some scribe's pen, *Callinisum*, for *Callinicum*, as in other authors it is found termed. It is rather therefore deemed to have been that which was in latter times, termed, *Ctesiphon*, sometime the head city of the Parthian kingdom, situate upon Tigris; the region thereabout from the ancient name of it, being commonly called *Chalonitis*, Strabo, l. 11. and 16. and Plinie, l. 6. ch. 26, 27.

*{Carchemish*} Of it, see 2 Chr. 39.20. a city situate upon Euphrates, Jer. 46.2. called in latter times, *Cercusium*.

*{is not Hamath*} This some take to be Amathus in Arabia, mentioned by Herodotus, l. 2. & 3. But others, rather, take it for a town, belonging to Syria, and situate not far from some of the others, here mentioned; all near upon Euphrates, 1 Chr. 18.3, 9. thence the Hamathites, deriving their pedigree from Canaan, Gen. 10.18. 1 Chr. 1.16. it is mentioned, as a boundary of the land of promise, Numb. 34.8. Josh. 13.5. 1 King. 8.65. 1 Chr. 13.5. and as Joseph the Jew witnesses in his *Antiquities*, l. 1. c. 7. it retained this name with the natives unto his times; though by the Greeks and Macedonians, termed *Epiphania*, from Antiochus Epiphanes, the reedifier of it. See ch. 63.19.

*{as Arpad*} Of this place, are the *Arvadites* supposed to have been; joined with the *Amathites*, both of the posterity of Cham and Canaan, Gen. 10.18. called by Ptolomy Arodites, and placed in Syria: See ch. 36.19. & 37.13. It is by Joseph the Jew, termed *Arphas*; by Isidore, *Arsa*, and in the register of the Roman empire, *Arisa*.

*{is not Samaria as Damascus?*} Of these, see chap. 7.8, 9. & 8.4.

**V. 10.** *{As my hand hath found the kingdoms of the idols*} He promises himself conquest of Judah and Jerusalem, in spite of God himself, from the success that he had attained against other kingdoms, cities, and countries, maugre all the power of their tutelar gods, ch. 36.15, 20. & 37.10, 12.

*{my hand*} My power, my might; as Deut. 8.17. Judg. 7.2. See ver. 13.

*{hath found*} Has reached, gotten, taken, subdued; as Levit. 12.8. and 14.21. Numb. 32.23. Prov. 1.13. So v. 14.

*{idols*} Heb. *idol*, collectively. See chap. 2.18. so he accounts the gods that other kingdoms and nations worshiped, because they were not able to protect their people against him and his forces, ch. 46.7.

*{and whose graven images*} Heb. *and their graven images*, for *and* those, *whose graven images*. A defect of the antecedent; as Ruth 1.16,17. 2 Chr. 1.4. Or, *though their graven images*, and, for, though, as Gen. 8.21. See on v. 5.

*{did excel them of Jerusalem and Samaria*} Heb. *were before Jerusalem, and Samaria*, before, for better, more excellent; as Prov. 22.1. Eccl. 7.1. Heb. 12.24. *Jerusalem, and Samaria*, for, the idols of Jerusalem, and Samaria. Of which manner of defective speech, see on v. 5. Thus this blasphemous beast, not only ranks and ranges God among idols; as v. 11. 2 Chr. 32.19. but prefers the base idols of other people before him, who is the only true God, Jer. 10.33–7,8–10.

**V. 11.** *{Shall I not, as I have done unto Samaria, and her idols, so do to Jerusalem, and her idols?*} Or, *May I not?* I will assuredly do it: or, who can hinder me from doing it? why should I not do the one, as well as the other? Of the success of his predecessors Tiglath-Pileser, and Shalmaneser, against Samaria; see 2 King. 15.19. & 17.5,6. for what was done by them, he takes to himself, as succeeding them in their power, and having no less than they had. All he esteems idols, in respect of his god Mithras, the Sun, whom the Assyrians worshiped.

*{her idols*} The latter term here used, comes of a word, that signifies to *put to pain, and grief*. Whence *Jabez* had his name, 1 Chron. 4.9. and idols, or false gods, are deservedly so called; not only because God is vexed, and grieved by them, with those that leave him, to adore them, and adhere to them, Psal. 78.58. ch. 63.10. Ezek. 6.9. but also, because they put those that serve them, and trust in them, to much pain, but can do them no good, Ps. 16.4. so he made account God would do with Jerusalem, ch. 36.11,15. but the issue proved otherwise, ch. 37.35,36. and he speaks of God, as if he were the God of that nation alone, who in power, and right, is God, and Lord of the whole world, Ps. 47.2,7,8.

**V. 12.** *{Wherefore it shall come to pass, that*} Heb. *And it shall be.* as c. 3.24.

*{wherefore*} Heb. *And.* The copulative for the illative; as ch. 3.17. & 9.11. as connecting together his pride, and his fall; as the cause, and effect, the one of the other; Prov. 11.2. & 16.18. & 18.12. or, *But*, the copulative for the adversative; as Psal. 64.7. as crossing his presumptuous expectation, with prediction of a sad and unexpected issue: or, *For*, as some; the copulative for the causative: as ch. 9.13. as having reference to vers. 1, and rendering a reason, to the woe there denounced against Ashur.

*{when the Lord hath performed his whole work upon Mount Sion*} When he has sufficiently chastised his own people, (for with them, he usually begins, Jer. 25.18. 1 Pet. 4.17.) he will proceed to reckon with him, and burn the rod, wherewith he chastised them, Jer. 30.11,16,21,23. Lam. 2.17. & 4.21.

*{the Lord hath*} For, *I have*. For it is the Lord that speaks it, the noun for the pronoun: as chap. 2.1. with chap. 6.1. chap. 7.3. 2 Tim. 1.18.

*{performed*} Heb. *perfected*, or, *finished*, Lam. 2.17. Zach. 4. ver. 9.

*{his whole work*} All that he intends to do, for the chastising of his people, ch. 28.21. & 40.2.

*{upon Mount Sion, and on Jerusalem*} As ch. 1.27. in the strait siege of her by Sennacherib's forces for some time, and the spoil made of the country round about her, ch. 36.1,2. & 37.3.

*{I will punish the fruit of the stout heart of the King of Assyria*} I will punish him, for this his impious, and presumptuous boasting; and his attempts against my people, chap. 37.23,29.

*{punish*} Heb. *visit upon them*. Punish him for them: as Exod. 20.5. ch. 26.14. Jer. 50.18. the phrase implies, that God neither chastises nor punishes; but with due consideration, and full cognizance of the crime, or fault, for which he does either, Gen. 11.5. & 18.21. and would have men to do the like, Deut. 13.14.

*{the fruit of the heart*} For, from the heart, issues, what comes forth at the mouth, Matth. 12.34,35. & 15.18,19. See ch. 9.13.

*{stout heart*} Heb. *greatness of heart*, ch. 9.9.

*{King*} Sennacherib, ch. 36.1. & 37.36–38.

*{and the glory of his high looks*} Heb. *the bravery*, (ch. 3.18, that is, the pride; because bravery both breeds, and bewrays pride) *of the loftiness of his eyes*, wherein pride also appears, ch. 2.11,12.
