**V. 13.** *{For he saith*} Heb. *Because he hath said*.

*{by the strength of my hand*} See v. 10.

*{I have done it*} A defect of the pronoun: as ch. 5.29.

*{and by my wisdom*} What God had done by him, and his antecessors, as his instruments, ch. 37.26,27, that, he arrogates to himself, and ascribes to his own power, and policy. That, which every man's heart is by nature, over-prone to, Deut. 8.17. Amos 6.13. Hab. 1.16.

*{for I am prudent*} Heb. *I understanding*. I am one of wisdom, and understanding (Gen. 41.33.) as well as of power, able to dispose mine affairs, to the best advantage for myself. See the like vaunting of wisdom, chap. 19.11. Jer. 8.8. but especially, Ezek. 28.3.

*{and I have removed the bounds of the people*} and, or, therefore; as ch. 9.11. ver. 12. By my prudent, and politic carriage, and managing of my designs, I have enlarged my dominions, and took away those bounds, wherewith other kingdoms and territories were before listed and limited, as therewith severed one from another; and excluding others from encroaching and entering in, upon them, Act. 17.26. they are said to *remove the bound*, that encroaches upon the possessions of others, Prov. 22.28. Hos. 5.10.

*{and have robbed their treasures*} As the enlargement of his territories, by the subduing of other countries, and adjoining them, to his own; so the increase of his wealth, by finding out, and making seizure of their hidden treasures, reserved for future uses, he ascribes as well to his policy, as his power. So Ezek. 38.4,5.

*{robbed*} So is the word rendered, 1 Sam. 23.1. but in this place it would rather, be some other ways rendered; because the Assyrian king is personated, as relating his own acts, and achievements: *I have seized*, or, *spoiled*, or *preyed upon*, made a spoil of their treasures. So it is rendered, Judg. 2.14. *spoilers, that spoiled them*: and chap. 17.14. *that spoil us*: and Hos. 13.15. *he shall spoil the treasures*.

*{treasures*} Heb. *preparations*, or *prepared things*. For the word it comes of, signifies to prepare, and the Hebrews use the feminine, commonly for the neuter: and it imports therefore such matters of special use and worth, as are wont to be treasured up and reserved, against times of necessary use and employment, such as the hidden treasures, that God promised, to make Cyrus master of, chap. 45.3. But because the word is nowhere else found in this form; and the Jewish critics, the Masorets, observe some misreading, or miswriting rather, in one letter of it; and yet whether letter we take, the sense will be the same; one that takes upon him to be a great critic, would instead of this feminine, substitute a masculine form, that signifies, as he says, rams, or bellwethers, but indeed, rather, *great he-goats*, Jer. 50.8. distinguished from rams, as oft, Num. 7. so Jer. 51.40. put here, says he, for princes and potentates: and so oft-times they are, chap. 34.6. Zach. 10.3. and again, because one letter in the other word rendered commonly, *robbing*, or *spoiling*, is of an ambiguous sound; like that of *Sibboleth*, and *Shibboleth*, Judg. 12.6. according to the pointing of it, nor is the word read elsewhere with that ambiguous character, he takes occasion thereby, to solicit the reading, and to bring him home, by aspiring the second letter, to another word much more ambiguous, used Ezek. 39.2. which because some render there *persuade*, he would have this here also so to signify, and so this branch of the Assyrian's speech, to have reference to his policy, as the next to his power, as if he had said, by my wiles I have persuaded great potentates to yield to me; and by my might, I have pulled them down from their thrones. But not to insist on the improbability of the sense here intended, as coming from the mouth of one that stood so much upon his valor and power; and whose prudence and policy, would seem to look another way: it is overmuch boldness thus to mangle the text, and to force in such senses, as the words will not admit.

*{and I have put down the inhabitants*} put down, or, *pulled*, or, *thrown down*, Heb. *made to descend*, or, *come down*: Jer. 49.16. Obad. 4. or, as a learned man of late, *stricken down*: as beasts, the greater sort of them, especially, are wont to be by the butcher or slaughterman: and consequently *slain*. So Jer. 51.40. to which purpose they are said *to descend*, or *come down to the slaughter*, ch. 34.6. Jer. 48.15. & 50.27. Hag. 2.22.

*{the inhabitants*} Heb. *the sitters*: those *that sit*, or, *inhabit*, as ch. 53.9. I have made havoc of the countries subdued by me. Howbeit, here, by *sitters*, some suppose, may be understood, such, as *sit aloft*, as ch. 6.1. & 9.7. and so the meaning should be, such as sit on the throne of state. See chap. 13.20. I have pulled them down from their regal power, and made them my vassals. v. 8.

*{as a valiant man*} Here also the Jewish critics observe some diversity about the text. For instead of that which our printed copies hold out, they with detraction of one letter, put in the margin, as so to be read, *cabbir*, which word signifies either *strong, and mighty*, as most take it, or *copious, and much*: as some other render that word. This reading, the Jewish commenters following, and of ours, also, not a few, refer the word here, to inhabitants, and expound it: Some, *those that sit*, or *dwell in a strong place*: and so the meaning should be, *I will pull, or throw down those that dwell, or sit most firmly*, that have the strongest, or surest seats, or places of abode. Others, *many inhabitants*, as the word is used, ch. 16.14. and whereas it might be objected that the word is singular, whereas that which it is joined unto, is plural; and that the adjective is seldom set before its substantive: it is answered, in defense of this version, that the word may be taken here substantively, as the word of contrary signification, for the most part, is: and this also, Job. 31.25. and so it may here be rendered, *a multitude of inhabitants, or sitters*: to which might be added: that sometime, though seldom, the adjective leads. See on ch. 9.6. *Wonderful.* Thus, they that follow the reading, as they term it: others follow the writing, as it is expressed in the text: and render it (not without the authority also of a Rabbine of great note) in the same manner, that our Bibles do, and the old Latin: *as a mighty, or, a valiant man*. Yea, some of the Jewish interpreters would make a medley of both expressions, imagining the term here used, to be composed of two words, *cabbir*, and *abbir*: which both they conceive to signify in substance the same: and to import a man of extraordinary might. But this exposition of that, which the text holds out, is controlled by the forementioned author. Who upon a general survey of all the places, where the word *abbir* is found, shows that it is, if not for the most part, yet very frequently, taken, substantively, and that it is oftentimes used, for a great *bull*, or, an *ox*, it is apparent by these places, Psal. 22.12. & 50.13. & 68.30. ch. 34.7. in which sense, he supposes it to be here used; as if he should say, I have stricken down, and laid along the people of those places, which with my forces I entered upon, like a company of *oxen*, or great *bulls*. The word is singular, but taken collectively; as *ox*, chap. 1.3.

**V. 14.** *{And my hand hath found*} Has gotten, or seized on. See before, v. 11,13. Yet there seems some emphasis here in the word: in comparing the treasures of the lands, surprised by him, to a bird's nest, or eggs in a nest, that are taken, without pains: all the labor is but to find them.

*{as a nest*} Or, *as in a nest*: as birds, or eggs in a nest, Deut. 22.6,7. a defect of the particle: as Job. 1.13.

*{the riches*} Or, *wealth*. The word signifies primarily, *strength*, whence, *men of might*, able to bear arms, Gen. 47.6. Deut. 3.18. Josh. 10.7. in the next place *wealth*, Ruth 2.1. Job. 20.15. because that is esteemed the strength and support of an estate, either public, or private: they seem to strain the text needlessly, who read it, *as a bird's nest, the nest of their riches*, the particle is observed to be divers times used as a note of the accusative. So 2 Sam. 2.30. Jer. 40.2.

*{of the people*} Heb. *peoples*. Of many people. as chap. 2.3.

*{and as one gathering eggs, that are left*} To wit, by the dam; forsaking them for fear.

*{have I gathered all the earth*} I have conquered the greatest part of the world, commonly known, and brought it under my command; so most interpreters. But the speech is here of seizing of wealth, and gathering of treasure; and that with as much ease and small difficulty, as a man, would take eggs out of a bird's nest. I should therefore rather choose to read it, *have I gathered the wealth of all the land*: the whole country wheresoever I come, or, (as in a vaunting manner, such a vainglorious boaster might speak) of *all the earth*, or the whole world. The like defect, and supply, from the foregoing words see Gen. 1.16. Job. 31.3. & 36.32.

*{and there was none that moved the wing, or opened the mouth, or peeped*} None, that did so, that is, none, that dared so do. There was none that dared stir; in way of opposition, against my forces, when I sent them to surprise and take away their treasures, 1 King. 20.5,6.

*{move the wing*} He persists in his former similitude from birds, that are wont to strike with the wing, at those, that offer to disturb them in their sitting, and to meddle with their eggs, or young under them; or, when they are driven off their nest, yet hover and flutter to and fro about those that take them away; and in a mournful manner, cry and make a noise after them.

*{moved*} *did move*, or, *wag*, for, *durst move*, or *wag*: as, *did lift up head* for, *durst lift up head*, Zach. 1.21.

*{the wing*} For, *with the wing*. So some of the Jewish critics, because the verb is not transitive; or, as some therefore, *no wing that moved*. Yet other of them say, that these neutrals have sometime a transitive notion: as the like to this, ch. 1.30.

*{or*} Heb. *and*, as ch. 8.19.

*{opened the mouth*} See the like expressions, Exod. 11.7. Josh. 10.21.

*{or peeped*} Spoken not of the young, as some would have it; but of the dam, bemoaning them. See chap. 8.19. and 38.14.

**V. 15.** *{Shall the ax boast itself against him, that heweth therewith?*} Hitherto were the Assyrian king's insolent and arrogant boastings. Which, in these words, the prophet controls, showing the unreasonableness, yea the absurdity and senselessness of them. Is it equal, or fit, that those, who are but God's instruments, (as all, even the wicked themselves are, ver. 5. Jer. 51.20.) and have not their action only from him, (as the *ax*, or *saw*, from the workman; the *rod*, or *staff*, from him that smites with it) but their power also to act, and fitness for such use, as they are applied unto, and employed in; should such advance themselves against him, whose instruments, and such instruments, they are, as can do nothing without him, and without such power as they have received from him? Joh. 19.11.

*{against him*} Or, as some, *above him*. The word will bear either: *against him*, by threatening to deal with him, as with the idols of other people, ver. 11. *above him*, by arrogating to himself what God has done by him, v. 13.

*{or shall the saw magnify itself against him that shaketh it*} Or, *moveth it*. The sawyer, that saws with it. An instance of the like stamp with the former.

*{as if the rod should shake itself, against them that lift it up*} Or, according to some, *as if the rod moved him, that lifted it up*; or, (to pass by many other version) as some other, *when one shaketh the rod*, (that is, when the rod is shaken) should it boast, or magnify itself, *against those that lift it up*? a supply from the former branches, neither unusual, nor unfit. See v. 14. Some of the Jewish doctors make it, an application unto God, and the king of Assyria; as he being the *rod*, ver. 5. and God the person, that smote by him: is but by way of excellency, spoken of in the plural number: as Josh. 24.29. Eccl. 5.8. and the ground of the action, proceeding not from the rod, but from the hand that smites with it.

*{as if the staff should lift up itself, as if it were no wood*} Or, *or if the staff should lift up itself, as if it were not wood*: and this version might peradventure receive some strength from that of the ostrich in Job, Job. 39.16. *she hardeneth herself towards her young ones, as if they were not hers*, or, *as to not hers*; save that there is a particle in the original there, which is not here. But see chap. 40.24. where the syntax seems the same with this here. The Hebrew has no more but this, *as lifting up a staff*; or *when one lifteth up a staff, not wood*, which some render, *as if the staff did lift up* (either itself, or him, that held it) and were *not wood*, or, *as if the staff*, because it is *lift up*, were *not wood*, or, *as if the staff should lift up* itself, against *not wood*, that is, against him, who is *not wood*, but able to move, and stir of himself. The Jewish writers, *when the staff is lift up, it is not the wood*; to wit, that lifts it up, but the man that holds it. Some of ours, *when the staff is lift up, the wood is nothing*: no regard is had of it, be it wood, or aught else; but of him that smites with it. Others lastly, *or, when the rod is lift up, is it not wood*: does it not still remain as it was before, a sorry piece of wood, unable to stir, or, to act aught of itself? and this last, without any strain at all flows most fitly from the text. So the heathen idols are vilified, that they are no better, many of them, than a parcel of searwood, chap. 44.13–20. Jer. 2.27. Hos. 4.12. in like manner, the king of Assyria, though raised up by God, and used as a bastinado, to cudgel his own people and others with, yet is still a poor, sorry, mortal, corruptible creature, such another piece of flesh, as before he was, Psal. 82.6,7. & 146.3,4. Eccl. 6.10. ch. 2.22. Ezek. 28.9. But all these exposition and readings also, a late writer of great note controls, conceiving them all to be mistaken in the word, *barim*, which they take for a verb, signifying, *to lift up*, when as indeed it is a noun, that signifies *mountains*; and renders the words, *as if the staff, were mountains*, (applied usually to men haughty and high-minded) *not wood*. I shall, having propounded it, leave it to the judgment of others.

**V. 16.** *{Therefore shall the Lord, the Lord of hosts, &c.*} His folly convinced, and laid forth; his doom from God follows, to wit; the sudden and unexpected destruction of the main body of his forces, wherein he so much confided; and whereof he so much boasted. Of the titles here given God, see ch. 3.1. Howbeit, it is by some of the Jewish writers well observed, that the style is for more special end, here given unto God, to wit, to intimate, that the successes, which the Assyrian kings, as well as others, had in the field, was not from themselves; but from him, who is their *Lord*, and *the Lord of hosts*: and from him therefore, both safety, and victory in fight is, Psal. 24.8. & 33.16,17. & 44.3,5,6. & 60.11,12. & 144.10. Prov. 21.30,31.

*{send among his fat ones leanness*} The Lord will waste his great forces, wherein he so much gloried, v. 8. ch. 35.9. as the body of man, or beast, is by a consumption wasted, and brought to extreme leanness. So ch. 17.4. Zeph. 2.11.

*{among his fat ones*} Heb. *upon his fatnesses, his fat ones*; the chief, and choice ones in his army, say all interpreters generally: as Judg. 3.29. Psal. 78.31. compared with, Psal. 106.15. So they; from whom I must crave leave here to dissent. The word here used, is an abstract, not a concrete. It is word for word, *his fatnesses*, as ch. 17.4. *the fat*, or, *the fatness of his flesh*, and, *the fatnesses of the earth*, Gen. 27.28,39. &, of the province, Dan. 11.28. by *his fatnesses*, therefore I here understand, not so much *his fat ones*, as his great and vast army, likened to the body of some creature overgrown with flesh, and fat, which God threatens here, to abate, and take down, by casting it into a consumption, by sending that upon it, that should make it thin and spare. The complement hereof, see ch. 37.36.

*{leanness*} That is, *death*, says the Jewish doctor, for that latter place of the Psalmist before mentioned. But the *leanness*, here mentioned, is not so much appliable to the bodies of the particular persons destroyed, as to the body of the army consisting of them, as limbs and members; which by the loss of so many thousands, could not but be much wasted and reduced to a very poor and thin scantling.

*{and under his glory he will kindle a burning, as the burning of a fire*} The same thing repeated, under a new notion, and expressed by another similitude. He will waste his forces, as with a consumption, and consume them as with fire; great, and sudden devastations and destructions, are in Scripture, commonly compared to great fires, Psal. 21.9. & 37.20. ch. 9.18. & 24.6. & 26.11. Jer. 17.27. Ezek. 20.47. Amos 7.4. Zach. 11.1.

*{under his glory*} That is, says one of the Jewish writers, in the *place of his glory*, or, *glorying*, where he glorified himself. Of which use of the preposition, see v. 3. But there seems rather to be an allusion to the manner of those, that burn dead bodies, which was the custom in old time, both of the Greeks and the Romans, their common use being not to bury as we do, the bodies of the deceased; but to burn them with a pile of wood kindled under them; and having so done, to gather their ashes and bones, if any remained of them, into an urn, and so lay them up in their places of sepulture. That which was done with a great deal of cost, huge piles of wood; yea, and curious fabrics of timber, together with abundance of odoriferous spices, at the funeral rites of great persons, as well women, as men. Somewhat like whereunto, was also used among the Jews, about their kings, 2 Chr. 21.19. and with them also, bodies of men were burnt, when they died, or were slain, in such multitudes that danger of infection might arise from them lying above ground, and the burying of them over-troublesome, ch. 66.24. Amos 6.10. Ezek. 39.9,10. See chap. 30.33. or if respect be had, as it may be, and is afterward, to the burning of a wood, or forest, as Psal. 83.14. *under his glory*; may be, under his great timber trees: as the fire that takes in the lower shrubs, and the underwoods; and from them, sets the whole wood or forest on fire. See v. 17,18. yet the former seems to me the more probable; and of this passage, more anon.

*{his glory*} The same with his *fatness*, or abundance of fat before mentioned; not as some would have it, his arms and his bravery: but his army; wherein he glories. See ch. 17.4. where both these terms are likewise used, as parallel.

*{he will kindle a burning*} Heb. *burning it shall burn*; or, *there shall a burning burn*, or, *it shall burn with a burning*. For whether it be a noun or verb infinite, is questionable. A great burning shall be. For these reduplications amplify. See v. 6.

*{as the burning of a fire*} Or, *as fire burneth*, or, *like the burning of fire* such a burning, as though it have no material fire used in it, yet should have the destroying force and efficacy of fire: and it may well be, that it was done by such a kind of blasting, as Aaron's sons were smitten with; who though they were stricken stark dead, yet neither were their bodies consumed, nor their garments, Levit. 10.2,5. or, wherewith the people were so many of them taken away in Taberah, Num. 11.2,3. and there are of the Jewish writers, who affirm, grounding in part upon this place, that by the stroke of the Angel sent to do execution on the Assyrian army, the bodies of those that were smitten, were so blasted and burnt, that they were dissolved into ashes. Which was, say they, that so many thousands lying dead on the ground, might not breed some contagion, especially being so near to the city: and they add hereunto, that though their bodies were dissolved, yet their garments were not burnt, that God's people might have the spoil of them, as those had, 2 Chr. 20.25. to which purpose also, some of them expound those words, *under his glory*, that is, under their goodly gorgeous apparel, such as the Assyrians usually wore, Ezek. 23.12. and that men are wont much to glory in, called therefore their glory, Ps. 93.1. Matth. 6.29. But these things are of no certainty.

**V. 17.** *{And the light of Israel shall be for a fire*} Or, *For*, &c. as ch. 8.21. & 9.11. God who is a light to his people, and will be so at this time, and upon this occasion, by giving them occasion of much joy upon their deliverance; as Esth. 8.16. Psal. 84.11. chap. 9.2. & 60.1,2,20. Mic. 7.8. shall be a consuming fire to destroy his, and their adversaries; as was intimated, v. 16. So Deut. 4.24. & 6.15. Psal. 97.3. ch. 26.11. & 30.30. See the like divers, yea, contrary use of that pillar, that conducted the Israelites in the wilderness, Exod. 14.20,24. See also Zach. 2.5. The Jewish doctors here dote, who would have by the *light of Israel*, to be understood, either the destroying Angel, or king Ezekiah; as so called from his constant study of God's law, Prov. 6.23.

*{and his Holy One for a flame*} The same thing, is in other terms repeated, but as usually, with some amplification. For *flame*, is somewhat more than fire, ch. 29.6. & 30.30. See the like, ch. 9.10,20. v. 1,7,14,16. There shall need no other fire, or fuel, to destroy and consume them, save God himself. See ch. 30.27,28. Of the title *Holy One*. See chap. 1.4.

*{and it shall burn*} To wit, that *flame* before spoken of.

*{and devour*} Heb. *eat up*, as ch. 9.18.

*{his thorns, and his briers*} By these the Jewish doctors, some of them understand the great ones in the Assyrian army, because, such are wont most to be, as pricking thorns, to vex and grieve others. Which some of ours also approve; supposing that the slaughter might begin at them. But the slaughter, it is evident, was sudden, and executed in an instant, as that in Egypt, Exod. 12.29. with that expedition, that little notice could be taken, nor regard needed be had, with whom it should begin. Rather, according to the similitude which the prophet still pursues of a fire; and here of a fire taking in wood, *thorns, and briers*, may have reference to the underwoods, where the fire is wont first to take, opposed to the tall timber trees, vers. 18. and should therefore, rather resemble the meaner sort of his soldiers. See chap. 9.18. Howbeit, thereby may be signified his whole army in general, and those in gross of whom it consisted, being all, as *thorns, and briers*: to annoy God's people, against whom they lay in siege, and whom they had before done much mischief to, in all parts of the land, chap. 36.1. See the like, Josh. 23.13. Ezek. 28.24.

*{in one day*} In an instant; at one and the same time, together, at once, 1 Sam. 2.34. chap. 47.9. Zach. 3.9. Or, *in one night*, ch. 37.36. being part of the natural day. Gen. 1.5. Levit. 23.32. Luk. 24.29,33,36. compared with Joh. 20.19. his great army, that required no small time, for the gathering, framing, fitting, and furnishing of it, destroyed in an instant! So ch. 15.5.

**V. 18.** *{And it shall consume the glory of his forest, and of his fruitful field*} Heb. *Carmel*. The proper name of a place; of which name, were two mountains, the one in Judah; of which Josh. 15.55. whereabout Nabal's dwelling was, 1 Sam. 25.2. the other situated in the confines of Asher, and Issachar Josh. 19.26, where Elias slew Baal's prophets, 1 King. 18.19,20. and it was near to the sea, 1 King. 18.42,43. Jer. 46.18. Now these mountains did not lie open, forest-like, or run wild, as Lebanon; but were enclosed, manured, tilled, and eared, or planted with great variety of fruitful trees, vines, olives, figs, and the like; and had much fat, and fertile soil, and arable ground. (whence *a green ear* of corn, also is so called, Levit. 2.14. & 23.14.) both upon them, and about them; whence it came to pass, that from the one, or both of them, the word *Carmel* was used, for any fertile, and fruitful place indifferently, whether higher, or lower ground, mountain or plain; as chap. 16.10. where mention is made of Moab's *Carmel*, and ch. 29.17. where *Lebanon* and *Carmel*, are opposed; and so it seems to be here taken. Hence therefore, some would infer, that by the *forest*, as a wild place, should be understood the meaner sort of Sennacherib's soldiery; by the *Carmel*, his chief commanders. Others imagine, that the desolation, or destruction of his state, and country is threatened; and as of persons of all ranks, high and low, rich and poor; so of places of all sorts. But this seems to divert too much from the prophet's present scope. I suppose rather, with others, that by his *forest*, and his *Carmel*, is meant the main body of his army, that seemed to resemble some great forest, or mountain, whether wild, or manured bethwacked with trees, whether for timber, fruit, or fuel, as thick as they can stand one by another, and by *the glory* thereof, the choice persons of command in it; as by *his glory*, ver. 16. was meant his glorious army, or his army wherein he gloried: so here, by *the glory* of that his glory, those that were the more glorious part of it, or of the more eminency in it, his stout and valiant warriors, and his rich and stately princes; which some also suppose to be respectively meant; by the forest, the one: by Carmel, the other. See Jer. 46.22,23. Some conceive that there is mention here of *forest* and *Carmel*: in regard that his army, being of large extent, was encamped, some in the higher, and wilder places; some in the lower, and better manured. I should rather think, but that it comes after, (and yet why might not the Lord have an eye to that, that in his person himself would afterward speak?) that some respect might in these terms, be had to Sennacherib's brags of surprising *Lebanon* and *Carmel*, chap. 37.24. as intimating, that his own *Lebanon* and *Carmel*, should be destroyed, before he should come to effect, what he threatened them with.

*{both soul and body*} Heb. *from the soul, and unto the flesh*, as Jer. 9.10. *from the fowl, and unto the beast*, for, *both fowl, and beast*, and Jer. 50.3. *from man, and beast*; for, *both man and beast*. Some would have the meaning to be, that they should be destroyed, both body and soul. Others, that they should be so smitten inwardly, that the evil yet should not stay there; but proceed also to the consumption of the outward parts of the body, because the *soul* is set first: contrary to the manner of material fire; which, in burning of bodies, seizes first upon the flesh, or outward parts, and from them pierces to the inward. The meaning is, rather, as one of the Rabbins well observes, that it should so seize on them, that it should, as fire is wont to do, with living creatures that are burnt, or persons condemned to the fire, not consume their *flesh* only, but take life away too, Levit. 20.14. & 21.9. The *soul* is commonly taken for the *life*, Gen. 9.4,5. Levit. 17.11,14. It is a proverbial speech intimating a total destruction of his army; not unlike those of *head and tail, branch and rush*, chap. 9.14. for the prophet returns here to the former similitude of a body, vers. 16. but he pursues it with a further amplification. It was *leanness*, or a consumption of flesh, that was there menaced; as ch. 17.4. which may yet be without loss, or danger of life: but here vitals, and all are wasted and consumed, as with fire: the very *soul* and *spirit* of this vast body, together with the *fat* and *flesh* of it, is utterly gone.

*{and they shall be, as when a standard-bearer fainteth*} Heb. *and he*, or, *it shall be*; or, *it shall be with him*, (as chap. 19.7,8.) *as when a standard-bearer melteth*, as alluding to the similitude before used. This some expound of the Assyrian king himself: He shall be like such a standard-bearer, whose *heart melting* within him: (as Psal. 22.14. Nah. 2.11.) when he sees his colors forsaken, he casts away his standard, and betakes himself to flight. So did Sennacherib, chap. 31.8. & 37.37. But some go further, adding, that he shall not be able to recover himself, or raise a new army again, no more than an army is able to recollect itself, when the standard-bearers are overthrown. Some such assurance seems to be given by God to Ezekiah, chap. 38.6. Others, rather understand it of his army, or the remainders thereof: it shall be with his forces, as with an army, whose standard-bearer fainting, and failing, the whole company is, together with him, quailed and quelled. Or, as when he having cast away his colors, the whole regiment is disordered, and soon routed by the adverse party: and so it was with Sennacherib's great host, they were suddenly, a great part of them, utterly destroyed; and the residue of them that survived, when in the morning they saw their camp full of dead corpses, chap. 37.36. their hearts also melted within them, and they fled away with their Lord. Of the army, the same term is used, that it *melted*, away, chap. 31.8.

**V. 19.** *{And the rest of the trees of his forest shall be few*} Very few shall remain of that his vast army, that seemed formerly, to be innumerable.

*{the trees*} The several soldiers in his army, of all sorts, the greater among them, as well as the meaner. Heb. *tree*. But the word is here collective; as Ezek. 15.6.

*{his forest*} His forces compared to a forest ver. 18.

*{few*} Heb. *a number*. That is, *a few*. For, though with us, *a number* be used, to signify a *multitude*: yet in the Hebrew phrase, it imports, *fewness*: so it is used, Deut. 33.6. *Let his men be*, or, (out of the foregoing branch, supplying the negative) *not be a number*: that is, *few*. And *days of a number*, for, *a few days*, Numb. 9.20. Contrary to which, is, Jer. 2.32. *days without number*: And Job. 16.22. *years of a number*; for few years: So *men of a number*, for, *few in number*, Gen. 34.30. Deut. 4.27. Ps. 105.12. Jer. 44.28. Ezek. 12.16. And the reason of the phrase is, because a small company may be easily numbered; a small number soon counted. In opposition therefore, whereunto, is that form *without number*, commonly used, Job 25.3. Psal. 40.12. & 104.25. & 105.34. Joel 1.6. Yet there seems to be a kind of defective speech, as in that of Moses, *His men a number*, for, *his men, men of a number*. So here, *the tree*, or, *trees of his forest, a number*, for *the trees of his forest, trees of a number*: a very small company that may soon be told. See ch. 11.17.

*{that a child may write them*} That is, as some, count them, and in counting point them out, *describe them*. Or, rather, as others, take a tale, or make a list of them: for, he seems to allude to the clerk of a band, or a muster-master, whose office is, to take a list of those, that are to be enrolled for service. It is as if he should say, there shall not need any officer to make a book of them; they shall be so few, that any child, that has but learned to make his letters, may soon set them down, either the number of them, or their names. Hence our Jewish doctors, or doters rather, gather that of Sennacherib's army there were but ten left; because the letter jod; that stands for ten in Hebrew, as it does also in Greek, is the least letter in the alphabet, which children therefore are first taught to write: and again, because children are seldom able to tell beyond ten; and so far they can count upon their fingers' ends. But these niceties we leave to such, whose lips suit with such lettuce. Heb. *and a child shall write them*, the copulative for the infinitive: as Job 5.11. & 7.15,19. Jer. 14.19. and the future for the potential, as chap. 33.23. Job 9.3. Jer. 2.13. & 13.23. Matth. 12.25. with Mark 3.24. for so I take it to be, rather than an ellipsis, as some would have it.

**V. 20.** *{And it shall come to pass in that day, that, &c.*} Hitherto of God's judgment, that should be inflicted upon the Assyrian king, for his pride, insolency, and arrogancy. When God had finished the work, that he intended to bring about by him. Now follows, both of the distress that God brought the whole land into by him, and his forces, and of the deliverance of some small parcel of them, by the judgment executed upon him and his army, to wit, the destruction of many wicked ones among them, and the reformation of the residue: see the like, ch. 1.24,25. Of the phrase, or manner of speech, see ch. 4.1,2,3.

*{the remnant of Israel, and such as are escaped of the house of Jacob*} Those of them, that shall escape and survive the Assyrian invasion: to wit, principally, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and such as for succor had resorted thither, chap. 37.35. as also, some other, in other parts of the land, though surprised and overrun by him, chap. 36.1. for *Israel* here, is put for the people of Judah, as chap. 1.3. and *the house of Jacob*, the same with *Israel*: as chap. 2.5. Howsoever, some would over-curiously distinguish them, and by *Israel*, understand Judah, that held still the faith of Israel: by *the house of Jacob*, the ten tribes, that fell from it, and were of Jacob's family; but not of Israel's faith, were not right, and true Israelites, Joh. 1.47. Rom. 9.6. but this seems not sound. See verse 21,22.

*{such as are escaped*} Heb. *the escapement*, or, *escaping*: as chap. 4.2.

*{shall no more again stay upon him, that smote them*} Being amended by the hand of God thus upon them, and better advised than before, by their late sufferings, they shall not seek to, or rely upon the Assyrians, for succor and support, as in former times they had wont to do, 2 King. 16.7. Hosh. 5.13. & 14.3.

*{no more again stay*} Heb. *no more add to stay*: chapter 7.10. Jer. 2.4.

*{stay*} As a man stays and upholds himself, by leaning on a staff, ch. 36.6. & 50.10. See ch. 3.1.

*{him that smote them*} The king of Assyria; (not Egypt; as some of the Jewish teachers) by whom God had smote them, chap. 9.12. using him, as a rod or staff, wherewith to chastise and correct them, ver. 5,24.

*{but shall stay upon the Lord*} This being the end of God's smiting them, not to drive them from him; but to reclaim and draw them home unto him, chapter 9.11,12. and by discovering to them the vanity of all other shores and supports; and their folly in relying on them, to their own hurt and ruin; to cause them to rely and rest now on him alone, chap. 17. ver. 7,8.

*{the holy one of Israel*} See ch. 1.4.

*{in truth*} In sincerity, as Ps. 145.18. (so Jer. 24.7.) not feignedly, as those Ps. 78.34,37. Jer. 3.10.

**V. 21.** *{The remnant shall return*} Or, *A remnant shall return*. Alluding to the name of the prophet's son, *Shearjashub*, ch. 7.3. and showing what was therein intimated: *a remnant*; denoting the paucity of those, that should escape and survive; in comparison of the whole, ver. 22.

*{even the remnant*} Or, *but a remnant*: a remnant only, ver. 22. as before: otherwise *the remnant* might import so many as escaped, were they fewer or more. So *a small remnant*, ch. 1.9. and *a seed*, Rom. 9.29.

*{of Jacob*} Of the main body of the people, called *the house of Jacob*, ver. 20.

*{unto the mighty God*} The name given to the Messiah, as part of his stately style, ch. 9.6. they shall return after the siege of Jerusalem, broken up upon the slaughter made by night in the Assyrian camp, chap. 37.36,37. not to their possessions and wonted places of abode only; out of which they had formerly by the Assyrian forces, been forced, or whence for fear of them, they had fled; but unto God also: whom formerly they had disregarded, and were fallen from: but now upon so pregnant proof and experience, had, and exhibited of his gracious goodness towards them, and powerful protection of them, they should more carefully seek after, more faithfully cleave to, and more firmly depend upon, Psal. 81.17,18. Jer. 32.40. See ch. 1.27.

**V. 22.** *{For though thy people Israel be as the sand of the sea, yet a remnant of them shall return*} As of Sennacherib's vast and numerous host, but a small number escaped, upon the judgment by God inflicted on it, ver. 19. so of the innumerable multitude of the Jewish people, but a small remnant in comparison, was to escape, and so did in that heavy judgment by the hand of Sennacherib, inflicted on them from him.

*{though*} Heb. *if*: and so Rom. 9.27. for, *though*, as Job 14.7,8. & 16.6.

*{thy people Israel*} Either, *thy people* to wit, *Isaias*: God speaking to the prophet: or, rather, *thy people*, that is thy posterity, *O Israel*, as turning his speech to their progenitor Jacob.

*{as the sand of the sea*} As was promised unto Abraham, that his seed should be, Gen. 22.17. fulfilled accordingly, Heb. 11.12. and hyperbolical phrase, and proverbial form of speech, used commonly, to signify an innumerable multitude, Judg. 7.12. chap. 48.19.

*{Yet a remnant of them shall return*} Or, *but a remnant in them*, or, *among them, shall return*: (for *Shear-jashub's* name is again alluded unto) that is, shall be saved, as the apostle renders it, Rom. 9.27. that remnant so delivered, and temporally saved, from the sword of the Assyrian, being a type of God's elect among that people, to be saved by Christ. See Rom. 9.27,29. & 11.5.

*{the consumption decreed shall overflow with righteousness*} The reason is here rendered, why he said, *but a remnant*: because God had determined in his just judgment, to bring in upon them a general inundation that should sweep away the greater part of them. This some of the Rabbines understand of the ten tribes carried captive by Salmanaser, 2 King. 17.6. in regard of whom the other two were but as a remnant. But the course of the context seems to carry it another way.

*{the consumption*} Or, *a consumption*: there shall be a consumption among the Jewish people, before that consumption in Sennacherib's army, ver. 18. So ch. 28.22.

*{decreed*} Heb. *decided, determined*, 1 King. 20.40. or, *precisely, cut out*, Job 14.5. as infallibly, and unfailably, or irrecoverably decreed, so exactly limited how far forth it shall proceed. So Dan. 11.36.

*{shall overflow*} Heb. *shall be overflowing*. He compares the Assyrian's invasion of the land, with his overspreading army, to a great inundation, overflowing the whole country. See chap. 8.7,8.

*{with righteousness*} Or, *in righteousness*; as the apostle renders it, Rom. 9.28. that is, through the just judgment of God; as noting out the ground of God's both determining to inflict, and inflicting those judgments on them: as Psal. 9.8. and vindicating of him from all aspersion of injustice in so doing, Neh. 9.33. Lam. 1.18. Dan. 9.7,14. or, as some other, with judgments, and punishments, the effects of his justice; as chap. 5.16. Howbeit the main stream of interpreters runs here another way; expounding the place; some of the *superabundant benefits*, that God would heap upon them, after that he had brought them thus low. For *righteousness*, is put sometime for *beneficence*, Psal. 112.3,9. chap. 56.1. Others, of that *righteousness*, and holiness, that should abound in the remainder of God's people, now reclaimed and refined in the furnace of affliction, ch. 48.10. wherewith the land should now flow; and that so as *to fill the whole world*, chap. 33.6. so, that by the *consumption cut out*, they would, many of them, have to be understood the *remnant left*, which should cause *righteousness* to overflow. But besides that, the construction seems overharsh; the apostle refers these words, *in righteousness*, to God's finishing and cutting out, or, cutting short: and I adhere therefore to our version, and the sense of it first given.

**V. 23.** *{For the Lord God of hosts shall make a consumption, even determined, in the midst of all the land*} The same thing is reiterated, with the author of it expressed; and some further amplification from the extent of it. For the style here given God, see on ch. 1.9. See also ver. 16.

*{shall make*} Or, *will shortly make*: Heb. *is making*: as ch. 5.5. & 43.19. See ch. 3.1.

*{a consumption*} Another word of the same notion and family with the former, ver. 22.

*{even determined*} Or, *and that determined*: as it is rendered, Dan. 9.27. See the like syntax, Mic. 2.10. Heb. *cut out*, as before; for both words are from one root. Yet some would have this word to be a substantive, as well as the word *consumption*: but so, as that the sense should not much vary; *consumption, and determination*, for, *a determinate consumption*; as ch. 1.14. *iniquity, and congregation*: for, *a wicked congregation*: or, rather, as ch. 4.5. *a cloud and smoke*, for, *a smoky cloud*. But I suppose it rather an adjective, as both the form of it shows, and the use of it also, Dan. 9.26. in those words, *a determinate desolation*; the same phrase is again found, ch. 28.22. Now, because instead hereof the apostle has, retaining the Greek version, *a word*, or, *speech, abbreviated*, or *abridged*; as they commonly render it: hence most of our ancient interpreters, and many later ones, Popish writers especially, do hence pick out much mysterious matter. Some of the Messiah, *the word contracted*, and *made flesh*, Joh. 1.14. Some, of the doctrine of salvation, drawn into a narrow compass, in the gospel, Mark 1.15. Joh. 3.16. Rom. 10.9. Some of one thing; some of another. All which to recite, is both needless, and would also be too tedious. Only, concerning the apostle's Greek, the term by him used, as that Hebrew one, which it answers, signifies as well *work*, as *word*, (which in Latin also, is held to come from the other in Greek; *opus* from ἔπος; or, rather, from the Greek word signifying either, as the verb whence it comes, signifies either, both *to speak*, and *to work*;) and as well *matter*, as *speech*, (as the Hebrew term also does, chap. 2.1. Dan. 10.1. Luk. 1.37. and in Latin, *res*, held to come from the Greek ῥῆσις) besides the word used by the apostle, and those ancient Greeks, signifies, as well *an account*, or *a reckoning*, as any of those two before mentioned, Matth. 18.23. & 25.19. Luk. 16.2. Phil. 4.17. and the apostle's words may well therefore be thus rendered; *The Lord will make short work*, or, *a short matter of it*. He will make a soon, and sudden consumption. It will neither be long before it comes; nor long in doing, when it comes: Or to come more nearly, and fully to the prophet's intendment: *The Lord will make a short reckoning*; alluding to a reckoning, where the matter is clear, the account is soon made: or to a bill of receipt and disbursements; which though it be long, yet being aright balanced, the foot of the account, or the remainder of the reckoning, may prove a very small sum: and so it would be, yea and fell out so here, when God had finished his work, and done his reckoning with his people, ver. 12. And thus much by the way for the clearing of that phrase, though not found in the text.

*{in the midst of all the land*} Heb. *earth*. Which some taking hold of; apply all this (as was in part, also, before hinted) unto Christ, of whom also they expound that in the Psalm, of *working salvation in the midst of the earth*, Psal. 74.12. Others refer it to the contracted number of the remaining, and returning faithful, ver. 21. &c. the apostles and others by them typified; who by their righteousness in preaching, and practice, should overflow, and fill the whole world with goodness and godliness, Dan. 12.3. Matth. 28.19. Mark 16.15. Joh. 7.38,39. & 15.16. Rom. 10.18. But the word here used, as the Greek also answering it, signifies as well *land*, as *earth*; and is commonly used of, and applied unto, particular coasts, and countries, chap. 9.1. Matthew 2.6. & 4.15. and *in the midst of the land*, is no more, than simply, *in the land*: as chap. 5.8. and so the apostle here renders it, Rom. 9.28. *in the midst of all the land*, no more, than *throughout the whole land*, chap. 8.8. & 28.22,15.

**V. 24.** *{Therefore thus saith the Lord God of hosts*} Upon this dreadful prediction of the great consumption to be made among the Jewish people, the prophet in God's name, and by message from him, comforts those few faithful ones, whom God had special care of among them, against those fears and distresses that might befall them, by occasion of the Assyrian invasion and surprisal of the greatest part of their cities; and that by giving them further assurance of a gracious deliverance from him; and of the speedy destruction of him, that had put them into such frights, and brought them into such distress. See the like, chap. 30.18–33. Of the style given to God here, look back to ver. 16.

*{O my people, that dwellest in Sion*} He directs his speech to the inhabitants of Jerusalem; (for *Sion*, is here put for *Jerusalem*; as ch. 1.8,27. & 27.12.) partly, because thither had a great party of the better sort fled for succor and protection: and partly, because they were to be in no small distress there, ch. 37.3.

*{be not afraid of the Assyrian*} Of Sennacherib; for all his proud menaces and vaunts of his forces, ch. 37.6.

*{he shall smite thee with a rod*} He shall lightly afflict you; God using him, as a rod, wherewith to chastise his people, ver. 5. not as a sword, to cut them off. He will not handle you by him, so roughly as he did the ten tribes, 2 King. 17.6,27. & 18.10,11. Howbeit, the Jewish writers are divided about the sense of these words. Some say, that they are to be understood of his purposes and menaces only: Others, of matter of fact also, and somewhat done by him; and these distinguish not amiss between *smiting*, and *slaying*: and true it is, that though no violent irruption, nor forcible assault, was made into, or against Jerusalem, chap. 37.33. Yet were many of her inferior cities, yea, the most of them, taken, ch. 36.1. the country round about her spoiled; as must needs be, by such an army lying about it, ch. 36.2. and the city itself, with those shut up in it, put to many difficulties, and reduced to much distress, ch. 36.12. & 37.3.

*{and shall lift up his staff against thee*} So the most render it. He shall not strike you, say some, but hold up the staff over you: as after, *he shall shake his hand at thee*, ver. 32. he shall shake the staff at you; but not hurt you with it. Others, he shall lay heavy taxes and tributes upon you; and so he did indeed, 2 King. 18.14,15. both suppose a reference here, as to the *rod*, so to the *staff* mentioned, ver. 5. Howbeit, some render the words otherwise; to wit, *but he shall lift up his staff for thee*: *but*, the copulative, in an adversative notion: as ch. 5.12. & 7.12. *he shall lift up*, or, *one* (to wit, God) *shall lift up his staff; his staff shall be lift up* (see chap. 14.30.) *for thee*. So is the particle used, 1 Chr. 6.49. Thus the meaning should be; the king of Assyria shall smite you with a rod; but the Lord your God, who is the Lord of hosts, will lift up his staff an heavier instrument, and more grievous, against him; that shall bring deliverance to you, and destruction to him; as did the staff, that Moses lift up at the Red Sea, Exod. 14.26,27. See ver. 26.

*{after the manner of Egypt*} Heb. *in the way*. Which some Jewish writers taking hold of, expound of Sennacherib's way, either toward Egypt, when he went thitherward to meet with Taracha, or when he returned from bickering with him; what time again he sent messengers in menacing manner to Jerusalem, chap. 37.9. Others, of Ezekiah's and his people's way; in sending to Egypt for help against the Assyrian, chap. 30.4. which occasioned the invasion, partly through the offense, that the Assyrian took at it, chap. 36.6. and partly through God's just indignation against them, for doing therein out of diffidence, against his command, ch. 30.1. & 31.1. And this exposition, the former way of it especially, some of ours follow; the rather, say they, because it sorts well with the story: and for the particle here used, it is not that which signifies *according to*: but *in*. But neither of these reasons seem valid enough, to put by the received reading. For neither does either of them suit so well with the context: nor is the use of the particle in the signification here given it in this form of speech unusual. For, so Ezek. 20.30. *in the way of your fathers*, is found, for *according to the manner of your fathers*: and these very words again in this form reiterated, ver. 26. do abundantly confirm it. Here therefore, *in the way of Egypt*, is, *after*, or, *according to the manner of Egypt*: that is as those who understand it of the Assyrian, and his dealing with God's people, either he shall inflict grievous things on you, as Pharaoh did on your ancestors in Egypt, Exod. 1.11–14. or, he shall pursue you, with a purpose to destroy you, as Pharaoh did the Israelites, after they were gotten out of Egypt, Exod. 14.5–9. & 15.9. but shall not prevail against you, no more than he then did. But as those, that understand it, of God's dealing with their enemy, the Assyrian; the same person that then *lift up* his staff against Pharaoh, for the safety of his people, will now *lift up his staff* against the Assyrian, to his confusion, and your deliverance, ver. 26. I will destroy the Assyrian, as I did the Egyptians, Exod. 14.26,27. & 15.6. and this I concur with.

**V. 25.** *{For yet a very little while, and mine indignation shall cease, and mine anger in their destruction*} As in the former verse, were two grounds of comfort to the godly: First, the lightness, in comparison of the chastisement, *a rod*: and secondly, the gracious issue of it: in the defeat of the enemy's intended purpose: so here are two more added: First, the shortness of it, God's wrath against his people shall not last long; and secondly, the diversion of it, it shall be turned upon their oppressors. See verse 12.

*{a very little*} Heb. *a little little*, or, *a small little*, or, *a little of a little*. A very short time: as chap. 29.17. So Psalm 30.5. *but a moment* lasts his anger: and, *for a moment, a small moment*, ch. 54.7,8.

*{mine indignation shall cease*} To wit, toward my people. I will no longer be angry, chap. 27.4. & 54.9. Ezek. 16.42. See Dan. 11.36.

*{and mine anger in their destruction*} This latter branch is diversely expounded, both by the Jewish doctors, and our writers. Some understand it of the Jewish people, and expound it of God's anger against them, for their sins and excesses: *for their detestable enormities*, says one: supposing the word to have the same notion with one in sound near unto it, that signifies *bestiality*, Levit. 18.23. & 20.12. or, *inveterate evils*, as coming from a word, which in all likelihood it does, that signifies *to wax old*. The works, says one, of the old Adam, Rom. 6.6. Eph. 4.22. But others rather understand it of the Assyrian. *Mine indignation* shall cease (supplied from the former branch) *upon their destruction*; or, shall have its end with them. Or, as others, *mine indignation*, shall be set *upon the consumption of them*. For the root, whence it springs, has a notion in it; as of oldness, so of decay, and consumption, which oldness brings with it, Heb. 8.13. So Psal. 32.3. & 49.14. Lam. 3.4. the meaning is, that God's anger being appeased and pacified towards his people, should be now turned against the Assyrians their adversaries, to destroy and consume them, as Psal. 81.14. The word is nowhere else found. For, as for those that would read *taclith*, for *tablith*; though it might come home to the same sense, this latter word issuing from the same spring with those other two before used, vers. 22,23. and seem to be also used in the same sense: as Job 26.10. yet they go against the general stream of the original copies, which are reported in all approved editions to represent the other term. The change of the number from the singular to the plural, as from the king to his forces, is so frequent, that it need not be insisted on here.

**V. 26.** *{And the Lord of hosts*} Or, *For*, chap. 9.11. Of *Lord of hosts*. See ch. 1.9. ver. 16. one greater than his hosts; and that has other manner of hosts at command, Ps. 103.20.

*{shall stir up a scourge for him*} Or, *will raise up a scourge against him*] This *scourge* is one of his host above, of his angels, ch. 37.36. termed God's hosts, Gen. 32.1,2. Psal. 103.21. here called *a scourge*, to answer the word *rod*, ver. 24. the king of Assyria has *a rod* for God's people; but God has *a scourge* in store for him; to whip him away from them, when he has by him, as with a rod, chastised them for their folly, ver. 5,12. See ch. 28.15,18.

*{according to the slaughter of Midian*} Heb. *stroke*; as chap. 27.7. God will smite him, as he smote the Midianites, and made a slaughter of them, in a strange and sudden manner, in the night, when nothing less was looked for. See ch. 9.4. and the story, Judg. 7.22.

*{at the rock of Oreb*} So called of Oreb, a chief prince of Midian; who after the discomfiture of his army, was in flight taken, and there slain, Judg. 7.26. Psal. 83.9,11. as was Sennacherib also, after the defeat of his forces, in the temple of his idol, chap. 37.37,38.

*{and as his rod was upon the sea; so shall he lift it up after the manner of Egypt*} Or, *and according to his staff lift over the sea*; (for so the Hebrew runs in way of connection to the former clause: nor is the word *as*, but *staff*) so (Heb. *and*: as ch. 53.7.) *shall he lift it up after the manner of Egypt*, (Heb. *in the way of Egypt*; as ver. 24.) at the time of their passage out of Egypt, as some; or rather, to destroy the Assyrians now, as he did the Egyptians then. He alludes to Moses his *staff* held up, over the Red Sea, Exod. 14.26. For there seems no ground for that exposition, that some give, applying this wholly to the Assyrians' expedition, to wit, that *his staff*; that is, his power, or, his army; and he with it, going against the Ethiopian; should pass the Red Sea into Egypt: and *in his way* from *Egypt*, should return again to Jerusalem: for, neither do the relations seem probable; nor does the exposition well cohere with the tenor of the text. See on ver. 24.

**V. 27.** *{And it shall come to pass in that day, that*} As ver. 20.

*{his burden shall be taken away from off thy shoulder, and his yoke from off thy neck; and the yoke shall be destroyed*} You shall not only be freed from those heavy exactions, that the Assyrian laid upon you, and delivered out of the present distractions and distresses, that he put you to by his forcible invasion and siege; but his might shall be so quelled, and his power impaired, that he shall not be able to afflict you again in like manner. See ver. 12,16–19. & ch. 28.6. A type of the deliverance of God's people in that manner from the tyranny of sin and Satan, that they never come to recover that power again, that they had in them, and over them before, Rom. 6.6–14. 1 Joh. 3.8,9. See ch. 9.4.

*{his burden*} The Assyrian's; by him imposed, ch. 14.25. *burden* for all manner of affliction, and oppression, Exod. 2.11.

*{shall be taken away*} Heb. *shall remove*, Ps. 81.6.

*{thy shoulder*} The part of man's body ordinarily employed for bearing of burdens. See ch. 9.6.

*{his yoke*} Used in the same notion with *burden*, but put more specially for servitude and bondage, Deut. 28.48. See chapter 9.4.

*{the yoke shall be destroyed*} Or, *corrupted*, as the Greek; as a thing perished and rotten, Job 17.1. and so the old Latin renders it; not barely taken off: for it might then come on again: nor broken only: for it might then be repaired; and being made up again, might afterward again be used as before. But *destroyed*, so corrupted, and spoiled, as disabled from recovery of the like strength, or made use of to the like purpose again, to yoke and vex any, as before it had done, fulfilled in Sennacherib and his forces, ch. 37.36–38. See ch. 14.25.

*{because of the anointing*} Heb. *from the face of*, or, *before*, (as Gen. 36.6,7. Exod. 9.11. ch. 7.3,16.) *the oil*, or *ointment*: as Eccles. 7.1. ch. 57.9. this some refer to the Assyrian yoke, which say they, was corrupted and spoiled, with excessive fatness: bodies, say they, overgrown with fat, become unwieldy, and pursy, and therefore blow much, and many times are suddenly stifled. Which they apply to the Assyrian, clogged with wealth, Hab. 2.6. puffed up with pride, ver. 13. breathing out blasphemies, ver. 11,15. 2 Chron. 32.19. and suddenly brought to nought, ver. 16,17. But this seems many bows wide from the scope of the prophet in this place. The Jewish writers generally carry it home, as the Chaldee also does, to the Messiah: but understanding by Messiah, not the Savior to come, but Ezekiah, partaker of that holy oil, wherewith David, his progenitor, and other the kings of Judah, had been anointed, Psal. 89.20. Nor do some of ours disallow it, acknowledging, that God, at Ezekiah's suit, and out of special favor to him, vouchsafed them this deliverance, 2 Chron. 32.20,21. adding further, some of them, that God had therein also regard to his people, his saints, his anointed ones, among them, and to that precious oil of spiritual grace, wherewith they are all, in some measure anointed, Psal. 105.15. 2 Cor. 1.21,22. 1 Joh. 2.20,27. But unto Christ principally, of whom Ezekiah herein was a type, the true Messiah, the anointed of God, in a peculiar and singular manner, far above and beyond all other, Psal. 2.1. & 45.7. Dan. 9.24. Luk. 4.18,21. Joh. 3.34. Act. 4.27. & 10.38. Heb. 1.9. and he, on whom are founded, all the gracious, both promises of deliverance, and performances thereof, at any time unto God's people, 2 Cor. 1.20. and unto him does this our evangelical prophet still carry them up, chap. 7.14. & 9.4–6. We need not therefore, with divers commenters upon this place, stand beating our brains to devise what *a yoke*, and *oil*, have to do the one with the other: one telling us, that *oil* takes away the hard knobs, and knotty parts of a yoke: another, that it helps to soften and dissolve the thongs, that fasten the parts of it one to another. Another, that *oil* spoils iron, and that that peradventure an iron, not a wooden yoke, may be meant here; as Deut. 28.48. Jer. 24.13,14. with other the like frivolous and groundless fancies: since, that the mention of *oil* here, is nor, as of an instrument, or means, whereby the yoke should be broken, and dissolved; but as of a motive, or inducement, in regard whereof, God would vouchsafe to do, what in this case and kind there was to be done.

**V. 28.** *{He is come, &c.*} The prophet here describes the progress of Sennacherib, with his army marching along from place to place in his several gests towards Jerusalem; as if it were a thing present; or as if he plainly beheld it, in a prophetical rapture or vision; or were going along in company with them. See ch. 2.1. and before-hand shows, which way he would come; to wit, through the land of Benjamin, whereunto most of the towns, hereafter mentioned, did appertain. See somewhat the like, of the enemies' march towards Babylon, ch. 13.5. and Jer. 4.7.

*{to Ayath*} Or, *the territory of Ay*, Gen. 12.8. Josh. 7.2. Ezr. 2.28. Neh. 7.32. for the city was by Joshua utterly overthrown, Josh. 8.28. & 10.1. another from that mentioned, Jer. 49.3.

*{he is passed to Migron*} Mentioned, as belonging to Gibea, 1 Sam. 14.2.

*{at Michmash, he hath laid up his carriages*} Heb. *made to visit his vessels*. Either left his luggage there, that he may march on with more expedition; as Jer. 36.20. or, *mustered*, and taken a survey of his train, and provisions, that what is any way defective, may be supplied, as Num. 1.29. & 2.33. ch. 22.10. Of the place, see 1 Sam. 13.1. & 14.5. Ezr. 2.27.

**V. 29.** *{They are gone over the passage*} Not the *fords* of Jordan; as some suppose; or some other brook, as others: but the straits, between the hills, near Michmash. Of which, see 1 Sam. 13.23. & 14.4,5.

*{they have taken up their lodging at Geba*} Heb. *lodged a lodging*. This place seemed to have been on the one side of the forementioned passage, as Michmash on the other. See 1 Sam. 14.5. & Neh. 11.31.

*{Ramah is afraid*} The inhabitants are terrified by the approach of the enemy. Of Ramah, see Joshua 18.25. Jer. 31.15.

*{Gibeah of Saul*} So called, because Saul was from thence, and there dwelt, 1 Sam. 10.26. & 11.4. & 15.34.

*{is fled*} Not the place itself, but those, that dwelt in it, for fear of the Assyrian army. So ver. 31.

**V. 30.** *{Lift up thy voice*} Heb. *cry shrill with thy voice*. See chap. 12.6. make a grievous outcry, as is wont to be done, upon discovery of some eminent and imminent danger, chap. 15.4,5. & 21.8. Matth. 14.26.

*{O daughter of Gallim*} Or, *O daughter Gallim*. Of the place, see 1 Sam. 25.44. of the phrase, chap. 1.8. The town seems to be so termed, from *heaps*, hillocks, or land-banks, near unto it, or about it. For so the word signifies, ch. 37.25.

*{cause it to be heard*} Cause your voice to be heard, that they may also take notice of the enemies' approach. See the like, chap. 15.5.

*{unto Laish*} A city possessed by the Danites, Judg. 18.14,27,29.

*{O poor Anathoth*} The place of Jeremy's birth and abode, Jer. 1.1. & 11.21,23. & 32.7. See Josh. 21.18. called *poor*, because surprised of the Assyrians, and plundered by them.

**V. 31.** *{Madmenah is removed*} Her inhabitants are gone, as those of Gibeah, ver. 29. Of the town, belonging to the tribe of Judah, see Josh. 15.31.

*{the inhabitants of Gebim*} This place seems so termed, from some store of *ditches* about it. For that the name imports. See on ch. 33.4. 1 King. 2.16.

*{gather themselves to flee*} Or, rather, *have retired*; *are fled*, as Jer. 4.6. & 6.1. For that appears to be the true notion of the word, from Exod. 9.19,20. by comparing the one verse with the other.

**V. 32.** *{As yet shall he remain at Nob, that day*} Heb. *Yet this day at Nob is he to stand*, or, *stay*; as Gen. 45.1. Deut. 5.31. 2 Sam. 7.18. (a place abused, to prove, that *David sat* at the commencing of that his solemn prayer) he shall make stay this day there: or, as the old Latin has it, *Yet a day* for him *to stand at Nob*, that is, he has now but a day's journey, to bring him thither, to arrive with his army there. Of the place, see 1 Sam. 21.1. Neh. 11.32.

*{he shall shake his hand, against the mount of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem*} Being come to Nob, from whence he might see Jerusalem; Sion especially, the higher part; he shall in contempt of the city, and as in a menacing way, intending to be with her ere long, shake his hand at her: (the same word is here used, that was before, ver. 15.) or, as some, he shall so do by his messengers, when he comes by them before her: and that is the worst he shall be able to do to her, in regard of what he intended against her. He shall threaten and straiten her, and by that means, it may be, affright her: but he shall not so much as assault her, and much less surprise her, chap. 37.33,35. Yea, as he wags his hand now, at her; so she after his defeat shall wag her head, in scorn and derision, at him, ch. 37.21. whereof, also, some would expound this passage; but the words will not well bear it. But a learned writer gives a different interpretation from others, of this whole verse: Which, having related only, I shall leave to the judgment of others. He thus renders the text, supposing it to be *more day yet, than to stay at Nob; he shall move his hand toward the mount of the daughter of Sion*; that is, he shall, by the motion of his hand, as he rides to and fro among his troops, make signs to them, not to stay; but to march on toward Jerusalem. The like haste in the Chaldeans' march thitherward, see described, Jer. 6.4.

*{mount*} Whereon Zion, that is, that strong fort, and the upper part of the city, called *the city of David*, 2 Sam. 5.7,9. was situate; as threatening her greatest strength, that it should be unable to withstand him.

*{daughter of Zion*} See ch. 1.8.

*{the hill*} For the city stood upon a knoll, or rising. See Jer. 17.3.

**V. 33.** *{Behold the Lord, the Lord of hosts, &c.*} The passage in these two verses, (which the prophet begins with a remarkable note, requiring more sedulous attention, and serious consideration; of which, see, ch. 3.1.) is by divers diversely expounded and applied. Some expounding it all of the defeat given to the Assyrian; some, of the havoc made by his forces among the people of Judah: others, the former part, ver. 33. of the one; and the latter, ver. 34. of the other. I shall follow the first, (though contrary to some of great note therein,) as most agreeable to the drift and tenor of the prophet's discourse; who having before encouraged God's people, those of Jerusalem especially, against the dreadful expectation of the Assyrian invasion; and yet, after that, related his progress and proceedings from place to place with his potent army; that affrighted and enforced to fly all before him, whithersoever therewith he advanced: and his approaches in menacing manner with it to Jerusalem; because this might minister matter of much terror, even to Jerusalem itself; and those that should resort thither for succor, he now, that they might not thereby be disheartened, informs them in the next place, how the Lord would deal with him, and these his forces, wherewith he threatened Jerusalem. He would take them down in an unexpected manner, and disable him and them from doing aught further against it.

*{Behold*} As if he had said, Mark yet, and behold a strange change. You have heard of a furious and forcible approach of an insolent tyrant. Wait but a while, and you shall see his pride pulled down, and his enterprise against you utterly frustrate.

*{the Lord, the Lord of hosts*} One mightier than he, as ver. 24,26.

*{shall lop the bough*} Heb. word for word, *shall branch*, or, *bough, the branch*, or, *bough*: *to branch*, or, *bough*; for, *to cut*, or *lop off*, either, as *to root*, for, *to root out*, Job 31.12. Psal. 52.5. See the like, ch. 22.5. the one word signifies not so much to *prune* and *pare away sprigs*, or the spray, or the lower washy branches next to the ground; as *to lop* and *fell* the bigger *boughs*, and great arms, of the loftiest of them that bear the most fruit; which the word, from whence that here used (as specially coined for this purpose, and nowhere else read) comes, does properly signify, Ezek. 31.5,6. chap. 17.6. and 27.10. in regard whereof, the highest *cliffs* of rocks are by the same term designed, Judg. 15.8,11. chap. 2.21. & 57.5. the other word imports, not *a bare bough*, or *branch*; but *a brave bough*, or, *branch*: (for thence the word, *bravery*, chap. 3.18.) a *bough*, or *branch*, adorned, adorned, and beautified with leaves, and fruit, Ezek. 17.6. & 31.5,6,8,12,13. put here collectively, *bough*, for *boughs*; as *tree*, for *trees*, ver. 19. So that, hereby is meant, that God would cut down the chief and principal, those of greatest state and might, in Sennacherib's army: such, as are likened to high boughs, and tall trees, ch. 2.13. ver. 18. ch. 18.5.

*{with terror*} Or, *with violence*. In most terrible manner, as the like word is used, ch. 8.14. & 29.23. For this word itself is also without fellow; but comes of one, that signifies both to *force*, and to *fright*.

*{and the high ones of stature shall be hewed down*} As Amos, 2.9. the same in effect, reiterated in other terms; but with some amplification: as if he had said, not the *boughs* only shall be *lopped*, but the *trees* also, even the tallest of them, *felled*, his *princes* whom he mated with kings, ver. 8.

*{and the haughty shall be humbled*} Thus shall Sennacherib's plumes be plucked, and his pride pulled down; as was before threatened, ver. 12. See ch. 2.11–17.

**V. 34.** *{And he shall cut down the thickets of the forests*} Or, *forest*, rather, for so it is in the original; that is, the main body of his army. For might, and multitude, compared to a wood, or forest full of trees, as before, ver. 18. See also ch. 9.18.

*{with iron*} Or, *as with iron*. The note of similitude to be supplied: as ver. 26. that is, as with iron tools, axes, and hatchets, or the like, wherewith boughs are wont to be lopped, and trees felled. See Jer. 46.22,23.

*{and Lebanon shall fall*} Hence some would infer, that this verse at least, must be understood, not of Sennacherib's army; but of the strength and glory of the Jewish people pulled down by him; because Lebanon was one of the boundaries of their country, Deut. 11.24. Josh. 1.4. and is sometime applied to it and them, and more specially, to Jerusalem, Jer. 22.6,20,23. Zach. 10.10. & 11.1. But to omit, that Jerusalem, *fell* not by Sennacherib, being defeated of his purpose: Mount *Lebanon* abounding with goodly tall cedars, and other timber trees, and famous far and near; for the same is commonly used to resemble, as well other states, persons, and people, as those of the Jews; in comparisons taken from woods and forests especially. Yea, the Assyrian king, in particular, is called *a cedar of Lebanon*, Ezek. 31.3. and *Carmel*, though a mount of Israel, is in this very argument applied to him and his forces, ver. 18. *Lebanon* therefore, as the Jewish Rabbines well observe, is no other here than the Assyrian vast host; for might and multitude, likened to that mountain, and the trees that it bore.

*{by a mighty one*} As Psal. 93.4. or, *an excellent one*: as the word is rendered, Psal. 8.1,9. & 76.4. or, *a goodly one*; as Ezek. 17.23. or, *a gallant one*, as chap. 33.21. or, *a glorious one*, as in the same place: that is, by an angel, ch. 37.36. so rather, (as most, both Jewish, and others agree) than as some; who, by *Lebanon*, understanding Sennacherib himself, who sustained that army, as mount Lebanon did the trees, that grew on it, would by this *great* and *gallant one*, have meant his son and heir, that slew him, which seems not to agree with the story, which tells us, that two of his sons slew him, and a third of them succeeded him, ch. 37.38. or, as others, who by *Lebanon*, would understand the temple at Jerusalem, built with the cedars of Lebanon, 1 King. 9.10,11. burnt down by Nebuchadnezzar, 2 King. 25.9.

### CHAPTER 11

**V. 1.** *{And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse*} Or, as some, *For*, as Chap. 10.17. whether way we read it, is not much material. The manner of this our prophet is, as has formerly been observed, upon occasion of particular deliverances, and restitutions, more remarkable than ordinary, related or foretold; to rise higher and proceed further, even unto that more general deliverance of mankind, and spiritual restoration and enlargement of the church by the Messiah at his coming; which is therefore not unfitly here annexed unto that, which he had in the close of the former chapter delivered, concerning the deliverance of Jerusalem and the remainder of Judah, by the defeat and fall of the Assyrian king and his forces; chap. 10.27,37,38. a type of the spiritual enemies of the church, utterly quelled by Christ, Col. 2.15. Howbeit, it may well be conceived to be, not in way of bare consecution, only annexed, but by way of declaration also subjoined to the former, as rendering a reason, why it was said that God would deliver and preserve that people, *for the anointing*, chap. 10.27. to wit, because of the Messiah, who was to come of that people, and that family, which God would therefore have preserved. Some of the late Jewish writers would draw all this to Ezekiah, wherein some of ours also go too far, yet not denying, but that Ezekiah is therein considered, as a type of the Messiah, of whom, also the most, even of the latter Jewish commenters, therein concurring with the ancient Talmudists, expound this place. And among these, some of them give this connection of this passage with the former. Having there expounded, that *excellent*, or, *gallant one*, by whom Sennacherib's forces should fall, to be Ezekiah; for whose purity, and piety wherein he *excelled*, being one of those, whom the psalmist gives that title to, Ps. 16.3. & the prophet, Jer. 30.21. (in both which places, the same word is used,) God should upon his prayer, give the enemy that defeat, and vouchsafe those of Judah that deliverance: because, say they, it might be further demanded, yea, but what shall become of those of Israel, that the Assyrian carried captive unto Halah, and Habor, 2 King. 17.6. to this prophet here answers, that the Messiah, when he comes, one of the same stock with Ezekiah, he shall gather them together, and bring them back again, and do more wonderful things for them, than ever was done for Ezekiah, alluding to the term of *wonderment*, used, ch. 9.6. which they apply to Ezekiah, thus they acknowledging, not Ezekiah, but the Messiah, to be here meant.

*{a rod*} Or, *a twig*, such as rods are made of. The word is nowhere else found, save here, and Prov. 14.3. where a fool's tongue is termed, *a twig of pride*, wherewith he is twitting, and twigging of others, or, for which by others, he comes to be twigged himself. Howsoever therefore, some following therein the Chaldee paraphrast, understand by it, a royal *scepter*; as another word seems to import, used of Christ, Gen. 49.10. Psal. 45.6. Yet in this place to me, it seems to have respect rather to the meanness and weakness of Christ's appearance in our human nature, and the low condition, wherein here he lived, rather like to some tender and sorry twig, than to a goodly bough, or a kingly scepter, chap. 53.2.

*{the stem of Jesse*} *Stem*, or, *trunk*, or, *stump*. For the word signifies properly, the stump of a plant, tree, or shrub, left in the ground, when the main body of it is felled, or cut away, Job 14.7,8. chap. 40.24. like that in Nebuchadnezzar's dream, Dan. 4.15,23. Whereupon, some suppose, that these words have reference to the lopping, and felling of the Jewish state and people, by the Assyrian mentioned, as they suppose, chap. 10.37,38. and so begin the chapter, with an adversative; *But*, or, *Yet*. As implying, that notwithstanding that state, compared to a goodly cedar, were so impaired, and impoverished, that it might justly be deemed, rather a sorry stump, than a tree: yet from it, should sprout out a sprig, that should do strange things. For the exposition of the former passage, and the connection of this with it, enough has been already said. But for the term here used, it is not denied, but that the house of David, and the strength, state, and wealth of it, was much impaired in those times, as well by the defection of the ten tribes, as the invasion of these their brethren, by the Syrians, Assyrians, and others. Nor is it improbable, that the prophet, had here an eye thereunto. But withal it is most likely, that he principally respected the mean and low estate, that the family of David was to be brought unto, at the time of Christ's birth, when Joseph, his father-in-law, and Mary his mother, both of the blood royal, and lineally descended from David, Matth. 1.1,16. Luk. 2.4,5. & 3.23,31. were the one a poor carpenter, and the other of as mean a condition as he, Matth. 13.55. Mar. 6.3. Luk. 4.22. So that the royal stem might then seem to be utterly withered, and in a manner cut clean away; in regard whereof he says, not, *the stock of David*; but the *stump of Jesse*, a private man of no power or state, nor of any great esteem, 1 Sam. 18.18,23. & 20.30. & 22.7. thereby to intimate from how mean a condition, in the eyes of flesh and blood, the Messiah, as man, should take his first rise, ch. 53.2.

*{and a branch shall grow out of his roots*} The same in effect (which in this prophet is very frequent) with the former.

*{a branch*} Or, *a sprig*, or a *scion*. Such as they are wont to graft with, ch. 60.21. and Babel is compared to a rotten *sprig*, or *spray*, ch. 14.19. The Messiah indeed is termed *a branch*, Jer. 23.5. & 33.15. Zach. 3.8. but it is another word that is there used. The word *sprig*, seems better here to suit with the word *twig*, that went before, and in sound comes somewhat near it, and they go yet further off, who with the Latin render it *a flower*. From the word here used, it is by many learned writers deemed, that the evangelist says, that Christ was to be called, not a *Nazarite*, such as Sampson was, though a type of Christ, Judg. 13.7. or such as those, in the law, that cut not their hair, nor drank wine, nor touched any dead corpse. For what is frivolously conceived of our Savior, concerning the first, is fabulous, and groundless; and for the latter two, it is certain, that he did both drink wine, Matth. 11.19. & 26.9. and touch dead bodies, Matth. 9.25. Luk. 7.14. (besides, that the word of *separation*, whence that name comes, is written with a divers character from the word here used,) nor a *Nazarene*, which signifies one of *Nazareth*, or, *Natsareth*, the town where he was brought up, Mar. 14.65. & 16.6. Luk. 4.34. which is supposed to have had its name, from the word here used, as a place, which being fit for fruit trees, had much planting of them about it. But a *Nazoree*, or a *Nazaree*, (for both readings are found, Act. 2.22. & 3.6.) that is, as well the *spriggy* one, here prophesied of, as one of *Nazareth's*, bred, or abode, Matth. 2.23.

*{shall grow*} Or, *bud*, as it is rendered, Ps. 132.17. or *sprung up*, as Ps. 85.12. ch. 44.4.

*{out of his roots*} Who these roots should be expositors dispute, and some run upwards and fetch in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, with all Jesse's ancestors. Others, run downward, and bring in David, and Nathan, with all Jesse's posterity, *his sons, and sons' sons*, as the Chaldee yields it. For Jesse say they, was as the grain cast into the ground, those of his posterity, were as the *roots*, or strings of the root, that from the grain swelling in the ground sprout out. The phrase imports the very same, but with further emphasis, that was before said, the *stump*, there; is the *roots*, here: the *stump*, is some small or short part of the stem, or stock above ground, Dan. 4.15. the *root* is that, that lies underground, Job 14.8. before Jesse, that is, his house or race, whence this twig was to shoot forth, was said to be, as *a stump*, that is, left near, but somewhat above the ground, when the main body of the tree is gone. Now it is likened to the *root* of a plant, or tree, so cut away that nothing of it is left to be seen above ground; so that the sprig that springs from it, must needs rise immediately from the root itself, nothing appearing above ground from whence it might sprout. So is Ezekiah said to proceed from the *root* of Ahaz his father, whose *rod*, that is, power, had been utterly broken, ch. 14.29. Yea, so in a parallel place, where the same terms here used, are found, Dan. 11.6,7. of the daughter of the southern king, given in marriage to the northern, it is said, that *out of a sprig from her roots, one should stand up*; when, *neither she should retain any power, nor her husband stand; and both he that brought her, and he that begat her*; (or, as some, *whom she begat*) *and he that supported her, should all be given up*. Which place conduces much to the clearing of this. See of the small beginnings in show of Christ and his kingdom, those parables, Matth. 13.31,32,33. Mark 4.30,31.
