**V. 2.** *{And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him*} He proceeds here, to show the transcendent excellencies, and endowments of this *rod*, or *sprig*, that should rise, and spring up from so poor and sorry a stock, by means whereof he should be enabled to effect and accomplish, such strange, and unheard of achievements as are hereafter mentioned.

*{The Spirit of the Lord*} The Holy Ghost, which proceeds from God the Father, Joh. 15.26. and which overshadowed the Virgin in the conception of our Savior, Luk. 1.35. though some understand by the *Spirit* here, God the *Father*, who is a *Spirit* also, Joh. 4.24. and is said to dwell in Christ, Joh. 14.10. Some, again, the Son, the second person, called his *Eternal Spirit*, Heb. 9.14. 1 Pet. 3.18,19. But that which was given in the first place, seems most probable; because the three persons are here distinctly propounded, as also, Psal. 45.6,7. chap. 61.1. and as distinctly appeared at his baptism; the Father in the *cloud*: the Son, in the *river*: the Holy Ghost in the *dove*, Matth. 3.16,17.

*{shall rest upon him*} Not *come upon* him only, as it did upon his mother, in the conceiving of him, Luk. 1.35. nor *be upon* him only; ch. 61.1. but *rest*, and abide with him, take up in a more special, yea singular manner, its perpetual and never interrupted, or eclipsed residence with him, and in him, typified by the Holy Ghost *descending in the likeness of a dove*, at the time of his baptism, and *resting upon him*, Matth. 3.16. the sign given John, who baptized him, whereby to know him, Joh. 1.32,33. Somewhat the like phrase is used; where it is said, that *the Spirit of Elias rested upon Elizeus*, 2 King. 2.15. as also of those elders, concerning whom God told Moses, that he would take of the Spirit that was upon him, and put it upon them, it is said, that when he so did, *the Spirit rested upon them, and when it rested upon them, they did incessantly prophesy*, Num. 11.17,25,26. yet not on them; or in them, so as on Christ; not *corporally*, in the apostle's sense, as in him, Col. 2.9. not *fully* as in him, Col. 1.19. but partially; *I will take of it*, says God, not, *incessantly*, and *inseparably*, as in him. For though they prophesied incessantly, while the Spirit rested upon them, yet it appears not, that, that prophetical Spirit was always so with them; for then should they have done nothing but prophesied; whereas they were sent apart for other employments, Num. 11.17.

*{The Spirit of, &c.*} The prophet having said in general that the Spirit of God should rest on him, goes on, to recite some heads of those particular endowments, wherewith the Messiah, in his human nature, should be superabundantly furnished, above all creatures, men or angels, not for his own private use, or honor alone; but for the managing of his spiritual kingdom, and the sufficient supply with the like graces, and endowments, according to their necessary employments, and due proportions of all those, that had interest in him, and dependence upon him, Joh. 1.14,16. & 3.34. & 4.14. & 7.38,39. Act. 2.33. Eph. 4.13,15,16. Col. 1.19. & 2.3,9,19. for the *Spirit* is put, sometime, for the *Holy Ghost* itself, the third person in the Trinity; Joh. 3.8. 1 Cor. 12.4,6,8. Rev. 22.17. and so it is to be understood, in the former branch: sometime, for the graces and spiritual endowments, that are given by the Spirit; either ordinary, or extraordinary, Joh. 7.39. Which place, would being compared with Acts, 19.2. help to clear that place, almost generally, much mistaken; as if the persons there spoken of, were wholly ignorant, of the being of the Holy Ghost; whereas the apostle's question, was of some extraordinary gifts of it; and their answer suitable to his demand. So Rom. 8.23. 2 Cor. 1.22. 1 The. 4.8. & 5.19. with 2 Tim. 1.6. And so is it to be taken in this latter branch, for the graces of the Spirit. And the word *Spirit*, is prefixed, and repeated again, and again, before these endowments; to intimate, that Christ, should not have these, or the like parts, and gifts, as men commonly have them; either as natural, or acquisite faculties, enabling them to the performance of natural offices, and the managing of worldly affairs: but that they should be in him, of a far more sublime, a spiritual, celestial, and divine nature; as proceeding from the Spirit of God, dwelling in him. Col. 2.9. Jam. 3.17. 2 Pet. 1.4. Howbeit, some take the *Spirit*, in this branch, also, as in the former, for the Holy Ghost itself, expounding the words thus, *The Spirit of wisdom*, &c. that is, The Spirit that works in men's hearts, these graces; and that should confer them, in a singular manner upon him: which yet in effect will come home to that, which was before said, for the substance of the matter here intended. Spiritual endowments here mentioned, are six in number; howsoever our Popish writers, following the old version, that without due regard, jumbles some passages together here; and swerves, both from the terms in the original, and the tenor of the context; make seven of them, to answer the number of the seven Spirits, mentioned, by John. Rev. 1.4. & 4.5. But the text mentions but six: and the addition of a seventh in the Apocalypse, say some, was to intimate a larger measure of the Spirit, exhibited in the times of the New Testament, than of the old. But neither was it the prophet's purpose, to relate all the endowments of Christ, or graces of the Spirit; which no tongue, or pen can do: and divers of them, as his humility, meekness, compassion, patience, &c. are not here expressed: nor need we in the number, to seek for any mystery; wherein wanton wits, to sport themselves are too prone. Suffice us it may, that by those here mentioned, is intended an absolute all-sufficiency, to be found in Christ, needful for the consummating of the work of his mediatorship; and the procuring of the eternal happiness of all his. See Rev. 3.1.

*{of wisdom and understanding*} This is the first pair of those spiritual endowments: and those two are here distinguished: as also Deut. 4.6. Prov. 2.6. & 4.5. & 7.4. But how to be limited in their distinct notions, is not easy to determine. Some would have the former such a gift, as fits one to be a teacher, 1 Cor. 12.8. The latter such a gift, as fits one to be a learner; able to understand that, that is delivered by the teacher. Mat. 24.15. 2 Tim. 2.7. Others by *wisdom* understand, skill, in divine matters; by *understanding*, prudence in politic affairs. Others distinguish them, as antecedent, and consequent; making *wisdom* the gift, of illumination, Eph. 1.18. Heb. 6.4. & 10.32. and *understanding*, the apprehending, and judging of things aright, by help of that light, Rom. 2.18. 1 Cor. 2.14,15. And this I take to be most probable; though some suppose, the one to be adjoined to the other, by way of exposition only. Many other distinctions of them, the schoolmen deliver: but such, as divers of them groundless; and most such, as do not so well fit this place: nor is it necessary to overclog this work with. These two, God promised to bestow upon Solomon, as two endowments most needful for the government of his people. 1 King. 3.12. And these therefore are in a far larger manner conferred upon him who was far greater than Solomon, Mat. 12.42. and of whose kingdom, Solomon's was but a shadow, Psal. 45.6. Heb. 1.8.

*{the spirit of counsel, and might*} This is the second pair of endowments, and contains two virtues, very requisite to the managing of a state, ch. 36.5. to wit, *counsel*, and *courage*. Where again by *counsel*, some understand ability to advise, and direct others, by *courage*, and ability, to execute advice given by others: as if they belonged to several persons, or subjects. But by *counsel*, I conceive be meant that faculty, whereby a man is enabled to manage his affairs to the best advantage, and to find out an issue in matters intricate and perplexed, Prov. 20.18. & 24.6. Luk. 14.31. By *courage*, (for so I would rather render it) that virtue, whereby a man is enabled, resolutely to undertake, and undauntedly to go through with, whatsoever his place, or office necessarily requires of him, seem it never so hazardous, 1 Sam. 14.6,13. & 17.32. 2 Sam. 23.16. Neh. 6.11. Esth. 4.16. Psal. 18.32. And these two proportionably mixed together, make an excellent composure.

*{the spirit of knowledge, and of the fear of the Lord*} The third pair of spiritual endowments found in Christ; which some again would so distinguish, as the one befitting a teacher, as importing skill, in interpretation of Scripture, Mal. 2.8. Luk. 11.52. The other belonging to a learner Deut. 17.19. Psal. 25.14. & 34.11. But that distinction suits nor so well with this place, where the Messiah is propounded; not so much, as a teacher, and much less, as a learner; but as a mighty Prince, able discreetly and righteously, to manage a large dominion, and to overreach, and overpower all the enemies thereof.

*{knowledge*} How to distinguish this from the two first, many much trouble themselves, and so cross one another, that it is hard to find any two that concur; too tedious it would be to relate their dissenting judgments. To leave them therefore to their jarring debates; the rather, because the words are in Scripture oft promiscuously used. By *knowledge*, we may well here understand the power of discerning the true nature of things, even the most hidden, and abstruse, as the secretest thoughts, and motions of men's hearts, 1 King. 8.39. Prov. 15.11. Jer. 17.9,10. Act. 1.24. & 15.9. 1 Joh. 3.20. that which is in special manner attributed to Christ, Matth. 9.4. Luk. 11.17. Joh. 21.17. Heb. 4.12,13. Rev. 2.23.

*{and of the fear of the Lord*} That which Solomon makes after David his father, Psal. 111.10. the *prime* part, if not, the *principal* piece of *wisdom*, Prov. 1.7. & 9.10. and Job before them both, *wisdom* itself, Job 28.28. But much doubt is made, how any *fear of God* should be in Christ; unto whom yet, some such thing seems to be attributed, Heb. 5.7. And if we shall consider, that there is not only a fear of wrath, which even the worst may have. Jam. 2.19. and a fear of sinning, which even the best must have, while they live here, Eccles. 9.2. Prov. 28.13. but a fear of honor and reverence also, that accompanies and seasons all service of God, Psal. 2.11. & 5.7. Heb. 12.28. such as even the blessed saints and angels, retain still in heaven, we need not doubt, but that Christ, who adored God, as he was man, Joh. 4.22. though, he were adored, and that by the angels themselves, as he was God, Heb. 1.6. did bear a reverent affection unto his Father whom he worshiped, Matth. 11.25. Joh. 11.41. & 17.1,2. and whose servant, also, he is said to be, chap. 42.1. and 53.11.

**V. 3.** *{And shall, &c.*} Before, were the excellent endowments of Christ; now follows the employment and exercise of these his parts and endowments, in the administration of his royal power and place.

*{shall make him of quick understanding in the fear of the Lord*} Heb. *he shall scent*, or, *smell*; or, *it shall make him scent*, or, *smell, in the fear of the Lord*. This, some, following the former version, understand of the party spoken of, on whom the Spirit does thus rest; he shall scent, or smell, or breathe of nothing, but what is pious, and religious. He shall send out such a sweet scent in all his course, as shall savor of that precious spiritual oil of piety, and godliness, wherewith he was so abundantly anointed, Psal. 45.7. See Cant. 1.2. See somewhat also the like of Jacob, Gen. 17.27. Of God's people in general, Hos. 14.6. and of the apostles, more especially, 2 Cor. 2.14,15. but they, so from Christ, through Christ, and the gospel of Christ, and the knowledge of Christ, which they bore about with them, 2 Cor. 4.6,7. nor do some of those, that admit the latter version, depart much from this sense, to wit, that the Spirit resting upon him, should make him to fill all places where he comes, as the apostle speaks of himself, and his associates, with such a sweet savor, as the scent of the ointment, poured upon his head, filled the whole house with, where he then was, Matth. 26.7. Joh. 12.3. But others, rather of those, that take the latter way, understand it of sharpness of judgment: the forementioned Spirit, shall make him *of quick understanding*, or, *judgment*; not in worldly affairs, Luk. 12.14. things far beneath his cognizance, Joh. 18.36. but either in matters of piety and godliness, in discerning of those things, that are agreeable thereunto, and that disagree from the same; whatsoever tincture they may bear with them, or gloss may be set on them, Rom. 2.18. Phil. 1.9,10. Col. 2.8,23. or, in judging of men's persons and inward dispositions, whether they have the power of piety within them, 2 Tim. 3.5. whether their hearts be sincere, and upright, or no, Joh. 1.47. and to discover the hypocrisy of hollow-hearted persons, through all those masks and semblances, veils and pretenses, under which they shroud, and wherewith they strive to cover and conceal their unsoundness, Matth. 22.18. & 23.25,27,28. Luk. 16.15. Joh. 2.23,25. & 6.26,70. It is a metaphor taken from the sense of *smelling*, which, says one of the Jewish doctors upon the place, is surer and less subject to deceit and mistake, where it is quick and vigorous, than, either the hearing, or the sight. And it is, as if the prophet had said, he shall be so quick of scent, in discerning things of this nature, that he will smell out an hypocrite, though he neither see his face, or hear his voice: or, though his face promise, or his voice protest the contrary, Matth. 6.16. & 7.21,22,23. And this exposition, the words following confirm.

*{in the fear of the Lord*} This term is used in Scripture, sometime for that reverent disposition that man bears unto God, either as his Sovereign Lord and Master, or as his Father in Christ. 1 King. 18.3,12. Neh. 7.2. sometime, for the service and worship of God, 2 King. 17.25,28,32,33,34,41. because it ought to proceed from it, and be seasoned with it, Heb. 12.28. Sometime, for all pious and religious affection towards God in general, Psal. 19.9. Jer. 32.40. and so it is taken here: though I accord not with those, who would have *the fear of the Lord*, here mentioned, to comprehend, synecdochially, all the endowments before named; rendering the words, *his scenting*, or, *smelling*, *shall be joined with the fear of the Lord*; the last of those graces, and consequently, (because they hang all on one string, and are links all of one chain) with the rest also of them: and the meaning to be, that he should not judge of things, slightly, and weakly, as the manner of men is; but wisely, understandingly, advisedly, resolutely, knowingly, religiously. Which, though all true, yet stuffs too much into the text; because more by much, than the word itself, simply, and singly considered imports.

*{and he shall not judge after the sight of his eyes*} Or, *So that he shall not*, &c. as ch. 10.19. for this is added, as an effect of his sagacity and expertness, in judging aright of matters, or persons presented unto him, to be decided, or tried by him, that it may keep him free in matter of judicature, from being either deluded with fair shows, and outsides; or misled by colorable, but false, reports.

*{after the sight of his eyes*} Not with respect of men's persons, 2 Chr. 19.7. Rom. 2.11. wherein men, many times are faulty, Psal. 82.2. Jam. 2.1,2. Christ is far from it, Job 34.19. Matth. 22.16. ver. 4. nor according to outward shows and appearances, as men are wont oft to do, Joh. 7.24. 2 Cor. 10.7. because they cannot pierce into men's hearts, or discern their secret intentions, and hidden dispositions, 1 Cor. 2.11. as Christ being God and man, thus furnished, can do, and does, 1 Sam. 16.7. whom no glittering outside, or goodly semblance, can deceive, Jer. 17.9,10. Gal. 6.7.

*{neither reprove after the hearing of his ears*} As he shall not, in regard of external shows, and appearances, acquit, or approve any, who is in truth, faulty, or inwardly unsound: so he shall not upon any flying report, or forged suggestion, proceed to the censuring, or disdeeming of any, (as men, even the best, now and then do, 1 Sam. 24.9,10. 2 Sam. 16.3,4. & 19.24–27.) who is not faulty, but free from that, wherewith he is charged, Job 1.8–12. & 2.3–6. Psal. 7.8–10. & 13.15,16. & 23.10. He shall not heed, or regard any reports from others, either for men, or against men, (which men are, of necessity, compelled to do, because they cannot come to the notice of things otherwise: and by reason thereof, being through untrue depositions, misinformed, do by mere mistake, therefore, many times, accordingly pass wrong judgment) but shall always proceed upon certain knowledge of his own, in whatsoever doom and sentence he shall pass upon any, Gen. 18.21. Joh. 2.23,25. in the judgment by God the Father, committed unto him, Joh. 5.22,27. Act. 17.31. Rom. 2.17. & 14.10,12. 1 Cor. 4.5. 2 Cor. 5.10. 2 Tim. 4.1. 1 Pet. 4.5.

**V. 4.** *{But*} Heb. *And*, as ch. 7.12.

*{with righteousness*} Heb. *in righteousness*; as Psal. 96.13. & 98.9. that is, justly, uprightly.

*{judge the poor*} That is, *judge for* them; give sentence in their behalf, and consequently, execute justice for them: as Psal. 7.8. & 26.1. ch. 1.17. He shall minister justice uprightly, equally, impartially, as well to poor, as to rich, Psal. 72.2,4.

*{and reprove with equity for the meek of the earth*} The same thing in effect, that was spoken before; but with some little further explication: for instead of *judge*, here is, *reprove*, or *debate*, for the word will admit either, *if debate*; it is *to plead* for them: as Job 13.15. If *reprove*; it is to *rebuke* for them, by word, Psal. 105.14. or to *punish* for them, by execution of judgment, Psal. 94.10. those that wrong, or oppress them, Psal. 72.4. for *justice*, he puts *equity*, or *evenness*, the same, see Psal. 45.6. & 67.4. a term taken from those, that cut out a thing, in dividing it, to an hair, as we say, or, a thread: for the *poor*, it is here the *meek of the earth*, or *land*, alluding to that peculiar place, wherein God's people did then most abide. So Zeph. 2.3. to *poor*, he adds *meek*, partly, to note the qualification of such poor, as Christ undertakes to protect; (for, all *poor*, are not *meek*, no more than all *poor* in state, *poor also in spirit*, Matth. 5.3. with Luk. 6.20.) and partly, because where poverty and *meekness* meet, ill-minded men are usually the more prone to abuse, and wrong such, while they observe them content quietly to bear and pass by those abuses and wrongs, that others will not so easily put up. Howbeit, there want not those of note, that expound this branch, not of Christ's dealing for such; but of his dealing with them: and they render the words thus; *and he will reprove*, or, *correct*, (as the word sometime imports, Psal. 6.1. & 38.1.) *in uprightness*, or *in evenness*, (that is, *uprightly, evenly*,) *the meek of the earth*, that is, as they conceive it, he will carry an even hand, between the one and the other, not sparing either, when they do amiss, nor bearing out either in what they are faulty; as God himself gives in charge, Exod. 23.2,3. or, he will carry a discreet, and moderate hand, in rebuking, or chastising the meek, and lowly; so as though to correct, and reclaim them, yet, not to dishearten; much less destroy them, ch. 27.7–9. & 48.9,10. Jer. 30.11. But I adhere rather to the former, see ch. 2.4.

*{and he shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth*} This some also understand of Christ's dealing with both sorts, good and bad, or elect and refuse; but in a different manner, by the power and scepter of his word, subduing, and bringing in and under, the one unto a voluntary obedience, and submission to his will, Psal. 110.2,3. and by the same word again, smiting the obstinate and refractory ones in their souls and consciences, and thereby, sealing them up, as it were, to condemnation and destruction, Joh. 12.48. For the word of God is double edged, Heb. 4.12. Rev. 1.16. as a *surgeon's knife*, unto those that are corrected and converted by it, Rom. 15.16,18. 1 Cor. 5.5. 1 Pet. 4.6. so a *slaughtering knife* unto those that stand out against it, Rev. 2.12,16. as a savor of life, by their conversion unto salvation, to the one; so a savor of death, unto their confusion, in their condemnation, and everlasting destruction, to the other, 2 Cor. 2.15,16. But I conceive it rather with others, as well Jews as Christians, to be understood only of his dealing with the wicked, called here, *the earth*, because earthly minded, Phil. 3.20. and having their portion only here upon earth, Matth. 6.20,21. Luk. 12.21. & 16.25. Jam. 5.5. And they are those, that possess the greatest part of the earth; being in most places, the most in number, in regard whereof, also, they are called the *world*, Joh. 16.19. & 17.9,25. 1 Joh. 5.19. and *the men of this world*, Psal. 17.14. These it is said, that Christ *smites*, that is, executes judgment upon them, in the behalf of his poor servants, whom they oppose and oppress: for the effecting whereof, he needs no other weapon, than *the rod of his mouth*, that is, a word of his mouth; that powerful word of his, whereby, as he created all things, Gen. 1.3. Psal. 33.6. Joh. 1.3. Heb. 11.3. and upholds all things, Psal. 145.5,6. Heb. 1.2,3. So is he able to bring all to nothing again, Psal. 104.29,30. his word being his will, and his will his work, Psal. 115.3. & 135.6. Dan. 4.35. This, I suppose to be the genuine sense of this clause, which requires therefore, to be brought in with an adversative, *But*, as denoting a passage from Christ's interposing for the one, to his proceedings against the other.

*{and with the breath of his lips shall he slay the wicked*} The same thing, in other terms, more emphatically repeated, *The earth*, there is *the wicked*, here: (the word singular, but taken collectively, as ch. 3.11.) though, by *the wicked*, some would understand *that wicked one*, the devil. 1 Joh. 3.10,12. the god and head of all wicked ones, Joh. 8.44. & 12.31. & 14.30. 2 Cor. 4.4. Eph. 2.2. & 6.12. But the term seems here more general; there he is said *to smite* there; which though it imply no less, as 1 Sam. 25.38. 2 Sam. 5.6. yet is it more fully and expressly said here, *he will slay*, that which he does oft-times with some of them by inflicting of exemplary judgments upon them, Dan. 7.10,11,12,14. Rev. 6.15–17. and will do with the whole body of them, at the last day, Luk. 19.27. 2 Thess. 1.8. And lastly, what was before said to be done, *with the rod of his mouth*, is now said, to be effected by *the breath of his lips*; both which some refer to that dreadful doom to be passed upon all wicked ones at the last day, Matth. 25.41. but it seems rather, to imply the same with the former, that Christ shall not need multitudes of men and store of ammunition, to bring down and confound the enemies of himself, and his people: he can do it of himself; with one word of his mouth, as John 18.6. yea without any word spoken, with a blast of his breath, or *the breath of his lips*; the least motion that may be, they are both joined together, also, Psal. 33.10. as in creating, there; so in destroying, here, see Job 4.9. and 15.30. chap. 59.19. Zach. 4.6,7. 2 Thess. 2.8. Rev. 19.14,15.

**V. 5.** *{And righteousness shall be the girdle of his loins, and faithfulness the girdle of his reins*} Or, *righteousness also*, &c. as chap. 8.5.8. or, as some, *for righteousness shall be*, &c. as chap. 8.21. Those that expound this whole prophecy of Ezekiah, (as we have formerly observed, that some both Jews and others, do understand hereby *righteousness*, and *faithfulness*, persons so qualified, men *righteous* and *faithful*, (the like whereunto, see on ch. 41.2.) and the meaning they suppose to be, that Ezekiah would have many righteous and faithful ones, constantly about him; and would not be attended by any, but such; therein following the example of David, his predecessor, and progenitor, Psal. 101.3,7. & 119.63,79,115. & 142.7. To which purpose also, some others, who understand it of Christ, yet give the same sense, that Christ will have his holy and faithful ones, always about him, and be himself also ever in the midst of them, to protect and support them, Psal. 46.5. Zach. 2.5. Matth. 18.20. & 28.20. Joh. 12.26. & 17.24. Rev. 14.4. & 17.14. & 19.14. But the words seem rather to be taken, for the virtues, or endowments of Christ himself, as they simply sound without trope or figure. For the better understanding whereof, we are to consider, that a *belt* or *girdle*, is sometime an ensign of honor, Job 12.18. Rev. 1.13. Sometime, an emblem of power, chap. 22.21. & 45.5. Psal. 18.32. & 93.1. Sometime, a note of preparation to fight, 1 King. 20.11. Sometime, of readiness for any affair or employment, journey, or handy work, 1 King. 18.46. Jer. 1.17. Luk. 12.35. Eph. 6.14. 1 Pet. 1.13. Of Christ therefore it is said, that *righteousness*, and *faithfulness*, shall be the *girdle* that he is girt with; to signify, that he shall not need such external ornaments, as worldly potentates are wont to wear: his gracious and honorable endowments, shall be sufficient to make him conspicuous and glorious: and from these, shall he be furnished, and enabled sufficiently for the execution of his office; nor shall he be idle and slothful, or loose and dissolute, (as earthly kings, and princes oft are, Eccles. 10.16,19.) but industrious in his place, and always ready for employment, in execution of justice, in the behalf of his people; and in faithful discharge in a constant course of whatsoever is necessary, for the procurement of their good. These are his *girdle*. These he counts, as his honor. These stick as close to him, as his girdle does to one's body; and this *girdle* he never puts off, or lays down. See Psal. 106.19. Jer. 13.11. The verse consists of two branches, where the same notion, is in other terms, redoubled, as one of the Rabbines well observes. What is called *righteousness*, in the former branch; is termed *faithfulness*, in the latter: *faithfulness*, being indeed a part of *righteousness*, 1 Joh. 1.9. (See of Christ, Rev. 2.24. & 19.11. though here some would have it to signify rather *firmness*, than *faithfulness*; and to note the perpetuity and constancy of the former, as Exod. 17.12. for they seem to me too wide, that would have the one meant of Christ's *righteousness*, whether imputed, or imparted to his, 1 Cor. 1.30. and the other of *faith*, whereby they apprehend him, and it 2 Cor. 13.5. Eph. 3.17. and for the other two words, that are rendered *loins* and *reins*, though they be several terms in the original, yet they note both the same things, nor does the latter word signify *reins*; there is another word or two for them, Exod. 29.13. Lev. 3.4. Deut. 32.14. Psal. 7.9. & 51.6. But *loins*, as well as the former, and is commonly so rendered; and that in this very argument, Job 38.3. & 40.7. chap. 5.27. & 32.11. Jer. 30.6. and would not therefore have been altered here, unless for some other word of the same signification.

**V. 6.** *{The wolf also, shall dwell with the lamb*} Heb. *And the wolf*, &c. as ch. 8.5. but some render it here, *wherefore*, as also, v. 3. I should rather yield it, *Then*, as Exod. 7.9. ch. 8.3. Here is laid down the strange effect, that this powerful government of Christ should have upon the souls of those, who by the ministry of the word shall be subdued unto him, and become loyal subjects of his spiritual kingdom; they shall through the efficacy thereof be so inwardly changed, that they shall seem new creatures, transformed out of beasts into men, Rom. 12.2. 2 Cor. 3.18. & 5.17. Gal. 6.15. Eph. 4.22,23. This is set forth by an allegorical illustration, wherein it is said, that such beasts, and other creatures, as are naturally ravenous, and harmful, as bears, and wolves, adders, and vipers, and the like, should now quietly, and harmlessly keep, and converse, with mankind, and with cattle, whom they were wont to prey upon, and do much mischief to before; thereby implying, that such persons, as had formerly been of a fierce, savage, unteachable, and untractable disposition, like to such forementioned creatures, should then become mild and gentle, tame and harmless, tractable and teachable; laying down that their former brutish, fierce, froward, and untoward disposition: and that therefore there should be abundance of peace, consequently, and safety, without fear of spoil and rapine, by one from another, in the kingdom of Christ. See ch. 2.4.

*{the wolf dwell with the lamb*} That is, *abide*, *stay*, as a stranger with his host: (So the word properly signifies, Judg. 17.7,9,10.) in peaceable and friendly manner; without doing any harm to them whom he had wont to worry, Matth. 10.16,17. See chap. 65.25.

*{and the leopard shall lie down with the kid*} They shall lodge quietly together, without fear of harm from the one to the other. Of the term *Leopard* see on Jer. 13.23.

*{and the calf, and the young lion, and the fatling together*} No wealth, or weakness, shall tempt them, to attempt aught one against another. Some of the Jewish writers suppose an allusion herein, to the state of the creatures in Noah's ark; wherein being shut up, they kept all quietly together, during the whole time of the deluge; and it may well be admitted, that the prophet so does. But that which they add, that it shall be so again, in the days of the Messiah; that all the creatures shall then do the like again, is a mere fable, and fiction of their own addle brains.

*{and a little child shall lead them*} Heb. *leading them*, or, *their leader*, which some have understood of Christ, who is called *a child*, Luk. 2.12,16. Act. 4.27. and was small, and abject in men's eyes; as David a type of him, says of himself, Psal. 119.141. But the meaning is plain, that those unruly and ravening creatures, should be so tame, that they should not need some stout and strong fellow, for a shepherd, to tend the one, and to defend them against the force and violence of the other; such an one as Sampson, or David, or one of his worthies, that were able to overmaster, a bear, or a lion, Judg. 14.5,6. 1 Sam. 17.35,36. 2 Sam. 23.20. Any *child*, though never so small would serve to tend them and to lead them out to pasture, and home again: and not them alone; but those other creatures also, where they were mixed with them, implying how, not harmless only, but tractable, men should be; and how meek, content to be directed and conducted, even by the meanest, that were able aright to inform them of aught, that might be useful for them to know, or concerned them to practice, and to follow their advice and direction therein. See the example of Apollos, Act. 18.24–26.

**V. 7.** *{And the cow, and the bear shall feed; their young ones shall lie down together*} Or, *The cow also, and the bear shall feed together* (supplied from v. 6. or from the next branch either) *and their young ones* (Heb. *their children*, as Joh. 38.41.) *shall lie together*; they shall not only feed, but breed together; nor shall the regard of their young ones prevail with them, as usually does with such creatures, to make them ravenous the rather.

*{and the lion shall eat straw like the ox*} It is an allusion, say some of the Rabbins, to the state of creation; and the harmless food, that the creatures then contented themselves with, feeding only on such food as the earth afforded them, either herbs, and grass on the ground, or, what the shrubs and trees yielded, Gen. 1.29,30. and not preying upon any other living thing, that is, creature endued with sensitive life: for had they so done, say they, at the first, there being but one pair of each made, (which, yet cannot be proved,) a male, and a female, the whole creation had soon been destroyed. I will not enter into the discussion of this difficult question, requiring larger discourse, than the nature of the present work will permit, especially, being but a by-matter. See ch. 65.25. Some expound it, that great and mighty men, should be content to be fed with the same food of the word and sacraments, that the poorest and meanest feed on, 1 Cor. 10.3,4. & 12.13. Gal. 3.27,28. But to such niceties we need not descend; an harmless course of life is intimated and that is enough.

**V. 8.** *{And the sucking child shall play upon the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand upon the cockatrice's den*} Or, *The sucking child, also, shall sport himself, over the hole, of the asp*; (a kind of serpent, noted for cruelty, Deut. 32.33. poisonful, Job 20.14,16. and untamable, Psal. 59.5.) *Yea, the child newly weaned* (as chap. 23.9. able now to go abroad) *shall thrust his hand*, out of a childish curiosity, to feel what is there, *into the cave* or, *hole* (for the word is of the same sense with the former, and the Rabbine observes, that such serpents' holes, in those parts, are oft-times so wide, that a little child's hand may easily enter into them) *of the basilisk* without hazard to the one, or hurt to the other. Of this latter kind of serpent, see Prov. 23.32. chap. 14.29. & 59.5. Jer. 8.17. Some expound it, that the great ones shall not oppress the mean ones, but great ones, should rather be lions, wolves, and bears, Prov. 28.15. Psal. 7.2. & 11.9. Dan. 7.5. Zeph. 3.3. If such particular application were necessary, I would rather say, the meaning were the subtle should not circumvent the simple. For serpents, are of note, rather for subtlety, for sleight, rather than for might, Gen. 3.1. Matth. 10.16. And for those, that would have *devils* meant here; because of the terms given him in Scripture, 1 Pet. 5.8. Rev. 12.3,9. stray a great deal further, from the intendment of the text. The thing intended, seems to be, that men who were formerly maliciously minded, and prone to do mischief unto others, should now be of an innocent and harmless disposition, no fear should be of hurt, from them, to any.

**V. 9.** *{They shall not hurt, nor destroy, in all mine holy mountain*} Or, *None shall hurt, nor destroy*, as ch. 49.10. Heb. *in all my mountain in holiness*, as Psal. 15.1. Jer. 31.23. mount Zion is meant, a type of the church. Hence our Jewish commenters control one another, confuting error with error. All the creatures, says one, throughout the whole world, shall grow harmless, in the Messiah's days. No, says another, that is not so. For, it is not said, *in the whole world*; but, *in all mine holy hill*. It is the holy land, only, where no harmful beasts shall be; according to that, Lev. 26.6. & ch. 25.9. or if any come into it occasionally, they shall hurt nobody, according to that Job 5.23. But it is of men, not of beasts, that the prophet here speaks; as they were *men*, not beasts, that our Savior bid his disciples *beware of*, when he talked to them of *wolves*, Matth. 10.16,17. His drift, is to describe, and assert, the innocency and harmlessness of those persons, on whose hearts his word should have its kindly work. See further, ch. 2.4.

*{for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord*} Or, *the land*. For though it be true, that the gospel of Christ should be dispensed unto all nations; and the knowledge of God, thereby, dispersed into all parts of the world: Matth. 24.14. & 28.18. Mar. 16.15. Act. 1.8. Rom. 10.18. Yet the prophet speaking here, of the church, typified by mount Sion; as the chief part, not of the city only, but of the whole country, Psal. 48.2. should be rendered according to the type, that he entreats of. Here is a reason rendered, and the ground declared, of this strange and stupendous change, to wit, the word of Christ; that spiritual, powerful spell, Psal. 58.5. by working into their souls, the sound and saving knowledge of God in Christ; (the want whereof is noted, as the main ground of all evil: Jer. 9.3. Hos. 4.1,2. 1 Cor. 15.32–34. Eph. 4.18,19.) should purge out of them, their former malignant disposition, and frame them, (as new molded thereby; and transformed into the image of God, and so made conformable to Christ,) into a clean contrary, both composure of heart, and tenor of life, Joh. 15.3. & 17.3,17. Rom. 6.17. & 8.28,29. 2 Cor. 3.18. Gal. 4.19. Eph. 4.20–24. Phil. 3.8,10. Col. 3.9,10. Jam. 1.18. 1 Pet. 1.22,23. 2 Pet. 2.20. 1 Joh. 2.3,4. Now this knowledge, was not to be barely, but to abound in the church, in the days of the Messiah. Jer. 31.33,34. Dan. 12.4. Joel 2.28. Hab. 2.13. Act. 2.17. Rom. 15.14. 2 Cor. 4.6. Eph. 3.19. Col. 1.9,10.

*{as the waters cover the sea*} That is, the channel, or the bottom of the sea, Job 36.30. Grace and knowledge, shall in those times be as plentiful, as water is in the sea: The land shall be as full of the knowledge of God, as the sea is full of water. See the like chap. 48.18. Or, as some other, more agreeably to the original, *as the waters of the sea*, (for so it is expressly) *do cover*, to wit, the land. It shall abound, as the sea-waters are wont to do: when having surrounded its walls, or wrought through its banks, it overflows, and covers the whole surface of the land; chap. 8.7,8. Jer. 51.42. Yet see, Hab. 2.14. where the same is almost word, for word, and it seems to go rather, the former way.

**V. 10.** *{And in that day, &c.*} Or, as some render it. *For* (as chap. 9.11.) *in that day*: that is, *at that time*. As chap. 3.18. The prophet here, proceeds to declare, that which shall be the main cause, of all this peaceable carriage and agreement; between people, and persons formerly of such different carriages, and contrary dispositions; to wit, the Messiah his calling in of the Gentiles, to be co-partners in grace, and salvation with the Jews; the restoration of his church, with a very considerable enlargement, consisting of both; and the co-uniting of them by his Spirit; in a nearer conjunction, than ever before either to others.

*{there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek*} Or, *It shall come to pass*; that (as ch. 10.20. v. 11.) *unto a root of Jesse, which shall stand up, for an ensign to people; the nations shall seek*, or, *resort*.

*{a root of Jesse*} The same, of whom before, v. 1. *a root*, that is, say some, one, who like a root, lay hidden before in the ground; as Job 14.8. but rather, *a root of Jesse*, that is, a *sprig*, sprouting out and springing up, *from Jesse, as a root*, as both Jews and Christians, most of them expound it; and as the word seems likewise used, ch. 53.2. Nor is it otherwise to be understood, where Christ is said to be *the root of David*, as here of *Jesse*, Rev. 5.5. & 22.16. See also ch. 14.30. Jesse *is a root*, as Abraham is one, Rom. 11.16. And though Christ be the *root*, that bears all the faithful, and the *stock*, whereinto they are engrafted; Rom. 11.17,18,24. Yet, here, he is considered in regard of the *root*, or *stock*, from whence he issued, as a man. See v. 1. & Rom. 15.12.

*{which shall stand*} Or, *stand up*, as Dan. 11.3,4.

*{for an ensign*} Not such as is used in fight, for soldiers to follow as some of the Jewish writers understand it; as Psal. 60.4. but such as is used to gather people together, so v. 12. Such an one shall Christ be, being lifted up in the ministry of his word. Joh. 3.14,15. & 12.32. Gal. 3.1.

*{of the people*} Or, *to peoples*, for the word is plural: not some one, but divers sorts of people; people indifferently, out of all parts. So did this ensign, at the very first advancing, or erecting of it, draw together divers sorts of people unto it, Act. 2.5–12.

*{shall the Gentiles seek*} Or, *repair*, as the word is used, Deut. 12.5. Though some, to express it, as they suppose, more fully, *repair for advice*, and *for prayer* because the word, sometimes, imports either, Deut. 18.11. chap. 8.19. & 55.6. Ezek. 36.37. But there seems here, to be the convention of them, only intended in it; that not Jews alone, but other nations, shall have recourse to the ensign, thus set up. See ch. 2.2,3.

*{and his rest shall be glorious*} Heb. *glory*, that is, *very glorious*: as *abomination*, for very abominable, chap. 1.13. or, *for glory*, as chap. 4.2. a *rest* of *glory*, a most glorious rest. See chap. 20.1. By his *rest*, here, some understand the *death* of Christ; because death is as *a sleep*, or *rest*, Joh. 11.11,13,14. Rev. 14.13. which, though ignominious in the eyes of the world; yet was glorious, in regard of the virtue, and efficacy of it, Col. 2.15. Heb. 2.14. Others understand, his *grave*, his *sepulcher*, because the grave is a place of rest, chap. 14.18. & 57.2. And Christ's sepulcher is, by resort to it, and miracles done at it, become famous. So our Popish writers, most of them, following the old version, and some of the ancients. Others, his *ascension*, after the conquest of his adversaries, for *rest* follows, when the fight is finished, and victory is glorious: where, that which some would have alluded to, to wit, the furling up of the ensign, when the fight is done, and the victory obtained; as if the word, *rest*, were referred to the ensign, and that were termed its rest; seems more nice and curious, than solid, or agreeable to the text. But, by *rest*, rather, is here understood, the place of Christ's rest, and residence; as the word *rest* is used, Mic. 2.10. alluding to that of mount Sion, said to be, *his rest*, in regard of the temple, there situate; Psalm 132.8,13,14. a type of God's church, the place of his special residence, and abode among them; said to be glorious, in allusion to both tabernacle, and temple; which are said, to have been filled with the glory of God; Exod. 40.35. Lev. 9.23. 1 King. 8.11. as also, unto great princes' courts, where they keep residence in state, which are usually of great note, 1 Kings 10.1,7,14,25. And such, much more, is God's church, through his residing in it, by his word and Spirit, and the effects of his divine power and presence, therein appearing; as also, by strange and remarkable things, wrought on the behalf of his people; for their deliverance, and their safety. 2 Cor. 10.4,5. See chap. 4.5. & 60.13.

**V. 11.** *{And it shall come to pass in that day, that, &c.*} Heb. *it shall be*, &c. So ver. 10.

*{the Lord shall set his hand again the second time*} Heb. *will add the second time his hand*: as, *the Lord added to say to me*, ch. 8.5. *add his hand*, that is, *add to stretch out his hand; stretch it out, again, the second time*. See chap. 1.25. what this *second time*, has reference to, is questioned: and what deliverance it is, that is, here, foretold. For the former, some think, this *second time*, has reference to the deliverance from the Assyrians, under Sennacherib, invading them, which he had spoken of before, ver. 12,24. Others, to the deliverance, from the Babylonian captivity, after seventy years expired, Jer. 29.10. But the most and best, both of the Jewish writers, and ours, to the deliverance out of the Egyptian thraldom; whence, he is said to have brought them, *with his hand stretched out*, Ezek. 20.6. for the *setting*, or, *stretching* out of his hand again, for a further deliverance, some understand it of the deliverance from the Chaldean deportation. But that others cross, and some of the Rabbines themselves: and their reason is good, because this is to be done in the days of the Messiah, ver. 10. though not by such a kind of restitution, as they poor souls dream of; but by calling home unto Christ, the elect of them, wheresoever dispersed, some at one time, some at another; and also, the main body of the residue, in his own appointed season, Act. 2.41. & 4.4. & 21.20. Rom. 11.5,25,26. 2 Cor. 3.16.

*{to recover the remnant of his people, that shall be left*} Heb. *to get, to buy, to purchase*. Which some suppose, to have some respect to Christ's buying his with his blood, Act. 20.28. Rev. 5.9. But it seems rather, here to intimate a getting of them into his possession again, which had made defection from him, and were now under the power of Satan; whereof their bodily servitude and restraint, in sundry places, was a type. See Jer. 16.14,15. & 23.7,8. Zach. 10.10.

*{the remnant*} A small parcel, in comparison of the whole that sometime was, ch. 10.21,22.

*{of his people*} Some understand this, of the elect, both Jew, and Gentile. But the distinction of those here mentioned, from the nations spoken of, ver. 10. does plainly show, that the parties here intended, are of the Jewish people only. See Rev. 7.4–9.

*{that shall be left*} The number of them, being much wasted by several deportations, dissipations, oppressions, and evil usage, in the places of their foreign abode, Deut. 28.62.

*{from Assyria*} Whither many of them had been carried, 2 King. 15.29. & 17.6.

*{and from Egypt*} Whither no small number of them fled, upon the murder of Gedaliah: whereof very few escaped, Jer. 43.5–7. & 44.27,28.

*{and from Pathros*} This some, in regard of the like sound of letters, have supposed to be *Parthia*; and some *Petra*, in Arabia, whereof Arabia Petrea: see chap. 16.1. Others, a part of Lybia, inhabited by the Phaurusii, mentioned by Pliny, and Ptolomy, and sited near the Atlantic Sea. But it appears to have been a province in Egypt, by Jer. 44.1,15. Ezek. 29.14. & 30.14. peopled by the *Pathrusim*, or, *Pathrusites*, which were of the lineage of Mitsraim, or Egyptus, Gen. 10.14. 1 Chr. 1.12. See more of it, on Jer. 44.1.

*{and from Cush*} A people descended from *Cush*, the son of Cham, and brother to Mitsraim, Gen. 10.6,7. of whom, and their place of abode, see further on ch. 18.1.

*{and from Elam*} People that issued from *Elam*; the son of Sem, and brother to Assur, Gen. 10.22. 1 Chr. 1.17. Hence the Elamites, or Elymei, possessing some part of Persia, and bordering upon the Medes, joined therefore together, chap. 21.2. Jer. 25.25. there is mention of them in Strabo, lib. 16. and in Pliny, lib. 6. cap. 26,27,34. Some gather from Act. 2.9. that they lay between Media, and Mesopotamia.

*{and from Shinar*} A region in Chaldea. Of which, Gen. 10.10. & 11.2. Hence the mountain *Singara*, mentioned by Ptolomy, in Mesopotamia; whereof Chaldea was sometime deemed a part, and a town of the same name in Pliny, lib. 5. cap. 24. *Singara*, of *Shinar*; by such interchange of letters: as in *Gaza, Gomorra*, and others. It is deemed by some, to have been so called, of a word signifying *to shake out*, or, *throw out*, Job 38.13. because they were thence dispersed that attempted to build Babel: but the region seems to have had that name, before they began to build there, and the letter *S*, to be radical; which in that word is wanting.

*{and from Hamath*} Of this place, see ch. 10.9.

*{and from the islands of the sea*} Or, *the lands* bordering upon *the sea*, the maritime countries. For so is the name *Island*, taken very commonly in Scripture; as where Judea, and Cappadocia are termed *Islands*, chap. 20.6. Jer. 47.4. So chap. 41.1,5. Jer. 25.22.

**V. 12.** *{And he shall set up an ensign*} Not a military ensign, as many interpreters imagine, for the conducting an army into the field, or the directing them in fight, when they are in the field; but a civil one rather, such as is wont to be set up, for the gathering of people together, upon any occasion whatsoever. See the like, ch. 49.12. & 62.10. as also, before, on ver. 10. of this ensign, what it is.

*{for the nations*} Or, *unto the nations*. To bring them in to Christ Rom. 15.16,18,19. or, rather as the Jewish doctors seem aright to understand it, for them to bring, or send in, the Israelites, that are in captivity with them, or that sojourn among them; as ch. 49.22. & 66.20.

*{and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah*} Or, *that he may gather up*; (the word properly so signifies, Jer. 10.17.) or, *gather together*: (as Numb. 11.17.) the use of this ensign, is, as in regard of the Gentiles before, ver. 10. so in regard of the Israelites, or Jews, whether of the ten, or, of the other two tribes, (for both were to be united, and made one, in and under Christ, Ezek. 36.16,19,21.) for the gathering of them together, out of the places of their dispersion, Luk. 21.24. Joh. 7.35. Jam. 1.1. 1 Pet. 1.1. the copulative designing the end of the action: as ch. 10.19. & 11.3.

*{dispersed*} Or, *dispersed women*. For the word is feminine; as intimating, that no sort, or sex, should, either, be neglected, or rejected, 1 Cor. 11.11. & 12.13. Gal. 3.27,28. Col. 3.11.

*{from the four corners of the earth*} Heb. *wings*, or, *skirts*. For it is applied to garments, as well, as to fowl, Deut. 22.12. Jer. 2.34. See chap. 18.1. & 24.16. So Ezek. 7.2. an end is said to be coming *on the four corners of the land*. The meaning is, that no place should be under heaven, where God would not find them; no country so remote, whence he would not fetch them. The gospel for this purpose, was to be preached, unto the ends, or utmost parts of the world, Act. 1.8. Rom. 10.18. and God had promised his people, that though they were driven away, into the utmost parts of heaven, yet from thence, he would gather them again upon their repentance, Deut. 30.4. And as God is said to gather his dispersed ones, *from the four wings* of the earth; so it is said, that Christ shall at the last day, by the ministry of angels, gather his Elect from *the four winds*, from the one end of heaven, to the other, Matth. 24.31.

**V. 13.** *{The envy also of Ephraim shall depart*} The Hebrew commenters, upon this place, take notice of some emulation from the first, between Judah, and the other tribes in David's time, 2 Sam. 2.9,10. & 3.1. & 19.41–43. But the envy here mentioned seems rather to have an eye to that, which ensued upon the revolt of them under Rehoboam, from the family of David. For Ephraim, the chief of the ten tribes, having then the royal seat of that kingdom among them; there was by occasion thereof, much emulation between it and Judah, and continual jars and wars, from time to time thence proceeding, to the great molestation and much mischief of either, and the exposing of them to the incursions, and invasions of other nations abroad; especially, while they sought help from them one against another, 2 Chr. 16.1–4. & 15.22,23. & 28.5,8,16,20. See chap. 7.1. But this emulation between the house of Joseph, and the house of Judah, was to cease, when united, either to other in Christ. See Ezek. 37.16. and they were then to be in terms of agreement, and amity, that had been at such deadly feud before, ch. 9.21. Luk. 9.52,53. Joh. 4.9.

*{and the adversaries of Judah shall be cut off*} Those of Israel, say the Jewish writers, and some of ours treading in their steps, that now are adversaries to Judah, and have of late put them to grievous frights, (as the word, properly, imports) shall be destroyed; so that Judah shall no more fear them. But they consider not, that this is spoken of the Messiah his time: and the meaning is; that the obstinate enemies of the church of God, whereof Judah is reckoned as a principal part, shall by Christ be destroyed. See chap. 60.12.

*{Ephraim shall not envy Judah*} This more plainly shows what *envy of Ephraim*, was before meant, to wit, that, wherewith it envied Judah: which then should cease. I cannot let slip, the ridiculous exposition, that a great Rabbi has of this place. The Messiah, says he, of the house of Joseph, shall not envy the Messiah of the house of David. The Talmudists tell us tales of two Messiahs: and they find them both, in this prophecy, ch. 32.20. where mention is of *an ox*, and *an ass*. The *ox*, says he, is the Messiah of the house of Joseph, because Joseph is likened to an *ox*, Deut. 33.17. the *ass* is the Messiah of the house of David, because he is said to come riding on an *ass*, Zach. 9.9. Such sottish toys, are those silly people taken with; and yet about the expounding and reconciling of such senseless absurdities, and abstracting strange and abstruse mysteries out of them, do some of ours spend grave, and serious discourses.

*{and Judah shall not vex Ephraim*} Or, *nor shall Judah put Ephraim to frights*; as Psalm 129.1,2. They shall not in Ezekiah's time, say the Jewish doctors, revenge themselves upon Ephraim, for the mischief done them by Pekah, 2 Chr. 28.6–8. But we are to look, and so should they have done, far beyond Ezekiah's reign, unto the reign of the Lord Jesus; under whom all such former enmities should be abandoned, and such hostile acts buried in utter oblivion, Jer. 3.18.

**V. 14.** *{But*} Heb. *And*; as ch. 5.12.

*{they shall fly upon the shoulders of the Philistines towards the west; they shall spoil them of the East together*} Or, *they shall together* (jointly) *fly upon the shoulder*, &c. *and spoil them of the East*. They shall join, in one, and combine themselves, against the common enemy.

*{fly*} A metaphor, from some great fowl, as an eagle; that flies swiftly, and eagerly to seize upon his prey, Job 9.26. Hos. 5.1. Though one of the Jewish great masters renders it, *they shall thrust with the shoulder the Philistines*, deducing it from another root of that notion, in use with them, but not found in Scripture.

*{upon the shoulders*} Heb. *shoulder*. Whence some of the Jewish commenters, following the Chaldee paraphrast, expound it, *by shoulder*; that is, *by consent*: as Hosh. 6.9. and as Zeph. 3.9. *with one shoulder*; for, *with one consent*, (or by mutual consent) which some also supply in that of Hoshea: and these thus read the words; *they shall fly with the shoulder*, (that is, by consent) *to smite the Philistines*: but the construction seems overharsh, and the place of Hoshea, is ambiguous. Others therefore conceive it to be *the Philistines' shoulder*, that they are said to fly upon; a metaphor, as some think, from a lion, or wolf, that are wont to fasten on the shoulder of the beast, that they prey upon; and why not from an eagle, also, or some such great ravenous fowl, which seize also sometime, in like manner on the lesser sort of cattle, their young ones especially, the lamb, or the kid? Others understand it, of subjugating and subduing them. The *burden* on the *shoulder*, being an emblem of servitude. See chap. 9.4,6. & 10.27. But against this latter is objected that the word *shoulder*, is not in a form of regiment here: and some use of the *shoulder*, proper, or tropical, seems to be employed in their falling upon them. I shall add my conjecture; and so leave it, the word rendered *a shoulder*, signifies sometime *a side*, Numb. 34.11. Josh. 15.8,12. I suppose the text may well be rendered, *they shall fly on the one side upon the Philistines westward*; the supplies are not unusual.

*{the Philistines*} The ancient ill neighbors and enemies, of God's people, 1 Sam. 4. & 13. & 17. & 31.

*{towards the west*} Heb. *to the sea*: as Josh. 15.4,11. that is the Midland Sea; which lay west from the land of Judah. See ch. 9.12.

*{them of the East*} Heb. *Sons of the East*; as Job 1.3. whence, some would have the Chaldeans, and Arabians, here meant. But I suppose, rather, the Syrians, as before, chap. 9.12. whose country lay east from Judea. See ch. 2.6. for Chaldea and Babylon is in Scripture commonly termed *North*, Jer. 1.12,13,14. and Arabia *South*, Mat. 12.42.

*{they shall lay their hand upon Edom, and Moab*} Heb. *Edom, and Moab* shall be *the immission*, or, *laying on of their hands*. See the like phrase, ch. 8.8. *to lay hand on*, imports, *to seize on*: as Esth. 9.10. or, *to slay*; as Ps. 55.20. they shall by force of arms surprise their lands, and subdue them; an inbred and inveterate enmity between Esau and Jacob, Edom, and Israel, Gen. 25.22,23. & 27.36,41. continued in their posterity, Ps. 83.6.

*{and the children of Ammon*} The offspring of Ammon; brother to Moab, (Lot's incestuous brood, Gen. 19.36–38.) the style commonly given to the Ammonites, Jer. 25.21. and 49.1. Both joined with the Chaldeans in the destruction of Judah, 2 Kings 24.2.

*{shall obey them*} Being subdued by them. Heb. *shall be their obedience*: at their command, at their service: as 1 Sam. 22.14. 2 Sam. 23.23.

**V. 15.** *{And the Lord shall utterly destroy the tongue of the Egyptian Sea*} The reducing of people to the obedience of Christ, and that spiritual freedom, that thereby accrues to them, being shadowed by the bringing of the people of Israel back again into their land, out of those countries, whither they had been dispersed; the prophet in this next passage, promises from God a removal of all impediments, that might hinder them in that their return. And because he had before, paralleled this their reduction, with the deliverance of them out of Egypt; as a second masterpiece of God's power, and providence showed in behalf of his people; he deciphers this removal of lets and obstacles, that might impeach them in their passage, by the drying up of the Red Sea, which he divided for them, at their departure out of Egypt, Exod. 14.21,22. See the like, chap. 42.15,16. & 51.10. & 63.11,12. Zach. 10.11. Rev. 16.12.

*{utterly destroy*} Heb. *make an anathema of it*: as Josh. 6.17,21. not divide it only, as Psal. 136.13. but even dry it clean up, chap. 50.2. so that it shall be no more, Rev. 21.1.

*{the tongue of the Egyptian Sea*} Not Nilus, as some of the Jewish doctors; but the Red Sea, that out of the main ocean shoots into the land, in form and fashion of a *tongue*; running up along, between Arabia and Egypt, and growing narrower towards the head: and as promontories, or headlands, that strike out into the sea, are in Latin called *tongues of land*; so such bays, as shoot in like manner into the land, are in Hebrew termed, *tongues of the sea*, Josh. 15.2,5.

*{and with his mighty wind, shall he shake his hand over the river*} He alludes here to the course, that God took, in making a passage for his people through the Red Sea.

*{he shall shake his hand over the river*} Not Euphrates, of which, ch. 7.20. though the Jewish writers, and others following them, so understand it; applying the former to those, that were to return out of Egypt; this, to such, as were to come from Assyria: (for of these, afterwards, ver. 16.) but Nilus, called *the river of Egypt*, Josh. 13.3. & 15.4. Jer. 2.18. Ezek. 29.3. because it runs down along through the midst of Egypt, dividing it into two parts, and once in the year overflows it, for the watering of it; to supply the want of rain in those parts, Deut. 11.10,11. *over this river*, or *against it*, as Zach. 2.9. it is said, God will *shake his hand*; as Moses by God's command, *stretched out his hand*, with his *staff lift up* in it, over the Red Sea, Exod. 14.16,21.

*{with his mighty wind*} Or, *by the might* (for which a word is here used without a brother) *of his breath*. He will do it with ease, *by his breath*, alone: as chap. 59.19. Zach. 4.6. See Exod. 15.8. but alluding to that stiff *East wind*, wherewith he beat back the Red Sea, Exod. 14.21. Ps. 74.13.

*{his wind*} As Ps. 147.18. which he has at command, Ps. 107.25. & 148.8. Mat. 8.27.

*{and shall smite it*} As Zach. 10.11. and as Elias and Elisha, successively, smote the river Jordan, 2 King. 2.8,14.

*{in the seven streams*} Or, *channels*, into which, the main body of the river Nilus branching, does as by so many mouths, empty itself into the sea, (see chap. 7.18.) where it is of the deepest, being nearest the main sea, see Psal. 74.15. & chap. 19.4. Of these *seven* outlets, for which, Nilus is famous, mention is made by Herodotus, lib. 2. Aristotle de mundo, cap. 2. Strabo, lib. 17. Pliny, lib. 5. cap. 9. and other authors, Latin and Greek, without number; geographers, historians, poets, and others. So that there is no reason, to divert the *streams* here mentioned, unto any other river, as some Jewish doctors do to Euphrates, cutting it out into seven streams, to make it passable for the return of the people out of those seven countries; mentioned before, ver. 11. that which neither suits well with the text, nor with the situation of some of those places: nor does that of those, sort well with the scope of the prophet, who understand this of Cyrus his dividing that river into many channels, for the readier surprisal of Babylon. Of which, see Jer. 51.31,32. for this smiting, and drying up, is of another kind, and for a far other end; not to enter upon her: but to come away from her.

*{and make men go over dryshod*} Heb. *and he shall*, or, *that he may* (as ver. 12.) *make to go in shoes*. Our English, fully expresses the sense of it; that men may pass over, without boat, or boot; on foot, and in shoes as they use to go, or *walk*, (for the word is indifferently used for either) on dry land, Exod. 14.22,29. Psal. 66.6. they shall not need to put off their shoes as they use to do, when they are to wade through some, though but shallow, water. The prophet's words then import, that God would not divide only, the Red Sea; as he did for them, at their departure out of Egypt; but dry up that whole bay, for that shoal sea is little better; nor drive back for a while, the stream of such a river, of no extraordinary wideness, as Jordan, being in divers places fordable, as he did at their entrance into Canaan, Josh. 3.16,17. & 4.18. & 5.1. but so smite that vast river Nilus, that all the several streams of it, near the entrance of the main sea, (far from which it was that the Red Sea was divided) should be clean dried up, to make free passage for his people. The meaning is, that no impediment, or obstacle should be so great, that might hinder those, who were to be brought home to Christ, and his church, out of all quarters; but it should be removed.

**V. 16.** *{And there shall be an highway for the remnant of his people which shall be left, from Assyria*} Because mention is made of drying up the Red Sea, and Nilus, as for the free passage of those that should come from *Egypt*, and *Pathros*, and from *Cush*, or, *Ethiopia*, ver. 11. But it might be demanded, what will become of those, that are in Assyria, and those parts; the prophet adds therefore, that, there shall be a course taken, for a fit and convenient passage also, for them.

*{there shall be an highway*} Or, *a causey*, chap. 7.3. such a way made by banks cast up and leveled; as is wont to be done by industry and careful provision for travelers and passengers, in countries where the ways are deep and miry, or stony and uneven. See ch. 40.3,4. & 49.11. Jer. 18.15. The Jewish writers expound it, of a passage through the waters, either of the river, or the sea; according to that Psal. 77.19,20. but neither is this word found there, and the frequent use of it in this argument, by collation of places, carries it rather, the other way.

*{the remnant, &c.*} See ver. 11.

*{from Assyria*} Whence it may appear that the river spoken of ver. 15. was not to be dried up for them in those parts.

*{like as it was to Israel, in the day that he came up out of the land of Egypt*} These words in the close of all, seem to reflect upon all that before was spoken, of drying up waters, and casting up ways; and to have respect to the whole course of the people's conduct in their passage from Egypt to Canaan, wherein seas and rivers were divided and laid dry in part for the present; and passages made by strange and uncouth ways through that wide and waste wilderness, that lay between these two lands, as fit and convenient, with supply of all necessaries, as if causeys had been raised for them all the way that they went, Exod. 13.21. Numb. 10.33. Deut. 1.31,33. & 8.2,4,15. & 32.10,11. See chap. 40.3,4. & 41.18,19. & 42.15,16. & 43.19,20.

*{in the day*} At that time, as Jer. 7.22. So ch. 12.1.

*{he came up*} Or, *came* simply: for the word is frequently used of passage, or departure, from place to place, without any reference to ascent or descent, see ch. 7.1.

### CHAPTER 12

**V. 1.** *{And in that day, thou shalt say*} That is, *at that time*, when you shall be set free, and fetched home again, then shall you sing this, or the like psalm, or song, as chap. 26.1. & 27.2. For this chapter contains certain forms, framed in songs, or hymns, of solemn praise, and thankful acknowledgment, of God's goodness to his people, and gracious workings for them; composed by the prophet, as ditties fit to be used by them; or a directory, to show them the way how to bless God upon such occasion, or both, so 1 Chr. 16.7,25,36.

*{O Lord*} The beginning of the first form.

*{I will praise thee*} Heb. *confess thee*, or, *confess to thee*, that is, acknowledge your goodness, and my thankfulness for it. So David, Ps. 138.1. and Christ, Mat. 11.25.

*{though thou wast angry with me, thine anger was turned away*} Or, *because*, though, or, *whereas thou wast angry, yet thine anger is turned away*. Heb. *because thou wast angry, thine anger is turned away*. See the like syntax, Rom. 6.7. *God be thanked, ye were the servants of sin: but ye have obeyed*, &c. That is, *that* whereas, or, although, *ye were the servants of sin, yet ye have obeyed*; or are now become *obedient*, &c.

*{thine anger is turned away*} And you turned from it, Psalm 85.3. chap. 10.25. Dan. 9.16. contrary to that, chap. 5.25. & 9.12.

*{and thou comfortedst me*} By reconcilement to me, mercy showed me, and good done for me, as Psal. 90.15. ch. 40.1. & 51.3,12. & 61.3.

**V. 2.** *{Behold God is my salvation*} That is, the author of it. So Psal. 27.1. whosoever or whatsoever the means or instruments are, my salvation is from him only, Psal. 3.8. & 33.16,17. & 44.6,7. Prov. 21.31. Jon. 2.9. To this is prefixed a note, or term, that calls for special consideration and regard, implying the deliverance of God's people, to be a matter very remarkable, and a mercy unexpected; considering, in what a low and forlorn condition, they seemed to be in before, as if they should say, either among themselves, or to others, their enemies especially, behold that now done, that was little looked for. So Ezek. 37.12.

*{I will trust*} Or, *I will be confident*, as Prov. 28.1. or, *I will trust* in him; as Ps. 18.2. a defect of the pronoun; as Job 13.15. his present deliverance shall make me rely on him for future preservation, chap. 26.3,4. 2 Cor. 1.9,10. 2 Tim. 4.17,18.

*{and not be afraid*} So upon the like ground, Psal. 3.6. and 27.1.

*{for the Lord is my strength*} The author and giver of it. So Exod. 15.2. (whence the latter part of this verse is taken) Psalm 18.2. & 28.7. I have it not from myself, or aught else; but from him, Psalm 62.7. Col. 1.11. he does and will by his powerful hand uphold me, and enable me to persevere and hold out to the end, chap. 40.29–31. Rom. 8.37–39. 2 Cor. 1.21. Phil. 4.13. 1 Pet. 1.5.

*{and my song*} The subject matter of it, as Ps. 89.1. & 104.34. and he that ministers matter for it, Ps. 32.7. & 40.3.

*{and he is become my salvation*} Heb. *Salvation to me*; that is, *my Savior*, as Luk. 2.30. So after Moses, David, Ps. 118.14. not that he was not so before, but that he has now manifested it in a more conspicuous and remarkable manner, Ps. 69.13.

**V. 3.** *{Therefore with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation*} Heb. *and with joy*, &c. as chap. 10.12. The effect of this their deliverance, the free and plentiful fruition of those benefits and blessings, that they had been deprived of, and debarred from before. You shall have free access now, unto the wellhead of all grace and goodness; from whence there shall be derived unto you abundance of saving grace, and sound comfort; as water drawn by full buckets from an incessant wellspring, Psalm 36.8,9. John 4.14. and 7.37,38. Rev. 7.17. There is in the words an allusion, as some deem, to the state and condition of those, that have liquor, to the full, unexpectedly afforded them, when they have been grievously vexed and afflicted for want of it, and were even now ready to perish, for thirst, Psalm 107.35. chap. 41.17. & 43.20. So chap. 55.3. Matth. 5.6. Rev. 22.17. and more especially to the *rock*, that afforded the Israelites water in the wilderness, Exod. 17.6. Numb. 20.11. or rather to the *well*, out of which God promised to give them water, when they wanted it, while they abode about the confines of Moab; and from whence with exceeding great joy and mirth, expressed in songs and ditties thereupon composed, it was received and entertained by them, Numb. 21.16–18. Others suppose, that this passage has respect to a solemn rite used in the feast of Tabernacles, at which their manner was, in the nighttime, with great variety of melodious music, and abundance of mirth and jollity, to fetch water in a golden vessel, from the spring of Siloam, unto the temple, and there to pour it upon the altar. See ch. 30.29. But whether this usage was so ancient as Esay's time, is uncertain. See somewhat the like phrase, and as many think, rite also, of drawing water, and pouring it out upon the ground, to a contrary purpose, in occasion of mourning, and to testify thereby their inward remorse, 1 Sam. 7.6.

**V. 4.** *{And in that day shall ye say;}* Or, *In that day, also, shall ye say*, as chap. 8.5. For this is a preface, or passage, unto a new form another ditty, of the like nature with the former; save, that it is conceived, as in way of exhortation; whereby the faithful invite, and incite one another unto this office of cheerful and constant praising and magnifying God for his mercies. See on vers. 1.

*{Praise the Lord; call upon his name; declare his doings among the people*} See the same, 1 Chr. 16.8. Ps. 105.1,2.

*{Praise the Lord*} Heb. *confess to the Lord*, as ver. 1.

*{call upon his name*} Or, *proclaim his name*, publish it abroad, as Jer. 2.2. & 4.16. Lam. 1.21.

*{declare, &c.*} As Ps. 3.11.

*{his doings*} The courses taken by him for your deliverance.

*{among the people*} Heb. *peoples*, not some one people; but the several nations abroad, throughout the wide world, ver. 5. So Psal. 57.9. & 108.3.

*{make mention*} Or, *record it*, as chap. 49.1. enter it upon record, for posterity, Psal. 45.17. or, *celebrate his name*, as Psal. 45.17.

*{that his name is exalted*} As Psal. 143.13. where it is rendered, *excellent*, but would rather be, *lofty*, as chap. 26.5. or, *high*, as chap. 30.13. or, *exalted*, as here, and ch. 33.5. Howbeit, there is by some observed, a trajection in the text: that which the points or pauses, also, seem to imply. In regard whereof, this whole branch might more fitly be thus conceived, *celebrate his name: for it is high*, or, *exalted*, as the sentence consisting of two distinct branches, whereof the latter contains a reason of the former: as Psal. 99.3,5,9. The word translated *make mention*, signifies also, *to celebrate*, as 1 Cor. 16.4. Ps. 71.16. ch. 63.7. and so may it well here.

**V. 5.** *{Sing unto the Lord*} *Sing*, or, *Play unto the Lord*: to his honor and praise: as Psal. 66.4. & 47.6. & 92.1. or, *Sing of the Lord*, as Psal. 66.2. & 101.1. & 138.5. So Numb. 21.17. chap. 27.2. The word properly signifies, to make a musical sound with instruments; at all sorts indifferently. For another word they have for music with voices, chap. 5.1.

*{he hath done excellent things*} Or, *done excellently*, or, *majestically*. Heb. *excellency*, or, *majesty*. For so the word signifies, taken in the better sense; as chap. 26.10. though in the worse sense, *pride*, c. 28.1,3. So, to *do valor*, for, *to do valiantly*, Psal. 60.12. & 118.15,16. to *do truth*; for, *to deal truly*, 1 Joh. 1.6. to *do righteousness*; for, *to deal righteously*, 1 Joh. 3.3,10.

*{this is known in all the earth*} Or, *this is made known*: as Levit. 4.23. or, *let this be made known throughout all the earth*: as c. 8.12. make all the world ring of it, by your publishing it abroad: as ver. 4.

**V. 6.** *{Cry out*} Or, *cry aloud*, or, as some render it, *cry shrill*. The word properly signifies, *to neigh*, as horses in heat, full fed, and lusty; or fitted for fight, Jer. 5.8. & 8.16. & 13.27. & 50.11. Is is used most commonly for *shouting*, or *hollowing*, in token of joy, Esth. 8.15. ch. 24.14. & 54.1. Jer. 31.7. Yet for *crying out*, upon affrightment, ch. 10.30.

*{and shout*} The same words are found joined together again, ch. 54.1. See ch. 14.7.

*{thou inhabitant of Zion*} Heb. *Inhabitress*, as Jer. 21.13. & 51.35. because such places, in Scripture, are commonly styled *daughters*, as like to young, choice, and beautiful daughters, or damsels. See ch. 1.8. & Jer. 46.19.

*{Zion*} A type of the church. ch. 2.2.

*{for great is the holy One of Israel, in the midst of thee*} Or *the holy One of Israel* (of which title, see ch. 1.4.) *who is great* (of great might and power, Psal. 48.1. & 135.5. & 145.5.) *is in the midst of thee*, to preserve, and protect you. Psal. 46.5. Zach. 2.5,11. and he has manifested the greatness of his might and power, in your deliverance.
